Readings

What there is

The library

Seven books that take experience apart and put it back together, and the long shelf of commentary that grew around them.

Manual Introduction (the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, commentaries, the Saṅgaha and its commentaries)

The Pāli Canon is a set of three baskets. The first holds the monastic discipline, the second the discourses, the suttas. The third is the Abhidhamma PiṭakaAbhidhamma Piṭaka the third basket of the Pāli Canon: seven books of analysis, and it reads like nothing else in the Canon. There are no stories in it, almost no people, hardly a setting. There are lists, and lists of lists, and questions asked of them with a patience that can feel inhuman.

Its name is usually rendered “higher teaching” or “special teaching”. The commentaries explain the prefix abhi as “excelling” and as “distinguishing”: the same Dhamma as the suttas, but taken apart further and set out without reference to any listener.The suttas teach in conventional terms to a particular person in a particular situation. The Abhidhamma is said to teach “in ultimate terms”, to no one in particular. That is the difference the two truths name; see the next reading.

Seven books

There are seven books, and their order has a logic.

The first, the DhammasaṅgaṇīDhammasaṅgaṇī the first Abhidhamma book: lists every kind of citta and its factors, the “enumeration of dhammas”, takes every state of mind and lists what is present in it. It opens with a matrix, a mātikāmātikā · matrix the Dhammasaṅgaṇī's opening lists, 22 triads and 100 dyads, that sort every dhamma: a table of headings under which anything at all can be sorted. Is it wholesome, unwholesome or neither? Is it joined with pleasant feeling, painful feeling or neither? The matrix runs through more than a hundred such pairs and triplets. The rest of the book fills the table in.

The Vibhaṅga, the “analysis”, takes familiar sutta lists, the aggregates, the bases, dependent origination, and analyses most of them three ways: as the suttas teach it, as the Abhidhamma teaches it, and by question and answer. The Dhātukathā asks how every dhamma is included in or excluded from the aggregates, bases and elements. The Puggalapaññatti is the odd one out: a book of types of person, the one place where convention is catalogued in its own right.

The Kathāvatthu is a book of debates, two hundred and more points on which the Theravāda disagreed with other schools, each refuted in turn. Tradition ascribes it to Moggaliputta Tissa at the Third Council, more than two centuries after the Buddha. The Yamaka, the “pairs”, tests the edges of every term by asking each question both ways round.

The last is the PaṭṭhānaPaṭṭhāna the seventh Abhidhamma book: relates all dhammas by 24 conditions, the “conditional relations”, the largest book of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Where the first book took things apart, this one puts them back together: it relates every dhamma to every other by twenty-four kinds of condition. Analysis at one end, synthesis at the other. Everything in between is method.

Where it came from

The tradition tells a story. In the seventh year after his awakening, the Buddha spent a rainy season in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven teaching the Abhidhamma to the gods, among them his mother, who had been reborn as a god in the Tusita heaven and came to hear it. Each day he came down to collect alms and gave the day’s teaching to Sāriputta in outline. Sāriputta passed it on in fuller form to five hundred monks, and that, the Atthasālinī says, is the Abhidhamma we have.

Modern scholars tell a different story. The earliest suttas already contain lists, and the monks who memorised them built matrices to keep them in order and to settle what they meant. Over several centuries, in different schools, these matrices grew into the Abhidhamma books. Other schools had their own seven: the northern Sarvāstivāda’s survive mainly in Chinese translation.The reading Other maps of the same ground, near the end of the site, sets the northern lists beside the Theravāda’s.

The two stories agree on one thing. The Abhidhamma is a reading of the Buddha’s teaching, carried out by people who took it very seriously, and it was not written to be read straight through.

The shelves below

Nearly everything since is commentary. In the fifth century Buddhaghosa wrote the Atthasālinī on the first book, and the Visuddhimagga, the “path of purification”, which sets Abhidhamma inside a manual of practice. Subcommentaries followed. Then, somewhere between the tenth and twelfth centuries, a monk called Anuruddha wrote the Abhidhammattha SaṅgahaAbhidhammattha Saṅgaha Anuruddha's manual of the whole Abhidhamma in nine chapters; Bodhi's CMA translates it: a summary of the whole system in nine short chapters, small enough to learn by heart. It is the book this site follows.

It became the doorway. In Burma and Sri Lanka students memorise the Saṅgaha before they open the canonical books, and commentaries on it multiplied. In the 1890s Ledi Sayadaw disputed one of them on hundreds of points and started a revival of lay Abhidhamma study that still continues.

In 1993 Bhikkhu Bodhi published a revision of Nārada Thera’s earlier English translation of the Saṅgaha with a full explanatory guide, as A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma. This site follows it chapter by chapter.

How to read the shelf

A library like this rewards a particular attitude. It is not a book to agree or disagree with page by page. It is a map, drawn by people who spent their lives looking at the same ground, and the right question to put to any part of it is the one a traveller asks of a map: what does this let me see that I could not see before?

To reflect on. The tradition says the Buddha taught the Abhidhamma; modern scholars say it grew over centuries from lists. Does it matter to how you read it which story is true?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, Introduction, and I §1. Nyanatiloka Thera, Guide through the Abhidhamma-Piṭaka. Atthasālinī, introductory discourse: the teaching in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Y. Karunadasa, The Theravāda Abhidhamma (2010). Erik Braun, The Birth of Insight (2013), on Ledi Sayadaw and the Abhidhamma controversy.

A chariot of parts

Where the Abhidhamma begins, with a nun's answer to Māra, and how a person is taken apart without being called a lie.

Manual I §2 (the four ultimate realities)

The nun Vajirā was sitting in meditation in the Blind Men’s Grove when Māra came to unsettle her. Who made this being, he asked her; where does it come from, and where does it go? Her answer is a good place to begin the Abhidhamma. Why do you assume there is a being? This is a heap of mere formations. When the parts are put together we say “chariot”. When the aggregates are present, we say “a being”.Retold after SN 5.10. Bhikkhu Sujato’s translation is in the public domain on SuttaCentral.

She did not say there is no chariot. She said what the word refers to. That distinction, between what is true in speech and what remains when speech is analysed, is the first thing the Abhidhamma asks a reader to hold.

Two ways of being true

The commentaries call them the two truths. Conventional truth, sammutisammuti · convention conventional truth: speech about persons and things; true, but not ultimate, is how people speak: persons, chariots, mangoes, “I” and “you”. It is not false. The Buddha used it all his life, and no vow, debt or kindness could be stated without it. Ultimate truth, paramatthaparamattha · ultimate what remains after analysis: citta, cetasika, matter and Nibbāna, is what the analysis ends in: things that keep their own nature however closely you look.The pair first appears as technical terms in the Kathāvatthu and is systematised in the commentaries. They connect it with a distinction the suttas already make (AN 2.25), between discourses whose meaning must be drawn out and discourses whose meaning is plain.

A chariot fails that test. Take away the wheels, the axle, the pole, and no chariot is left over among them; nor is it anywhere else. Take apart a moment of anger and something is left that cannot be taken further: ferocity, the same wherever it occurs. That is a dhammadhamma an ultimate reality, bearing its own nature; not a mere name or concept.

Four kinds of reality

The Abhidhamma’s catalogue of what remains is short. There are four kinds of ultimate reality.

Cittacitta · consciousness one moment of knowing an object; 89 kinds, or 121 counted in detail, consciousness, is the bare knowing of an object, one moment at a time. The Abhidhamma counts 89 kinds of it, or 121 when the higher states are counted in detail.

Cetasikacetasika · mental factor a mental factor: arises and ceases with a citta, sharing its object and bases, mental factors, are what colour each knowing: feeling, perception, volition, attention, and fifty-two in all, from greed to compassion. They arise and cease together with the citta, sharing its object and its base.

Rūparūpa · matter matter: the third reality, 28 kinds; as an aggregate it is called form, matter, comes in twenty-eight kinds: the four great elements and what is derived from them, from hardness and heat to the eye’s sensitivity and the nourishment in food.

Nibbānanibbāna the unconditioned: the ending of craving; object of path and fruition is the fourth, and it is unlike the other three. It does not arise and does not pass away. It is not made of anything, and nothing is made from it.

The aggregates, counted again

The suttas sort experience into five khandhakhandha · aggregate one of the five heaps into which the suttas sort all experiences: form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. The Abhidhamma does not replace this list; it recounts it. Form is matter. Consciousness is citta. Feeling and perception are two of the cetasikas, important enough to stand alone. Formations are the other fifty mental factors.

Nibbāna appears in none of the aggregates. The aggregates are what clinging takes up; Nibbāna is where clinging ends.

In one sutta the Buddha compares the aggregates to a lump of foam on a river, bubbles in the rain, a mirage, the trunk of a plantain tree, which has no heartwood, and a conjuror’s illusion (SN 22.95). Each simile points to the same absence: when you look for the thing itself, the core is not there.

Why begin here

A manual could begin with ethics or with meditation. Anuruddha begins with this list, and every later chapter assumes it. It changes what the rest of the book is about. Processes of mind will be sequences of cittas. Kamma will be a cetasika, volition. Rebirth will be a relation between one citta and the next. At no point will the book need a self to hold the story together.

That is the claim the Abhidhamma makes, and the reason for its patience with lists. If experience can be described completely without an owner, the owner was never needed. Vajirā was sitting in meditation when she said it, and she spoke from what she had seen.

If “chariot” is not a thing, what is the word? The Manual answers at the very end of its account of conditions: see Names and the named.

To reflect on. Pick something you call "mine", a hand or a habit or a name. Taken apart into the four realities, where does the "mine" go, and what still works without it?

Sources. SN 5.10, Vajirā Sutta: the chariot simile, spoken by the nun Vajirā. Milindapañha II.1: Nāgasena and the chariot of King Milinda. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, I §2, and the Introduction on the two truths. SN 22.95, Pheṇapiṇḍūpama Sutta: the five aggregates as foam, bubbles, mirage, plantain and illusion.

The All, counted twice

Twelve bases and eighteen elements: the Buddha's "all" as six doors and what comes through them, and why the same ground was counted three ways.

“What is the All?” the Buddha asks in a short sutta, and answers: the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and smells, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, the mind and mental objects. Anyone who claims to describe some other “all”, he says, would be speaking of what is outside their range (SN 35.23).

It is a startling definition. The All is not a world out there, nor a world in here. It is six doors and what comes through them.

Twelve bases

The twelve āyatanaāyatana · base (the twelve) one of twelve bases: six internal (five sense organs and the mind base) and their six objects, bases, count the two sides of each door. Six are internal: the eye, ear, nose, tongue and body, which are sensitive matter, and the mind. Six are external: visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.

The mind base is the whole of consciousness, all eighty-nine kinds. The mental-object base is everything else that the mind can know and the senses cannot: the fifty-two mental factors, the sixteen subtle kinds of matter that no sense can touch, and Nibbāna. Concepts are left out, though the mind knows them: a base must be something real in its own right, and a concept is only constructed (VII §36).

Eighteen elements

The eighteen dhātudhātu · element (the eighteen) one of eighteen elements: the twelve bases, with the mind base split into seven, elements, take the same doors and add what arises at each: the consciousness. “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact” (MN 18). So for each door there are three elements: the organ, the object, and the knowing.

In doing so the elements split the mind base into seven. Five are the sense consciousnesses. The sixth is the mind element, the cittas that turn toward a sense object and receive it. The seventh is the mind-consciousness element: every other citta, from investigating up to the moments of awakening.The division follows function. The mind element only adverts and receives; it does no more. Everything that examines, judges, wants, gives or understands is mind-consciousness.

Why three lists for one thing

The aggregates, the bases and the elements cover the same ground. The commentaries give a reason for having all three: the Buddha taught the aggregates to those confused mainly about mind, the bases to those confused mainly about matter, and the elements to those confused about both. Each list suits a temperament.

What the three have in common is that none leaves a remainder. Everything that can be experienced is an aggregate, a base or an element. Look for a self among them and it is not there; look for it outside them and there is no outside to look in.

The Manual has a fifth way of cutting the whole, after the aggregates, the aggregates of clinging, the bases and the elements: the four noble truths (VII §§34, 38–40). It sorts the same realities by the task each calls for, and it leaves some of them outside: the path and fruition cittas and their factors, all but the path’s eight (VII §40). It has its own reading, The four noble truths.

Practising at the doors

This is also why the bases are a practice and not only a list. Sense restraint, in the suttas, means guarding the six doors: seeing what is seen without grasping at its signs. The reading The mango and the moment, later on, shows where that guarding works. Seeing itself is given; greed or calm arises only in the moments that follow, the javanas, where the mind acts.

The Buddha’s instruction to the ascetic Bāhiya is the shortest form of this teaching: in the seen there will be only the seen, in the heard only the heard. When that is so, he said, there is no “you” in it, and that is the end of suffering (Ud 1.10). Bāhiya was liberated on the spot. The eighteen elements are the same instruction worked out in full.

To reflect on. For the next sound you hear, try to find something in the experience that is neither the ear, nor the sound, nor the hearing. What do you find?

Sources. SN 35.23, Sabba Sutta: the All is the six internal and six external bases. MN 18, Madhupiṇḍika Sutta: eye, forms and eye-consciousness; their meeting is contact. Ud 1.10: the instruction to Bāhiya. Visuddhimagga XV and the Sammohavinodanī: why the aggregates, bases and elements are all taught. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, VII §§34–39.

A map of the eighty-nine

Every kind of consciousness the Abhidhamma knows, sorted by plane, by root and by feeling, and what the sorting reveals.

Manual I §§3–32 (all 89/121 cittas)

If you were asked how many kinds of mind there are, you might answer: one, mine. The Abhidhamma answers eighty-nine. It does not mean eighty-nine minds sitting side by side. It means that every moment of knowing, every cittacitta · consciousness one moment of knowing an object; 89 kinds, or 121 counted in detail, is of one kind or another, and that the kinds can be counted.

Each citta knows one object and lasts one moment. What makes it the kind it is: whether greed or hatred or delusion is present as a root, or their opposites; whether the moment is pleasant, painful or neither; whether it makes kamma, is the result of kamma, or merely functions; and in what plane of existence it belongs. Fix those, and you have fixed the citta.

Four planes of mind

The first sorting is by plane. Fifty-four cittas belong to the sense sphere, the ordinary mind of seeing, hearing, wanting, giving, worrying. Fifteen belong to the fine-material sphere: the minds of the jhānas, the meditative absorptions (four in the suttas; the Dhammasaṅgaṇī gives both a fourfold and a fivefold scheme, and the Manual follows the fivefold), absorbed in a meditation object. Twelve belong to the immaterial sphere, the formless attainments, where the object is boundless space, the consciousness that knew it, nothingness, or the consciousness that knew that. Eight are supramundane: the moments of path and fruition that take Nibbāna as their object.Counted in finer detail, each supramundane citta can occur at any of five jhāna levels, which gives forty instead of eight, and a total of 121. The Manual gives both counts.

The plane of a citta and the plane of a world are linked. A human being lives in the sense sphere but can, in deep meditation, have fine-material cittas. A being reborn in a fine-material world is reborn by such a citta.

Twelve that are unwholesome

The sense-sphere cittas begin with twelve that are unwholesome, akusalaakusala · unwholesome unhealthy, blameworthy, bringing painful results; rooted in greed, hatred or delusion. Eight are rooted in greed, lobhalobha · greed grasping at an object; roots eight cittas; as craving, a root of the wheel, and differ by three switches: with joy or with neutral feeling, with wrong view or without it, spontaneous or prompted (needing a push, from oneself or another). Two are rooted in hatred, dosadosa · hatred aversion, from irritation to rage; root of two cittas, always with displeasure, and both carry displeasure. Two are rooted in delusion alone: one with doubt, one with restlessness.

That sorting has a quiet consequence, which the figure below shows by colour. Domanassadomanassa · displeasure painful mental feeling; only in the two hate-rooted cittas, mental displeasure, occurs in only those two hate-rooted cittas, nowhere else among the eighty-nine. Grief, sadness, dejection are all, in this analysis, forms of aversion.The Dhammapada commentary tells the story of Kisāgotamī, who carried her dead child from house to house looking for medicine. She sought a mustard seed from a house where no one had died, found none, and understood. Her grief was aversion toward loss; the search turned it into a fact about the world.

Rootless, and beautiful

Eighteen cittas have no roots at all. Most of them are results: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching, each in a wholesome-result and an unwholesome-result version, and the cittas that receive and investigate what the senses bring. They are the passive, given part of experience. Three are functional: two adverting cittas, which turn the mind toward an object, and the smile-producing citta, a rootless moment of joy found only in arahants (I §10).

Then twenty-four “beautiful” (sobhanasobhana · beautiful the 59 cittas other than unwholesome and rootless ones, and their 25 factors) sense-sphere cittas: eight wholesome, eight resultant, eight functional. Twelve, eighteen and twenty-four make the fifty-four of the sense sphere. The wholesome eight are the ordinary good mind, generous, kind, clear, and differ by the same switches as the greed-rooted eight: with joy or neutral feeling, with knowledge or without, spontaneous or prompted. Their functional twins are the same states in an arahant, who still acts with kindness and understanding but makes no kamma by it.

What the count is for

There is a temptation to treat the eighty-nine as trivia. The list does something else. It replaces the single, continuous mind that we assume is doing our knowing with many kinds of knowing, each brief, each conditioned, none of them owned.

It also makes the mind legible. Painful bodily feeling occurs in just one citta, body-consciousness that is the result of unwholesome kamma; pleasant bodily feeling in one, its wholesome counterpart. Every other painful feeling is mental: displeasure, in the two hate-rooted cittas. Joy occurs in wholesome and unwholesome minds alike, so joy alone is no test of a good state. Neutral feeling, equanimity, occurs in the dullest mind and in the arahant’s, and only the roots tell them apart.

None of this is meant to be memorised as a table first. It is meant to be met, one citta at a time, in the moments when you notice which kind you are in.

To reflect on. Displeasure occurs in only two of the eighty-nine cittas, both rooted in aversion. Think of a recent sadness. Can you find the aversion in it?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, I §§3–32, and III §§2–4 on feeling. Dhammasaṅgaṇī, the analysis of states of mind. Dhammapada commentary on verse 114: Kisāgotamī.

The twelve unwholesome cittas

Eight rooted in greed, two in hatred, two in delusion alone: what each label means, the scenes the old commentaries chose to show each one, and where the teachers disagreed about prompting.

Manual I §§4–7 with the Guides and Table 1.2 (the greed-, hate- and delusion-rooted cittas

A map of the eighty-nine placed twelve cittas at the head of the sense sphere and called them unwholesome. This reading takes them one at a time. The Manual gives them in three short paragraphs and a verse (I §§4–7), Bodhi sets them out in Table 1.2, and the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, where they first appear, describes each at length (Dhs §§365–430). The labels are terse: “accompanied by joy, associated with wrong view, unprompted”. Each word in them does work, and it is worth knowing what before meeting the twelve.

What the labels mean

Rooted. A root, hetuhetu · root one of six factors that steady a citta: greed, hatred, delusion, or their opposites, is a mental factor that gives a citta stability; cittas without roots are the weaker for it (Guide to I §8). There are three unwholesome roots: greed, hatred and delusion. Delusion is in all twelve. Greed and hatred cannot stand in the same citta. So a citta is called after its most prominent root: eight are rooted in greed, two in hatred, and in two delusion stands alone (Guide to I §4). Greed here is any wanting, gross or faint; hatred, which the Manual names by its synonym paṭighapaṭigha · aversion “striking against”: the Manual's name for hatred in the two hate-rooted cittas, from rage to slight irritation; it always comes with displeasure, aversion, is any pushing-away, fierce or mild (Guides to I §§4–5).

Joy or neutral feeling. Every citta has a feeling. Joy, somanassasomanassa · joy pleasant mental feeling; it accompanies 62 of the 121 cittas, is pleasant feeling of the mind. The other option is upekkhāupekkhā · equanimity (feeling) neutral feeling, neither pleasant nor painful; in 55 of the 121 cittas, which the Manual’s translation calls equanimity; but here, the Guide notes, it names only neutral feeling, neither glad nor sad, and not the meditator’s even-mindedness (Guide to I §4). Greed can be cheerful or flat; hatred always comes with displeasure, domanassadomanassa · displeasure painful mental feeling; only in the two hate-rooted cittas; delusion alone is always neutral.

Accompanied by wrong view. Wrong view, diṭṭhi, can come with greed in two ways. It may give the wanting a reason, or be itself the thing held dear (Guide to I §4). The cittas “dissociated from view” are greed with no reason given.

Prompted. The last switch is prompting, sasaṅkhārikasasaṅkhārika · prompted arising after urging or persuasion, by oneself or by another. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī itself marks only the second, fourth, sixth and eighth citta of a set “with prompting”; it has no word for unprompted, and the Atthasālinī says the first is to be understood by contrast with the second (on Dhs §1). The Atthasālinī defines prompting as effort and means added to the same conditions that would otherwise produce the citta (on Dhs §146). The Visuddhimagga puts it as a prior effort, by oneself or by others, and gives the difference in two words: the unprompted citta is naturally keen and unurged, the prompted one sluggish and urged (Vism XIV §§452–453). The Guide adds that the push may work through the body, through words, or in the mind alone, as when one talks oneself into acting against reluctance (Guide to I §4).

Two consequences follow. Prompting is not a moral grade: nothing in these sources makes a prompted deed better or worse than an unprompted one. And the sluggishness is real: sloth and torpor can arise only in the five prompted unwholesome cittas, never in the unprompted, which are naturally keen (II §13 with the Guide).

Two sets of examples

The commentaries illustrate the cittas with scenes, and there are two sets. The Visuddhimagga gives a short standard one (Vism XIV §453), repeated almost word for word by Buddhadatta’s Abhidhammāvatāra and by the Vibhāvinī. The Atthasālinī, the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, has a different and livelier set (on Dhs §§365–429). The Guide’s examples, a boy stealing an apple and a murder, are modern; they are not the commentaries’ (Guide to I §7). All are only illustrations. The citta is the state of mind, and the same state can show in many deeds.

The eight rooted in greed

1. Joy, with view, unprompted. The Visuddhimagga’s case: someone happily enjoys sense pleasures, keen of himself, holding that there is no harm in them, or trusts lucky sights and other auspicious signs as things of real worth (Vism XIV §453). The first is a view the suttas already know: MN 45 describes ascetics who say there is no harm in sensual pleasures. The Atthasālinī gives no scene here, but lists how such a view comes about: hearing false teaching, bad friends, not wishing to see the noble ones, unwise attention, a taste for omens and festivals (on Dhs §365).

2. Joy, with view, prompted. The Atthasālinī tells a story (on Dhs §399). A young man wants to marry a girl from a family of another faith. Her people refuse, until his relatives promise that he will do as they do. He goes with them to their teachers, doubtful at first, and in time comes to like their ways and takes up their view. The view arrived with help. The Visuddhimagga simply repeats case 1 with a sluggish mind that has to be urged.

3. Joy, without view, unprompted. The Visuddhimagga gives plain appetite: sexual indulgence, coveting another’s wealth, stealing another’s goods, with joy and keen of itself (Vism XIV §453). The Atthasālinī puts us in a crowd: watching shows, wrestling and dance festivals, or absorbed in pleasant sounds, without any view at all (on Dhs §400). Here, it adds, conceit may come in. The Manual agrees: conceit can arise only in the four greed-rooted cittas without view, though they need not have it (II §13 with the Guide).

4. Joy, without view, prompted. The same crowd, but now people are spitting and kicking dust about, and you have to work to keep watching, peeping between their heads; or the royal dancers come out, the crowd is pushed back, and you peer through the gaps (on Dhs §402). The pleasure is still there, but it takes effort.

5–8. The same four with neutral feeling. The Visuddhimagga says when they arise: when the sense objects are nothing special, or some other cause for joy is lacking (Vism XIV §453). Greed does not need delight. Much of it is flat: the habitual reach, the idle wanting. The Atthasālinī treats these four as the first four without joy and without zest (on Dhs §§403, 409–412).

One small difference between the sets: the Guide uses stealing for all eight greed-rooted cittas; the Visuddhimagga names stealing only among the cittas without view, though its sub-commentary also counts views that excuse some theft under the first (on Vism XIV §453).

The two rooted in hatred

9. Displeasure, aversion, unprompted. The Visuddhimagga says it arises in killing and the like when the mind is keen (Vism XIV §453); the Atthasālinī, that it arises in one who is displeased, as aversion to any of the six objects (on Dhs §413). The Guide’s example is a murder in a sudden fit of rage (Guide to I §7).

10. Displeasure, aversion, prompted. The Atthasālinī’s example is more telling (on Dhs §421). Someone is stirred up by others, or reminded of another’s offence; or, recalling it himself, grows angry. The last needs no one else. The Guide’s example for this citta is a murder after premeditation (Guide to I §7), which can suggest that “prompted” means “worse”; the commentary’s examples do not.

Displeasure and aversion always go together, but they are two things: displeasure is the feeling, aversion the attitude, and they fall in different aggregates (Guide to I §5). These two cittas never carry wrong view. A view may lead to hatred, but in an earlier citta (Guide to I §5). And they never take an object as predominant: an angry man, the Atthasālinī says, holds nothing in esteem (on Dhs §421). Greed can prize its object; hatred cannot. Envy, avarice and worry, when they arise, arise only here, one at a time (II §§13, 26).

The two rooted in delusion

In the last two cittas there is no greed and no hatred, only delusion, and the Manual calls these two momūhamomūha · sheer delusion delusion with neither greed nor hatred: the two delusion-rooted cittas, one with doubt and one with restlessness, “sheer delusion” (I §6 with the Guide). Their feeling is always neutral. The Guide’s reason is that a mind caught in doubt or agitation cannot form a clear liking or disliking of its object, so neither joy nor displeasure can arise (Guide to I §6).

11. With doubt. The Visuddhimagga says only: at the time of indecision (Vism XIV §453). The canon lists eight things one doubts: the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, the past, the future, both, and dependent origination (Dhs §1008). The Guide’s example is doubting the Buddha’s awakening or the Dhamma as a way to freedom (Guide to I §7).

12. With restlessness. At the time of distraction, the Visuddhimagga says (Vism XIV §453): the mind cannot settle on anything (Guide to I §7). Restlessness is in all twelve unwholesome cittas, but only here is it the chief factor (Guide to I §6).

The Atthasālinī compares the two (on Dhs §§427–429). Restlessness wavers on one object, doubt between several. Both roll on their object, but the doubting citta rolls freely, while the restless one has a foothold, since it has adhimokkhaadhimokkha · decision resolves on the object; absent from doubt and from sense consciousness, decision, and doubt does not: like a round gem and a square gem let go on a slope. The restlessness citta is also the only one of the twelve that cannot produce rebirth-linking; the Guide explains this by its weakness. Any of the other eleven, as kamma, can bring rebirth in a woeful plane; the twelfth gives results only in the course of a life (V §27 with the Guide). The Atthasālinī gives its own reason: it is not among the states abandoned by the first path (after Dhs §429). It does not call the citta weak: with its foothold of decision it is the stronger of the two, and the sub-commentary to the Visuddhimagga names the doubt citta the weakest of all (on Vism XIV §453).Where teachers differ. On one point the commentators all agree: the push behind a prompted citta may come from oneself or from another (Atthasālinī on Dhs §146; Vism XIV §452; Vibhāvinī on I §4; Ledi, Paramatthadīpanī §22). They differ on what the word names. For the Atthasālinī it is the effort or means added to the usual conditions; for the Visuddhimagga, an earlier effort. The Vibhāvinī takes it as a keenness that the earlier effort gives the citta. Ledi Sayadaw objects that on that reading the prompted citta would be the keen one, the reverse of the teaching; for him the word qualifies the set of conditions the citta comes from. They also differ on the two delusion-rooted cittas, which carry no label (I §6). The Vibhāvinī and the sub-commentary on the Visuddhimagga say neither word fits: these cittas have no natural keenness, and no one sets out to arouse them. Ledi holds they are always unprompted, since they arise in beings of themselves, without effort (Guide to I §6; Vibhāvinī on I §6; sub-commentary on Vism XIV §453; Paramatthadīpanī §28). The Guide’s count for the sense sphere, 17 unprompted, 17 prompted and 20 neither (Guide to I §17), follows the Vibhāvinī; if the two delusion-rooted cittas are counted as unprompted, as Ledi holds, the figures become 19, 17 and 18 (our arithmetic).

Which path removes which

The twelve do not fall all at once. Stream-entry removes five for good: the four greed-rooted cittas with view, and the citta of doubt. Once-returning removes none, but weakens sensual desire and ill will. Non-returning removes the two hate-rooted cittas. Arahantship removes the last five: the four greed-rooted cittas without view, and restlessness (Guide to I §§26–28). The Atthasālinī pictures this as a king at war with twelve bandit chiefs, taking them in turn (after Dhs §362, closing its commentary on the wholesome).

So a stream-enterer can still want, cheerfully or flatly, with or without a push; what is gone is wanting backed by a view, and doubt. What an arahant lacks is not only greed with joy but the quiet, unjustified liking, and the faint restlessness that came with every unwholesome state. How the paths do this is told in Four noble persons.

None of this is a catalogue to memorise first. Each label names something that can be noticed: a want with a reason attached, a want without one; a pleasure that comes of itself, and one that has to be worked up; an irritation kept alive by going over it. The cittas that have no roots at all, and the beautiful ones, are the subject of Rootless and beautiful cittas.

To reflect on. The Atthasālinī's example of the prompted hate-rooted citta includes someone who, with no one urging him, recalls an old offence and grows angry all over again. Why would the commentary count that as "prompted", when nobody else was involved?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, I §§4–7 with the Guides, and Table 1.2; I §8 (roots give stability); II §§13, 26 with the Guide (which unwholesome factors go with which citta); Guide to I §§26–28 (which path removes which citta); V §27 with the Guide (the restlessness citta and rebirth); Guide to I §17 (the counts by prompting). Dhammasaṅgaṇī, the unwholesome cittas, CS §§365–430 (SuttaCentral ds2.1.6); the eight objects of doubt, CS §1008 (ds2.3.1:24.2). Visuddhimagga XIV §§452–453 (the standard examples; prompting as a prior effort by oneself or others). Paragraph numbers are those of the Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana edition. Dhammapāla's sub-commentary on Vism XIV §453 (views that excuse theft; the doubt citta the weakest; sub-commentarial). Atthasālinī on Dhs §146 (what prompting is: the monk and the shrine terrace), §365 (how wrong view arises), §§399–402 (the young man and the sectarian bride; the shows and the dancers), §421 (the prompted hate citta; no object-predominance), §§427–429 (doubt and restlessness compared; restlessness and rebirth); the twelve bandit chiefs, after Dhs §362, closing its commentary on the wholesome. Commentarial. Buddhadatta, Abhidhammāvatāra ch. 1 (the same examples as the Visuddhimagga). Sumaṅgala, Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī on CMA I §§4–6 (CS §§4–6); Ledi Sayadaw, Paramatthadīpanī, CS §§22, 28. MN 45, Cūḷadhammasamādāna Sutta: those who hold there is no harm in sensual pleasures (SuttaCentral mn45).

Rootless and beautiful cittas

The eighteen cittas with no root at all, the arahant's smile among them; the twenty-four beautiful cittas of the sense sphere and who has them; and, briefly, the jhāna, formless and supramundane cittas, with how eight became forty.

Manual I §§8–16 with the Guides and Tables 1.3–1.4 (the rootless and the sense-sphere beautiful cittas)

The twelve unwholesome cittas took the first part of the sense sphere one citta at a time. This reading goes on through the rest of the eighty-nine: the eighteen rootless cittas (I §§8–11), the twenty-four beautiful cittas of the sense sphere (I §§12–16), and, more briefly, the cittas of jhāna, of the formless attainments, and of the path (I §§18–32).

Eighteen without roots

A rootless citta, ahetukaahetuka · rootless a citta with none of the six roots; there are 18, has none of the six roots: not greed, hatred or delusion, and not their opposites either. Since roots give a citta stability, these are the weaker cittas (Guide to I §8). Ledi Sayadaw adds that the roots are great states, and do not arise in cittas born of weak kamma or with weak bases and functions (Paramatthadīpanī §38). Fifteen of the eighteen are results of kamma; three are functional.

Fifteen results. Seven come from unwholesome kamma and eight from wholesome kamma (I §§8–9). In each set are the five sense consciousnesses, seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching; receiving, which takes up what was sensed; and investigating, which examines it. The word “unwholesome” in “unwholesome-resultant” qualifies the kamma, not the citta: the seeing of an ugly sight is not itself bad (Guide to I §8). Four of the sense consciousnesses always come with neutral feeling. Only touch is felt as pain or pleasure, because only there does the object strike the faculty hard (Guides to I §§8–9). The wholesome set has one more citta than the unwholesome: investigating with joy, which arises when the object is especially desirable (Guide to I §9).

These are the given part of experience, and they are not tied to the realm one lives in. The Atthasālinī gives an example (on Dhs §498). When Mahāmoggallāna made a lotus appear in hell and sat on it teaching, the beings there saw him with wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness and heard him with wholesome-resultant ear-consciousness. They smelled the sandalwood scent of his robe, tasted the rain he made fall on the fires, and felt a gentle breeze. Reborn there by unwholesome kamma, they still had old wholesome kamma to ripen.

One rootless result does more than register a sense. The wholesome-resultant investigating citta with neutral feeling can serve as rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death consciousness: for human beings born with a deep defect already in the kamma that made the birth, such as those born blind or deaf, and for some lower deities (V §11 with the Guide). Its unwholesome counterpart does the same for every being in the four woeful planes (Guide to III §9).

Three functional. A functional citta, kiriyakiriya · functional a citta that neither makes kamma nor results from it, such as adverting, is neither kamma nor its result. The Atthasālinī compares those that never reach the javana stage to wind-flowers, which set no fruit, and those that do to the flowers of a tree whose root has been cut (on Dhs §566). The first of the three is five-door adverting, which turns to an object at a sense door and does no seeing itself (Guide to I §10). The second is mind-door adverting, which does the same at the mind door and, in a five-door process, determines the object. The Atthasālinī calls it the great elephant, since there is no object it cannot take: even the Buddha’s unique knowledges take only what it has turned to first (on Dhs §574).

The arahant’s smile

The third functional citta is the smile-producing one, hasituppādahasituppāda · smile-producing an arahant's rootless functional citta that causes smiling at sense-sphere things, joyful and rootless (I §10). It has no root of any kind: not greed, and not non-greed either. The canon has it as one citta among the indeterminate, without the name (Dhs §568); the name, and the rule that only arahants have it, are the commentaries’ (Atthasālinī on Dhs §568; Vism XIV §454). Buddhas and paccekabuddhas are arahants too, so they have it (Guide to I §10).

What does it smile at? Small things, says the Visuddhimagga (Vism XIV §454); “sense-sphere phenomena”, says the Guide (Guide to I §10). The Atthasālinī gives examples at each door (on Dhs §568). An arahant sees a place fit for meditation; hears the din where goods are handed out and greedy people grab, and knows that craving is gone in him; shares good almsfood and reflects that he has kept the rule of sharing. At the mind door, it says, the Buddha smiled with this citta when he recalled what he had done as the potter’s friend Jotipāla (MN 81) and as King Maghadeva (MN 83): both suttas open with him smiling at a certain place. The recalling was the work of his knowledges; the smile came at their end.

A smile, in the Abhidhamma, is an act of the body made by a citta. Thirteen joyful javana cittas can produce one: a worldling smiles with any of eight, a trainee with six, an arahant with five, the four joyful great functionals and this one (VI §11 with the Guide).Where teachers differ. Did the Buddha smile with it? The root sub-commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī objects: this citta has no wisdom in it, while the canon says all the Buddha’s bodily action follows knowledge (Mahāniddesa; Paṭisambhidāmagga, ps3.1:26.1); so the Atthasālinī’s statement “should be examined” (on Dhs §568). The later teachers answer that the smile does follow knowledge, since it comes at the end of the work of his knowledges; and that if the objection held, the Buddha could not have mind-door adverting either, which also moves the body (second sub-commentary on Dhs §568; sub-commentary on Vism XIV §454; Vibhāvinī on VI §11; Ledi, Paramatthadīpanī §158). Does it smile at the five doors? The second sub-commentary says that there it only gladdens, since five-door cittas make no bodily act; the actual smile comes at the mind door (on Dhs §568). The Manual lists the smiling cittas without such a limit (VI §11).

Twenty-four beautiful

“Beautiful”, sobhanasobhana · beautiful the 59 cittas other than unwholesome and rootless ones, and their 25 factors, is wider than “wholesome”. It covers every citta with beautiful mental factors, so it takes in resultant and functional cittas that make no kamma (Guide to I §12). In the sense sphere there are twenty-four: eight wholesome, eight resultant and eight functional, each set sorted by the same three switches: joy or neutral feeling, with or without knowledge, unprompted or prompted (I §§13–16). With knowledge they have three roots; without it, two, non-greed and non-hatred (Guide to I §13). Without knowledge does not mean deluded: it means only that the factor of wisdom is absent (Guide to I §13).

The great wholesome eight. The Visuddhimagga’s examples run parallel to those for greed (Vism XIV §452). Someone meets a fine gift, a worthy recipient or some other cause for joy, and with the right view that there is fruit in giving, the view of MN 41, gives without hesitation and unurged: that is the first. The same person, hesitating for want of free generosity, or urged by others, gives with the second. Small children who have seen their relatives do it, catching sight of monks, joyfully give whatever is in their hands or bow: the third. When their relatives tell them “give, bow”, the fourth. When the gift or recipient is nothing special, the same four arise with neutral feeling.

The Atthasālinī’s examples are close to home (on Dhs §§146–149). A monk living at the edge of the monastery thinks the shrine terrace, or the elders’ service, or the Dhamma talk is too far, and decides not to go; then reflects that it is unfitting for a monk not to go, and goes. Whether he goes by his own effort, because another admonishes him, or because he is told “come, do this”, the citta is prompted. Small children see a monk, think “this is my elder”, and bow; or their parents take them by the head and make them bow, and, though they did not want to, they bow gladly. The Guide’s examples are of generous deeds done with or without understanding, spontaneously or after deliberation (Guide to I §13).

These eight arise in worldlings and trainees, not in arahants (Guide to I §13). The Guide says that “according to the commentary” one acts unprompted from fitness of body and mind, good food and climate, and past practice; that list is the Vibhāvinī’s (on I §13, CS §15; climate and food at CS §4).

The great resultants. Each wholesome citta has its result of the same shape (I §14). They do not act: they carry a life, as rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death, and register an object after the javanas, all within the sense sphere (Vism XIV §454). Anyone reborn in the happy sense-sphere planes with two or three roots, a human being or a deva, is carried by one of them (V §11), arahants included, whose life-continuum is still a result (Guide to III §9). The Visuddhimagga gives an image: the result is like a face in a mirror, there without effort, while the wholesome citta is like the face (Vism XIV §454). The Atthasālinī adds that every bodhisatta takes his last rebirth with the first of them, joyful, with knowledge and unprompted, as the fruit of loving-kindness; the elder Mahāsīva held it was the neutral one, and the commentary sets that aside (on Dhs §498).Where teachers differ. What makes a result “prompted”? Not effort, since a result makes none. The Atthasālinī reports three elders (on Dhs §498). Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga let it depend on the conditions present: strong, clear conditions give an unprompted result, weak ones a prompted, whatever the deed. Mahādatta of Moravāpi held a stricter rule: an unprompted deed gives only unprompted results, a prompted deed only prompted ones; Mahādhammarakkhita held the same rule within a different count. The Atthasālinī tells us to take what is sound in each. The Manual gives Cūḷanāga’s view and then the strict rule as “some teachers” (V §§29–30); the Guide, following the Vibhāvinī, ascribes it to Mahā Dhammarakkhita’s school (Guide to V §30), and Ledi Sayadaw corrects the name to Mahādatta (Paramatthadīpanī §153). Ledi also gives a concrete case: a rebirth citta is prompted if, at the previous death, relatives set the object before the dying person, unprompted if kamma brought it up of itself (§44).

The great functionals. In arahants the same eight shapes occur as functional cittas, mahākiriyamahākiriya · great functional the eight beautiful sense-sphere functional cittas: the arahant's counterparts of the great wholesome, which make no kamma: their twins, which act and leave nothing behind as kamma (I §15 with the Guide). An arahant still gives, bows and teaches, with or without the factor of knowledge in a given moment, and the giving makes no kamma. The Atthasālinī says these are the great wholesome cittas become functional because they arise in an arahant (on Dhs §576).

Beyond the sense sphere

Fifteen fine-material. These are the jhāna cittas, each defined by its jhāna factors (I §§18–20). The Manual counts five jhānas: the first with initial and sustained application, zest, happiness and one-pointedness, each later one dropping a factor, the fifth with neutral feeling and one-pointedness. It is often said that the suttas have four jhānas and the Abhidhamma five, but the Dhammasaṅgaṇī itself gives both schemes, fourfold (Dhs §§160–166) and fivefold (§§167–175), and the Manual keeps the fivefold. The Atthasālinī explains the second: for some hearers only initial application seemed gross, and the suttas already know a concentration with sustained application but without initial (on Dhs §167, citing DN 33; the same three concentrations are in MN 128). Wholesome jhānas belong to worldlings and trainees; their results arise only in beings reborn in the fine-material world; the functional jhānas are the arahant’s (Guide to I §§18–20). All have three roots (Guide to I §21).

Twelve immaterial. The four formless attainments have the same two factors as the fifth jhāna and are named by their objects (I §25; Table 1.6). The first takes infinite space; the second, the consciousness that took infinite space; the third, nothingness, the absence of that first consciousness; the fourth, the consciousness that took nothingness. Each is wholesome, resultant or functional, as before (I §§22–24).

Eight, or forty, supramundane. Four paths and four fruitions take Nibbāna as their object (I §§26–28). A path citta arises only once in a person, for one moment; its fruition follows at once and can be entered again later. There is no supramundane functional citta (Guide to I §§26–28). The Manual then counts again (I §§30–32). Every path and fruition has the factors of one jhāna or another, so each of the eight can occur at five levels: eight become forty, and the eighty-nine become a hundred and twenty-one.

Which jhāna a path has, the Guide says, the ancient teachers explained in three ways; a bare-insight meditator’s path is of the first jhāna (Guide to I §§30–31).Where teachers differ. Prompting above the sense sphere. The Manual leaves prompting out of the jhāna, formless and supramundane cittas. The Vibhāvinī gives two reasons: neither word fits, since no jhāna comes without preliminary work, nor from preliminary work without past aptitude; or “unprompted” never fits and “prompted” would add nothing (on I §18, CS §21). The Guide holds that the effort belongs to the approach, not to the attainment, so the distinction does not apply (Guide to I §21). Ledi Sayadaw keeps it, reading prompted and unprompted into the painful and pleasant modes of progress, as the commentaries’ own wording allows (Paramatthadīpanī §§50–51).

Who counted

None of these totals is in the canon. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī describes the cittas one after another, without a sum. The count of eighty-nine is the commentaries’: it stands in the Atthasālinī’s introduction, the Visuddhimagga (Vism XIV §455) and Buddhadatta’s Abhidhammāvatāra (ch. 1 v. 64); the forty supramundane cittas already stand behind the Visuddhimagga’s count of joyful cittas (Vism XIV §456), and the total of a hundred and twenty-one is given in the Abhidhammāvatāra (ch. 3 vv. 90–91), before the Manual (I §§30–32). And it is one count among several: the commentaries also multiply the great wholesome cittas by the bases of merit, the objects and the doors of action into many thousands, and add that their variety by time, place and person is beyond counting (Vibhāvinī on I §13; Abhidhammāvatāra ch. 1 v. 27).

The count is a tool. What it sorts is ordinary: a moment of seeing, a turning toward, a gift that comes of itself and one that needs a nudge, a smile at a small thing.

To reflect on. The Atthasālinī says that when Mahāmoggallāna sat on a lotus in hell, the beings there saw him with wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness. What does that tell you about the relation between where a being is and what it experiences?

Commentarial. Visuddhimagga XIV §§452–456 (examples; the mirror simile; the smile citta; the totals 89 and the forty). Paragraph numbers are those of the Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana edition. Dhammapāla's sub-commentary on Vism XIV §454; the root and second sub-commentaries on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, on Dhs §568 (sub-commentarial). Buddhadatta, Abhidhammāvatāra ch. 1 v. 64 (89) and ch. 3 vv. 90–91 (121).
