MN 81, Ghaṭikāra Sutta (SuttaCentral mn81); MN 83, Maghadeva Sutta (mn83); MN 41, Sāleyyaka Sutta (mn41); DN 33, Saṅgīti Sutta (dn33); MN 128, Upakkilesa Sutta (mn128); Paṭisambhidāmagga, the Buddha's actions follow knowledge (ps3.1).

An ensemble of fifty-two

Seven factors present in every moment of mind, two families that never meet, and why the Abhidhamma thinks of a mind as a chord.

Manual II §§1–9 (the 52 in four groups), with the guide's definitions

A citta never arises alone. It comes with company: the mental factors, cetasikacetasika · mental factor a mental factor: arises and ceases with a citta, sharing its object and bases, which arise with it, cease with it, take the same object and depend on the same base. Citta is the knowing; the factors are what the knowing is like. If citta is a note, the factors make it a chord.

The Abhidhamma counts fifty-two, and their arrangement is one of the most useful things in the system.

Seven that are always there

Seven factors occur in every citta, from the dullest moment of hearing to the path that sees Nibbāna. They are the minimum equipment of any experience at all.

Phassaphassa · contact the meeting of object, base and consciousness; the first universal factor, contact, is the meeting of mind and object. Vedanāvedanā · feeling feeling: the pleasant, painful or neutral tone of a moment; not emotion, feeling, is the tone of that meeting: pleasant, painful or neither. Saññāsaññā · perception perception: marks an object's features so it can be recognised again, perception, marks the object so it can be recognised again. Cetanācetanā · volition the willing that organises the other factors; as kamma, it bears results, volition, organises the rest toward the object; in some cittas it is kamma. One-pointedness, ekaggatāekaggatā · one-pointedness unifies the mind on its object; when strong it is concentration (samādhi), fixes the mind on its single object. The life faculty sustains the mental factors for their moment. Manasikāramanasikāra · attention turns the citta and its factors toward the object; present in every citta, attention, turns the citta toward its object.The suttas already say that feeling, perception and consciousness are “conjoined, not disjoined”: you cannot separate them and point to the difference between them (MN 43). The Abhidhamma lengthens the list and keeps the principle.

It is a striking list. There is no moment of mind without feeling, without some recognising, without some willing. Even the most neutral glance has a tone and a direction.

Six that come and go

Six more are “occasional”: they occur in many cittas but not all. Initial application, vitakkavitakka · initial application lays the mind onto its object; a factor of the first jhāna only, lifts the mind onto the object; sustained application, vicāravicāra · sustained application keeps the mind moving over its object; a factor of the first two jhānas, keeps it there. Decision, energy, zest, and the desire to act complete the set. These are ethically variable, like the universals. They take on the colour of whatever citta they join, so energy can serve greed as well as kindness.

Two families

The remaining thirty-nine divide into two families that never occur together.

Fourteen are unwholesome. Four of them occur in every unwholesome citta: delusion, mohamoha · delusion mental blindness to an object's true nature; present in every unwholesome citta, which hides the nature of the object; shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing, the absence of a conscience; and restlessness. The others come in groups: greed with wrong view or conceit; hatred with envy, avarice or worry; sloth and torpor; and doubt.

Twenty-five are beautiful. Nineteen of them occur in every beautiful citta, and the list reads like a portrait of a good moment. They are faith, mindfulness, shame and fear of wrongdoing, non-greed, non-hatred, neutrality of mind, and six pairs of qualities, tranquillity, lightness, malleability, wieldiness, proficiency and rectitude, each of mental body and of mind. Then three abstinences, from wrong speech, wrong action and wrong livelihood; two illimitables, the boundless attitudes toward beings: compassion and appreciative joy; and wisdom.Loving-kindness and equanimity, the other two illimitables, appear in the list, the commentaries explain, under other names: non-hatred and neutrality of mind. That is why only two are listed separately.

A good moment is complete

The arrangement makes a moral point without stating it. Every beautiful citta has nineteen beautiful factors at once. In any single beautiful moment you cannot have mindfulness without faith, or non-greed without non-hatred: in this analysis the good qualities arrive together. And every unwholesome citta has its four companions, so any greed is also, at that moment, delusion and a lapse of conscience.

It also means the two families never mix. In the moment of a generous gift there is no greed in the gift. If the giver then wants thanks, that is a later citta, in another process: the seven javanas of one process are all of one kind. What feels like mixed motives is a rapid alternation of whole states, each complete in its kind.

That is good news for practice. A beautiful moment is not diluted by the selfish one that follows it. It happened, whole, and it conditions what comes next.

To reflect on. Greed and generosity never occur in the same citta. Yet people often feel they give and want at once. How would the Abhidhamma describe that experience?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, II §§1–9, with the guide's definitions. Dhammasaṅgaṇī, the factors present in the first wholesome citta. MN 43, Mahāvedalla Sutta: feeling, perception and consciousness are conjoined, not disjoined.

Which factors meet which cittas

One table read two ways: across, the cittas a factor joins; down, the factors a citta takes. How the Abhidhamma assembles a moment of mind.

The second chapter of the Manual asks two questions of one table. Put the fifty-two factors down the side and the eighty-nine cittas across the top. Read across a row, and you have the method of association: which cittas does this factor join? Read down a column, and you have the method of combination: which factors does this citta take?

It is the Abhidhamma’s way of assembling a moment of mind from its parts.

Reading across

Some rows are full. The seven universals appear in every column. Some rows are nearly empty: doubt appears in one citta only, the delusion-rooted citta that bears its name. Envy, avarice and worry share the two hate-rooted cittas, but never together, since each has a different object. Compassion and appreciative joy appear in twenty-eight cittas, and only occasionally, when a being in suffering or in success is actually the object.The Manual calls such factors “unfixed”: they may be present in a citta, but are not always. Eleven factors are unfixed in this way.

The three abstinences behave the same way. Right speech, right action and right livelihood join the great wholesome cittas only at the moment of actually refraining from a wrong. In path and fruition, all three are present together.

Reading down

A column is a recipe. The simplest cittas, the sense consciousnesses, take only the seven universals: seeing is contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, life and attention, and nothing else. The first greed-rooted citta takes nineteen: the seven universals and six occasionals, the four unwholesome factors present in every unwholesome citta, then greed and wrong view. An unwholesome citta takes at most twenty-one factors at once. A great wholesome citta (one of the eight wholesome cittas of the sense sphere) with knowledge can count thirty-eight, though not all at once: at most thirty-four arise together, because the abstinences and the illimitables exclude one another.

Two families that never meet

The table has one rule that is visible at a glance. The fourteen unwholesome factors and the twenty-five beautiful ones never fall in the same column.

What the table is for

It is tempting to treat this chapter as a reference table and move on. But it carries a picture of mind that is worth absorbing slowly. Every moment is assembled anew, from a fixed menu, according to rules. Nothing carries over from one column to the next except by condition. Name the kind of citta, and the table tells you everything that came with it.

To reflect on. An unwholesome citta takes at most twenty-one factors at once; a great wholesome one up to thirty-four. Is a good moment richer than a bad one, or only busier?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, II §§10–30. Dhammasaṅgaṇī: the factors of each kind of citta.

What each citta does

From what a citta is to what it does: fourteen functions, six doors, six bases, and the few cittas that do the most work.

Manual III §§5–7 (roots), §§8–11 (functions), §§12–15 (doors), §§16–19 (objects), §§20–22 (bases)

A map of the eighty-nine sorted the cittas by what they are. The third chapter of the Manual sorts them by what they do. It is the bridge from the map to the moments of a process: before you can follow a sight through seventeen moments, you need to know which cittas can fill each slot.

Fourteen jobs

The Manual counts fourteen functions, kiccakicca · function (of a citta) one of fourteen jobs a citta can do, such as seeing or javana. Three happen outside any process: rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death. The rest are the stations of a process: adverting; seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching; receiving; investigating; determining; javana, the run of moments in which the mind acts; and registration, which takes up the same object once more after the javanas.

Most cittas have one job only. Sixty-eight of the eighty-nine do just one thing: seeing only sees; a greed-rooted citta only ever runs as javana. A few are versatile. The two equanimous investigating cittas each do five jobs: they investigate and register in ordinary processes, and in beings reborn with a rootless citta, in the lower worlds or with a severe impairment, they also serve as rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death.The eight great resultant cittas do four jobs each: registration, rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death for human beings and gods of the sense sphere. The nine fine-material and immaterial resultants do three.

So a single kind of citta can open a life, carry it through every pause, and close it.

Six doors

A dvāradvāra · door the channel by which a process meets its object: five senses and mind, door, is where a process meets its object. Five are the sensitive matter of the senses. The sixth, the mind door, is the life-continuum itself, at the moment it is disturbed by an object.

Forty-six kinds of citta can arise through the eye door; sixty-seven through the mind door. Nineteen are “door-freed” when they serve as rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death: in those roles they arise outside any process and through no door. Ten of them also work inside processes, as investigating or registration; the other nine never do (III §§13–14). The counts overlap, because one citta can arise through more than one door.

Six bases

Every citta in a being with a body stands on a physical base, a vatthuvatthu · physical base the matter a citta arises from: a sense organ or the heart-base. The ten sense consciousnesses, a pair for each sense, stand on their own sense organ: five bases. Every other citta stands on the sixth, the heart-base, which the commentaries name as the physical support of mind. In the immaterial planes there is no matter and so no base; cittas there arise without one.

The base is not the same as the door. Seeing stands on the eye as its base, and the eye is also its door. But the javanas of that process arise through the eye door while standing on the heart-base.

Why this chapter matters

Read as a table, the chapter is dry. Read as a description of a mind, it says something precise about freedom. Of the fourteen functions, only one, javana, makes kamma. Every other function is either a result of past kamma or merely functional. A process has seventeen moments, a life has millions of processes, and in all of it the room for doing something new is a single station, seven moments long.

The same chapter sorts the cittas three more ways, by feeling, by roots and by object; those are in Feeling, roots and objects.

To reflect on. The same kind of citta that links a life to the last one also runs as the life-continuum and ends that life as death. What does it mean that a life begins, idles and ends in the same kind of mind?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, III §§8–22. Visuddhimagga XIV: the functions of consciousness.

Feeling, roots and objects

Three more ways to sort the eighty-nine cittas: by the feeling each one carries, by the roots that make it firm, and by what it is able to know.

Chapter III of the Manual is called the compendium of the miscellaneous. Having listed the cittas and their factors, it sorts the cittas six more ways: by feeling, by roots, by function, by door, by object and by base. What each citta does takes up functions, doors and bases. This reading takes the other three. Each is a lens: the same eighty-nine cittas, seen from a different side.

Three feelings, or five

Every citta has a feeling, because vedanāvedanā · feeling feeling: the pleasant, painful or neutral tone of a moment; not emotion is one of the seven universal factors, the mental factors present in every citta (see An ensemble of fifty-two): it is how the object is tasted. Counted simply, feeling is threefold: pleasant, painful, and neither (III §2). Counted by the faculty that governs it, it is fivefold, because pleasant and painful each divide into a bodily and a mental kind: bodily pleasure, sukhasukha · bodily pleasure pleasant bodily feeling: only in wholesome-resultant body-consciousness, and mental joy, somanassasomanassa · joy pleasant mental feeling; it accompanies 62 of the 121 cittas; bodily pain, dukkhadukkha · bodily pain painful bodily feeling: only in unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness, and mental displeasure, domanassadomanassa · displeasure painful mental feeling; only in the two hate-rooted cittas; and equanimity, upekkhāupekkhā · equanimity (feeling) neutral feeling, neither pleasant nor painful; in 55 of the 121 cittas.

The counts are lopsided (III §3–4). Bodily pleasure and bodily pain occur in one citta each, the two kinds of body-consciousness. Displeasure occurs in only two, the cittas rooted in hatred. Joy occurs in sixty-two, and equanimity in the remaining fifty-five.The Manual’s sixty-two and fifty-five count the supramundane cittas by jhāna, as in the reckoning of 121: eight paths and fruitions in each of five jhānas. Among the eighty-nine, the lens above counts thirty-eight with joy and fifty-five with equanimity, the eight paths and fruitions being in both.

Why should only touch be pleasant or painful? The Guide gives the commentary’s image. In seeing, hearing, smelling and tasting, a derived kind of matter strikes another derived kind of matter, like balls of cotton striking balls of cotton on an anvil: the impact is soft, and the feeling neutral. In touch, the object is the great elements themselves, and they strike the great elements of the body, like a hammer through cotton onto the anvil. So the bare moment of seeing a lovely sight is neutral. The pleasure comes after, in the javanas, as mental joy: the liking is added.

The suttas sometimes speak of feeling as only two, pleasant and painful, and the Buddha once said that whatever is felt is included in suffering (SN 36.11). The Guide reads that in the wide sense: not painful feeling, but the unsatisfactoriness of everything that passes.

Six roots

A root, hetuhetu · root one of six factors that steady a citta: greed, hatred, delusion, or their opposites, is a mental factor that makes the citta it joins firm and stable. Cittas with roots are compared to trees; those without are like moss (III §5). There are six: greed, hatred and delusion, always unwholesome; and non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion, which are wholesome in wholesome cittas and neither good nor bad in resultant and functional ones.

Eighteen cittas have no root at all: the sense consciousnesses, receiving, investigating, adverting and the arahant’s smile (III §6). Two have one root, the cittas of sheer delusion. Twenty-two have two: the other ten unwholesome cittas, with greed or hatred together with delusion, and the twelve sense-sphere beautiful cittas without knowledge, with non-greed and non-hatred. Forty-seven have all three beautiful roots: the twelve sense-sphere beautiful cittas with knowledge, and every jhāna, path and fruition.

The count matters later. The roots of the rebirth-linking citta decide what a life can reach: a being reborn with a rootless or two-rooted citta cannot attain jhāna or the path in that life, however hard they practise. That is taken up in From kamma to its results.

Six kinds of object

Every citta knows something. The Manual names six kinds of object (III §16): visible form, sound, smell, taste, the tangible, and the mental object. The first five are matter. The tangible is three of the great elements felt directly, earth as hard or soft, fire as hot or cold, air as pressure; the fourth, water, cannot be touched and is known only by the mind. The mental object is itself sixfold: the five kinds of sensitive matter, the sixteen kinds of subtle matter, cittas, mental factors, Nibbāna, and concepts, paññattipaññatti · concept a concept: a name, or what a name refers to, such as “chariot”.

A citta can know an earlier citta, in its own stream or another’s, but never itself in the same moment: the knower does not know itself.

Doors also limit time (III §17). The cittas of an eye-door process know only a visible form, and only a present one. The cittas of a mind-door process can know any of the six, past, present or future, or timeless: Nibbāna and concepts are outside time, Nibbāna because it does not arise or pass, concepts because they have no being of their own. And the door-freed cittas of a life, in their three jobs of rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death, all keep one object: the one the last process of the previous life held, as a kamma, a sign of kamma, or a sign of destiny.

Who can know what

Last, the Manual sorts the cittas by the range of objects each can take, in seven groups (III §18–19, Table 3.5):

  • Sense-sphere objects only: twenty-five. The sense-sphere resultants, five-door adverting, and the smile.
  • Anything but the supramundane: twenty. The unwholesome cittas, and the wholesome and functional beautiful ones without knowledge. The paths, their fruitions and Nibbāna are too pure and deep for them.
  • Anything but the arahant’s path and fruition: five, Nibbāna included. The wholesome cittas with knowledge, and the wholesome direct knowledge. An ordinary person, or a trainee (a noble disciple short of arahantship), cannot know an attainment they have not reached.
  • Anything at all: six, Nibbāna included. The functional cittas with knowledge, the functional direct knowledge, both arahants’ only, and mind-door adverting, the citta that also does the job of determining, which turns to every kind of object.
  • Sublime cittas: six. The second and fourth immaterial jhānas, which take the first and third as their objects.
  • Concepts: twenty-one. The fine-material jhānas and the first and third immaterial. Their object is a counterpart sign, beings for the illimitables, infinite space, or nothingness (Table 3.6).
  • Nibbāna only: eight. The paths and fruitions. The sense-sphere cittas with knowledge above turn to Nibbāna only at change-of-lineage and in reviewing (Guide to III §18; IX §34).

That makes ninety-one, because the two cittas of direct knowledge are fifth-jhāna cittas as well, and so they are counted twice.

Taken together, the three lenses show that no citta is simply “a mind”. Each has a tone, a footing or none, and a range, and each of these sets limits on what that moment can do.

To reflect on. The Abhidhamma says seeing itself is always neutral in feeling, and that pleasure in a beautiful sight comes a moment later, in the javanas. Next time you enjoy something you see, can you find the gap between the seeing and the liking?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, III §§2–7 (feeling and roots) and §§16–19 (objects), with Tables 3.1, 3.2, 3.5 and 3.6. Atthasālinī, on why bodily feeling alone is pleasant or painful (cited in the Guide to III §4). SN 36.11: whatever is felt is included in suffering.

How matter is made

Four great elements, twenty-four kinds of matter derived from them, four ways matter is produced, and the smallest groups in which it ever occurs.

Manual VI §§2–5 (enumeration), §§6–8 (classification), §§9–15 (origination), §§16–22 (kalāpas), §§23–29 (occurrence)

The Abhidhamma is a teaching about mind, and yet one of its four kinds of ultimate reality is matter, rūparūpa · matter matter: the third reality, 28 kinds; as an aggregate it is called form. It is there because experience needs it. The eye that sees, the colour seen, the body that walks and the breath that is watched are all matter. And matter, like mind, turns out on inspection to be a set of brief, conditioned events rather than a solid thing.

Four great elements

Everything material rests on four mahābhūtamahābhūta · great elements earth, water, fire and air: the primary matter all other matter depends ons, the great elements. They are named earth, water, fire and air, but they are not substances. Each is a quality defined by what it does.

The earth element is extension: hardness and softness, what resists. The water element is cohesion: what holds things together and lets them flow. The fire element is heat: hot and cold, what ripens and decays. The air element is motion and support: what moves, what distends.The suttas already teach the elements this way, as qualities found inside the body and outside it: the hair and bones are the earth element, the blood and sweat the water element, and so on (MN 28). The Abhidhamma keeps the teaching and defines each one exactly.

The four never occur apart. Wherever there is any matter, all four are present, though one or another predominates in strength. In a stone earth predominates, in a river water, but there is water in the stone and earth in the river.

Twenty-four derived from them

On the four great elements depend twenty-four kinds of derived matter. Five are the sense faculties, the pasādapasāda · sensitivity the matter of eye, ear, nose, tongue or body that receives sense impactss: the sensitive matter of eye, ear, nose, tongue and body, which can be struck by an object. Four are sense objects: visible form, sound, smell and taste. Touch is not listed separately, because what the body touches is three of the great elements themselves: hardness, heat and motion.

The other fifteen are:

  • the heart-base, which the commentaries name as the physical support of mind-consciousness;
  • the material life faculty, and nutritive essence;
  • femininity and masculinity;
  • two kinds of intimation, the bodily and vocal expressions by which a mind makes itself known;
  • space, as what separates groups;
  • lightness, malleability and wieldiness;
  • four marks: production, continuity, decay and impermanence.

The last eight are qualities of matter rather than kinds of it.

Four ways matter is produced

Matter does not come from nowhere, and the Abhidhamma names four origins.

Some matter is produced by kammakamma wholesome or unwholesome volition, which later ripens as results: the sense faculties, the heart-base, the life faculty, the sex faculties. They begin at the moment of conception and are renewed at every moment of a life by past action. Some is produced by citta: the posture of the body, its gestures, the movements of speech. Some is produced by temperature, by the fire element itself, inside and outside the body. Some is produced by nutriment, by the food that is eaten.The Manual traces which matter has one origin and which has several. A sound, for instance, can be mind-born, as in speech, or temperature-born, as in thunder.

So a body at any moment is four streams of matter interwoven. One comes from the past, one from the present mind, one from heat, within the body and around it, one from the last meal.

The smallest groups

Matter never occurs as a single kind. Its smallest unit is a group, a kalāpakalāpa the smallest group of matter: eight or more kinds arising and ceasing together, and the smallest group of all has eight members: the four great elements with colour, smell, taste and nutritive essence. These eight are inseparable. Every group of matter has them.

Other groups add to the eight. The eye-decad adds the eye’s sensitivity and the life faculty. A sound group adds sound. The Abhidhamma counts twenty-one kinds of group, each with its origin. A kalāpa, the commentaries hold, lasts seventeen mind-moments: long enough to carry one complete process of seeing, and no longer.

Why look at matter this way

The body is the first object of mindfulness in the suttas, and the place where the idea of a self is most stubborn. “This is me” is said of a body before it is said of anything else.

Seen as the Abhidhamma sees it, the body is no single thing to say it of. There is hardness, heat, cohesion and motion. There are groups that arise and break up far faster than they can be seen. There are four streams of production, one of which you are adding to with every movement of mind. The body works perfectly well described this way. What is missing from the description is only the owner.

To reflect on. Some of the matter in your body right now was produced by kamma, some by mind, some by temperature and some by food. Which of these can you influence today, and how?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, VI §§2–29. Visuddhimagga XI, the definition of the four elements; XIV, the aggregate of matter. MN 28, Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta: the elements within and without.

Mind and matter together

The nāma–rūpa model. Two currents that hold each other up, moment by moment: matter gives mind its bases and objects, mind makes and sustains matter, and at conception the two arise together.

The readings so far have taken the Abhidhamma’s lists one at a time: the eighty-nine cittas, the fifty-two mental factors, the twenty-eight kinds of matter. Experience never comes in lists. Every moment of a life in this world is mind and matter at once, each holding the other up. The tradition calls the pair nāmarūpanāmarūpa · mentality-materiality (link 4) mind and matter. As link 4 of the wheel: the resultant mental factors and kamma-born matter of a new life; in the suttas, feeling, perception, volition, contact and attention with the elements; in the Abhidhamma, citta with its factors, and the 28 kinds of matter, mind and matter, and this reading is about how they fit together. It is the hinge of the whole study: after it, and two shorter readings that round off the first part, the readings turn from what there is to how it unfolds.

Two words, two depths

The word is older than the Abhidhamma. In the suttas, name-and-form is the fourth link of dependent origination, and the Buddha defines it there: “name” is feeling, perception, volition, contact and attention; “form” is the four great elements and the matter derived from them (SN 12.2). Consciousness is not part of it; it is the link just before, on which name-and-form depends.

The Abhidhamma keeps the pair but takes it down to its ultimate terms. Mind, nāmanāma · mind mind: citta with its factors, which “bend” toward objects; the word also means “name”, is citta together with its mental factors; matter, rūparūpa · matter matter: the third reality, 28 kinds; as an aggregate it is called form, is the twenty-eight kinds. Together they are everything conditioned. The fourth ultimate reality, after citta, its factors and matter, is Nibbāna, and it is neither: nothing produces it, and it conditions only as an object (VIII §17, §19). The path and fruition cittas take it, and so, briefly, do change-of-lineage and reviewing (IX §34).The Dhammasaṅgaṇī, sorting all dhammas into the pair “nāma and rūpa”, puts Nibbāna on the side of nāma, because, like mind, it is not matter and the mind bends towards it as an object. In the model here it stands apart, since it is not one of the two currents.

Two currents that hold each other up

In the worlds that have both, mind cannot arise without a physical base, and much of the body is produced and kept going by mind. Each side feeds the other, and the arrows run both ways.

Matter feeds mind in two ways. Every citta rests on a vatthuvatthu · physical base the matter a citta arises from: a sense organ or the heart-base, a base: the five sense organs for the five kinds of sense consciousness, and the heart-base for all the rest. And the five kinds of sense object, colour, sound, smell, taste and the tangible, are all matter.

Mind feeds matter in two ways too. Seventy-five of the eighty-nine kinds of citta produce matter, each at the moment it arises, from the first life-continuum after rebirth on: posture, gesture, speech, a smile. And volition, which is kamma, produced the living core of this body from conception on: the sense organs, the heart-base, the life faculty.

Meanwhile temperature and food keep renewing the body without asking the mind. The fire element in every group of matter gives rise to new groups, and the nutritive essence of food does the same.

Nine ways they meet

The model below draws nine of these relations as moving threads. On the left is mind, a single citta with its factors circling it; on the right, a body drawn as a cloud of tiny groups of matter, with the heart-base and the eye inside it. Around them are the outside sources: a visible object, past kamma, temperature and food.

  1. Heart-base supports mind(matter → mind; every moment of life, in worlds with matter). Every citta except the ten sense consciousnesses rests on the heart-base, a piece of matter that arose before it and is still present. The Paṭṭhāna names it only as “the matter in dependence on which the mind-element and mind-consciousness element occur”; the commentaries identify it with the heart.Conditions: support, prenascence, dissociation, presence, non-disappearance.
  2. A sense organ supports its consciousness(matter → mind; whenever a five-door process occurs). Eye-sensitivity, already arisen and still present, is the base of eye-consciousness and governs it as a faculty. The same holds for ear, nose, tongue and body. Seeing depends on the eye; it is not produced by it.Conditions: support, prenascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, non-disappearance.
  3. Matter as object(matter → mind; whenever matter is known). The mango's colour is a piece of matter in its presence phase. It strikes the eye door and becomes the object of the whole process of seventeen mind-moments. At the mind door, any of the 28 kinds of matter can be an object, past, present or future.Conditions: object, prenascence, presence, non-disappearance, object predominance or object decisive support, when the object is esteemed.
  4. Mind produces matter(mind → matter; from the first life-continuum after conception until death). Seventy-five of the 89 cittas produce matter at their arising sub-moment: posture, gestures, speech, a smile. The factors of that citta, its roots, its volition, its jhāna and path factors, and, if it is a resultant, its being a result, support the same matter. Intimation, the matter of a gesture or a word, lasts only as long as the citta that makes it.Conditions: conascence, support, dissociation, presence, non-disappearance, root, predominance, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path.
  5. Later mind sustains earlier body(mind → matter; throughout life). A citta supports the bodily matter that arose before it and is still present. It is the one condition in which what is conditioned is older than its condition.Conditions: postnascence, dissociation, presence, non-disappearance.
  6. Past volition builds the body(mind → matter; from conception until seventeen mind-moments before death). Volition from a past life produces the eye, ear, nose, tongue and body sensitivities, sex, the heart-base and the life faculty, with their eight inseparables. It does so at every sub-moment, from rebirth-linking until seventeen mind-moments before the death consciousness.Conditions: kamma, asynchronous kamma, from a past life.
  7. At conception, they arise together(mind ⇄ matter; only at rebirth-linking). For a being born from a womb, the resultant rebirth-linking citta arises together with three groups of kamma-born matter, the body, sex and heart-base decads (some beings lack the sex decad). The mental aggregates and the heart-base support each other. It is the only moment in a life when mind and matter condition each other mutually. As with any citta that has matter arising with it, the citta's volition, nutriments, faculties and jhāna factors, and its roots and path factors if it has roots, also help the kamma-born matter arising with it.Conditions: conascence, mutuality, support, result, dissociation, presence, non-disappearance, root, kamma, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path.
  8. Food sustains the body(matter → matter; whenever food is absorbed). Edible food conditions the body as nutriment, and its nutritive essence produces new matter in its presence phase. The mind has nutriments too: contact, volition and consciousness nourish the mind and matter that arise with them.Conditions: nutriment, presence, non-disappearance.
  9. Heat keeps matter renewing(matter → matter; from conception, through life, and after death). The fire element in each group of matter, in its presence phase, gives rise to new groups. This begins at the presence phase of rebirth-linking and continues all life. It is the only origin that outlasts death: the matter of a corpse is temperature-born.Conditions: temperature, the fourth origin of matter, not one of the 24 conditions.

Each relation is made of several of the Paṭṭhāna’s twenty-four kinds of condition working at once (they are introduced in The web of twenty-four conditions). The heart-base, for instance, helps a citta in five ways at once: as its base (support), by having arisen before it (prenascence), as matter helping mind (dissociation), and by being present and not yet gone (presence, non-disappearance). Choose a relation to see which.

Who supports whom

Seen from the other side, the Paṭṭhāna’s twenty-four conditions can be sorted by which way they run. Here is every condition that crosses between mind and matter, or runs within matter, with what it means in that direction.

Matter → mind · 11

  • 2. object A visible form is the object of eye-consciousness, a sound of ear-consciousness; any matter can be the object of mind-consciousness.
  • 3. predominance Object predominance: an object esteemed highly, such as a cherished possession, dominates the mind that takes it. A mental state, or Nibbāna, can do the same.
  • 6. conascence At rebirth, the heart-base and the rebirth-linking citta arise together and help each other.
  • 7. mutuality At rebirth the heart-base supports the rebirth-linking citta and its factors, and is supported by them in return.
  • 8. support The eye-base supports eye-consciousness, and so on for the five senses; the heart-base supports the other cittas.
  • 9. decisive support Climate, food and lodging can decisively support good or bad states of mind.
  • 10. prenascence The six bases, arisen earlier and still standing, support the cittas that depend on them; an object already arisen supports the consciousness that knows it.
  • 16. faculty The five sense faculties, eye and the rest, govern the five kinds of sense consciousness.
  • 20. dissociation The bases help the cittas that depend on them, across the divide of mind and matter.
  • 21. presence Present bases and objects support the cittas that depend on them.
  • 24. non-disappearance Bases and objects, while they last, support the cittas that depend on them.

Mind → matter · 15

  • 1. root The roots also support the matter their citta produces, and, at rebirth, the kamma-born matter arising with it.
  • 3. predominance A conascent predominant also leads the matter produced by its citta.
  • 6. conascence A citta helps the matter that arises with it: mind-born matter in the course of life, kamma-born matter at rebirth.
  • 7. mutuality At rebirth the rebirth-linking citta and its factors support the heart-base, as it supports them.
  • 8. support A citta supports the matter that arises with it.
  • 11. postnascence A later citta sustains the body that arose before it; the Manual's Guide compares it to later rain helping plants already grown (Guide to VIII §15), the Visuddhimagga to young vultures kept going by their longing for food (Vism XVII §604).
  • 13. kamma Past volition also produces kamma-born matter, from rebirth onwards; present volition supports the matter its citta produces.
  • 14. result Resultant cittas also support the matter arising with them, such as kamma-born matter at rebirth.
  • 15. nutriment The mental nutriments also sustain the matter that arises with them.
  • 16. faculty The mental faculties also govern the matter that their citta produces.
  • 17. jhāna The jhāna factors also support the matter that their citta produces.
  • 18. path The path factors also support the matter that their citta produces.
  • 20. dissociation Mind helps matter, a different kind of thing: the matter its citta produces, and, later, the body arisen earlier.
  • 21. presence Present cittas sustain matter, both what arises with them and the body arisen earlier.
  • 24. non-disappearance Cittas that have not disappeared sustain matter.

Matter → matter · 7

  • 6. conascence The four great elements arise together and help each other and the derived matter arising with them.
  • 7. mutuality The four great elements support one another, each by the others.
  • 8. support The great elements are the support of all derived matter.
  • 15. nutriment Edible food nourishes this body.
  • 16. faculty The physical life faculty sustains the kamma-born matter it is part of. The two sex faculties are not faculty conditions: they shape the body but do none of a condition's three works, producing, supporting or maintaining (Guide to VIII §24; Vism XVII §609).
  • 21. presence Present great elements, food and the life faculty sustain matter.
  • 24. non-disappearance Great elements, food and life faculty, while they last, sustain matter.

Mind → mind · 21

  • 1. root The roots, such as greed or non-greed, make firm the citta and the factors they arise with.
  • 2. object Any citta or factor, past, present or future, can be the object of a later citta, as when one recollects.
  • 3. predominance Conascent predominance: desire, energy, consciousness or investigation leads the citta and factors it arises with; only one at a time, and only in javanas with two or three roots.
  • 4. proximity Each citta, as it ceases, conditions the very next one: the life-continuum gives way to adverting, adverting to seeing, and so on.
  • 5. contiguity The same relation stressed as seamless: no gap between one citta and the next.
  • 6. conascence A citta and its factors arise together and help one another to arise.
  • 7. mutuality A citta and its factors hold each other up, like the three sticks of a tripod.
  • 8. support A citta and its factors are each other's support, as the earth supports trees.
  • 9. decisive support Faith, a past resolve, or a habit of anger strongly supports later states; each citta also strongly supports the next.
  • 12. repetition Each mundane javana repeats and strengthens the next of its kind, like a lesson made firm by practice. A path citta does not, since a fruition follows it, not another path.
  • 13. kamma Volition coordinates the citta and factors it arises with; past volition, ripening later, produces resultant cittas.
  • 14. result Resultant cittas and factors, arising without effort, support one another.
  • 15. nutriment The three mental nutriments, contact, volition and consciousness, sustain the mind they arise with.
  • 16. faculty The mental faculties, such as mindfulness and wisdom, each govern their own domain in the citta.
  • 17. jhāna The jhāna factors, such as initial application and one-pointedness, fix the citta closely on its object: in every citta but the ten sense consciousnesses.
  • 18. path The path factors, right or wrong, lead the mind in their direction: in every citta but the eighteen rootless ones.
  • 19. association A citta and its factors are associated: they arise and cease together, with one object and one base.
  • 21. presence A citta and its factors help each other by being present together.
  • 22. absence A citta helps the next by ceasing: its absence gives the next room to arise.
  • 23. disappearance The same as absence, seen from the side of disappearing.
  • 24. non-disappearance The same as presence, seen from the side of not disappearing: a citta and its factors, while they last.

The same ways are drawn as strands in the 3D model of the 24 conditions.

Notice how much more traffic runs from mind to matter than the reverse. Matter helps mind mainly by being there first, as base and object. Mind helps matter in many ways at once, through its roots, its volition, its jhāna and path factors, its nutriments and faculties. And only once in a life do the two hold each other up as equals: at conception, when the rebirth-linking citta and the heart-base arise together, each the mutual support of the other.

Where they meet: the six doors

Every kind of knowing needs an object, a door it comes through, and a base it rests on. At five of the six doors, everything but the knowing is matter. The eye-door is the eye-sensitivity, its object is colour, its base is the same eye-sensitivity, and its consciousness is eye-consciousness. The mind-door is different: its door is a citta, the life-continuum, though the mind still rests on the heart-base. The six doors are drawn in The All, counted twice.

Matter in time

Mind and matter do not keep the same time. A citta lasts one mind-moment, with three sub-moments: arising, presence and dissolution. A unit of matter lasts seventeen mind-moments, fifty-one sub-moments. That is why a sense object that strikes a door lasts exactly long enough for one complete process, the seventeen moments traced in The mango and the moment.

It also means that at any instant, dozens of generations of matter are alive in the body at once. In the model below, each bar is one unit of matter from its arising to its ceasing, in four lanes for its four origins; the row of discs is the stream of cittas.

An interactive 3D model goes here on the site: /explore/3d/#D3.

Kamma makes new matter at every sub-moment; a citta makes matter at its arising. Kamma-born matter stops arising seventeen mind-moments before death, so that it ends together with the death consciousness. Temperature-born matter alone outlasts death: the matter of a corpse is temperature-born.

The smallest groups of matter

Matter never arises alone. It comes in small groups, kalāpakalāpa the smallest group of matter: eight or more kinds arising and ceasing togethers, built on the same core: the four great elements and the four kinds of matter that always go with them, colour, smell, taste and nutritive essence. These eight are called the inseparables. Kamma, mind, temperature and nutriment each add their own members. The model shows the twenty-one groups, with the eight inseparables at the corners of a cube.

An interactive 3D model goes here on the site: /explore/3d/#D2.

The four great elements hold up all the rest. The Visuddhimagga defines each by what it is, what it does and how it shows itself:

ElementCharacteristicFunctionManifestation
pathavī, earthhardnessto act as a foundationreceiving
āpo, watertrickling, cohesionto intensifyholding together
tejo, fireheatto maturea continued supply of softness
vāyo, airdistensionto cause motionconveying

The body, the Visuddhimagga says, is founded on earth, held together by water, maintained by fire and distended by air. Of the four, only water cannot be touched, which is why the tangible object is the other three: hardness or softness, heat or cold, pressure or motion.

Inside the mind side

On the side of mind the unit is a citta with its factors. A factor arises with its citta, ceases with it, takes the same object and rests on the same base. The citta is the knowing; the factors colour it. Choose a citta to see which factors make it up.

An interactive 3D model goes here on the site: /explore/3d/#D2.

Mind makes matter

Not every citta can produce matter, and those that can do different things with it. The ten kinds of sense consciousness are too weak; the four immaterial resultants arise where there is no matter. A smaller set can move the body and the voice, and a smaller set again can make a smile.

Not every world has both

Which bases a being has depends on its plane. In the immaterial worlds there is mind with no matter at all, and the citta needs no base. Among the non-percipient beings there is matter with no mind. Everywhere else the two currents run together, and the groups of matter present at the moment of rebirth-linking differ by plane.

Why this matters

For practice, all of this comes down to one first step. The Visuddhimagga makes the discerning of mind and matter, nāmarūpa-paricchedanāmarūpa-pariccheda · defining mind and matter discerning mind and matter as they are, without a self; the purification of view, first of the insight knowledges, the purification of view: the first knowledge of insight, on which the rest are built (see The tree of purification). To see a moment of hearing as sound, ear and the hearing, and nothing over and above them, is the beginning of seeing that there is no one behind the hearing. The model on this page is a map of what such seeing finds.

To reflect on. Sit still for a minute and notice one moment of seeing, or of hearing. What in it is matter, and what is mind? Where exactly do they meet?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, VI §§2–32 (matter, its origins, groups and occurrence) and VIII §§11–28 (the conditions). Visuddhimagga XI (the four elements), XIV (the aggregate of matter), XVIII (purification of view: defining mind and matter). SN 12.2, Vibhaṅga Sutta: name-and-form in the suttas; Dhammasaṅgaṇī, the pair nāma and rūpa. Y. Karunadasa, The Theravāda Abhidhamma (2010), on the heart-base and on matter.

Names and the named

If a chariot is only a name, what is a name? The Manual's last word on what there is: concepts, the things they make known, and the six ways of naming, from "feeling" to "king's son".

A chariot of parts takes the chariot away and leaves its parts. But the word “chariot” did not vanish. People still say it, understand it, and steer by it. The Manual waits until the end of its chapter on conditions to say what such words and their meanings are (VIII §§29–32). Having counted every reality, it turns to what is left over.

What is left over

The realities fall into two classes. Matter is one: the twenty-eight kinds, a single aggregate. The other is called nāma, name, or the immaterial: citta and the mental factors, which make up the four mental aggregates, and Nibbāna. The Guide explains the word. Mind is nāma because it bends toward its object; Nibbāna is nāma only because it makes something else bend, drawing the cittas of awakening, called path and fruition, onto itself as their object.

Everything else that the mind can take up is paññattipaññatti · concept a concept: a name, or what a name refers to, such as “chariot”, concept. A concept has no nature of its own, and yet the mind meets concepts constantly: in every word, every plan, every person thought of.

Two sides of a concept

Every concept has two sides (§29). One is what is made known, the meaning: attha-paññattiattha-paññatti · meaning-concept a concept as what is made known: the meaning a name conveys, such as the idea of a chariot. The other is what makes it known, the name: nāma-paññattināma-paññatti · name-concept a concept as what makes known: the name or designation itself, the word “chariot”. The Guide’s example is a dog. The idea of a four-legged, furry, domestic animal of a certain kind is the meaning; the word “dog” is the name that calls it up.

What is made known

The Manual lists the meanings by what each is built on (§30):

  • land, mountain, built on the elements in their changing shapes; the Guide calls these formal concepts;
  • house, chariot, built on materials put together: collective concepts;
  • person, individual, built on the five aggregates;
  • east, morning, month, built on the course of the moon and sun: concepts of place and of time;
  • well, cave, built on a place where nothing strikes: concepts of space;
  • the kasiṇa sign, the image that arises in meditation on a device such as a coloured disk, built on an element and on the work of meditation.

None of these exists in the ultimate sense. The Manual’s image is that they reach the mind as shadows of real things: real enough to be objects of consciousness, never real enough to be found when looked for.

What makes known

Names come in six kinds (§31). Two are simple: a name for something real, as “matter” or “feeling”; and a name for something unreal, as “land” or “mountain”. The other four are compounds that name one thing by means of another, real or unreal. The Manual gives one example of each:

  • “possessor of six direct knowledges”: the knowledges are real, the possessor is not;
  • “woman’s voice”: the sound is real, the woman, as a whole, is not;
  • “eye-consciousness”: both the eye-sensitivity and the consciousness that depends on it are real;
  • “king’s son”: neither the king nor the son is real in the ultimate sense.

The grid is less a puzzle than a habit worth learning. Ordinary speech mixes the two registers in nearly every phrase, and the mix is where the trouble starts: a real feeling, named through an unreal owner, seems to belong to someone.

How a word is understood

The chapter ends with how a name works at all (§32). A spoken word is a sound, and it is first known like any other sound, by a run of cittas at the ear. Then further runs of cittas follow at the mind alone. They take up the concept the sound stands for, and only then is the meaning understood. Concepts, the Manual says, are made by the world’s agreement.So the same sound can carry different concepts in different languages, or none, to someone who does not know the language. The sound is real; the meaning rides on convention.

Why the Abhidhamma bothers

Concepts are not dismissed. They are real objects of real cittas. The kasiṇa sign is the object of the fine-material jhānas, and beings are the object of loving-kindness (see Feeling, roots and objects). A person remembered can inspire faith years later; the Paṭṭhāna counts that as a strong form of support, called decisive support (VIII Table 8.3). What concepts cannot be is a base or an element: those lists hold only things with a nature of their own (VII §36).

So the two truths are not two worlds. There is one world of realities, and over it a net of names that lets beings speak, plan and practise. Insight does not tear the net. It looks through it to the realities it was laid over.

To reflect on. "Woman's voice" names something real by means of something that is not. Pick a sentence you said today and sort its words: which name realities, which name constructions, and which do both at once?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, VIII §§29–32 with the Guide; VII §36 (concepts and the bases); VIII Table 8.3 (concepts as decisive support). Puggalapaññatti, the Abhidhamma book of concepts of persons. SN 5.10, the nun Vajirā's chariot; Milindapañha II.1.

Nibbāna, the unconditioned

The fourth ultimate reality, the one the analysis does not take apart: what the suttas and the Manual say it is, why the commentaries deny that it is mere absence, and which few moments of mind ever take it as their object.

Manual VI §§30–32 with the Guide (Nibbāna: definition, analysis, summary)

The analysis so far has taken things apart: a person into mind and matter, and what was left over into names. One ultimate reality remains that it does not take apart, because it has no parts and no conditions: nibbānanibbāna the unconditioned: the ending of craving; object of path and fruition. The Manual gives it three short paragraphs at the end of the chapter on matter (VI §§30–32). This reading opens them out, with the suttas behind them and the commentaries that argued over them.

One, and unmade

In the Udāna the Buddha describes a sphere in which there is no earth, water, fire or air, none of the formless spheres, neither this world nor another; no coming or going, no arising or passing away; without support, not continuing; and that, he says, is the end of suffering (Ud 8.1). A little later comes the passage most quoted: there is something not born, not become, not made, not conditioned; if there were not, no escape from what is born, become, made and conditioned would be known (Ud 8.3, repeated in It 43). The Itivuttaka’s verse adds that it is peaceful, stable, and beyond the reach of reasoning.

Elsewhere the definition is short. Asked what Nibbāna is, Sāriputta answers: the destruction of greed, of hatred, of delusion (SN 38.1). A whole collection of short suttas asks what the unconditioned is and gives the same answer, then repeats it under thirty-two other names: the far shore, the island, the refuge, the deathless, the peaceful, the subtle, and more (SN 43).

The Abhidhamma takes all of this as one thing. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī, sorting every dhamma into the conditioned and the unconditioned, puts on the second side a single entry, the unconditioned element, asaṅkhata-dhātuasaṅkhata-dhātu · unconditioned element Nibbāna, the one element not made by conditions (Dhs §§1090, 1092). It is indeterminate, neither wholesome nor unwholesome (Dhs §583). The Manual states it in a line: Nibbāna is supramundane, to be realised by the knowledge of the four paths, and the object of paths and fruits (VI §30). Of the four ultimate realities it is the only one not made by conditions; citta, its factors and matter all are (Guide to I §2).

The word itself has two explanations. Its plain sense is a fire going out, the fires of greed, hatred and delusion. The Manual gives another, which the commentators prefer: Nibbāna is a departure (nikkhanta) from craving, which entangles (vāna) and binds one life to the next (VI §30 with the Guide).

What it is like, if it is like anything

The commentaries describe every dhamma by four marks: characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause. For Nibbāna the Visuddhimagga gives the first three and names no proximate cause; nothing causes it. Its characteristic is peace, santisanti · peace peace; the characteristic of Nibbāna (Vism XVI §556). Its function is not to pass away, or, in a second reading, to comfort. It shows itself as the signless, or as freedom from proliferation, nippapañcanippapañca · non-proliferation freedom from proliferation, the spreading out of craving, conceit and views (the commentaries' gloss); a manifestation of Nibbāna (Vism XVI §556) and a sutta name of it (SN 43.23) (Vism XVI §556).

The Manual’s closing verse gathers its names: a footing (pada), not passing away (accuta), endless, unconditioned, unsurpassed (VI §32). Most are negations.

Two elements, one Nibbāna

The Itivuttaka speaks of two Nibbāna elements (It 44). One is the element with residue, sa-upādisesasa-upādisesa · with residue the Nibbāna element with residue: the defilements ended while an arahant's aggregates remain (It 44; VI §31): in a living arahant, greed, hatred and delusion are destroyed, yet the five faculties remain, and he still meets the agreeable and the disagreeable. The other is the element without residue, anupādisesaanupādisesa · without residue the Nibbāna element without residue: named by the absence of aggregates after an arahant's last citta (It 44; VI §31 with the Guide; Vism XVI §561): for that same arahant, everything felt, no longer delighted in, will grow cool right here. The verse calls the first visible in this life and the second what comes after, where all becoming stops.

The Manual keeps the two but insists they are one thing seen two ways. By its own nature Nibbāna is single; it is twofold only by way of a ground for naming it (kāraṇapariyāyena, VI §31). The basis, the Guide explains, is whether the aggregates are still there. The Visuddhimagga says the same: the element with residue is named by reference to the residue still present, and the element without residue by reference to its absence once the last citta has passed (Vism XVI §561). Nibbāna does not change when an arahant dies; only the aggregates to name it by are gone.

Three names, and three doors

By aspect, the Manual says, Nibbāna is threefold: void, suññatasuññata · void void; an aspect of Nibbāna itself (VI §31), and, with signless and desireless, one of the three emancipations named after the insight that leads to the path, signless, animittaanimitta · signless without sign; an aspect of Nibbāna (VI §31), and the emancipation reached through the contemplation of impermanence, and desireless, appaṇihitaappaṇihita · desireless without hankering; an aspect of Nibbāna (VI §31), and the emancipation reached through the contemplation of suffering (VI §31). The Vibhāvinī gives two reasons for each name. Nibbāna is empty of greed, hatred and delusion, has none of their marks and none of their longing; and, read more widely, it is empty of every formation, bears none of their marks, and is nothing craving can long for (Vibhāvinī, ch. 6, CS §64; Guide to VI §31).

The same three words return in the chapter on insight with a different job, and the two uses are easy to blur. There they name doors: ways of contemplating the conditioned that lead out of it. Contemplating non-self is the door of the void, impermanence the door of the signless, suffering the door of the desireless (IX §35). A path is named after the door by which it was reached (IX §36). But by its object and its own quality every path and every fruition has all three names, because the Nibbāna they take is void, signless and desireless at once (IX §37 with the Guide). The doors are three; what they open on is one. Ten knowledges follows the doors further.

Not nothing, and not mere ending

Perhaps Nibbāna is just the absence of everything conditioned. The Visuddhimagga answers this in a short debate, the tradition’s main defence of Nibbāna as a reality (Vism XVI §§557–561).

It cannot be found, says the objector, like the horn of a hare. It can, comes the reply, by the right means, the practice that fits it, just as another person’s supramundane mind is found by the knowledge that reads minds. What the foolish cannot find is not therefore absent (§557). If it did not exist, right practice would bear no fruit (§558). Nor is it the absence of the aggregates. Past and future aggregates are already absent, yet that is not Nibbāna; present ones cannot simply be absent; and the element with residue is reached while the aggregates are present (§558).

Then the strongest objection: the sutta itself calls Nibbāna the destruction of greed, hatred and delusion. The reply is that arahantship is described with the same words (SN 38.2), and arahantship is not mere destruction either. Worse, a destruction is an event. If Nibbāna were one, it would last only a while, would bear the mark of the conditioned, and could be reached without right effort. The path, which does the destroying, would itself be Nibbāna. The sutta’s word is therefore a figure: Nibbāna is called destruction because it is the decisive support for the destruction, the ceasing by which defilements never arise again (§559). Last, the path reaches Nibbāna but does not make it. What the path does not make has no origin, and what has no origin does not age or die (§560).

Later manuals add an argument from the mind that knows it. Buddhadatta’s Abhidhammāvatāra asks what change-of-lineage, cleansing and the path would take as object if Nibbāna were the destruction of defilements. At change-of-lineage they are yet to be destroyed; at the path they are being destroyed; only at fruition have they been destroyed. On that view only fruition would have an object (Abhidhammāvatāra, ch. 11, after v. 770). The Vibhāvinī, the standard commentary on the Manual, puts the point as an inference. Knowledge that takes conditioned things or concepts as object cannot cut off defilements; yet defilements are cut off; so there is a dhamma unlike both, the object of paths and fruits, and that is Nibbāna (Vibhāvinī on VI §30).

The Milindapañha makes the same case by simile. Space and Nibbāna, Nāgasena says, are the two things not born of kamma, of a cause or of season. A path to realise Nibbāna can be taught, but no cause to produce it, as a man can walk to the Himalaya but cannot carry it home. And it exists though it cannot be shown, like the wind, which no one can show by colour or shape (Milindapañha, Akammajādipañha).Where teachers differ. How many unconditioneds? The Theravāda counts one. The Kathāvatthu rejects those who would add others, among them space, dependent arising, the attainment of cessation and two kinds of cessation: a second unconditioned would mean two deathless refuges with a boundary between them (Kv II.11, VI.1–6, XIX.3–5). It names no school; its commentary does. Another school entirely, the Sarvāstivāda, counted three unconditioned dharmas: space, cessation through discernment, which is nirvāṇa, and cessation without discernment, the mere non-arising of what lacks its conditions. Destruction itself, or what destruction depends on? SN 38.1 says plainly that Nibbāna is the destruction of greed, hatred and delusion; the Visuddhimagga reads this as a figure (Vism XVI §559). Read literally, the sutta would make Nibbāna the extinction of the fires in a living person, a state of a life, not a further element. The commentaries’ answer is the debate above. The Udāna’s “without object” (anārammaṇa, Ud 8.1) is read in a similar split: its commentary takes it to mean that, unlike feeling and the other mental states, Nibbāna takes no object (Udāna commentary, CS §71; so too Kv XIX.6). Read the other way, as “not an object for the mind”, it would contradict the Abhidhamma, for which Nibbāna is the object of path and fruit.

Outside time, outside the aggregates

Every conditioned dhamma has a moment of arising, a moment of standing and a moment of passing. Nibbāna has none of these, and so it is not past, present or future. The Manual allows mind-door cittas objects that are free of time (kālavimutta, III §17), and the Guide names them: Nibbāna and concepts. Nibbāna stands outside time because what it is has no arising, change or ceasing; a concept stands outside time because it has no nature of its own to arise (Guide to III §17).

For the same reason it stands outside the five aggregates, which are sorted as past, present and future, near and far, and the rest (VII §40). Among the twelve bases it belongs to the base of mental objects (VII §39). It is not a place: the Milindapañha says there is no spot where it is stored (Nibbānasannihitapañha). And it is not a consciousness, for it is not citta.

The moments that take it

Most cittas can never take Nibbāna as object: not the unwholesome, not the beautiful sense-sphere cittas without knowledge, for which it is too pure and too deep (III §18 with the Guide), not the sublime cittas of the jhānas (Table 3.5), and not insight, which comprehends only the formations of the three planes (IX §32). The moments that can are few (the Manual’s rule for the direct knowledges, III §18, would add them; the Visuddhimagga’s list of their objects, XIII §§416–419, does not), and each has its place in a process.

Change-of-lineage, gotrabhūgotrabhū · change-of-lineage the javana that leaves the sense-sphere lineage for jhāna, or turns to Nibbāna, is the first. It is a sense-sphere wholesome citta with knowledge, at the end of the insight before the first path (Guide to III §18). It is the first moment to advert to Nibbāna, and it removes nothing (IX §34 with the Guide). Before the three higher paths the same moment is called cleansing, vodānavodāna · cleansing the name of the change-of-lineage javana in the processes of the three higher paths, because the person already belongs to the noble lineage.

The four paths and four fruitions come next: the supramundane cittas, whose only object is Nibbāna (III §18; VI §30). Counted by jhāna, they are forty (I §§30–32).

Reviewing, paccavekkhaṇapaccavekkhaṇa · reviewing after attainment, knowledge looking back on path, fruition and Nibbāna, and usually, not always, on the defilements abandoned and those that remain, follows each path, in ordinary mind-door processes. The disciple reviews the path, the fruition and Nibbāna, and usually the defilements abandoned and those that remain (IX §34 with the Guide). Each process opens with mind-door adverting and runs on sense-sphere javanas with knowledge: wholesome ones for trainees, functional ones for the arahant (Guide to III §18). The Paṭṭhāna names each of these moments as taking Nibbāna as object (Paṭṭhāna, Kusalattika, question chapter, CS §§410–411).

Last, the attainment of fruition, phalasamāpattiphalasamāpatti · attainment of fruition a noble one's absorption in their own fruition, with Nibbāna as object, in which a noble person enters his own fruition again, with Nibbāna as object, to dwell in the happiness of Nibbāna in this very life (IX §42 with the Guide). Here no change-of-lineage comes before the fruition: the moments just before it are conformity, still taking formations, and the Visuddhimagga says that in this process “change-of-lineage” is to be understood as conformity (Vism XXIII §§863, 866). The process of the path is described in Other processes, and who reaches which fruition in Four noble persons.

What about everyone else? The Vibhāvinī draws the line. That Nibbāna is to be realised by the four paths shows it is known by direct perception to the noble ones, each at their level; that it is the object of paths and fruits shows that the good worldling, who has not reached a path, can establish it only by inference, by the argument given above (Vibhāvinī on VI §30). A worldling can still think about Nibbāna, but outside change-of-lineage that thought cannot have Nibbāna itself as its object; presumably it takes the idea of it. That is our inference from III §18 and its Guide, not something the Manual says.

What it gives

Nibbāna is a condition, and never conditioned (Guide to VIII §1). It produces nothing, as a seed produces a sprout; it conditions only by being taken as object, in three forms. It is an object condition for every citta that takes it (VIII §17). For the cittas that take it with weight, those of change-of-lineage and cleansing, path, fruition and reviewing, it is also object predominance, ārammaṇādhipatiadhipati · predominance the one factor leading a citta: desire, energy, citta or investigation; or, as object predominance, an object held in high regard, the object that dominates the mind attending to it (VIII §19), and object decisive support, the object that, prominent, gives strong support to the mind that takes it (VIII §17; Table 8.3). Mind-door adverting takes it only as plain object (Paṭṭhāna CS §§410, 416). It is not prenascent like a visible form, nor a natural decisive support like past faith (Table 8.3).

This is also why the Abhidhamma counts Nibbāna as nāma, though it is no mind. Citta and its factors are nāma because they bend toward an object; Nibbāna is nāma only because it makes the supramundane cittas bend toward itself, as their predominant object (Guide to VIII §29).

The Manual’s account ends there. It says what Nibbāna is, how it differs from everything else, and which minds can know it; it does not describe what it is like to know it, and makes no promise about who will. How insight ripens toward it is the subject of The tree of purification.

To reflect on. The suttas say that Nibbāna is the destruction of greed, hatred and delusion; the Visuddhimagga says that this is a figure of speech, and that Nibbāna is rather that on account of which they are destroyed. What would be lost if the sutta phrase were taken literally?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, VI §§30–32 with the Guide; I §§30–32 (the forty supramundane cittas); III §§17–18 with the Guide and Table 3.5; VII §§39–40 (the mental-object base; Nibbāna outside the aggregates); VIII §§17, 19 with the Guide, §29 with the Guide, and Table 8.3; IX §§32, 34–37 and 42 with the Guide. Visuddhimagga XVI §§556–561 (characteristic, function and manifestation; the discussion of Nibbāna), XXIII §§863, 866 (conformity before fruition in the attainment of fruition). Paragraph numbers are those of the Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana edition. Udāna 8.1 and 8.3 (SuttaCentral ud8.1; ud8.3); Itivuttaka 43 and 44 (iti43; iti44). SN 38.1 and 38.2 (SuttaCentral sn38.1; sn38.2); SN 43, the connected discourses on the unconditioned, with its names of Nibbāna (sn43.12; sn43.14–43). Dhammasaṅgaṇī CS §§1090, 1092 (the one unconditioned element) and §583 (it is indeterminate); Paṭṭhāna, Kusalattika, question chapter (pañhāvāra), CS §§410–411 (object), §416 (object predominance), §423 (object decisive support). Buddhadatta, Abhidhammāvatāra, ch. 11, the section on Nibbāna, prose after v. 770 (what change-of-lineage and the path would take as object if Nibbāna were destruction). Sumaṅgala, Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī on CMA VI §30 (CS §62): known directly by noble ones, by inference by good worldlings. Milindapañha, Akammajādipañha (neither produced by kamma, cause or season; the path to realise it can be taught, no cause to produce it; the wind simile) and Nibbānasannihitapañha (no place where it is stored). The commentary on the Udāna, on Ud 8.1, CS §71: anārammaṇa read as "taking no object" (commentarial); so too Kathāvatthu XIX.6. Kathāvatthu II.11, VI.1–6, XIX.3–5 (debates on further unconditioneds; the schools are named only in the commentary).

The commentators' picture-book

A heap of coins, a struck bell, a bird gliding: how the old teachers made a list of dhammas memorable, and what each picture is pointing at.

Manual II guide (each factor's characteristic, function, manifestation, proximate cause)

The canonical Abhidhamma gives lists and definitions. It rarely gives pictures. The pictures came later, from the commentators, who had to teach the lists to people who had to remember them. Their similes are some of the best teaching tools in Buddhist literature, and they share a discipline worth learning: each is chosen to show one property, and only one.

Four questions for every dhamma

First, the method behind the pictures. The commentaries describe each dhamma by four questions. What is its characteristic, lakkhaṇalakkhaṇa · characteristic a dhamma's own nature: the first part of its identity card, the mark by which it is known? What is its function, rasarasa · function (of a dhamma) what a dhamma does: the second part of its identity card, what it does? What is its manifestation, paccupaṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhāna · manifestation how a dhamma shows itself in experience: the third part of its card, how it shows up in experience? And what is its proximate cause, padaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhāna · proximate cause what a dhamma most directly depends on: the fourth part of its card, the condition it most immediately depends on?Applied to contact: its characteristic is touching, its function is the impact of mind and object, its manifestation is their coming together, and its proximate cause is the object that has come into range.

A simile usually illustrates one of the four. It makes a definition visible.

Three people and a heap of coins

A child, a villager and a money-changer look at the same heap of coins. The child sees shapes and colours, bright and round, but does not know they are money. The villager knows they are money and that they can be spent. The money-changer knows which coins are genuine and which are false, where each was struck and what it weighs.

The Visuddhimagga uses the picture to separate three things that are easily confused. Perception, saññāsaññā · perception perception: marks an object's features so it can be recognised again, is the child: it notes surface features so they can be recognised again. Consciousness, viññāṇaviññāṇa · consciousness (aggregate) consciousness, the fifth aggregate: all 89 cittas, the same reality as citta, is the villager: it knows the object as an object. Understanding, paññāpaññā · wisdom understanding things as they are; also called non-delusion and the faculty of wisdom, is the money-changer: it penetrates the object’s real nature.

It is a picture of depth, not of separate people. All three can be present in a single moment: in a citta that has understanding, perception and consciousness are there too.

A struck bell, a gliding bird

Two of the occasional factors, those found in some cittas but not all, are hard to tell apart: vitakkavitakka · initial application lays the mind onto its object; a factor of the first jhāna only, initial application, and vicāravicāra · sustained application keeps the mind moving over its object; a factor of the first two jhānas, sustained application. The commentaries offer several pictures. Initial application is like striking a bell; sustained application is the bell’s resonance. Initial application is like a bird spreading its wings to take off; sustained application is the bird gliding on outstretched wings. Initial application is like a bee diving toward a flower; sustained application is the bee buzzing above it.The images come from the Visuddhimagga IV and the Milindapañha. L. S. Cousins’s study of the two terms shows how much their meaning shifts between the suttas and the Abhidhamma.

Each picture adds a nuance. The bell shows that sustaining follows striking. The bird shows that the first is effortful and the second smooth. The bee shows that one goes toward the object and the other stays near it. Together they say what a definition struggles to: that these are two phases of one act of attending.

What a simile hides

Every picture can also mislead. The child, the villager and the money-changer are three people, and the factors they illustrate are not people. A bell rings on after it is struck, and a dhamma does not linger after its moment. The commentators knew this, which is why they used several similes for one factor and dropped each one quickly.

That is the reader’s discipline too. Ask what a picture is pointing at, take that, and leave the rest. The Buddha called his teaching a raft, for crossing over and not for carrying (MN 22). A simile is a small raft of the same kind: use it to reach a dhamma that lasts a single moment, then put it down.

To reflect on. Choose a simile you rely on for your own mind, a river, a monkey, a mirror. Which single property is it pointing at, and which does it hide?

Sources. Visuddhimagga IV and XIV: the coins, the bell, the bird. Milindapañha II: Nāgasena's similes for the mental factors. Atthasālinī, on the factors of the first wholesome citta. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, II, the guide's definitions. MN 22, Alagaddūpama Sutta: the simile of the raft.

How it unfolds

The mango and the moment

A man asleep under a mango tree, a fruit that falls, and the seventeen moments in which seeing happens and kamma is made.

Manual IV §§1–11 (six kinds of process, the five-door process and intensity of objects)

A man is asleep at the foot of a mango tree with his head covered. A breeze moves the branches and a ripe mango falls beside his head. He wakes at the sound, uncovers his face and sees the fruit. He reaches out and picks it up, squeezes it to test it, and smells it. Then he eats it.

That is the whole story. Buddhaghosa tells it in the Atthasālinī to explain something that takes far less time than the story does: one act of seeing.The simile is commentarial, not canonical. The suttas describe the same ground more loosely: eye and form give rise to eye-consciousness, the three together are contact, and contact conditions feeling (MN 18). In the Abhidhamma’s account a single sight is a process, a vīthivīthi · cognitive process a fixed series of cittas taking one object at one door of seventeen mind-moments, each a citta with its own job. The man and his mango are a way of keeping them in order.

Asleep

Before anything happens, the man is asleep, and the mind is not doing nothing. It runs as the bhavaṅgabhavaṅga · life-continuum the resultant citta, of the same kind as rebirth-linking, that runs between processes, the life-continuum: a stream of identical resultant cittas that keeps a life going whenever no process is active. It is the same kind of citta that linked this life to the last, and it holds the same object it held then. It knows nothing of the mango tree.

Three moments of this stream belong to our process. In the first, the visible form of the mango has already struck the eye, but the stream flows on unchanged. In the second it vibrates; in the third it is arrested, and the stream stops. A sense object is matter, and a unit of matter lasts exactly seventeen mind-moments, so the clock has started.Why seventeen: the commentaries hold that matter arises and ceases seventeen times more slowly than mind. A strong object can therefore carry one complete process before it is gone. Weaker objects strike later and leave fewer moments; some never get past vibrating.

Waking and looking

The fourth moment is the man waking and turning toward the sound. In the process it is pañcadvārāvajjanapañcadvārāvajjana · five-door adverting citta 28: turns toward an object arriving at one of the five sense doors, adverting at a sense door: the mind turns to whatever has arrived. It is a kiriyakiriya · functional a citta that neither makes kamma nor results from it, such as adverting citta, merely functional. It does its work and leaves no trace.

The fifth moment is seeing itself, eye-consciousness. It is worth staying with, because it upsets an assumption. Seeing is a vipākavipāka · resultant a citta that is the ripening of past kamma; it makes no new kamma, a result of past kamma. The man did not choose to see the mango, nor whether the sight would be pleasant. Whether one meets a desirable sight or a repulsive one is the ripening of what was done before. The moment of seeing is the most passive moment in the process. It knows only colour.

Handling the fruit

Three more moments follow, and the story gives each a gesture. Taking the mango in his hand is receiving (sampaṭicchanasampaṭicchana · receiving the citta that takes up the object just after sense consciousness), which takes up the object just seen.
