Squeezing it is investigating (santīraṇasantīraṇa · investigating the rootless resultant citta that examines the object just received), which examines it. Smelling it is determining (voṭṭhapanavoṭṭhapana · determining the moment that defines the object; done by mind-door adverting, citta 29), which settles what the object is for this process.

Receiving and investigating are results again. Determining is functional, like adverting. None of them makes kamma. Everything so far has happened of itself, the way water finds its level.

But determining, with adverting before it, is where the commentaries locate the hinge. How attention turns there, wisely or unwisely, yoniso manasikārayoniso manasikāra · wise attention attending in a way that leads to wholesome javanas; unwise attention leads to unwholesome or its opposite, decides what kind of citta follows.The Guide says only that wise or unwise attention decides whether the javanas are wholesome or unwholesome; it places that attention at no single moment (Guide to III §13). The Atthasālinī names both moments: when adverting and determining both turn wisely, unwholesome javanas cannot follow, and when both turn unwisely, wholesome ones cannot.

Eating

Now the man eats the mango. These are the seven javanajavana · impulsion the active phase of a process, usually seven alike cittas; here kamma is made moments, moments nine to fifteen, and in the whole process they are the only ones in which the mind acts. Here, and only here, kamma is made.

The javanas are seven cittas of one kind, each strengthening the next. In our story they are greed with joy: a sense-sphere citta rooted in lobhalobha · greed grasping at an object; roots eight cittas; as craving, a root of the wheel, wanting the mango, liking it. They could as easily have been wholesome: the same ripe fruit seen with a generous mind, meant for someone else, or seen with clarity as colour, smell and taste arising and passing. The object does not decide this. The javanas do.

Cetanācetanā · volition the willing that organises the other factors; as kamma, it bears results, volition, arises in every citta, but in the javana it does what the word kamma names: it wills, and the willing has consequences. A habit is a long run of javanas of one kind. A character is what those habits have become.In an arahant the javanas are merely functional: they act, perceive, even smile, but they leave no result. This is one of the Abhidhamma’s most exact ways of saying what liberation changes.

Swallowing, and sleep

Two moments of registration (tadārammaṇatadārammaṇa · registration resultant cittas that hold the javanas' object after a strong object) follow when the object is strong: resultant cittas that hold the object the javanas held, like the last taste of the fruit as it is swallowed. Then the process is over, exactly as the matter that started it falls away, and the mind sinks back into the life-continuum. The man lies down and sleeps.

The swallowing and the sleep are not in the Atthasālinī. Later teachers, the Vibhāvinī-ṭīkā among them, added them (Guide to IV §6) so that the simile would cover every moment. It is a reminder that this is a teaching device, extended over centuries to fit an analysis, not a report of a man’s afternoon.

What the story leaves out

The man thinks “a mango”, and later “I ate a mango”. None of the seventeen moments contains that thought. The five-door process knows a colour, and the javanas want or do not want it. Recognising mango, naming it, placing oneself as the one who sees: all of that is done by later processes at the mind door, which take this one as their object.The atlas’s Plate 7b sets out these mind-door processes and how a sight becomes a named thing.

So “I see a mango” is true as convention and is built afterwards. In the moment itself there were cittas and their factors, an eye, and a colour. There was no one behind them.

And it was fast. The commentaries say that many thousands of millions of cittas arise and pass in the time of a lightning flash. It is the commentaries’ figure of speech for more than can be counted, not a measurement. The seventeen moments are not a slow story. They describe a structure: what must happen, in what order, for seeing to become wanting. The story is slow so that the structure can be seen.

Read slowly, the simile leaves a practical question. Most of what happens in seeing is given. A small part is not, and that part decides what continues. The Buddha’s instruction to Bāhiya, “in the seen there will be only the seen” (Ud 1.10), can be read as practice at exactly this point: letting the process complete without javanas of wanting.

To reflect on. The seeing was a result of past kamma; the wanting was new kamma. Can you find the seam between them in your own experience, the moment when a sight becomes a want?

Sources. Atthasālinī, Buddhaghosa's commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī: the mango simile; the role of attention at adverting and determining (Abyākatapada, Vipākuddhārakathā). Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, IV §§1–11 and the guide to them; Guide to III §13 (wise and unwise attention). Vibhāvinī-ṭīkā: the later additions of swallowing and sleeping again. MN 18, Madhupiṇḍika Sutta: from eye and form, through contact and feeling, to proliferation.

When the object is weak

Not every sight or sound gets the full seventeen moments. How late an object comes into range decides where the process stops: after registration, after javana, at determining, or before it has begun.

You are reading. Somewhere in the street a door closes. A moment later you could not say whether you heard it or not. Or something moves at the edge of sight, and by the time you look there is nothing to look at.

A caution first. Any sound you could half notice was not one process but, on this account, a great many, at the ear door and the mind door by turns, many of them cut short (Guide to IV §12). What follows concerns single processes, far below anything you could notice. A half-heard sound is a run of courses in which few went the whole way.

The mango of the last reading fell beside the sleeper’s head, and nobody could have missed it. Most of what reaches the senses is not like that. The later Theravāda Abhidhamma tradition, its commentaries and manuals, has an account of the half-heard and the barely seen (whose words these are, a later section asks). It is the same account as before, cut short.

A clock that is already running

What is seen or heard (the visible form, the sound itself, not the experience of it) is classed as matter, rūparūpa · matter matter: the third reality, 28 kinds; as an aggregate it is called form, and the Theravāda tradition gives a unit of matter a fixed life: as long as seventeen mind-moments (IV §6). Other Abhidharma schools held matter to be as momentary as mind; the long life of matter is a Theravāda teaching. A mind-moment, cittakkhaṇacittakkhaṇa · mind-moment the life of one citta, in three sub-moments: arising, presence, dissolution, is the life of one citta, and the Manual divides it into three: arising, presence and dissolution (IV §6). The tradition gives no clock time for it, only the ratio, and the commentators say that billions of mind-moments pass in a flash of lightning (Guide to IV §6). Many modern readers take the numbers as a scheme for ordering rather than a measurement.The sub-commentaries record dissent on both counts. Some held that matter lasts sixteen moments, not seventeen, and some, Ācariya Ānanda among them, denied that a citta has a moment of presence, since the Yamaka names only arising and dissolution. The Vibhāvinī rejects both views, and the Manual follows the seventeen and the three (Guide to IV §6).

The object does not wait for the mind. It arises, and its seventeen moments begin to run whether anything notices or not. Until it comes into range, the mind goes on as the bhavaṅgabhavaṅga · life-continuum the resultant citta, of the same kind as rebirth-linking, that runs between processes, the life-continuum: a stream of resultant cittas, one at a time, each holding the object taken at rebirth, that fills every gap between processes. It runs between processes, never beneath them, and stores nothing. Those moments are spent.

An object comes into range when its impact on the sense door is enough to disturb that stream. The tradition ties weakness and lateness together: a feeble impact comes into range late, and an object that arrives late has little life left and is too feeble to carry the process further (Guide to IV §5; Vibhāvinī on IV §8). So the grades rank the presentation of the object, not the thing presented. A loud sound can make a slight presentation if the ear is weak or the sound nearly over, and a sight can be slight in dim light; a keen organ and good light raise the grade. The grade measures the force of the impact, and it shows in how many cittas of the process arise (Guide to IV §5).

On the commentary’s reckoning the question then becomes one of arithmetic. How many moments have already gone when the object comes into range? Whatever is left is all the process has to work with, and two rules decide what fits: in the ordinary course javana runs seven times or not at all (IV §§6, 21), and registration twice or not at all.The rule for registration was not uncontested: an older view allowed a single moment of it. The Vibhāvinī, following the Sammohavinodanī, rejects that view. The Abhidhammattha Saṅgaha (the Manual itself) calls the result the presentation of objects, visayappavattivisayappavatti · presentation of objects very great, great, slight or very slight: decides how far a process runs, and at the five sense doors it names four grades (IV §5). Bhikkhu Bodhi’s explanatory guide in the same book, the Guide, does the counting.

Four grades, four endings

Very great. One moment passes before the object is in range (moment 1), for matter can strike a sense door only once it has reached its stage of presence (IV §6). The stream vibrates (2) and is arrested (3). Then the full course runs: adverting, sense consciousness, receiving, investigating and determining (4–8), seven moments of javanajavana · impulsion the active phase of a process, usually seven alike cittas; here kamma is made (9–15), and two of registration, tadārammaṇatadārammaṇa · registration resultant cittas that hold the javanas' object after a strong object (16–17), where registration can occur at all (IV §§17–20). The object ends with the process (IV §6; Table 4.1). This is the mango.

Great. Two or three moments pass first. Everything runs as before up to the last javana, and then one moment is left, or none. Registration always takes two moments. With only one left, or none, it cannot happen, so it is skipped, and the mind sinks back into the life-continuum. The object and the sense door perish together (IV §7 and its Guide).

Slight. Four to nine moments pass first. Now the seven javanas do not fit, so, on the commentary’s reckoning, none arise. The process reaches determining, voṭṭhapanavoṭṭhapana · determining the moment that defines the object; done by mind-door adverting, citta 29; determining occurs two or three times in all, and the mind sinks back (IV §8 and its Guide). There has been a moment of ear-consciousness, in the technical sense, and no javana: nothing in the course likes, dislikes or understands.

Very slight. Ten to fifteen moments pass first. The object is close to its end when it arrives. The life-continuum vibrates twice and flows on. No citta of a process arises: no adverting, no ear-consciousness (IV §9 and its Guide; Table 4.2). The Manual calls this the futile course, moghavāra (IV §10).

Each possible number of moments gone is one case, so counted out there are fifteen: one very great, two great, six slight and six very slight (Guide to IV §10; Table 4.2). The strips show the first of each.The Manual says only that one moment or several have passed (IV §6). The reasons (registration needs room for two moments, javana for seven) are the Vibhāvinī’s, and so are the counts of moments gone; Bhikkhu Bodhi’s Guide sets them out as fifteen cases (Guide to IV §§7–10; Table 4.2). The four endings are the four courses at the five doors: the course ending with registration, with javana, with determining, and the futile one (IV §10).

At the mind door

A thought or a memory strikes no sense organ, and its object need not be present at all: it may be past or future, or a concept, which stands outside time (III §17). The Manual does not count moments at the mind door. It asks only whether the object is clearvibhūta · avibhūta · clear and obscure an object's strength at the mind door; only a clear one gets registration or obscure. When it is clear, the stream vibrates and is arrested, mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjanamanodvārāvajjana · mind-door adverting citta 29: opens mind-door processes, and does determining in five-door ones) turns to the object, seven javanas run, and two moments of registration follow (in the sense sphere). When it is obscure, the javanas run and registration does not (IV §12 and its Guide; Table 4.3).

That gives the mind door two grades where the sense doors have four. Ledi Sayadaw, the Burmese teacher who wrote some eight centuries after the Manual, held that it gives only the fullest case of an obscure object, and the Guide reports his fourfold version (Guide to IV §12). The Manual’s clear he calls very clear; the Manual’s obscure he calls clear. Below these he adds two: obscure, where mind-door adverting occurs two or three times and no javana follows, and very obscure, where the life-continuum only vibrates. Clarity, he adds, can come from either side: a prominent object can appear clearly to a weak mind, and a strong mind can clearly know a subtle object (Guide to IV §12). Everyday examples, ours and not his: a vivid memory is a clear object; a name on the tip of the tongue, turned to again and again and never taken up, an obscure one.

Whose words these are

None of this is in the suttas or in the canonical Abhidhamma books. They do not speak of seventeen moments or of graded objects.

The fourfold ladder (very great, great, slight, very slight) belongs to the later manuals, the Abhidhammattha Saṅgaha above all. The Visuddhimagga (XIV) already speaks of a great and a very great object, and of a clear one at the mind door; slight and very slight are not yet there. Buddhaghosa’s Atthasālinī speaks more loosely of a strong or a weak object, and of three futile rounds that a weak object produces: one in which the life-continuum is never turned from its course (our very slight), one that gets as far as determining and falls back (our slight), and one in which javana runs but no registration follows (our great). For the second it gives the report anyone will recognise: it is as if seen by me, as if heard by me.The Vibhāvinī notices the difference in wording: the older commentary calls all three shortened courses futile, because they lack registration or javana; the Manual keeps the word for the last, where no process arises at all.

For the third, where javana runs but registration does not, it has a simile. A river is dammed and its water turned into a channel. The water fills the fields on both banks, and what is left over drains back to the river through the crab-holes. The river is the life-continuum, the dam is adverting, the channel is the process, the filling of the fields is javana. The draining back is the return to the life-continuum, with no registration in between.

Why it matters

The four endings are not equally important. What registration adds is slight: two resultant moments more. For kamma, the line that matters is the one between the great object and the slight one, because that is where javana drops out.

Kammakamma wholesome or unwholesome volition, which later ripens as results is made only in the javanas. Everything before them is a result or functional (Guide to III §8). So in the slight and very slight courses, and in Ledi Sayadaw’s two obscure ones, no kamma is made. No citta in them wanted the object or pushed it away; there was no room for one to, and no merit in it either.

The Visuddhimagga (I) puts restraint of the senses and its lack at the javana stage, though they are named after the door: guard the city gate and the whole city is guarded. So a slight course is not a restrained one; there was no room in it for restraint, or for its lack. Restraint belongs to the courses that run in full. And since, on Ledi Sayadaw’s account, a strong mind can know clearly what a weak one barely meets, the mind’s side of the grade is the side that practice can work on.

To reflect on. Think of something today that you only half heard or half saw. What was actually missing from it: the sound itself, or everything the mind usually does with a sound?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, IV §§5–10 and §12, with their Guides and Tables 4.1–4.3. Vibhāvinī-ṭīkā on the same sections: the moments gone for each grade, why each ends where it does, and the older use of 'futile'. Atthasālinī: the futile courses, the weak object and the simile of the dammed river. Visuddhimagga XIV: a great and a very great object, and a clear one at the mind door. Ledi Sayadaw, Paramatthadīpanī, as reported in the Guide to IV §12: four grades at the mind door, and the naming of an object in later processes.

Other processes

The mind door, the last process of a life, absorption, the path, fruition and cessation: how the building blocks of the mango moment make every other kind of process.

The mango reading followed one process: a strong visible object at the eye door, seventeen moments, seven javanas. The same few building blocks make every other process the Abhidhamma describes: adverting, javana, registration, and the life-continuum before and after. This reading counts the others out one by one. In every strip below, one cell is one mind-moment, except the dotted gap in the last.

At the mind door

The next day the man remembers the mango. Nothing strikes his eye. The object is the mango as remembered: a past thing, now present to the mind. It arrives at the sixth door, the mind door. There is no sense organ for it. On the Theravāda account, the mind door is the resting stream itself, the life-continuum, at the moment an object disturbs it.The commentaries do give this mind a physical base, the heart-base, which the canonical Abhidhamma does not name (Guide to III §20). Which moment of the life-continuum counts as the door is disputed: the Vibhāvinī says the arrest, Ledi Sayadaw the whole stream (Guide to III §12). What follows is a mind-door process, manodvāra-vīthimanodvāra-vīthi · mind-door process a process at the mind door alone: adverting, seven javanas, and two registrations when the object is clear and the conditions for registration hold. Counted out, it goes like this.

  • Moment 1. The life-continuum vibrates (bhavaṅga-calanabhavaṅga-calana · vibration of the life-continuum the life-continuum moment that is shaken when an object comes into range; the next is the arrest). The remembered mango has come into range.
  • Moment 2. The life-continuum is arrested (bhavaṅgupacchedabhavaṅgupaccheda · arrest of the life-continuum the last life-continuum moment before a process; after it the stream stops and adverting arises). This is the last moment of the stream.
  • Moment 3. Mind-door adverting, manodvārāvajjanamanodvārāvajjana · mind-door adverting citta 29: opens mind-door processes, and does determining in five-door ones, turns to the object. It is the same functional citta that did the determining in the mango process. Here it has the job of adverting, and it makes no kamma.
  • Moments 4 to 10. Seven javanas run. “Javana” names a place in the process, the one after adverting. Usually kamma is made there, and so it is here: the seven are cittas of one kind, wholesome or unwholesome. He may want another mango, or be glad he shared it. In an arahant the same places hold functional cittas, which make no kamma (Guide to III §13). And the four fruitions, met below, are the only results that ever stand in a javana place (III §9).
  • Moments 11 and 12. Two moments of registration, tadārammaṇatadārammaṇa · registration resultant cittas that hold the javanas' object after a strong object, hold the object once more.

Then the life-continuum flows again. Counting from the vibration, that is twelve moments. Two are the life-continuum being disturbed; the other ten are the process proper, ten cittas doing three kinds of work: one adverting, seven javanas, two registrations (IV §12–13).

Three things are missing compared with the mango. There is no sense consciousness, because nothing is seen or heard. There is no receiving, investigating or determining, because those cittas handle what a sense has delivered. And there is no past moment counted before the vibration. At a sense door the object is matter, and the commentaries explain the past moment by saying matter needs one moment to reach full strength. A memory, a plan or a concept is not present matter, so nothing needs to be waited for.The reason is Ledi Sayadaw’s, in his Paramatthadīpanī: objects of any time, or of no time, come into range at the mind door, so no rule about moments already past applies there.

A mind-door object can be anything: a sight or sound just past, something that happened years ago, something expected, a concept, a name, another citta. A sense object is graded by how many of its seventeen moments are left when it strikes, as When the object is weak tells. A mind-door object is graded only by how plainly it appears. A clear object, vibhūtavibhūta · avibhūta · clear and obscure an object's strength at the mind door; only a clear one gets registration, gets the full course above. With an obscure one, avibhūtavibhūta · avibhūta · clear and obscure an object's strength at the mind door; only a clear one gets registration, the javanas still run seven times, but no registration follows and the mind sinks straight back into the life-continuum (IV §12).

Registration has conditions of its own, whatever the door. In plain words: it belongs to everyday experience of everyday things, and nowhere else. Exactly: it follows only sense-sphere javanas, only in beings of the sense sphere, only when the object is itself a sense-sphere thing, and only with a clear or very great object (IV §19–20). When one of these fails, the process ends at the last javana.The Manual fixes registration at two moments or none. The Visuddhimagga (XIV) says “twice or once”, and reports elsewhere that the Majjhima commentary allowed a single moment. The later tradition settled on two.

How a colour becomes a mango

The eye-door process of the mango reading knew a colour and nothing else. It did not know “mango”. That is added afterwards, at the mind door, by processes of exactly the kind just counted.

The Manual’s own text does not describe them. The Guide does: Bhikkhu Bodhi’s explanatory guide, printed with the Manual in the same book (Guide to IV §12). It follows the Burmese teacher Ledi Sayadaw. After the eye-door process ends, seven mind-door processes follow it in this order:

  1. One repeats the colour just past. The eye-door process has dropped it; the mind door takes it up again.
  2. One grasps it as a whole. The separate glimpses are put together, the way a torch whirled in the dark looks like a circle of fire.
  3. One recognises the colour.
  4. One grasps the thing: a shape, an object.
  5. One recognises the thing.
  6. One grasps the name.
  7. One recognises the name: “mango”.

Together they may run to many thousands of processes. Ledi Sayadaw’s image for this is a bell. Struck once, it goes on sounding; in the same way one touch of a colour at the eye sets off process after process at the mind door.Ledi Sayadaw’s own Paramatthadīpanī gives both accounts: these seven processes, and also, more briefly, four kinds of grasping that follow each sense door: of the past object, of the whole, of the thing and of the name. The Guide follows the fuller list.

Only then is a mango known. Only in the recognising processes, Ledi Sayadaw holds, does one know “I see” anything: first the colour, then the thing, then its name. This is an analysis of recognition, not a description of what it feels like. On this account the “I” in “I see” is a name put together late in the chain, not a seer standing behind the seeing.A comparison with another school: the Buddhist logicians Dignāga and Dharmakīrti also held that perception proper is free of conceptual construction, and that names and kinds are added afterwards by thought. Ledi Sayadaw’s chain draws a similar line in the Abhidhamma’s own terms, with the name coming last.

The last process

Every life has one process of its own kind, the last. At the end of a life an object appears to the dying mind: the deed itself, recalled or re-lived, or a sign of it, or a sign of the world to come (V §35–36). The last process takes that object. It may run at the mind door or at a sense door, and it is weak. Its javanas run five times, not seven (IV §21; V §38). They have no rebirth-producing power of their own; they are the channel for the past kamma now set to produce the next birth (Guide to V §37). If that kamma is a death-proximate one, it was done or recalled just before this process, which is why, in Buddhist countries, the dying are customarily reminded of their good deeds (Guide to V §19).

After the javanas, the last citta of the life arises: death consciousness, cuticuti · death consciousness the last citta of a life, of the same kind as its life-continuum. It is not a process citta. It is the life-continuum’s own kind of citta, doing its final job. It may follow the fifth javana directly, or two moments of registration, or some moments of life-continuum (Guide to V §37). On the Abhidhamma’s account, when it ceases, rebirth-linking, paṭisandhipaṭisandhi · rebirth-linking the first citta of a life: a resultant that links it to the last, arises with no gap as the first citta of the next life, and takes the object of that last process. The one exception is an arahant: their death consciousness is followed by no further citta at all. This is the final passing away (Guide to V §40; Guide to VIII §13). The story is told in full in Kamma, death and rebirth.

Absorption

The Abhidhamma sorts cittas by sphere. The sense sphere is our everyday world and the cittas that belong to it: seeing, wanting, remembering a mango. The fine-material and immaterial spheres are the levels of deep meditation, and the worlds that match them. So far every javana in this reading has been a citta of the sense sphere. In a meditator the mind-door process can carry something more: jhānajhāna · absorption deep concentration fixed on one object: five fine-material levels, then four immaterial, absorption.

The process begins as before. The object is a meditation sign, nimittanimitta · meditation sign the preliminary, learning or counterpart image of the meditation object, such as the bright image of a disc that the meditator has been attending to. The life-continuum vibrates and is arrested, and mind-door adverting turns to the sign. Then the javanas run, but they are not seven of one kind. The first few are sense-sphere cittas with knowledge, and each has a name for what it does (IV §14):

  • Preliminary, parikammaparikamma · preliminary the first stage of concentration; also the first javana leading into absorption: it prepares the mind for absorption.
  • Access, upacāraupacāra · access concentration just short of jhāna; also a javana in the run-up to absorption: it comes close to absorption.
  • Conformity, anulomaanuloma · conformity the javana that fits the mind to what follows, just before change-of-lineage: it fits the mind both to the moments before it and to the absorption about to come.
  • Change-of-lineage, gotrabhūgotrabhū · change-of-lineage the javana that leaves the sense-sphere lineage for jhāna, or turns to Nibbāna: the last sense-sphere javana. With it the mind leaves the lineage of the sense sphere and takes on that of the higher sphere.

Then comes the next javana, and it is not a sense-sphere citta at all. It is the first-jhāna citta of the fine-material sphere: absorption itself, appanāappanā · absorption the jhāna or path javana itself, after access; the third stage of concentration.

How many preparatory javanas run depends on the meditator’s faculties; Ledi Sayadaw speaks of dull or keen wisdom. In one whose faculties are slow (the Guide’s “average”), mandatikkha · manda · keen and slow of a meditator's faculties: a keen one needs three preparatory javanas before absorption or path, a slow one four, all four arise, and absorption is the fifth javana. In one whose faculties are keen, tikkhatikkha · manda · keen and slow of a meditator's faculties: a keen one needs three preparatory javanas before absorption or path, a slow one four, the preliminary moment is not needed: access, conformity and change-of-lineage are enough, and absorption is the fourth. It is never earlier, and never later. The commentaries give a reason for each side. It cannot come earlier, say the Vibhāvinī and Ledi Sayadaw, because change-of-lineage needs conformity javanas before it that have been strengthened by repetition. It cannot come later, says the Visuddhimagga (IV), because by the sixth or seventh place a run of javanas is already close to falling back into the life-continuum. It illustrates this, without proving it, with a man who runs to the edge of a cliff and cannot stop there.The Visuddhimagga records the elder Godatta’s view that absorption could come at the sixth or seventh javana, and rejects it.

Three more rules belong here. The preparatory javanas and the absorption share one feeling: joyful javanas lead into a joyful absorption, equanimous ones into an equanimous one (IV §15). No registration follows absorption, and its object is never obscure (IV §14). And the first time a meditator reaches a jhāna, the absorption citta arises once and the mind sinks back into the life-continuum. With practice the same citta can be made to repeat without any fixed limit, for as long as the meditator has resolved, for hours or even days (IV §22 and its Guide).

Direct knowledge runs the same way. The Manual counts five mundane kinds, abhiññāabhiññā · direct knowledge a mundane power worked from the fifth jhāna, such as the divine eye or recalling past lives; its citta runs for one moment: supernormal powers, the divine ear, knowing the minds of others, recalling past lives, and the divine eye (IX §21). All of them are worked from the fifth jhāna (IX §21), by one who, the commentaries add, has mastered it.The Abhidhamma counts five fine-material jhānas where the suttas count four, by taking in two steps what the suttas pass in one. Its fifth jhāna is the suttas’ fourth. After three or four preparatory javanas, one moment of the fifth-jhāna citta does the work of direct knowledge, and only one, however practised the meditator is (IV §14, §22).

The path

The noble ones, ariyaariya · noble one anyone who has reached a path or fruition, from stream-entry up, are those who have seen Nibbāna for themselves. Anyone who has not is a worldling, puthujjanaputhujjana · worldling an ordinary person who has reached no path. On the Theravāda account, Nibbāna is the one unconditioned reality: it does not arise from conditions or pass away. It is an “object” only in the sense that the mind can take it up; it does not strike a door as a colour does. There are four paths, one for each stage of awakening, and here is the first, the moment a worldling becomes a noble one. The tree of purification tells how insight ripens up to this point; here is the process itself. It has the same shape as absorption, and the path is itself an absorption, a supramundane one (IV §14; IX §34).

It runs at the mind door. The preparatory javanas are moments of insight. They take some conditioned thing as their object and see it as impermanent, as suffering or as non-self. They are named as before: preliminary, access, conformity. Then comes change-of-lineage, and here the name means more. It is still a sense-sphere citta, but it drops the conditioned object and, for the first time, takes Nibbāna as its object. With it the lineage of the worldling is left for that of the noble ones.In the processes of the three higher paths the person is already noble, so the same javana is called cleansing, vodānavodāna · cleansing the name of the change-of-lineage javana in the processes of the three higher paths, and not change-of-lineage (Guide to IX §34).

Change-of-lineage sees Nibbāna but removes nothing. The next citta does: the path, maggamagga · path (citta) a supramundane citta that arises once, cutting defilements, with Nibbāna as object. It arises for one moment only, and in that one moment it does four things at once: it fully understands suffering, abandons craving, its origin, realises Nibbāna, its cessation, and develops the path itself (IX §34 and its Guide). It is said to abandon, for good, certain defilements, the states that stain the mind. The first path removes wrong view and doubt, and with them every defilement strong enough to lead to a woeful rebirth (IX §38 and its Guide); what remains of greed, hatred and delusion falls to the later paths. Straight after it comes its result, fruition, phalaphala · fruition the supramundane resultant citta that follows its path, also taking Nibbāna as object, with the same object. So in a path process the javana places hold not only kamma but its result.

Path-kamma differs in kind from all other kamma. Its result is its own fruition (Guide to I §§26–28), and it builds no rebirth. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī calls the path a jhāna that tears down, and its commentary explains: it pulls down the deaths and rebirths that other kamma has built up (Atthasālinī; commentarial). Compare ordinary kamma, whose result may ripen lives later: here the result follows at once, in the same process.The tradition also recognises noble ones who reached the path by insight without jhāna, of “dry insight” (Visuddhimagga XXIII). How much concentration the path needs is a question on which modern teachers differ.

The javana counts here come from the Guide to IV §22 and the Manual’s Table 4.4; that one adverting can carry seven javanas at most is the Visuddhimagga’s rule (XXII). The path process uses all seven. With slow faculties there are four preparatory javanas, one path and two fruitions. With keen faculties there are three preparatory javanas, one path and three fruitions. Then the life-continuum resumes. The process is short, and the tradition holds the change irreversible.

Fruition again

Afterwards come processes of reviewing, paccavekkhaṇapaccavekkhaṇa · reviewing after attainment, knowledge looking back on path, fruition and Nibbāna, and usually, not always, on the defilements abandoned and those that remain (IX §34 and its Guide). Each is an ordinary mind-door process, adverting and then seven sense-sphere javanas with knowledge. One reviews the path, one the fruition, one Nibbāna, and usually, not always, the defilements abandoned and those that remain (an arahant has none remaining). When the object is the path, the fruition or Nibbāna, no registration follows, since none of these is a sense-sphere thing (IV §19–20).

A noble person can also return to the fruition they have reached and stay in it, as a meditator stays in jhāna: the attainment of fruition, phalasamāpattiphalasamāpatti · attainment of fruition a noble one's absorption in their own fruition, with Nibbāna as object (IX §42). Each noble one enters only the fruition of their own stage (IX §42 and its Guide). They resolve on it and develop insight again. A process then runs with a few javanas of insight, all of them called conformity here (Visuddhimagga XXIII). After them come fruition cittas, taking Nibbāna as object, one after another with no fixed number, for as long as was resolved (IV §22).

Cessation

One attainment goes further than any jhāna. The attainment of cessation, nirodha-samāpattinirodha-samāpatti · attainment of cessation the temporary stopping of citta and mental factors, open only to non-returners and arahants with all eight jhānas, is described as one in which the stream of cittas stops for a time (IX §43–44). The Theravāda Abhidhamma holds that in it there is no citta at all, not even the life-continuum.This is not the path-and-fruition moment that some modern insight teachers also call “cessation”. That moment has Nibbāna as its object; in the attainment of cessation there is no citta to take any object.

Who can enter it. Only a non-returner or an arahant who has mastered all eight absorptions, the four fine-material (five in the Abhidhamma’s count) and the four immaterial, and only in the sense sphere or the fine-material worlds: not in the immaterial worlds, since the fine-material jhānas that lead up to it cannot arise there (Guide to IX §43). It needs both calm and insight at full strength. Stream-enterers and once-returners cannot enter it: they have not yet abandoned sensual lust, which obstructs concentration, so their calm is incomplete. Nor can noble ones of dry insight, who lack the absorptions. Calm alone, the Visuddhimagga says, stops at neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and insight alone at the attainment of fruition; only the two together reach cessation (Visuddhimagga XXIII; commentarial).

How it is entered. The meditator enters each absorption in turn, emerges, and sees its factors with insight as impermanent, suffering and non-self. After the third immaterial absorption they make certain resolves, among them how long the attainment is to last. Then they enter the fourth and highest immaterial absorption, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Its process begins like any absorption process, but the absorption javana runs just twice (IV §22). After the second, no citta arises.The Visuddhimagga (XXIII) says the last absorption runs “one or two” times; the Manual says two. The detail of the resolves is also from the Visuddhimagga, and is told in Four noble persons.

How it is described. The tradition holds that for the time resolved, up to seven days, there is no citta and no mental factor, and so no matter produced by mind. The body remains, kept going by kamma, temperature and nutriment. The suttas mark the difference from death. In the Mahāvedalla Sutta (MN 43), one who has entered the cessation of perception and feeling differs from a dead body in this: life is not exhausted, heat has not subsided, and the faculties are clear. The Abhidhamma reads this as the stopping of all citta.Cessation is not Nibbāna. The Visuddhimagga (XXIII) calls it neither conditioned nor unconditioned, since it has no nature of its own, and the Kathāvatthu (VI.5) rejects the view that it is unconditioned.

What emerges. The first citta to arise afterwards is one moment of fruition: the fruition of non-returning for a non-returner, the fruition of arahantship for an arahant (IV §22). No adverting comes before it, the commentators note. Then the life-continuum flows, and reviewing follows (IX §44).

How can a citta arise after days with none? The Paṭṭhāna’s answer, quoted in the Visuddhimagga (XXIII), is that the last citta of neither-perception-nor-non-perception before the gap is the proximity condition for the fruition after it. “Proximity” means that no citta comes between them (Guide to VIII §13), not that they are near in time; the Visuddhimagga (XVII) uses this very case to make that point.A comparison with other schools, which asked the same question: in Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośa the Vaibhāṣikas, much as the Paṭṭhāna does, let the citta before the gap condition the one after it, while the Sautrāntikas have mind return from seeds kept in the body. The Yogācāra puts a store-consciousness, ālaya-vijñāna, beneath the gap, so that some mind never stops.

One pattern

What these processes share is a rhythm: a disturbance, a turning, a run of javanas, and a return to the life-continuum. Remembering a mango, dying, entering deep concentration and awakening are all made of it. What changes is which cittas fill the javana places, and how many times they run.

  • A sense-sphere process, at any door: seven javanas of one kind, or six when the object is weak (IV §21).
  • The last process of a life: five (IV §21; V §38).
  • A first attainment of jhāna: three or four preparatory javanas, then absorption once (IV §14, §22).
  • Direct knowledge: three or four preparatory javanas, then direct knowledge once (IV §14, §22).
  • The path: three or four preparatory javanas, the path once, then three or two fruitions (Guide to IV §22; Table 4.4).
  • Jhāna or fruition entered as an attainment: no fixed limit (IV §22).
  • Entering cessation: the fourth immaterial absorption twice, then nothing (IV §22).

The Abhidhamma’s claim is not that awakening is ordinary, but that it happens in the same stream of cittas: in moments of the same kind, under the same fixed order.

Which of these processes, and which cittas in them, can arise for a given being in a given world is the subject of Who has which cittas.

To reflect on. Recognising a mango, entering jhāna, awakening and dying are all, on this account, runs of the same few kinds of moment in the same order. What, then, changes when a mind changes?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, III §9, §§12–13 and §20 (javana, the mind door and its base); IV §§12–16 (the mind door and absorption), §§19–22 (registration and the javana counts) and Tables 4.3–4.4; V §19, §§35–38 and §40, and Table 5.6 (the last process); VIII §13 (proximity); IX §21, §34, §38 and §§42–44 (direct knowledge, the path, the stream-enterer, fruition and cessation); with the Guide to each. Ledi Sayadaw's Paramatthadīpanī, followed in the Guide to IV §12: the processes that follow a sense-door process, and the mind door. Vibhāvinī-ṭīkā, the classic sub-commentary on the Manual: why absorption cannot come earlier than the fourth javana. Visuddhimagga IV, XIV, XVII, XXII and XXIII: the absorption process, registration, death and rebirth-linking, the path process, and the attainments of fruition and cessation. Commentarial. MN 43, Mahāvedalla Sutta: how one who has entered cessation differs from one who has died. Kathāvatthu VI.5: whether cessation is unconditioned. The Paṭṭhāna on the proximity condition across cessation, as quoted in Visuddhimagga XXIII. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī and its commentary, the Atthasālinī, on the path as a jhāna that tears down.

Who has which cittas

The object decides what is seen; the person decides what is done with it. Which of the eighty-nine cittas can arise depends on how a being was reborn, what they have attained, and the world they live in.

The mango and the moment follows one process of seeing. Chapter IV of the Manual ends with two questions. In any process, what depends on the object and what on the person? And which cittas can arise at all, for which beings, in which worlds?

Three grades of object

The Manual sorts sense objects into three grades (IV §17): the undesirable, aniṭṭhaaniṭṭha · undesirable of an object, undesirable; met through unwholesome kamma; the moderately desirable, iṭṭhaiṭṭha · desirable of an object, desirable (moderately, or extremely, ati-iṭṭha); met through wholesome kamma (also called iṭṭha-majjhatta); and the extremely desirable, ati-iṭṭha. The Guide insists this is a quality of the object, judged by an average person, and not of anyone’s taste: someone who finds a desirable object repugnant is misperceiving it.

Which grade one meets is the work of past kamma. An undesirable object comes through unwholesome kamma, so the cittas that simply receive it, the sense consciousness, receiving, investigating and registration, are all unwholesome results. A desirable object comes through wholesome kamma, and the same positions are filled by wholesome results; an extremely desirable one even brings investigation and registration with joy. These cittas match the object without deliberation, the Guide says, as a reflection in a mirror matches a face.

The javanas do not. They follow the person. Faced with something extremely desirable, one person’s javanas run with greed and another’s with calm equanimity; faced with a corpse, a meditating monk’s run with knowledge and joy. The object sets the results; the response is made in the javanas.

When registration happens

Registration, the two moments after the javanas that hold their object a little longer, does not always come. It happens only after sense-sphere javanas, only to beings of the sense sphere, only when the object is of the sense sphere (IV §19), and only when the object is very great at a sense door or clear at the mind door (§20).

There is a further rule about feeling. A citta with joy cannot follow one with displeasure directly, nor the reverse. Suppose javanas of displeasure end in someone whose life-continuum is joyful, and no registration comes to bridge them. Then, the teachers say, a single investigating citta with equanimity arises on some familiar object, only to pave the way back. They call it the adventitious life-continuumāgantuka-bhavaṅga · adventitious life-continuum an equanimous investigating citta that bridges displeasure in the javanas and a joyful life-continuum (§18).

Who you are reborn as

The first fact about a person, for the Abhidhamma, is the citta they were reborn with, since it runs all life long as the life-continuum (IV §§24–26). There are three kinds of rebirth:

  • Rootless: by an investigating citta with equanimity. In the woeful planes every rebirth is of this kind; in the happy ones it means a weakened birth.
  • Two-rooted (duhetukaduhetuka · two-rooted a being reborn by a great resultant citta without knowledge; jhāna and the path are closed to them in that life): by a great resultant without knowledge.
  • Three-rooted (tihetukatihetuka · three-rooted a being reborn by a great resultant citta with knowledge; every attainment is open to them): by a great resultant with knowledge.

The roots of rebirth set a ceiling. For the rootless and two-rooted, no jhāna and no path can arise in that life, however they practise: absorption needs a three-rooted base (§24). The three-rooted may become anything. Then attainment changes the set of cittas a person can have. Stream-enterers lose the four cittas with wrong view and the one with doubt; non-returners lose the two with aversion; arahants lose every wholesome and unwholesome javana, and act only through functional cittas (§25).

The Manual’s own summary is simpler: those beyond training, the arahants, experience forty-four kinds of citta; trainees, the other noble persons, fifty-six (counting the three lower fruitions together and adding the four paths), and everyone else fifty-four (§26).The Guide fills in the rest: worldlings in the woeful planes, thirty-seven; the rootless and two-rooted in happy planes, forty-one; stream-enterers and once-returners, fifty; non-returners, forty-eight. Each figure is a maximum; someone who lacks a jhāna lacks its citta too.

Where you are

The plane removes more (IV §§27–29). In the fine-material worlds there are no cittas of aversion, suppressed in the training that led there, and no registration; and since those beings have no working nose, tongue or body, the consciousnesses of smell, taste and touch never arise. In the immaterial worlds there is no matter at all: no sense-door process, no smile, no fine-material jhāna, no immaterial jhāna lower than the one that brought the being there, and no first path.

So, of the eighty-nine, eighty can arise in a process in the sense sphere, all but the nine sublime resultants, which only ever serve as rebirth and life-continuum. Sixty-four can arise in the fine-material worlds, and forty-two in the immaterial (§29). Two special cases complete the picture (§28): a being without an eye has no eye-door process at all, and the non-percipient beings have no process of any kind.

The point to carry away is the first one: results come with the object, and the javanas are where a person can work. The highest attainments, and what each path removes, are followed in Four noble persons; how kamma decides the rebirth that starts all this, in From kamma to its results.

To reflect on. Two people see the same beautiful thing. The Abhidhamma says their seeing is the same kind of citta, but their javanas may be utterly different. What, in your own experience, belongs to the seeing, and what to you?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, IV §§17–20 (registration) and §§24–29 (individuals and planes), with the Guide and Table 4.5. Sammohavinodanī, on the desirable and undesirable object, as cited in the Guide to IV §17.

The web of twenty-four conditions

The Abhidhamma's last book relates every dhamma to every other. How one thing helps another to arise, and why the help is never a cause acting alone.

Manual VIII §§11–28 (the Paṭṭhāna method

The suttas teach that things arise dependent on conditions. The PaṭṭhānaPaṭṭhāna the seventh Abhidhamma book: relates all dhammas by 24 conditions, the last and longest book of the Abhidhamma, asks how. In what way does one dhamma help another to arise or to continue? It answers with twenty-four kinds of paccayapaccaya · condition a dhamma that helps another to arise or persist, in a specific way, condition, and it applies them to every dhamma in every combination. The printed text fills several volumes.

The Manual condenses all this into a few pages, and a few pictures are enough to see what kind of thing a condition is.

Some of the twenty-four

A root condition is like the root of a tree: greed, hatred and delusion, or their opposites, make the states that grow from them firm and stable. An object condition is anything that a citta takes as its object; it helps simply by being known. A proximity condition is the citta that has just ceased, which makes way for the next, as a runner hands on a baton.

A conascence condition, sahajātasahajāta · conascence support between things arising at the same moment, like a lamp and its light, helps by arising together: a citta and its factors help one another into existence at the same moment, like a lamp and its light. Mutuality is the same help in both directions, like the three legs of a tripod. Support is help by being a basis, as the earth supports a tree, or the eye supports seeing.

Decisive support, upanissayaupanissaya · decisive support a strong earlier cause, such as a habit, a teacher or a climate, is the strong, often distant help: a good friend, a suitable climate, a past habit, a resolution made years ago. Repetition is the way each javanajavana · impulsion the active phase of a process, usually seven alike cittas; here kamma is made strengthens the next, like a lesson learned by recitation. Kamma condition is the help volition gives: at once, to the citta and matter it arises with, and across any span of time, as past kamma, to its results. And absence is the help a ceased state gives simply by being gone.Some conditions restate others. Absence and disappearance are proximity seen as making way; presence and non-disappearance are help by being there at the same time. Association and dissociation, by contrast, are two different relations: between mental states, and between mind and matter.

Six directions

The Manual sorts the conditions by direction, and that sorting shows what they are for. There are six directions:

  • Mind to mind: the previous citta to the next.
  • Mind to mind and matter at once: volition to the mental factors and to the matter it produces.
  • Mind to matter: later cittas sustaining a body that already exists.
  • Matter to mind: the eye supporting seeing.
  • Concepts, mind and matter to mind: anything at all as an object or a decisive support. (Concepts, such as names and ideas, have no nature of their own, yet they can be objects.)
  • Mind and matter to mind and matter: arising together, supporting, feeding, governing, being present: nine ways, from the great elements holding up derived matter to food sustaining the body; and once in a life, at conception, the citta and the heart-base holding each other up (VIII §18; §21).

Matter, in other words, is not only helped by mind, and mind does not only ride on matter. The relation runs both ways, by different conditions.

Four that hold them all

At the end of its account the Manual says that all twenty-four conditions can be folded into four: object, decisive support, kamma, and presence. Everything that helps anything does so by being known, by leaning on it strongly, by being the volition that ripens in it, or by being there at the same time.

Never a cause alone

The most important thing about the Paṭṭhāna is what it never says. It never names a single cause of anything. The Manual’s Guide says the same of dependent arising: a collection of conditions always gives rise to a collection of effects, and the formula only singles out the chief of each (VIII §3). Every dhamma arises from many conditions, and every condition helps in a particular way. No dhamma is self-produced, and none produces another by itself alone.

The suttas give a picture of this: two sheaves of reeds that stand because they lean on each other; take one away and the other falls (SN 12.67). The Paṭṭhāna makes that picture exact. And in doing so it leaves no place for an agent standing outside the web and pulling its strings. What we call a person acting is the web itself, seen from inside.

To reflect on. Name something you did today and look for more than one condition that helped it arise. Which of them was "you"?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, VIII §§11–28. Paṭṭhāna, the method of conditional relations. Nyanatiloka Thera, Guide through the Abhidhamma-Piṭaka, on the Paṭṭhāna. SN 12.67, Naḷakalāpī Sutta: two sheaves of reeds leaning on each other.

One moment, twenty-four questions

Two moments of the mango process, seeing the fruit and wanting it, put to each of the twenty-four conditions in turn: which hold, what gives them, and why the others do not.

Manual VIII §§11–27 with the Guides and Tables 8.2–8.4 (the conditions one citta receives: eye-consciousness and a greed-rooted javana)

The web of twenty-four conditions named the kinds of help the Paṭṭhāna distinguishes. This reading puts them to work. It takes two moments from the mango and the moment: the fifth, in which eye-consciousness sees the fruit, and one of the seven javanas in which the mind wants it. Of each it asks twenty-four questions. Is it helped by a root? By an object? By a predominant? And so on down the list: for each condition that holds, what gives it; for each that does not, why not.

The exercise is an old one. The Burmese teacher Ledi Sayadaw, in his Paṭṭhānuddesa-dīpanī, counts the conditions each type of citta receives (in the section Paccayaghaṭanānaya), and checked against Table 8.3 of the Manual row by row they hold. Two cautions. The counts are of kinds of condition, not of helpers: one helper can give several kinds, and one kind can come from several helpers. And Ledi’s figures are ceilings for a type; a single moment may fall short, as the first javana will.

The setting is the mango reading’s: a human being, an object strong enough to run all seventeen moments, and a pleasant sight, so that the seeing ripens from some past wholesome kamma. The colour of the mango and the eye-sensitivity that sees it both arose with the first of the seventeen moments, the past life-continuum, and both last through the process (Guide to IV §6; Guide to VIII §24 puts the sensitivity’s arising at that moment’s static phase).

Seeing: eighteen of twenty-four

Eye-consciousness here is a wholesome-resultant citta with neutral feeling, and it has no roots. It receives eighteen kinds of condition (Ledi, Paṭṭhānuddesa-dīpanī, on the sense consciousnesses), and they come from six places.

From the eye. The eye-sensitivity arose four mind-moments before and is still standing. It helps the seeing in six ways: as its base, which is support; by having arisen first, which is vatthu-purejātavatthu-purejāta · base prenascence a physical base, arisen earlier and still standing, helping the cittas that rest on it, base prenascence; as a faculty, whose rule sharp sight and dim sight show; as matter helping mind, which is dissociation; and by being present and not yet gone, which are presence and non-disappearance (Vism XVII §641; Table 8.3 rows 8, 10, 16, 20, 21).

From the colour. The visible form helps in four ways: as object; by having arisen first, which is ārammaṇa-purejātaārammaṇa-purejāta · object prenascence a present object of matter, arisen earlier, helping the cittas that take it, object prenascence; and by presence and non-disappearance (Paccayaniddesa §§2, 10, 21, 24; Vism XVII §642 says the same of eye-contact; Table 8.3 row 10). It does not dominate the seeing, nor lean on it heavily. Object predominance, and the object decisive support that goes with it, reach only certain javanas, and sense consciousness is not among them (Table 8.3 rows 3, 9).

From the moment before. Five-door adverting has just ceased. Its ceasing gives the seeing proximity, contiguity, proximity decisive support, absence and disappearance: five conditions with the same giver and the same receiver (§13 with the Guide; Guide to §17). The Paṭṭhāna’s definition fixes the next steps of the order itself: eye-consciousness for the mind element that receives, and that for the mind-consciousness element that investigates (Paccayaniddesa §4, and its general clause, 16.1). The commentary fills in the rest by the same method.

From past kamma. The volition of a past wholesome act helps the seeing across time, as asynchronous kamma, nānākkhaṇika-kammanānākkhaṇika-kamma · asynchronous kamma a past volition helping its results at a later time; kamma condition across a gap (§14; Table 8.3 row 13). The Manual adds, closing its account of decisive support, that kamma is also a natural decisive support for its results (§17), and the Paṭṭhāna gives the same case: wholesome kamma for its result (Pañhāvāra, CS §423).

From further back. Climate, food, lodging and persons, and the ignorance and craving behind the old kamma, help as natural decisive support (Ledi, Paṭṭhānuddesa-dīpanī, on the sense consciousnesses; Paccayaniddesa §9).

From within. The citta arises with the seven universal factors, eight states in all, and they hold each other up by conascence, mutuality, conascent support, association, presence and non-disappearance, and, since all eight are results, by result. Contact, volition and the citta itself feed the rest as nutriment. Volition organises them as conascent kamma. The citta, the feeling and the life faculty each govern their share as faculties; those are the three the Dhammasaṅgaṇī names for this citta (Dhs §§431–442).

That makes eighteen. Six do not hold, each for a plain reason. There is no root, because the citta is rootless, and therefore no path, which reaches only rooted cittas (Vism XVII §611; Table 8.3 rows 1, 18). There is no jhāna: the sense consciousnesses are the one class the jhāna factors do not reach (Vism XVII §§610–611; Table 8.3 row 17). There is no predominance: a conascent predominant leads only in javanas with two or three roots (Guide to §19), and the colour, as said, cannot be an object predominance here. There is no repetition, which passes only from javana to javana (Guide to §13). And there is no postnascence, which never helps mind at all, only a body that arose before (§15).

What the seeing gives is soon told. To receiving it gives proximity and its four companions. To its own factors it gives the conascent set. To the body already standing it gives postnascence, for every citta from the first life-continuum on supports matter that arose earlier and is still present (Table 8.3 row 11). That body includes the eye-sensitivity on which the seeing rests: the eye helps the seeing by prenascence, and the seeing helps the eye by postnascence. Both rows are in the Table; that they meet on one piece of matter is our application of them. What the seeing does not do is produce matter. The ten sense consciousnesses are too weak to (VI §11 with the Guide), so the seeing gives nothing to matter by conascence.

Wanting: twenty, or twenty-one

In the mango reading the javanas are greed with joy, without wrong view, unprompted. Ledi’s ceiling for the greed-rooted cittas is twenty-two, everything except postnascence and result (Paṭṭhānuddesa-dīpanī, on the unwholesome cittas). A single javana sits a little below it.

From the roots. Greed and delusion are the two roots of this citta. By root condition each helps the other, the rest of the citta, and the matter the citta produces (Pañhāvāra, CS §402; Table 8.3 row 1).

From the heart-base. The eye is no longer the base: every citta of the process except the seeing rests on the heart-base. It helps in five ways: support, prenascence, dissociation, presence and non-disappearance (Vism XVII §641; Guide to §16). The faculty that the eye gave the seeing has no counterpart here, for the heart-base is not a faculty.

From the colour. The javana takes the same colour, still present, and receives from it object, object prenascence, presence and non-disappearance. Object prenascence reaches beyond the sense consciousness to the sense-sphere cittas that take a present object (Pañhāvāra CS §424, patthana1.2:816.1; Table 8.3 row 10(2); the Vibhāvinī on Saṅgaha VIII §19 (CS), which is CMA §16, extends it to mind-door processes).

From the moment before. For the first javana, determining has just ceased and gives proximity and its four companions (Pañhāvāra, CS §417). From the second javana to the seventh the giver is the javana before, and it gives one thing more: repetition, āsevanaāsevana · repetition Repetition is the way each javana strengthens the next, as a lesson is learned by reciting it., the help a state gives the next of its own kind, making it more practised, as a lesson is by recitation (Guide to §13; Pañhāvāra CS §426, patthana1.2:822.1). The first javana receives none, since determining is not a javana, and repetition passes only between javanas of one kind (Table 8.3 row 12).

From within. The citta and its factors give one another the conascent set, nutriment and conascent kamma, as in the seeing. What is new comes in three groups that the seeing lacked. As faculties: energy, concentration, the mind, joy and life. As jhāna factors: initial and sustained application, zest, joy and one-pointedness. As path factors: wrong intention, wrong effort and wrong concentration. That is three, because this citta has no wrong view; the greed cittas with view have it as a fourth (Dhs §§400–401; the variant with view, §§365, 398; Table 8.3 rows 16–18). A path factor here is a road to a bad destination, not the noble path (Guide to §14).

From far away. Natural decisive support, pakatūpanissayapakatūpanissaya · natural decisive support strong help from what came before: earlier lust or faith, pleasure or pain, a person, food, climate, lodging, past kamma, is the widest condition in the list, and the javana takes it from many places: earlier greed, an old liking for mangoes, an earlier pleasure, the weather, food, company. The Manual names lust and faith, pleasure and pain, persons, food, season and lodging among such supports (§17). The Paṭṭhāna gives greed as the decisive support of later states, and bodily pleasure, climate, food and lodging as supports of unwholesome ones (Pañhāvāra, CS §423).

So the first javana receives root, object, proximity, contiguity, conascence, mutuality, support, decisive support, prenascence, kamma, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, absence, disappearance and non-disappearance: twenty. Each later javana adds repetition, for twenty-one. Result is missing because an unwholesome citta is not a result, and postnascence because it never helps mind.

Possibly, predominance. Two kinds of predominance could raise the count by one. A conascent predominant, desire, energy or the citta itself, may lead the javana, but only one at a time, and only on some occasions (Guide to §19; Guide to VII §20). The Paṭṭhāna commentary makes a predominant certain only in unwholesome cittas fixed in wrong view, and in the others present only when it leads; it also rules investigation out of the unwholesome altogether (on Paccayaniddesa §3). Ledi says the predominants of the greed cittas operate kadāci, “sometimes”. Investigation could not be one here in any case, for this citta has no wisdom, and no source we have read says whether an ordinary passing want has a predominant at all. The colour too may become an object predominance, ārammaṇādhipatiārammaṇādhipati · object predominance an object held weighty, which dominates the mind that takes it, and with it an object decisive support, if it is made weighty. The Paṭṭhāna gives exactly this case, a visible form made weighty and relished, and lust arising (Pañhāvāra, CS §416), and its commentary allows matter to be weighty in this way only for greed. Whether the javanas of a single glance can make the colour weighty, or only the mind-door processes that follow, no source read decides. We mark both kinds possible, not necessary, so the count is twenty or twenty-one for the first javana and twenty-one or twenty-two for the rest, never a fixed twenty-one.

What the javana gives. To the next javana it gives proximity’s five and repetition; the seventh gives registration proximity’s five alone, since registration is a result and not of its kind (Table 8.3 row 12). To the matter it produces it gives much of what it gives its own factors: root, a predominant if there is one, conascence, support, kamma, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, dissociation, presence and non-disappearance, but never mutuality or association (§14; §§19–26). To the body standing from earlier moments it gives postnascence. And to the future it gives two things. Its volition becomes asynchronous kamma, which can ripen as unwholesome results and kamma-born matter (Pañhāvāra CS §427, patthana1.2:828.1), and its greed becomes a natural decisive support for later states (Pañhāvāra, CS §423), the nearest the conditions come to describing a habit. Ledi sets a limit worth keeping: the Paṭṭhāna maps only the chief result. A long chain, from greed to work to wealth to gifts, belongs to the suttas’ method of “this being, that is”, not to the twenty-four (Paṭṭhānuddesa-dīpanī, closing section).

The seam between seeing and wanting

The mango reading asked where a sight becomes a want. The twenty-four give an exact answer, and the Visuddhimagga states it when it reads the links of dependent origination through the conditions. Contact helps the feeling in eye-consciousness in eight ways, arising with it and sharing its moment; but for the feelings of receiving, investigating and registration, which come later, contact is a decisive support and nothing more (Vism XVII §643). And feeling helps craving by decisive support alone, because the feeling meant in that link is resultant feeling (§644). In the mango process, then, the neutral feeling of the seeing and the joy of investigating do not make the greed. They help it from a moment or more away, strongly, but not as part of it.

Inside the javana it is different. The joy and the greed arise together in one citta and help each other by conascence, mutuality and association. The Vibhaṅga, in its Abhidhamma section, reads the whole series of links within one such citta (Vibh §243 ff.; the greed-rooted citta from §248). The two readings do not contradict each other. One follows the links across moments and lives, the other within a single moment: across the seam, feeling helps craving from a distance; inside the want, once it has arisen, joy and greed hold each other up. That the distance is where restraint can work is the site’s reading of §644, not the text’s claim.Where teachers differ. Proximity and contiguity. The Guide calls the two identical in meaning and then gives them different emphases: nothing comes between, and the next arises in its fixed order (Guide to VIII §13). The Visuddhimagga puts the fixed order under proximity itself, reads sam- as “well”, that is, without a seam, and rejects a view of some teachers that the two differ in meaning (Vism XVII §598). How many faculties in seeing? The Dhammasaṅgaṇī names three in eye-consciousness: mind, feeling and life (Dhs §§431–442). Ledi has one-pointedness govern there as a faculty too (Paṭṭhānuddesa-dīpanī, on the sense consciousnesses); we have not found his reason. The count of eighteen kinds is the same either way. Can one glance make the mango weighty? The Paṭṭhāna illustrates object predominance with a visible form relished (Pañhāvāra, CS §416); its commentary limits weighty matter to greed; Ledi counts object predominance among the conditions of the greed cittas. None says whether a five-door javana can do it. Does decisive support ever reach matter? Table 8.3 and Ledi say no: only mind is decisively supported, and past kamma builds the body by kamma condition alone. The Visuddhimagga once says that the kamma-forming consciousness helps kamma-born matter by decisive support, but it marks this as the suttas’ way of speaking, not the Paṭṭhāna’s (Vism XVII §640).

How mind and matter hold each other up

The Manual does not walk through the twenty-four in order. It sorts them by what helps what, in six kinds, and its verse gives the count of each (VIII §12). Mind helps mind in six ways: proximity, contiguity, absence, disappearance, repetition and association (§13). Mind helps mind and matter together in five: root, jhāna, path, kamma and result (§14). Mind helps matter in one, postnascence (§15). Matter helps mind in one, prenascence (§16). Concepts, mind and matter help mind in two, object and decisive support (§17). And mind and matter help mind and matter in nine: predominance, conascence, mutuality, support, nutriment, faculty, dissociation, presence and non-disappearance (§18). Six, five, one, one, two and nine make twenty-four, and on our count each condition is placed exactly once.

That is where a reader can trip. “Matter helps mind in one way” sounds as if the eye did little for the seeing, yet above it helped in six ways and the colour in four (Vism XVII §641; Paccayaniddesa §§2, 10, 21, 24). In effect, each condition sits under the widest kind of relation it can serve. Support, faculty, dissociation, presence and non-disappearance can run between mind and matter in either direction, so they sit under §18; object sits under §17. What §16 says is that prenascence is the one condition that runs only from matter to mind. The same holds the other way: postnascence is the one condition that runs only from mind to matter (§15), though a javana helps the matter it produces in eleven ways, or twelve with a predominant.

The heart-base shows the whole pattern in one piece of matter. In the course of a life it helps every citta but the sense consciousnesses in the five ways met above (Vism XVII §641). At rebirth it cannot be prenascent, for it arises at the same moment as the rebirth citta. Then the two help each other by conascence and mutuality, with support, dissociation, presence and non-disappearance, and that is the only moment in a life when mind and matter help each other by mutuality (Vism XVII §641; §§20–21, 25; Table 8.3 rows 6–8; Guide to §16). From the first life-continuum on, the help also runs back: each later citta supports the body that arose before it, the heart-base included, by postnascence (§15 with the Guide). The Paṭṭhāna never names the heart. It speaks only of “the matter in dependence on which the mind element and the mind-consciousness element occur”, their support (§8), prenascent to the mind element and to the mind-consciousness element at some times only (§10); and it says material states are conascent with mental states at some times (§6), which the Visuddhimagga takes as the heart-base (Vism XVII §599). Identifying it with the heart is the commentaries’ work, and the conditions say nothing more about where the mind is.

Matter can also help mind from far off, but only in one direction. Food, climate and lodging are natural decisive supports for states of mind (§17; Paccayaniddesa §9). The reverse does not happen in the Paṭṭhāna’s sense: only mind is decisively supported, and past kamma helps the body it builds by kamma condition alone (Table 8.3 rows 9, 13).

Between the links

The same questions can be put to the twelve links of the wheel, and the Visuddhimagga puts them, reading the links across three lives as the wheel across three lives does (Vism XVII §§616–651). Some joints are held by many conditions at once, some by one.

  • Ignorance helps meritorious formations of the sense and fine-material spheres as object and decisive support, and the imperturbable formations of the formless spheres as decisive support only. Demeritorious formations it helps in many ways, since it arises within them as a root (§616).
  • Formations help consciousness by asynchronous kamma and decisive support (§636).
  • Resultant consciousness helps resultant mentality in nine ways; at rebirth it helps the heart-base in nine and other matter in eight (§640).
  • The eye-base helps eye-contact in six ways, and the visible form helps it in four (§642).
  • Contact helps the feeling of its own citta in eight ways, and later feelings only as decisive support (§643).
  • Feeling helps craving as decisive support only (§644).
  • Craving helps sensual clinging as decisive support only, and the clingings of view in seven ways, or eight (§645).
  • Clinging helps the becoming it shares a citta with by the conascent conditions, and other becoming as decisive support (§650).
  • Becoming, here kamma, helps birth by kamma and decisive support; birth helps ageing-and-death as decisive support (§651).

The joints held by decisive support alone are the ones that work across a gap in time, and feeling to craving is the one the mango process crosses. The Vibhaṅga’s single-moment reading ties the same links by conascence instead, so a table of conditions between the links has to say which reading it follows; these counts belong to the reading across three lives.

Ledi draws the point of the exercise at the end of his grouping of the conditions. Every conditioned dhamma depends on conditions, none on anyone’s will, and none arises from a few conditions, only from many (Paṭṭhānuddesa-dīpanī, Paccayasabhāga; compare Vism XVII §617). Eighteen kinds of help for one glance, twenty or more for one want: the count is the argument. There is no one in the list who sees or wants, only what helps, and how.

To reflect on. The seeing receives eighteen kinds of condition and the wanting twenty or more, yet the feeling in the seeing helps the wanting in only one way, and from a distance. If the feeling does not make the greed, what in the javana's list made the greed likely?

Sources. Paragraph numbers are those of the Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana edition.
