Taints, floods, bonds, ties

Nine lists of what binds the mind, and why the tradition kept all their names: each name has its own reach, a latent tendency is a defilement not yet abandoned, and the paths do not end every name at the same time.

Manual VII §§3–14 with the Guides and Table 7.1 (the nine lists of the unwholesome and the factors they name)

The seventh chapter of the Manual opens with nine lists of what binds the mind: taints, floods, bonds, ties, clingings, hindrances, latent tendencies, fetters and defilements (VII §§3–12). Then, in two short paragraphs, it reduces them: all their members are a few of the fourteen unwholesome mental factors (VII §§13–14). The lists reduced does that arithmetic. This reading asks what the arithmetic leaves open: why keep the names, what it means for a defilement to lie latent, and what a path abandons.

Nine lists, in brief

Each list has an image behind its name. The images are mostly the commentaries’, and the Visuddhimagga gathers them in one paragraph (Vism XXII §829).

Taints, āsavaāsava · ogha · yoga taints, floods, bonds: sense desire, desire for existence, views, ignorance: sensual desire, existence, views, ignorance (VII §3). Factors: greed twice, wrong view, delusion. The Atthasālinī gives “long fermented”, like old liquor, as the one sense common to every use of the word (on Dhs §1102, and on the mātikā’s cluster of taints); the Vibhāvinī adds that they ooze through the six doors like fluid from a sore (on VII §3). The Visuddhimagga reads the prefix as “up to”: they flow as far as the summit of existence and, as object, as far as change-of-lineage (Vism XXII §829; Guide to VII §3). The suttas usually count three taints, without the taint of views (DN 33; SN 38.8); the fourth appears in the Abhidhamma (Dhs §1102) and in Khuddaka books such as the Paṭisambhidāmagga and the Niddesa.

Floods, oghaogha · flood the four taints seen as floods that drag beings into the sea of becoming: sensual desire, existence, views, ignorance, and bonds, yogayoga · bond the four taints seen as bonds that keep beings from coming unyoked from suffering: sensual desire, existence, views, ignorance: the same four (VII §§4–5). As floods they drag beings down into the sea of becoming, a sea hard to get across; as bonds they never let one come unyoked from the object or from suffering (Vism XXII §829). Here the suttas already count four (SN 45.171; DN 33).

Ties, ganthagantha · tie, knot four ties of the mental and physical body: covetousness, ill will, rites and rituals, the dogma 'this alone is true', which Bodhi calls bodily knots: covetousness, ill will, rites and rituals, and the dogma “this alone is true” (VII §6). Factors: greed, hatred, wrong view twice. They knot both the mental and the physical body (Vism XXII §829); the Vibhāvinī says they tie mind to body, or this body to bodies to come (on VII §6; Guide to VII §6).

Clingings, upādānaupādāna · clinging intense grasping: at sense pleasures, views, rites, a self; link 9 of the wheel: to sense pleasures, to views, to rites, to a doctrine of self (VII §7). Greed once, wrong view three times. The prefix makes the grasping firm (Atthasālinī on Dhs §1219); the Vibhāvinī pictures a snake holding a frog (on VII §7).

Hindrances, nīvaraṇanīvaraṇa · hindrances obstacles to jhāna and to wisdom: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, doubt; the Abhidhamma adds ignorance: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, doubt, ignorance (VII §8). Eight factors: greed, hatred, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, doubt, delusion. They obstruct and cover the mind (Vism XXII §829). Six is the Dhammasaṅgaṇī’s count (Dhs §1158); the suttas (SN 45.177), and even the Vibhaṅga (Vibh §836), have five, without ignorance.

Latent tendencies, anusayaanusaya · latent tendencies seven (six factors) that lie latent, unabandoned and gone to strength, ready to arise when conditions meet; only the paths remove them: sensual lust, lust for existence, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, ignorance (VII §9). Seven names, six factors. They “lie along” with the mind because, having gone to strength, they lie in wait as the cause of their own arising again and again (Vism XXII §829); unabandoned as well, the Vibhaṅga commentary adds (on Vibh §949). The Dhammasaṅgaṇī also has nine clusters of defilements, but not these nine: it has none for latent tendencies, and has one the Manual leaves out, misapprehension, which is wrong view. The seven latent tendencies are found in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh §949), in the Yamaka, and in suttas such as AN 7.11–12.

Fetters, saṃyojanasaṃyojana · fetter one of ten defilements that bind to rebirth; the four paths cut them, in two lists of ten (VII §§10–11). The first, found in the suttas and the Abhidhamma alike, splits greed three ways: sensual lust, lust for fine-material and for immaterial existence. The second, the Abhidhamma’s own (Dhs §1118; Vibh §969), adds envy and avarice (Guide to VII §§10–11). Fetters bind aggregate to aggregate, kamma to its fruit, beings to suffering (Vism XXII §829).

Defilements, kilesakilesa · defilement one of ten states that torment the mind, from greed to fearlessness of wrongdoing: greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing (VII §12). Ten names, ten factors. They are defiled and defile what comes with them (Vism XXII §829); they afflict the mind (Guide to VII §12).

Bodhi’s Table 7.1 sums this up, and its last column is easy to misread. Greed’s “9” counts the nine kinds of list it appears in (both lists of fetters counted as one), not its number of names, which is larger.

One factor, different reach

Why keep the names? One might answer that each name catches a different behaviour of the same factor. The commentaries say something sharper: the names cut the factor at different widths. Three names for greed show it.

The taint of sensual desire is narrow. The Atthasālinī says that lust for the mansions, wishing-trees and ornaments of the Brahmā gods is not this taint; nor is lust that comes with a wrong view, which it calls view-lust (on Dhs §1102). The tie of covetousness is wide. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī defines it not with the short formula for sensual desire but with its long string of words for greed, and the Atthasālinī explains why: the tie is every kind of greed, lust for the Brahmā worlds included (on Dhs §1140). The clinging to sense pleasures is wide in another way. “Sense pleasures” here means every object of desire, not only the five strands of sensual pleasure, so that even a non-returner, free of sensual lust, still has this clinging (Atthasālinī on Dhs §1220).

The consequence shows in the Visuddhimagga’s table of what each path abandons (Vism XXII §830). The taint of sensual desire falls at the third path, the path of non-returning. The tie of covetousness and the clinging to sense pleasures last until the fourth, and the Visuddhimagga gives the reason for the clinging: lust for fine-material and immaterial existence also counts as sensual there.

Greed, then, is seen through several windows of different widths, and the paths close them at different times. Knowing only that each name “is greed”, one could not say why a non-returner, free of the taint of sensual desire, still has the tie of covetousness. That is reason enough to keep them. (The image of windows is ours; the widths and the path assignments are the commentaries’.)

What lies latent

In MN 64 the Buddha asks how a young baby lying on its back could have identity view, when it has not even the notion “identity”; or doubt, clinging to precepts, sensual lust or ill will, when it has no notion of teachings, precepts, sensual pleasures or beings. Yet the latent tendency to each, he says, lies within it. The same sutta then describes the ordinary person whose mind is obsessed by identity view, which, having gone to strength and not been removed, is a fetter; and the noble disciple, in whom identity view is abandoned together with its latent tendency (MN 64). Latent, obsessing, gone to strength: the three ideas the commentaries later systematise are already here.

Other suttas tie the tendencies to feeling. In MN 44 the nun Dhammadinnā says that the tendency to lust lies in pleasant feeling, to aversion in painful feeling, to ignorance in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; and then that it does not lie in every such feeling, since in the first jhāna lust is abandoned and no tendency to it lies there (MN 44; also SN 36.3). The Yamaka draws a different grid, placing the tendency to sensual lust in neutral as well as pleasant sense-sphere feeling (Yamaka VII §2) (the two feelings, as the commentary reads them).

The Vibhaṅga sets the seven latent tendencies beside seven fetters and seven obsessions, pariyuṭṭhānapariyuṭṭhāna · obsession a defilement risen into the mind and taking it over, but not yet in deed; the middle of the commentaries' three levels, with the same names (Vibh §949): canonical evidence that “obsession” is a category of its own. Its commentary defines a latent tendency as a defilement that lies along because it is unabandoned and gone to strength, thāmagatathāmagata · gone to strength a canonical word (MN 64) that the commentaries make the mark of a latent tendency: a defilement not only unabandoned but grown firm, ready to arise when its cause is met (on Vibh §949). The Vibhāvinī presses the second mark. If being unabandoned were enough, every defilement would be a latent tendency; what makes these seven so is that they have gone to strength (on VII §9). The Guide takes the wider view: any defilement may be called latent, these seven being only the chief (Guide to VII §9). The canon’s own use is wider than seven, as MN 64’s tendencies to identity view, rites and ill will show.

Is a latent tendency a mental factor at all? Other early schools said no. A worldling whose present citta is wholesome is still called “with latent tendencies”, and they cannot be in that citta; so, these schools argued, they are dissociated from mind, without object or root, indeterminate, and a different thing from the obsession. The Kathāvatthu rejects each thesis (Kv IX.4; XI.1–3; XIV.5–6; also III.5), and its commentary names the holders: Andhakas, Sammitiyas, Mahāsaṅghikas and some Uttarāpathakas. The Theravādin’s reply is by parity: the same worldling is also called “with lust” at that moment; is that lust then without object too? The commentary on Kv IX.4 explains: he is “with latent tendencies” only because they are unabandoned, not because they are occurring. The commentary on the Yamaka goes further: the latent tendency is the defilement gone to strength, a real, citta-associated, conditioned, wholly unwholesome dhamma (Pañcappakaraṇa commentary on Anusayayamaka §1).

Why does this matter for the whole Abhidhamma? Because the Manual rests rebirth on it. Rebirth-linking, it says, is produced by a volitional formation wrapped in latent ignorance, with latent craving at its root (V §37). What carries the round on is not only the craving that bends the mind at death (Vism XVII §631), but that craving and ignorance are still unabandoned: the liability the path removes (cf. Vism XXII §835).

That is also what the path removes. The Paṭisambhidāmagga asks whether the path abandons past, future or present defilements, and answers: none of them, for the past are gone, the future not yet arisen, and a path with present defilements would be defiled. Yet abandoning is real, as cutting the root of a young tree means fruit not yet born will never be (ps3.3:17–18). The Visuddhimagga builds on this (Vism XXII §§831–838). The path abandons defilements “arisen as having soil”: liable to arise in aggregates not yet fully understood. The soil is the aggregates as the defilement’s basis, not its object; defilements can take even an arahant’s aggregates as their object, yet those aggregates are not their soil (§834). The roots of the round lie in all five aggregates, as the sap of earth and water runs through a whole tree, not its root only; the path is like a poison thorn driven into that tree, after which it bears no more fruit (§§835–836).Where teachers differ. Past, present or future? The commentary on the Kathāvatthu says an unabandoned defilement is none of the three, and “exists” only as not yet abandoned by the path (on Kv IX.4). The Pañcappakaraṇa commentary says the latent tendency can be past, future or present, and arises (on Anusayayamaka §1). The Vibhāvinī says that strictly they are future defilements, called so in the past and present because their nature is the same, and that they lie along the continuity “as it were” (on VII §9). Ledi Sayadaw answers the Vibhāvinī: they really lie along, are not future, and are present only in a loose sense until they rise to obsession (Paramatthadīpanī, CS §162). All agree that what the path removes is the defilement as unabandoned and liable to arise; they differ on how to place it in the Abhidhamma’s scheme of time. The reach of a name. The Atthasālinī and the Vibhāvinī count lust that comes with the eternalist view as the taint of existence (on Dhs §1102; on VII §3). Ledi disagrees: the Dhammasaṅgaṇī puts the taint of existence only in greed-cittas without view (Dhs §1465), so that lust belongs to the taint of sensual desire (Paramatthadīpanī, CS §162). Each side argues from the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. Which path ends worry? The Atthasālinī, on the hindrance cluster, puts worry with doubt at stream-entry (on Dhs §§1158 ff.); Vism XXII §830 and Table 9.3 put it at non-returning.

Three levels, three abandonings

The commentaries give a defilement three levels. It can lie latent; it can rise into the mind and take it over, as an obsession; and it can break out in body and speech, as a transgression, vītikkamavītikkama · transgression a defilement broken out in body or speech; the coarsest of the commentaries' three levels, opposed by virtue. The Visuddhimagga sets these against the three trainings in its first chapter: virtue opposes the transgression of the defilements, concentration their obsession, wisdom their latent tendency. In the same paragraph virtue abandons by substitution, tadaṅgatadaṅga-pahāna · abandoning by substitution removal of a defilement by its opposite, as a lamp removes darkness, for as long as the opposite lasts; given to virtue in Vism I §5, to insight in Vism XXII, concentration by suppression, vikkhambhanavikkhambhana-pahāna · abandoning by suppression the holding down of defilements by concentration, as a pot pushes moss aside on water; they can return, and wisdom by cutting off, samucchedasamuccheda-pahāna · abandoning by cutting off the path's way of abandoning a defilement: for good, never to arise again (Vism I §5). Its sub-commentary defines the levels: transgression at the doors of body and speech; obsession, defilements that, given an opening, rise and take over the wholesome course of the mind; latent tendency, the seven gone to strength. The wisdom that cuts off, it adds, is the wisdom of the four paths (sub-commentary on Vism I §5). The introductions to Buddhaghosa’s commentaries on the Abhidhamma, the Dīgha Nikāya and the Vinaya give the same three levels to the three baskets: the Vinaya abandons transgression, the Suttanta obsession, the Abhidhamma the latent tendency (Atthasālinī, Sumaṅgalavilāsinī and Samantapāsādikā, introductions).

A caution belongs beside this. The same three words appear elsewhere with a different distribution. The Paṭisambhidāmagga counts five abandonings: suppression of the hindrances by one developing the first jhāna; substitution of views by one developing the concentration that partakes of penetration, that is, insight; cutting off by one developing the supramundane path; tranquillisation at fruition; and escape, which is Nibbāna (ps1.1:125). The Visuddhimagga’s chapter on the paths keeps the first three. Suppression is mundane concentration, like a pot pushing aside moss on water; it holds the hindrances back so that, before and after the jhāna, they do not suddenly overwhelm the mind (Vism XXII §848). Substitution is insight: each knowledge removes its opposite as a lamp removes darkness, as defining mind and matter removes identity view, and seeing rise removes the annihilationist view (§849). Cutting off is the path, like a tree struck by lightning (§851). So substitution is given to virtue in Vism I §5, and to insight in Vism XXII and the Paṭisambhidāmagga. Both uses mean removal by the opposing quality, and both are temporary. Only cutting off is the path’s own; the other two prepare for it (§851).

What each path removes

The Manual itself names little: view and doubt at stream-entry, the attenuation of lust, hatred and delusion at once-returning, sensual lust and ill will at non-returning, and all the rest at arahantship (IX §§38–41). The fuller accounting, list by list, is the Visuddhimagga’s (Vism XXII §830), and Bodhi’s Table 9.3 gives the factor-level result.

  • Stream-entry: the taint, flood and bond of views; the ties of rites and of “this alone is true”; the clingings to views, rites and a doctrine of self; the hindrance of doubt; the latent tendencies to views and doubt; the defilements of view and doubt; the fetters of identity view, doubt and rites; in the Abhidhamma list, envy and avarice as well (Atthasālinī on the fetter cluster).
  • Once-returning ends no list item outright. It ends the gross forms of sensual lust and aversion: as fetters in both the Paṭisambhidāmagga (ps1.1:349) and Vism XXII §830, and as latent tendencies in the Paṭisambhidāmagga only; the Visuddhimagga gives the second path no latent tendency.
  • Non-returning: the taint (with the flood and bond) of sensual desire, the tie of ill will, the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will and worry, the latent tendencies to sensual lust and aversion, the defilement of hatred, and the subtle forms of sensual lust and aversion as fetters.
  • Arahantship: the taints (floods, bonds) of existence and ignorance, the tie of covetousness, the clinging to sense pleasures, the hindrances of sloth and torpor and restlessness (the Visuddhimagga counts five hindrances), the latent tendencies to conceit, existence-lust and ignorance, the other seven defilements, and the five higher fetters.

The Visuddhimagga adds a rule (Vism XXII §830): whatever is assigned to a higher path has already, through the lower ones, lost its power to lead to the woeful states. Stream-entry does not leave sensual lust and aversion untouched; it removes the grade of them that leads to a woeful rebirth. Who these four persons are, and what else marks them, is told in Four noble persons.

The reduction to factors says what the defilements are; the names say how far each reaches and when it ends.

To reflect on. In the Majjhima Nikāya a baby lying on its back has no idea of "identity" or of "sensual pleasures", yet the latent tendencies to identity view and to sensual lust are said to lie within it. What is being claimed about the baby, if nothing in its mind at that moment is greedy or deluded?

Sources. The lists reduced to their factors

Taints, floods, bonds, clingings, hindrances, fetters: chapter VII's many names for what binds, and the fourteen factors they all come down to.

The seventh chapter of the Manual is a compendium of lists. It opens with nine lists of what binds the mind: the taints, the floods, the bonds, the bodily ties, the clingings, the hindrances, the latent tendencies, the fetters and the defilements (VII §§3–12). Most come from the suttas, though the taint of views and the sixth hindrance, ignorance, are not in the suttas’ usual counts. Read as they come, they make a dense thicket of names. The Abhidhamma’s contribution is to ask, of each item, which mental factor it really is.

The answer clears the thicket. Dozens of names come down to only fourteen factors, the unwholesome factors of the fifty-two (VII §§13–14).

Many names, few factors

Take the four taints, āsavaāsava · ogha · yoga taints, floods, bonds: sense desire, desire for existence, views, ignorance: sensual desire, attachment to existence, wrong views and ignorance. The first two are greed; the third is wrong view; the fourth is delusion. Three factors, four names. The four clingings, upādānaupādāna · clinging intense grasping: at sense pleasures, views, rites, a self; link 9 of the wheel, are greed once and wrong view three times. The six hindrances (six in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī’s count; the suttas have five, without ignorance) are eight factors: greed, hatred, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, doubt, and delusion as ignorance.

Count across all nine groups and a pattern appears. Greed is in every one of the nine groups (Table 7.1), in seventeen items if both lists of fetters are counted, under sixteen different names. Wrong view is in eight groups, delusion in seven. A handful of factors does almost all the binding.The atlas counts by factor: each circle on the plate gives the number of items in a list that are, ultimately, that factor, counting both lists of fetters.

Why keep the names, then? Not only because each has its own image. The commentaries give them different reach: the taint of sensual desire is lust for the five sense pleasures and ends at non-returning, while covetousness as a bodily tie is every kind of greed and ends only with arahantship (Atthasālinī on Dhs §§1102, 1140; Vism XXII §830). Each list, its images, what a latent tendency is, and which path ends which name are taken up in Taints, floods, bonds, ties.

Categories that are conditions

The chapter’s second section, its mixed categories (lists that hold wholesome, unwholesome and neutral factors together), holds a further surprise. Six of them are six of the twenty-four conditions. The six roots work as root condition. The jhāna factors work as jhāna condition. The path factors, the faculties, the predominants and the nutriments each have a condition of the same name. Only the nine powers have no condition of their own. Five of them (faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration and wisdom) are also counted as faculties; the other four are shame, fear of wrongdoing and their two opposites. All nine are called powers because their opposites cannot shake them (Guide to VII §19).

So the lists of chapter VII and the web of chapter VIII describe the same factors from two sides: what they are, and how they help.

The requisites

The chapter ends with the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment: the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of success, the faculties and powers, the factors of awakening, and the eightfold path. Reduced the same way, thirty-seven items are fourteen states (a different fourteen from the defilements). Energy appears nine times, mindfulness eight, wisdom five, concentration four, faith twice. The path, too, is a few qualities under many names, each name marking a stage or a use. The seven sets and their fourteen states are drawn out in Thirty-seven requisites, fourteen states.

To reflect on. Greed turns up in every one of the nine groups of defilements, under sixteen different names. Why might the tradition have kept so many names for one factor?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, VII §§3–33 with the Guide, and Table 7.1; Guide to VII §19 (why the powers are so called). Dhammasaṅgaṇī CS §§1102–1235: the clusters of defilements; Atthasālinī on Dhs §§1102, 1140; Visuddhimagga XXII §830 (Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana paragraph). Nyanatiloka Thera, Buddhist Dictionary, on paccaya.

The wheel across three lives

Twelve links, three periods, twenty modes and three rounds: how the Abhidhamma reads dependent origination, and where the wheel can be stopped.

Manual VIII §§2–10 (dependent origination: formula, periods, factors, modes, connections, groups, rounds, roots)

“When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.” The suttas state the principle in a sentence, and then apply it as a chain of twelve links: paṭicca-samuppādapaṭicca-samuppāda · dependent origination the twelve links by which suffering arises, and by whose ending it ceases, dependent origination. It explains how suffering arises and continues, and how it ends.

The twelve are these, each conditioning the next:

  1. Ignorance: not knowing the four noble truths, in the sutta explanation (Guide to VIII §3)
  2. Formations: volitions, wholesome and unwholesome
  3. Consciousness
  4. Mentality-materiality: mind and matter, the nāmarūpa of Mind and matter together
  5. The six sense bases
  6. Contact
  7. Feeling
  8. Craving
  9. Clinging
  10. Becoming
  11. Birth
  12. Ageing and death, with sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair

Three lives

The Abhidhamma’s commentaries read the twelve across three lives.This is the commentarial reading, systematised in the Visuddhimagga and the Manual. The suttas themselves give several variants, and some modern teachers read the chain within a single life or a single moment. The Vibhaṅga itself, in its Abhidhamma section, applies the whole series to one moment of citta. Avijjāavijjā · ignorance not knowing the four noble truths; delusion as a root of the wheel, ignorance, and the formations it conditions belong to the past: they are the kamma of a previous life. Consciousness, mentality-materiality, the six bases, contact and feeling belong to the present as results: the rebirth-linking consciousness and the life it begins. Craving, clinging and becoming belong to the present as causes: the defilements and the kamma of this life. Birth and ageing-and-death belong to the future.

So the twelve links describe two turns of a wheel: past causes producing present results, and present causes producing future results.

Twenty modes

The commentaries then notice something about this arrangement. Wherever ignorance and formations are present, craving and clinging are present too, since one does not occur without the others. Becoming has two sides: kamma-becoming, the kamma that leads to a new existence, and rebirth-becoming, the existence it leads to. Wherever kamma-becoming is, ignorance and formations are. So each set of causes is really five. The results are five too: consciousness, mentality-materiality, the sense bases, contact and feeling; and birth and ageing-and-death in the future are those same five seen arising and decaying.

That gives twenty “modes”: five past causes, five present results, five present causes, five future results. The twelve links are a sketch; the twenty modes fill it in.

Three rounds, two roots

The links can also be sorted into three rounds, vaṭṭavaṭṭa · round one of three cycles turning in the wheel: defilements, kamma, results. The round of defilements is ignorance, craving and clinging. The round of kamma is formations and kamma-becoming. The round of results is everything else. Defilements give rise to kamma, kamma gives rise to results, and results, met with ignorance and craving, give rise to new defilements.

And the wheel has two roots. Ignorance is the root that runs from the past into the present, and its run ends in feeling; craving, taṇhātaṇhā · craving greed as thirst: for sense objects, for existence or for non-existence; a root, is the root that runs from the present into the future, and its run ends in ageing and death (VIII §9). Neither is a first cause. The Manual adds that ignorance itself arises from the taints (VIII §10; the Guide traces this to MN 9), so the wheel has no beginning that can be found.

Where it can be stopped

A wheel with no beginning sounds hopeless. The teaching is the opposite. A wheel of conditions is held together only by its links, and any one link that fails stops the whole.

Teachers often point to the joint between feeling and craving. Feeling is a result: as long as there is a body and a mind, there will be pleasant, painful and neutral feeling. Craving is not a result. It is a defilement arising in the javanas, where new kamma is made, and it can fail to arise. Insight teachers stress this joint: where feeling is seen clearly, as feeling, craving does not get its hold. The commentaries call this kind of release abandoning by the opposite factor (tadaṅga-pahāna): insight keeps a defilement away only while it lasts (Vism XXII §849, after the Paṭisambhidāmagga). Craving, with ignorance one of the wheel’s two roots (VIII §9), is cut for good only by the paths, the last of it by the path of arahantship (IX §38–41).

That is why the twelve links are taught at all. They are not a cosmology to be admired. They are a diagram of a machine, drawn so that you can see where to put your hand.

To reflect on. The wheel has no first link. Ignorance conditions formations, but ignorance is itself conditioned. Does a wheel without a beginning make liberation harder to imagine, or easier?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, VIII §§2–10. SN 12.1–2: the twelve links stated and analysed. MN 9, Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta: ignorance arises from the taints, and the taints from ignorance (SuttaCentral mn9). DN 15, Mahānidāna Sutta: a variant series beginning from consciousness and mentality-materiality. Visuddhimagga XVII: the three periods, twenty modes and three rounds.

Kamma, death and rebirth

Four ways to sort kamma, the signs that appear to a dying mind, and the hinge between two lives, where nothing passes over and yet nothing is lost.

Manual V §§18–33 (kamma: four ways, unwholesome and wholesome kamma, results), §§34–41 (death and rebirth)

“It is volition, monks, that I call kamma. Having willed, one acts by body, speech and mind” (AN 6.63). In the Abhidhamma this sentence becomes exact. Kammakamma wholesome or unwholesome volition, which later ripens as results is the volition, cetanācetanā · volition the willing that organises the other factors; as kamma, it bears results, that arises in wholesome and unwholesome javanas. The act itself, the gift or the blow, is the expression. The kamma is the willing.

A volition does not vanish without trace. It leaves a potency that can ripen, later, as a resultant citta: as a pleasant or unpleasant sight, as a sound, as a rebirth. The Manual sorts this ripening four ways.

Four ways to sort kamma

By function: some kamma produces results, giving rise to resultant cittas and kamma-born matter. Some supports kamma that is already ripening, some obstructs it, and some destroys it, cutting off a weaker kamma and taking its place.

By order of ripening: weighty kamma ripens first. On the unwholesome side this means the five heinous deeds, such as killing a parent, and wrong views that deny the results of deeds, held firmly; on the wholesome side, the jhānas. Next comes death-proximate kamma, an act done or remembered just before death. Then habitual kamma, āciṇṇaāciṇṇa · habitual kamma what one does again and again; next in line after death-proximate kamma, what one has done again and again. Last is reserve kamma: anything else done that is strong enough to ripen.

By time: some kamma ripens in this life, some in the next, some in any later life, and some lapses without ripening at all.

By place of result: unwholesome kamma ripens in the sense sphere; wholesome sense-sphere kamma ripens there too; the jhānas ripen in the fine-material worlds; the immaterial attainments in the immaterial ones.

Four ways a life ends

Death, in the Abhidhamma’s terms, is the cutting off of the life faculty that belongs to one existence. The Manual names four ways it comes (V §34). The life-span may run out, as it does in worlds with a fixed span, or in old age. (Then, if the kamma that made the life still has force, it can bring a new birth on the same level or higher.) The kamma may run out while the life-span still has years to give. Both may run out together. Or a destructive kamma may cut the life short, overriding the kamma that sustained it.

The first three are timely deaths; the fourth is untimely. The Guide’s image is an oil lamp, which goes out when the wick is spent, or the oil, or both, or when a gust of wind blows it out.

The last moments

As death approaches, the Manual says (V §35), one of three kinds of object presents itself to the mind. It may be the kamma itself, the deed recalled or re-lived (Guide to V §36). It may be a sign of the kamma, kamma-nimittakamma-nimitta · kamma sign at death, an object linked with a past deed, such as offered flowers, an image connected with the act. Or it may be a sign of destiny, gati-nimittagati-nimitta · destiny sign at death, an image of the coming birth, an image of the world about to be entered. The last process of the life takes this object, and its javanas, weak now, run five times instead of seven (IV §21; V §38).

Counted out, the last process is short. The life-continuum vibrates and is arrested. Adverting turns to the object: at the mind door if it is a kamma recalled, and at any of the six doors if it is a sign of kamma. Where a sign of destiny appears is read two ways (V §38 and its Guide; see the note). The five javanas run. Then death may come at once, or after two moments of registration, or after a few more moments of life-continuum; the figure below shows the shortest case.The Manual’s wording, as the Burmese teacher Ledi Sayadaw reads it, lets a sign of destiny appear at any of the six doors; the Visuddhimagga (XVII) has it appear at the mind door, its sub-commentary says only there, and the Vibhāvinī follows them (Guide to V §38). This is a difference among commentators. The principle is the same for both: the last process carries the object that the next life will begin with.

The hinge

Then comes the death-consciousness, cuticuti · death consciousness the last citta of a life, of the same kind as its life-continuum: the last citta of a life, the same kind as the life-continuum and with the same object as it. It ceases. Immediately after it, with no gap at all, the rebirth-linking consciousness, paṭisandhipaṭisandhi · rebirth-linking the first citta of a life: a resultant that links it to the last, arises in a new life, taking as its object the sign that the dying process presented.

Nothing, the Abhidhamma holds, passes across. No soul migrates, no consciousness is carried over. The new citta is a different citta. But it is conditioned by the old: by the kamma that ripens in it, and by the dying citta as the proximity condition that makes way for it. The commentaries compare this to a seal pressed into wax, to an echo answering a voice, to a flame lit from another flame. The impression is not the seal. It is not unrelated to the seal either.

A life of one kind

The rebirth-linking citta sets the tone of the new life. The same kind of citta then runs as the bhavaṅgabhavaṅga · life-continuum the resultant citta, of the same kind as rebirth-linking, that runs between processes, the life-continuum, whenever no process is active, and at the end it will be the death-consciousness. One kamma, ripening as one kind of resultant citta, holds a whole life’s background together.

The foreground is different. Every process in the new life has its own javanas, making new kamma, which will ripen in their turn. The wheel turns on these two at once: the given background of a life, and the choices made against it, moment by moment.

To reflect on. Habitual kamma ripens at death when nothing weightier or nearer takes precedence. What would your habits bring to mind if you had to die today?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, V §§18–41. AN 6.63: "It is volition that I call kamma." MN 135, Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta: why beings differ. Visuddhimagga XVII and XIX: the similes of the seal and the echo.

Ten ways to act

Kamma is made through three doors, body, speech and mind, in ten typical ways for ill and ten for good. Which root drives each, when an intention becomes a full course of action, and the ten bases of merit.

Kamma, death and rebirth sorts kamma by when and how it ripens. The Manual also sorts it by where it is done (V §§22–26). The answer is three doors: the body, speech and the mind. It is the Abhidhamma’s account of what counts as a deed.

Three doors

A door here is the medium a volition acts through. The door of the body is bodily intimation, the change in the body’s matter by which a mind expresses itself (VI §4); the door of speech is vocal intimation. The door of mind is the mind itself, acting without either.

The Manual says each kind of deed occurs “mostly” through its door, and the qualification matters. Killing done by giving an order uses speech, but it is still a bodily deed; a lie told in writing uses the hand, but it is still false speech (Guide to V §22). The door names the kind of act, not the muscles that carried it out.

Ten for ill

Three are bodily: killing, stealing and sexual misconduct. Four are verbal: false speech, slander, harsh speech and idle chatter. Three are purely mental: covetousness, ill will and wrong view. These are the ten unwholesome courses of action, kammapathakammapatha · course of action one of ten typical deeds of body, speech or mind, unwholesome or wholesome; complete, it can produce a rebirth (V §22).

Each of the first seven is a volition, and the volition is already kamma when the effort starts, whether or not it succeeds. If it reaches its aim, the victim dead, the goods taken, the lie believed, it becomes a full course of action: a kamma strong enough to produce a rebirth.The commentaries list the conditions that complete each course; killing, for instance, needs a living being, the knowledge that it is one, the intention to kill, the effort, and the death that follows from it. The tips in the figure give them in short. The last three are not volitions but other mental factors grown strong: covetousness is greed that has become the wish to own what is another’s; ill will is hatred that has become the wish that someone be harmed; wrong view counts only when it denies that deeds have results at all.

Which root drives each

The Manual assigns each course a root (V §23). Killing, harsh speech and ill will come from hatred. Sexual misconduct, covetousness and wrong view come from greed. Stealing, lying, slander and idle chatter can come from either. And delusion underlies all ten.

The Guide adds a careful point. Someone may kill for gain, or misbehave sexually out of spite. Still, the Abhidhamma holds that the volition that actually cuts off a life is always aversion to that life continuing, and the one that drives sexual transgression is always desire. The motive may be elsewhere; the act itself has its fixed root.

Ten for good

The wholesome courses run through the same doors. The first seven are abstaining from the seven unwholesome deeds of body and speech: in the Abhidhamma’s terms, the abstinences (mental factors that hold back from a wrong act) right action and right speech, with the volition that goes with them. The last three are non-covetousness, non-ill will and right view, which are the three wholesome roots at work (Guide to V §24).

The Manual adds a second list, the ten bases of merit:

  • giving, virtue, meditation;
  • reverence, service;
  • sharing one’s merit, rejoicing in others’ merit;
  • hearing the Dhamma, teaching it, and straightening one’s own view.

The first three, giving, virtue and meditation, are the classical threefold summary.The commentaries fold the other seven into the three: sharing and rejoicing into giving, reverence and service into virtue, hearing, teaching and straightening view into meditation, though straightening view is also said to belong to all. All twenty courses of action, ten for ill and ten for good, are made by the twelve unwholesome cittas and the eight great wholesome cittas: kamma of the sense sphere.

Beyond the three doors

The jhānas are kamma too, but only of the mind. Fine-material wholesome kamma is meditation that has reached absorption, fivefold by its jhāna factors; immaterial kamma is fourfold, by its object (V §§25–26). In every case the deed is made in the mind; the doors only say how it went out. What each kind of kamma gives as result is followed in From kamma to its results.

To reflect on. The Abhidhamma counts covetousness, ill will and wrong view as actions, though nothing is done or said. Is a thought you never act on really a deed?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, V §§22–26 with the Guide; VI §4 (intimation). MN 41, Sāleyyaka Sutta, and AN 10.176, on the ten courses of action. Atthasālinī, on the conditions that complete each course.

From kamma to its results

How each kind of kamma is matched to the rebirth it can give, why the quality of a good deed matters as much as the deed, and what ripens within a life.

A volition ceases as soon as it arises, and yet it can ripen much later. The Manual traces two ways it does so. It can ripen as the first citta of a new life, the rebirth-linking consciousness. And it can ripen within a life, as the resultant cittas of seeing, hearing and the rest: the pleasant or unpleasant sights and sounds that come to a being without being chosen.

Matching kamma to rebirth

The Manual matches each kind of kamma to the rebirths it can give. Twenty kinds of rebirth-linking cover all thirty-one planes.Nineteen kinds of citta can link a new life; the twentieth is the purely material rebirth of the beings without perception, who have no citta at all at rebirth.

Wholesome kamma comes in grades, weak, middling and excellent, by its roots and by how it was done (next section). Unwholesome kamma gives rebirth in the four woeful planes, by the unwholesome-resultant investigating citta. Weak wholesome kamma, two-rooted and done half-heartedly, gives a rootless rebirth as a human or as one of the lesser spirits: a life with serious disadvantages from the start. Middling wholesome kamma gives a human or divine rebirth with two roots, without understanding. Excellent wholesome kamma, three-rooted and done well, gives a three-rooted rebirth, with the capacity for jhāna and for the path in that very life.

How the deed is done

What makes kamma weak, middling or excellent is not only what is done but how. The Manual weighs the roots of the citta, whether understanding was present, and the manner: whether the act was done gladly, with a clear mind before and after, or reluctantly and with regret. A gift given grudgingly and a gift given with joy and understanding are different kamma, though the gift is the same.

Jhāna and the higher planes

The jhānas ripen in their own planes. In each of the first three jhāna levels, a jhāna developed weakly, moderately or fully leads to the lowest, middle or highest plane of that level. The highest jhāna leads to the plane of great fruit, or, with a turning away from perception, to the plane of beings without perception; the Pure Abodes receive only non-returners. The immaterial attainments likewise lead to the immaterial planes. This is weighty kamma: if a jhāna is maintained to the end of life, it takes precedence over everything else.

Results within a life

Within a life, results arrive constantly. Unwholesome kamma ripens as the seven unwholesome-resultant cittas: unpleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes, the pain of body-consciousness, and the receiving and investigating of such objects. One unwholesome citta, the restlessness citta, gives results in life but can never produce a rebirth.

Wholesome kamma of the sense sphere ripens too, and here the Manual records a disagreement between teachers (V §§29–30). On the usual view, a wholesome citta of the best kind, with three roots and done well, can give all sixteen sense-sphere wholesome results in the course of life: the eight rootless ones and the eight great resultants. A weaker kind gives twelve, and the weakest only the eight rootless. Some teachers held a stricter rule: an unprompted deed gives only unprompted results, and a prompted deed only prompted ones. On their count the three grades give twelve, ten and eight.The Guide names the two schools: the usual view goes back to the elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, the stricter one to the school of Mahā Dhammarakkhita at the Moravāpi monastery in ancient Sri Lanka. Table 5.5 of the Manual sets the two side by side. The Atthasālinī gives this view to Mahādatta of Moravāpi, and Ledi Sayadaw corrects the name accordingly (As on Dhs §498; Ledi, Paramatthadīpanī §153).

The practical lesson the tradition draws is about urgency. The kind of rebirth decides what is possible in the life that follows: only a three-rooted being can attain the path in that life. Each life is the field prepared by the last, and each moment of javana is preparing the next.

How kamma is made through the three doors is set out in Ten ways to act; which worlds can follow a death in each world, in Who is reborn where.

To reflect on. A generous act done grudgingly gives weaker results than the same act done gladly and with understanding. Think of something kind you did recently: what were its roots, and how was it done?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, IV (individuals), V §§18–33. Visuddhimagga XVII. MN 135, Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta.

Thirty-one planes

The worlds of the Theravāda cosmology, from the hells to the formless realms, and how each one corresponds to a kind of mind.

Manual V §§2–8 (the four planes), §§9–17 (four kinds of rebirth-linking, lifespans)

The Abhidhamma inherited a cosmology and gave it a structure. There are thirty-one planes of existence, bhūmibhūmi · plane one of 31 planes of existence, each matched to a kind of mind, in four tiers. A being is reborn into one of them, lives out its span there, and dies into another. None of them is permanent, the highest included.

No single sutta lists all thirty-one; the count is a later synthesis of material scattered through the Canon.The suttas speak of five destinations: hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, humans and gods (MN 12). The thirty-one planes refine this into a ladder. But the structure has a logic the suttas already imply, and the Abhidhamma makes it explicit: each plane corresponds to a kind of mind.

Four tiers

At the bottom are four woeful planes, apāyaapāya · woeful planes hell, animals, ghosts and titans: the four unhappy destinations: hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the realm of the asuras. Rebirth here is the result of unwholesome kamma.

Above them are seven happy planes of the sense sphere: the human world and six heavens of the devadeva a being of the six sense-sphere heavens, above the human worlds, the gods. Together with the woeful planes these make eleven sense-sphere planes, the worlds of the five senses and the desires that go with them.

Above the sense sphere are sixteen fine-material planes, the worlds of the BrahmāBrahmā a being of the fine-material planes, reborn there through jhāna gods. Beings are reborn here by the power of the jhānas. Among them is a plane of beings without perception, and five Pure Abodes, where only non-returners (those who have reached the third of the four paths) are reborn and from which they attain Nibbāna.

At the top are four immaterial planes, named after the four formless attainments: boundless space, boundless consciousness, nothingness, and neither perception nor non-perception. Here there is no body at all, only mind.

Time

The spans grow almost beyond imagining. In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, one divine day is a hundred human years, and a god lives a thousand divine years. In the fine-material planes lifespans are counted in aeons; in the highest immaterial plane, in eighty-four thousand great aeons, mahākappamahākappa · great aeon one cycle of a world's arising and passing; four incalculable aeons.A great aeon is described by simile: longer than it would take to wear away a mountain of solid rock a league high by brushing it with a cloth once a century (SN 15.5).

The plate draws the planes on a logarithmic scale of time, and the effect is dizzying. Even so, every bar on it ends. The longest life in the cosmos is a conditioned thing, and it ends like any other, when its lifespan runs out or its kamma is spent (V §34).

A place, and a state of mind

The key to the cosmology is the match between planes and cittas. A sense-sphere citta that makes kamma can lead to rebirth in a sense-sphere plane. A first-jhāna citta, if the jhāna has not been lost by the time of death, leads to the corresponding Brahmā world. A citta of the base of boundless space leads to that plane.

So the planes are worlds, but they are also a map of kinds of mind. Who is reborn where works out which citta opens a life in each. A human being in the course of a day can pass through states that resemble many of them: moments of hungry-ghost craving, of hellish anger, of heavenly delight, even, in deep meditation, of Brahmā-like calm. Read this way, and many modern teachers do read it so, what is visited in a moment can, made habitual, become a place to live.

Why it matters

The tradition takes the planes as real worlds, each reached by the kind of mind that matches it: a jhāna kept until death, for example, ripens as rebirth in its own Brahmā world (V §31 and Guide). Some modern teachers also read the planes as states of mind met within this life, the hells in hatred and the heavens in calm; that reading is theirs: the commentaries take even the sutta’s “hell of the six contact-bases” (SN 35.135) as a real hell. On either reading the teaching points in the same direction. Every plane is a result, and every result ends. The way out is not upward through the tiers but out of the ladder altogether, to what the planes do not contain.

To reflect on. The highest formless plane lasts eighty-four thousand great aeons, and still ends. What does the impermanence of even the longest heavens say about where to look for peace?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, V §§2–17. MN 12, Mahāsīhanāda Sutta: the five destinations. AN 8.43, Visākhā Sutta: divine lifespans. Visuddhimagga VII and XIII.

Who is reborn where

Nineteen cittas can begin a life, and each belongs to its own kind of world. Where a being can go next depends on where it dies and with what, and for the noble ones there is no going down.

Kamma, death and rebirth describes the last process of a life and the first moment of the next. Thirty-one planes describes the worlds. This reading joins them. It asks two questions: which citta can begin a life in which world, and, after a death in one world, where the next birth can fall. The answers show why, on this reading, the path, not a high rebirth, is the only real safety.

Four kinds of beginning

The Manual counts four kinds of paṭisandhipaṭisandhi · rebirth-linking the first citta of a life: a resultant that links it to the last, rebirth-linking (V §9). The citta that links a new life is the same citta that then runs all life long as the life-continuum and finally ends it as the death citta: one type, with one object, for the whole of a life (V §17).

  • In the woeful planes, one citta does it: the investigating citta with equanimity, born of unwholesome kamma (§10). Every hell-being, animal, ghost and asura begins this way.
  • In the human world and the sense heavens, nine cittas (§11). The eight great resultants, two- or three-rooted, are the usual ones. The ninth, the investigating citta born of wholesome kamma, is rootless, and it begins the lives of those born with a defect already in the kamma that made them: those blind, deaf or mentally impaired from conception, and some minor earth-deities and a class of “fallen” asuras distinct from the asuras of the woeful planes.The Guide is careful: blindness from an accident in the womb is a different matter, and can happen to a being with a two- or three-rooted rebirth. Only a defect built into the generating kamma marks a rootless rebirth.
  • In the fine-material worlds, six modes (§13): the five fine-material resultants, each in the worlds of its jhāna, and, for the non-percipient beings, no citta at all, only matter.
  • In the immaterial worlds, four cittas (§15): each immaterial resultant in its own plane.

That makes nineteen rebirth cittas, and one rebirth with none.

Where a worldling can go

The Manual closes chapter V with a verse on the order of death and rebirth (V §40), and the Guide and Table 5.7 work it out world by world. For an ordinary person, a worldling (the roots counted here are the three wholesome ones: non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion, or wisdom):

  • Dying in a woeful plane, or dying in the sense sphere with a rootless or two-rooted citta, one is reborn only in the sense sphere, woeful or happy.
  • Dying in the sense sphere with three roots, one can be reborn anywhere, since a three-rooted being can make any kind of kamma, including a jhāna.
  • Dying in a fine-material world, one is never reborn without roots: into the sense sphere with two or three roots, or into a fine-material or immaterial world by a jhāna one still has. The non-percipient beings return to the sense sphere.
  • Dying in an immaterial world, one is reborn in the same plane or a higher one, if the jhāna is kept; if it is lost, in the sense sphere, with three roots, by the force of access concentration (Guide to V §40).

Never lower

For noble disciples, those who have reached at least the first path, the rule is simpler and stricter (Guide to V §40). A “trainee” is a noble disciple short of arahantship. A noble disciple always dies with a three-rooted citta, since the path cannot be reached without three roots, and is never reborn into a lower world or with a lower citta. A trainee who dies in the sense sphere goes to the sense sphere or higher, never to a woeful plane; one who dies in a world of form or of formlessness goes to the same world or a higher one. The Pure Abodes receive only non-returners, who climb from one to the next and reach arahantship there at the latest. An arahant is not reborn at all.

So the grid has a shape. For worldlings it spreads in every direction, because a jhāna can raise a being high and its fading can let it fall. For the noble it only rises.

To reflect on. A being in the highest heaven of form can be reborn as a human, but a stream-enterer in the human world can never be reborn as an animal. What, in the Abhidhamma's terms, makes the difference?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, V §§9–17 (the four kinds of rebirth-linking), V §40 with the Guide, and Table 5.7. III §9 (the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death).

The way out

The four noble truths

The first sermon's frame, read the Abhidhamma way: the realities sorted under the truths, with a remainder left outside, each truth with its own task, and all four seen in a single moment.

Manual VII §§38–40 (the four noble truths, and what falls outside them)

In the Deer Park at Isipatana the Buddha told the five ascetics who had once practised with him that one gone forth should take neither of two dead ends: a life given over to sense pleasure, and a life of self-torment. The middle way he had found between them, he said, is the noble eightfold path (SN 56.11, sn56.11:2.1–3.4). Then he set out four truths, the ariya-saccaariya-sacca · noble truth suffering, its origin, its cessation, the path: the four noble truths (sn56.11:4.1–4.10). There is suffering: birth, ageing, sickness and death, meeting what is unloved, parting from what is loved, not getting what one wishes; in short, the five aggregates of clinging. There is its origin: craving, which brings renewed existence, craving for sense pleasures, for existence and for non-existence. There is its cessation: the complete fading and ending of that same craving. And there is the way there: the eight factors of the path.

The four noble truths, one page each ›

While this was being spoken, Koṇḍañña, one of the five, saw that whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease (sn56.11:11.1–11.2). That this “eye of Dhamma” was the first path, stream-entry, is the commentary’s reading (Sāratthappakāsinī on SN 56.11, CS §1081). The story is told in Koṇḍañña's eye of Dhamma.

Every Buddhist school teaches the four truths, though not every school makes them its frame or reads them alike. What this reading adds is the Theravāda Abhidhamma’s way of reading them: as a sorting of ultimate realities, each truth with its own task, and all four penetrated in one moment.

Four truths, three turnings, twelve aspects

The sermon does not stop at naming the truths. For each, the Buddha says, three knowings arose: this is the truth; it is to be fully understood, or abandoned, or realised, or developed; and it has been (sn56.11:5.1–8.3). Four truths, three turnings each: the sermon calls this knowledge tiparivaṭṭatiparivaṭṭa · three turnings each truth in the first sermon turned three ways, as this is it, it is to be done, it has been done: twelve aspects in all, three-turned and twelve-aspected. He did not claim awakening, he says, until all twelve were fully clear (9.1–10.3).

The middle column carries the point of the whole frame. Each truth has its own task (SN 56.29). Suffering is to be fully understood, pariññāpariññā · full understanding the task of the first truth, which is to be fully understood, not abandoned; its origin, craving, is to be abandoned; its cessation is to be realised; the path is to be developed. The tasks do not swap. Suffering is never the thing to be abandoned, and cessation is never the thing to be developed. The names for the three turnings, knowledge of the truth, of the task and of the task done (sacca-, kicca- and kata-ñāṇa), are the commentary’s (CS §1081).

What each truth is, in ultimate realities

The Manual closes its compendium of the whole with the four truths, the last of five ways it divides ultimate realities: aggregates, aggregates of clinging, bases, elements and truths (VII §§38–40; see Bases and elements). Here the sermon’s words become counts of paramatthaparamattha · ultimate what remains after analysis: citta, cetasika, matter and Nibbāna, ultimate realities. The Guide to VII §38 (p. 289) gives the reckoning.

The truth of suffering, dukkhadukkha · bodily pain painful bodily feeling: only in unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness, is everything of the three mundane planes except craving. Spelled out, which is the site’s counting and not the Guide’s: the 81 mundane cittas, every mental factor that arises in them except one, and all 28 kinds of matter. The origin, samudayasamudaya · origin the origin of suffering, the second noble truth: craving, for sense pleasures, for existence and for non-existence, is that one exception, craving, taṇhātaṇhā · craving greed as thirst: for sense objects, for existence or for non-existence; a root, which is the mental factor greed, in its three aspects. Cessation, nirodhanirodha · cessation (third truth) the cessation of suffering, the third noble truth, which is Nibbāna, to be realised; not the attainment of cessation, is nibbānanibbāna the unconditioned: the ending of craving; object of path and fruition, realised by the eradication of craving. It is not an event the path brings about: Nibbāna is unconditioned, reached by the path and not produced by it (Vism XVI §560, commentarial). It is called cessation because in reaching it craving ceases, and the Manual explains the word nibbāna itself as a departure from craving (VI §30 and Guide). The path is the noble eightfold path, and here the Guide is exact: in the teaching of the truths it is only the eight factors as they arise in the four supramundane path cittas. They are wisdom as right view, initial application as right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, energy as right effort, mindfulness and one-pointedness as right concentration. In the requisites of enlightenment the same factors may be mundane or supramundane; as the fourth truth they are only supramundane.

It follows, and it is surprising, that the path factors of ordinary good moments belong with suffering. In the teaching of the noble truths the path is only supramundane (Guide to VII §38), so a moment of mundane right view, or of real effort, or of mindfulness, is counted under the first truth: Buddhaghosa puts into it everything but craving and the taint-free states (Vism XVI §564). The objection is obvious: is a kind thought suffering? “Suffering” here does not mean what hurts. It names the aggregates of clinging, craving aside: what is conditioned and can be clung to, the stuff of the round. The supramundane states are conditioned too, and in that broad sense suffering, but they are not aggregates of clinging, and so not this truth (Vism XVI §566, commentarial). The suttas know three kinds: suffering as pain, suffering in change, and the suffering of formations (SN 38.14; SN 45.165), and the commentary places pleasant feeling under the second and neutral feeling, with all the other formations of the three planes, under the third (Vism XVI §539). So the first truth takes in pleasant and wholesome states too. A good mundane state is still to be developed as practice. As a reality, it belongs with what is to be fully understood, not with what is to be clung to.Sacca means both “true” and “real”, and the last of the Guide’s four reasons for calling the truths noble is that they are real and unalterable (Guide to VII §38). The sermon states the truths (“this is suffering”); the Abhidhamma counts what they are about, so that on its use a truth is also a set of dhammas, and “noble realities” would fit as well as “noble truths”.

What falls outside

The sorting leaves a remainder, and on the Manual’s count it is a large one. Its summary verse says that the states associated with the paths, and the fruits, are excluded from the four truths (VII §40). The path’s eight factors are the fourth truth, and nothing else in the path citta is: the citta itself and its other factors, and all four fruitions, fall outside the four truths (VII §40; the Guide to §40 says “strictly speaking”). Fruition holds the same eight factors again, as results, but on this count they are not the fourth truth (Guide to VII §40).Where teachers differed: Ledi Sayadaw counts what is left out: twenty-nine states in the path moment besides the eight, and thirty-seven in fruition (Paramatthadīpanī, CS §165). These match a path at the first or second jhāna level and a fruition at the first (II §19); that is our reading of his figures, not his statement. The Vibhāvinī (CS §53) allows a looser count: the fruit’s path factors under the path, since the Dhammasaṅgaṇī still calls them “included in the path”, and the other states of path and fruit under suffering, as conditioned, so that the truths can cover everything. And the Vibhaṅga itself, in one round of its Abhidhamma method, counts the whole path citta as the way to cessation (Vibh 4, vb4:97.1–105.3).

Why craving, and why this order

The tradition’s reasons are the commentaries’, and they are worth having. Why four truths? Because nothing can be added or taken away: the Buddha taught occurring with its cause, and stopping with its means, and four exhausts it (Vism XVI §535). Why this order? Suffering comes first because it is gross and shared by all; then its cause; then cessation, to show that when the cause ends the result ends; then the way to it (Vism XVI §536). Cessation is defined as the ending of craving, not of suffering directly, because the Tathāgatas, Buddhaghosa says, are like lions, who go for the cause, while other teachers are like dogs, who go for the result: they would end suffering by tormenting the body (Vism XVI §554).

Why craving, of all the causes of suffering? The Vibhāvinī answers that craving is the chief cause: it makes kamma varied and keeps kamma company (CS §52). Ledi Sayadaw takes up the harder objection, that ignorance is the root of the whole round. In dependent origination, he says, ignorance stands first in the chain of conditions; in the teaching of the truths craving is the owner and chief that produces the aggregates. A park is made by a gardener from ground and seed: asked whose park it is, we name the gardener (Paramatthadīpanī, CS §165). And ignorance, in the sutta explanation, is just not knowing these four truths (Guide to VIII §3, p. 295).

The two teachings fit together in the suttas themselves. AN 3.61 gives the origin of suffering as dependent origination in its forward order, and its cessation as the same chain ceasing, link by link (an3.61:13.6–17.4). The wheel across three lives draws that chain.Where teachers differed (two methods): The Vibhaṅga teaches the truths twice. Its sutta method gives the sutta definitions, with craving alone as the origin. Its Abhidhamma method drops the word “noble” and widens the origin step by step: craving; then all the defilements; then all unwholesome states; then the three wholesome roots that still carry taints; then all tainted wholesome states. Each time suffering is “the rest” of the mundane (Vibh 4, vb4:55.2–80.2). Dropping “noble”, the Sammohavinodanī explains, is what lets these other causes in, since they too produce suffering (CS §§206–214); at the widest step good mundane moments count under the origin, not under suffering. The Manual’s count matches the sutta method.

Similes

The commentaries set the four truths beside images with the same four parts, every one of them commentarial (Vism XVI §565). Suffering is a burden; its origin is taking the burden up; cessation is laying it down; the path is the means of laying it down. Or a disease, its cause, its cure and the medicine. Or a famine, a drought, plenty, and the rain that brings it. The same paragraph adds an enemy and the root of enmity, a poison tree and its root, fear and its cause, and a near shore, the flood, the far shore and the effort of crossing.Comparison: The four truths are often presented today as a physician’s diagnosis. In the commentaries the disease is one image among several (Vism XVI §565), beside the burden, the famine and the rest, not the frame of the teaching.

One knowledge, four tasks, one moment

Before the path, the truths are known one at a time, and not all of them directly. The Visuddhimagga calls this following knowledge, anubodha: mundane, and for cessation and the path only by learning and hearsay. Penetration, paṭivedha, is supramundane, and takes all four at once (Vism XVI §563).

At the path moment the twelve aspects collapse into one act. The path citta, taking Nibbāna as its object, does the four tasks together: it fully understands suffering, abandons craving, realises cessation and develops the path (IX §34 and the Guide, pp. 354–356). This happens four times, once at each path. Each path does all four tasks, but abandons only its share of the defilements: the first cuts wrong view and doubt, and craving is gone entirely only at the fourth (IX §§38–41 with the Guides). Seeing any one truth, the elder Gavampati reports, is seeing all four (SN 56.30).

The Visuddhimagga gives three images for this, quoting “the ancients” for the first (XXII §§839–841). A lamp, in one moment, burns the wick, dispels the darkness, makes light appear and uses up the oil. The rising sun lights up forms, dispels the darkness, shows light and allays the cold. A boat leaves the near shore, cuts across the stream, carries its cargo and reaches the far shore. Each act is one of the tasks, and none comes before another. In all three, the path is said to be developed by conascence: its factors arise together and support each other.Comparison: The Theravāda holds a single penetration of the four truths (SN 56.30; Kathāvatthu II.9, which argues that seeing them one by one would make a quarter-arahant). Its commentary names the Andhakas, Sabbatthikas, Sammitīyas and Bhadrayānikas as holding, in its description, a gradual realisation in sixteen parts, the four truths at each of the four paths (CS §339).

Practice

The frame gives a practice that is easy to get wrong. The task for suffering is not to get rid of it but to understand it: to see the conditioned as conditioned, the pleasant as well as the painful. Before the path this understanding is insight: seeing the formations of the three planes as impermanent, suffering and not self (IX §§32–33), in the stages the commentaries call full understanding as the known, as investigating and as abandoning (Vism XX §693, commentarial). The task for craving is to abandon it where it arises, and the suttas say where that is: wherever something is pleasing, in the six-door process itself, in the eye and the sight, the seeing, the contact, the feeling and the rest, sixty places in all (DN 22, dn22:19.4–19.67). The mango and the moment shows where in a process of seeing the wanting begins. The third task is not done by working on cessation itself: it is realised when the path that is developed reaches it. The fourth is the only one to be developed.

The fourth truth, the path, is the next reading but one, The noble eightfold path, after the meditation subjects that supply its concentration.

To reflect on. Each truth has its own task: suffering is to be fully understood, its origin abandoned, its cessation realised, the path developed. Which of the four tasks do you most often confuse with another?

Sources. SN 56.11, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta: the middle way, the four truths, the three turnings and twelve aspects, Koṇḍañña's insight (SuttaCentral sn56.11). SN 56.29, the four tasks (sn56.29); SN 56.30, who sees one truth sees all (sn56.30). MN 141, Saccavibhaṅga Sutta: the truths analysed word by word (SuttaCentral mn141). AN 3.61: origin and cessation as dependent origination arising and ceasing (an3.61:13.6–17.4). DN 22: the sixty pleasing places where craving arises (dn22:19.4–19.67). SN 38.14 and SN 45.165: three kinds of suffering (sn38.14, sn45.165). SN 36.6: the second dart (sn36.6). Vibhaṅga 4, Saccavibhaṅga: the sutta method and the Abhidhamma method (SuttaCentral vb4). Kathāvatthu II.9: one penetration, not a gradual one (kv2.9). Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, VII §§38–40 with the Guide (pp. 289–291); IX §§32–34 and §§38–41 with the Guides (pp. 350–356, 358–362); VI §30 and the Guide (pp. 258–259); Guide to VIII §3 (p. 295); II §§18–19 and Table 2.3. Visuddhimagga XVI §§535, 536, 539, 554, 560, 563–566, XX §693 and XXII §§839–841 (Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana paragraphs; commentarial). Commentaries (Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana paragraphs): Sāratthappakāsinī on SN 56.11, CS §1081; Sammohavinodanī on Vibh 4, CS §§206–214; Kathāvatthu commentary on II.9, CS §339; Vibhāvinī-ṭīkā on the Saṅgaha VII, CS §§52–53; Ledi Sayadaw, Paramatthadīpanī VII, CS §165.

Forty meditation subjects

The *Manual*'s catalogue of calm, after the *Visuddhimagga*: subjects matched to temperaments, the signs that arise on the way, and how far each subject can take the mind.

Manual IX §§2–21 (calm: subjects, temperaments, stages of development, signs, jhānas, direct knowledges)

The Manual’s last chapter turns from analysis to practice. It describes two kinds of meditation: calm, samathasamatha · calm meditation that develops concentration, up to the jhānas, which unifies the mind, and insight, vipassanāvipassanā · insight seeing mind and matter as impermanent, suffering and non-self, which sees its nature. Calm comes first in the order of the chapter, and the Manual, following the Visuddhimagga, gives it a catalogue: forty subjects of meditation, with notes on who should use which, and how far each can go.

The forty

Ten are kasiṇakasiṇa a device for concentration, such as a disc of earth or a colours, devices: earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, white, light and limited space. Earth is often a prepared disc of clay; air is the wind seen moving in leaves. Each is attended to until its image is held with the eyes closed. Ten are kinds of foulness: ten stages of a decaying corpse. Ten are recollections: of the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, of virtue, generosity and the qualities of the gods, of peace, of death, of the body’s parts, and of breathing.

Then four illimitables, appamaññāappamaññā · illimitables (factors) compassion and appreciative joy as mental factors, taking suffering or happy beings as object: loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity. One perception, of the repulsiveness of food. One analysis, of the four elements in the body. And four immaterial states, the formless attainments, reached by going beyond a kasiṇa.

Six temperaments

The Manual matches subjects to people (IX §13). It describes six temperaments: greedy, hating, deluded, faithful, intelligent and speculative. A greedy temperament is given the kinds of foulness and the body’s parts, which cool desire. A hating temperament is given the four illimitables and the four colour kasiṇas. A deluded or speculative one is given mindfulness of breathing. A faithful one, the first six recollections. An intelligent one, the recollection of death and of peace, the perception of food, the analysis of elements.The matching is a guide. The Visuddhimagga presents it as what most directly counters each temperament, and adds that every wholesome development suppresses greed and the rest. Teachers in practice often give loving-kindness and mindfulness of breathing to almost everyone.

Three signs, three stages

As a subject is developed, a sign, nimittanimitta · meditation sign the preliminary, learning or counterpart image of the meditation object, arises. First the preliminary sign, the object as it is attended to. Then the learning sign, the object held in mind with the eyes closed, still with its flaws. Then the counterpart sign: a purified, stable image, bright and without blemish, like a mirror just taken out of its case.

The stages of development run in parallel. Preliminary development is the effort to attend. Access concentration, upacāraupacāra · access concentration just short of jhāna; also a javana in the run-up to absorption, arises, in the subjects that have one, with the counterpart sign: the hindrances are suppressed and the mind is near absorption. Absorption, appanāappanā · absorption the jhāna or path javana itself, after access; the third stage of concentration, is the jhānajhāna · absorption deep concentration fixed on one object: five fine-material levels, then four immaterial itself: the mind fully merged with its object.

How far each can go

This is the most practical part of the chart. Not every subject reaches absorption. Ten subjects reach only access: the eight recollections other than the body’s parts and breathing, the perception of repulsiveness in food, and the analysis of the four elements. They call for so much reflection that the mind cannot settle into jhāna. The kinds of foulness and the body’s parts reach the first jhāna only, since they need initial application to keep them vivid. Loving-kindness, compassion and appreciative joy reach the jhānas up to the one that still has happiness; equanimity reaches only the last, which has equanimity in place of happiness. The kasiṇas and mindfulness of breathing reach all the jhānas, and the kasiṇas open the way to the formless attainments.

What calm is for

A jhāna is a wholesome citta of the fine-material sphere (or, for the immaterial attainments, of the immaterial sphere), as the map of the eighty-nine showed. It is powerful kamma: weighty, as the reading on kamma said, and able to lead to rebirth in the Brahmā worlds. But it does not uproot anything. The hindrances are held down, so that for a while even before and after it they do not overwhelm the mind, but they can return, because nothing has uprooted them (Vism XXII §848; §837).

Its value on the path is the mind it leaves behind: unified, bright and workable, able to look at itself without flinching. For the meditator who goes by the vehicle of calm, that is the basis for insight: calm makes the instrument, and insight uses it. It is not the only route. The suttas name four ways to arahantship, among them insight before calm and the two yoked together (AN 4.170), and the Guide describes a vehicle of pure insight, whose concentration is momentary, not jhāna (Guide to IX §29; see Ten knowledges, one by one).

To reflect on. The tradition matches subjects to temperaments: the reflection on foulness for a greedy one, loving-kindness for a hating one. Which subject would your own temperament call for, and which would you rather avoid?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, IX §§2–21. Visuddhimagga III–XI: the subjects, the temperaments and the signs. MN 118, Ānāpānasati Sutta: mindfulness of breathing. AN 4.170, Yuganaddha Sutta: four ways to arahantship (SuttaCentral); Guide to IX §29: the vehicles of calm and of pure insight.

The noble eightfold path

Eight factors named as the mental factors they are: scattered over many moments in ordinary practice, and together, in one citta, at the moment of the path.

Manual VII §30 with the Guide (the eight path factors as mental factors)

In the first sermon the Buddha begins not with the truths but with a way between two dead ends, indulgence in sense pleasure and self-torment. That middle way, he says, is the noble eightfold path (SN 56.11, sn56.11:2.4–3.4). Elsewhere he defines each of its eight factors, and the first of them closes a circle: right view is knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation and the way to its cessation (SN 45.8, sn45.8:3.1–3.2). The path begins by knowing the truths that The four noble truths set out, and it is itself the last of them.

The eight factors, one page each ›

This reading asks what the eight factors are, in the Abhidhamma’s terms, and when they are there.

Eight path factors, eight mental factors

Each path factor, maggaṅgamaggaṅga · path factors twelve: eight right factors and four wrong ones; the eight right ones in path consciousness are the truth of the path, is one of the fifty-two mental factors (Guide to VII §30). Right view is wisdom, understanding the four truths. Right intention is initial application, vitakkavitakka · initial application lays the mind onto its object; a factor of the first jhāna only, the factor that directs the mind onto its object, here directed toward renunciation, goodwill and harmlessness. Right speech, right action and right livelihood are the three abstinences, virativirati · abstinences right speech, right action, right livelihood; singly in mundane cittas, together in a path: not good speech, good deeds and a good trade, but the deliberate holding back from false, divisive, harsh and idle speech, from killing, stealing and sexual misconduct, and from wrong ways of living (II §6, Guide). Kind and true words are still wholesome; what the path factor names is the refraining. Right effort is energy, working as the four supreme efforts. Right mindfulness is mindfulness, as the four foundations. Right concentration is one-pointedness, which the suttas define by the four jhānas (Guide to VII §30; SN 45.8).

Eight factors, eight distinct mental factors. The count matters most at livelihood. If right livelihood were only right speech and right action done for money, the path would have seven factors, not eight.Where teachers differed. The Atthasālinī (CS §301) gives livelihood its own work: killing or lying done for a living, as by a hunter or a bribed witness, is wrong livelihood, and abstaining from it is right livelihood; the same deeds done for sport are wrong action or wrong speech.
