The elder Mahāsīva drew the line elsewhere: for him wrong livelihood proper is getting one’s requisites by trickery, and the deeds themselves, for gain or not, are wrong action and speech.Comparison: is right speech mental or material? For the Theravāda the abstinences are mental factors (II §6), and the Kathāvatthu argues against the thesis that the path is matter (Kv X.2). The thesis was held, so the commentary says, by the Mahīsāsakas, Sammitīyas and Mahāsaṅghikas (CS §§573–575). The Manual’s insistence that right speech is an abstinence, a cetasika, takes a side in an old debate.

Four senses of “path”

The word path does four different jobs in the Abhidhamma, and the claims of this reading hold only for the sense they are made in.

  1. The path condition. Here a path is whatever leads somewhere, to the happy states, to the woeful states, or to Nibbāna. The Manual counts twelve path factors: the eight right ones and four wrong ones, wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort and wrong concentration (VII §17). Wrong view is the factor wrong view; the other three are initial application, energy and one-pointedness in an unwholesome citta. All four arise together in a citta rooted in greed and accompanied by wrong view (Dhs §§365–398). The suttas do speak of wrong speech, action and livelihood, and even of wrong mindfulness (MN 117, mn117:35.7–35.11). The Abhidhamma counts none of them as a path factor of its own. The first three are unwholesome conduct, not separate mental factors. Mindfulness is only ever beautiful (Guide to VII §17). The commentaries take “wrong mindfulness” as a name for the unwholesome mental states together, not for one factor (Papañcasūdanī on MN 8, CS §83; Ledi Sayadaw, Paramatthadīpanī, CS §163; commentarial). This is the sense of the path condition, one of the twenty-four conditions of Chapter VIII (VIII §11).
  2. The requisites of enlightenment. The eight right factors are the last of the seven sets of thirty-seven requisites, and there they may be mundane or supramundane (VII §§30, 33).
  3. The fourth noble truth. In the teaching of the noble truths the path is only the eight factors as they arise in the four supramundane path cittas, the lokuttaralokuttara · supramundane beyond the world: the four paths, four fruitions and Nibbāna moments of awakening (Guide to VII §38). So on this count the path factors of an ordinary good moment, mundane right view and the rest, belong with the truth of suffering: conditioned, of the round, still to be fully understood.
  4. The path citta. The whole citta of that moment, maggamagga · path (citta) a supramundane citta that arises once, cutting defilements, with Nibbāna as object. On the Manual’s strict count only its eight factors are the fourth truth; the citta itself and its other factors fall outside all four truths, and so do the fruitions that follow (VII §40 and Guide).

The first sense is the widest and the fourth the narrowest. The surprise is in the third: in the teaching of the noble truths, kind and mindful moments are not yet the path of the four truths, though they are the path in the second sense.Not every text counts so strictly. Ledi Sayadaw calls the mundane factors “path” in a looser sense (Paramatthadīpanī, CS §165).

Right view first, virtue first

The list starts from view, and MN 117 says why: right view comes first (mn117:4.1). It knows wrong view as wrong and right view as right, and so for intention, speech, action and livelihood. Each of those five is twofold, says the sutta: one kind is tainted, meritorious and ripens in further existence; the other is noble, taint-free and supramundane, a factor of the path (mn117:6.3–6.4). And beside each of those five run three others: right view, right effort and right mindfulness (mn117:9.3, 15.3, 21.3, 27.3, 33.3). One sees the wrong, strives to drop it, and stays mindful while one does.

The suttas also gather the path into three trainings, sikkhāsikkhā · training one of the three trainings, virtue, concentration and wisdom, under which the eight path factors are grouped. Speech, action and livelihood fall under virtue; effort, mindfulness and concentration under concentration; view and intention under wisdom. The nun Dhammadinnā puts it with care: the path is included in the three trainings, not the trainings in the path (MN 44, mn44:11.2–11.5).

The trainings are developed in the opposite order to the list. The Manual’s seven purifications start from purification of virtue (IX §28) and of mind, which is access and absorption concentration (IX §29), and the last five belong to wisdom (IX §22, Guide; Table 9.2). The first six are mundane; the seventh is the supramundane paths. Neither order is wrong. The list follows what leads; the training follows what supports what.The commentary on MN 117 counts five kinds of right view: insight, the view that beings own their kamma, and the right views of the path, of the fruit, and of reviewing (Papañcasūdanī, CS §142). This is commentarial.

Before the path: the factors one at a time

In ordinary life the factors turn up a few at a time. The abstinences are the clearest case. On the Manual’s account a mundane abstinence arises only in a sense-sphere wholesome citta, and only on an occasion of actually refraining, when a chance to do the wrong is there (II §6 and §15, with the Guides). It arises singly: if you hold back from a lie, right speech is present and the other two are not. And it reaches only the wrong in view: refraining from taking this life is abstinence from killing, not from stealing (II §15, Guide). Mundane abstinences never arise in the sublime cittas of jhāna, whose object is the counterpart sign and offers nothing to refrain from, nor in an arahant’s functional cittas, since an arahant has no tendency left to hold back (II §15, Guide).

The other factors come and go in the same way. Giving with understanding has five: view, intention, effort, mindfulness and concentration, with no abstinence, since nothing is being refrained from. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī itself counts a five-factored path in that first wholesome citta of the sense sphere (Dhs §§58, 89). Without understanding there are four, and right view is missing (Dhs §147). A mundane second jhāna has four again, now without initial application (Dhs §161). A rootless citta, such as eye-consciousness, has none (VII §22).

The Manual sums this up in a line: in the mundane, the factors occur according to circumstances in the course of the six purifications (VII §33). The commentaries call this the preliminary stage of the path, pubbabhāga-maggapubbabhāga-magga · preliminary path a commentarial name for the path factors as developed in ordinary moments, before the supramundane path: before the path the factors arise at different moments with different objects (Sammohavinodanī, CS §205); one abstains from lying with one citta and from slander with another (Atthasālinī, CS §299). On the strict count it is not yet the fourth truth. It is how the fourth truth is approached.

At the path: all together, in one moment

At the path moment the scattered factors arise together, in one citta, and all of them take one object, Nibbāna (IX §34; Guide to I §§30–31). The three abstinences are there at once, and each works in full: right speech now cuts the disposition to every kind of wrong speech, right action to every wrong deed, right livelihood to every wrong livelihood (II §15, Guide). This is abstinence by eradication, samucchedavirati, the only one of the three kinds of abstinence that is supramundane (II §6, Guide).

How many factors that is depends on the jhāna the path corresponds to. A path at the level of the first jhāna has all eight. From the second jhāna up initial application is absent, and with it right intention, so the path has seven (II §19; Guide to VII §§32–33). One who reaches the path by bare insight, without jhāna, has a path at the level of the first jhāna (Guide to I §§30–31), and the commentaries draw the conclusion: such a path has all eight factors (Vism XXI §798; Atthasālinī, CS §350). For such a meditator the Guide counts momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi), as strong as access, as purification of mind (Guide to IX §29).Where teachers differed: what fixes the jhāna level. The Guide reports three views of the ancient teachers: the jhāna used as a basis, the jhāna examined by insight, or, for one who has mastered several, the meditator’s wish (Guide to I §§30–31). The commentaries add their own answer: whichever view one follows, it is the final insight before the path that settles the factors (Vism XXI §797; Atthasālinī, CS §350).

Two or three moments of fruition follow the path (IX §34). They have the same factors, now as results, the moral purity the path has won (II §15, Guide). They are not the fourth truth. On the Manual’s strict count the fruitions fall outside all four (Guide to VII §40).Eight or five? The canon counts two ways. The Vibhaṅga runs the supramundane path once as eightfold and again as five-factored, leaving the three abstinences among the “associated” states (Vibh 11, §§490–503). The Kathāvatthu, though, rejects the thesis that the path is five-factored (Kv XX.5); its commentary says the Mahīsāsakas held it, taking right speech, action and livelihood to be matter. The Sammohavinodanī reconciles the two: there is no five-factored supramundane path; the five-count shows the five factors that do the work of abandoning when one wrong is given up. A disputant who will not accept this, it says, should be sent off to drink his gruel (CS §493).

The path in practice

MN 117’s three strands can be read as a practice. Know the wrong as wrong and the right as right; that is view. Make the effort to drop the one and take up the other; that is effort. Do it mindfully; that is mindfulness. Most of the time you will meet the virtue factors in the precepts: the commentators call keeping them abstinence by undertaking, still mundane, and it happens only at the moment you actually hold back (II §6, Guide).

The tree of purification is this same path unfolding in time, from the roots of virtue to the crown of knowledge. In each path moment its factors stand together, for that one moment; at the fourth its work is complete.

To reflect on. On the Abhidhamma's analysis, as already in the suttas' definition (SN 45.8), right speech is not the kind word but the holding back of a wrong one. When did you last notice that moment of refraining, and what else was present in it?

Sources. SN 45.8, Vibhaṅga Sutta: each factor defined (SuttaCentral sn45.8); SN 56.11, the middle way (sn56.11). MN 117, Mahācattārīsaka Sutta: right view first; mundane and noble factors; view, effort and mindfulness around the first five (mn117). MN 44, Cūḷavedalla Sutta: the path in the three trainings (mn44). MN 149: conduct already purified (mn149). Dhammasaṅgaṇī §§58, 89, 147, 161: the path factors of ordinary wholesome cittas (ds2.1.1). Vibhaṅga 11, §§490–503: the path counted as eightfold and as five-factored (vb11). Kathāvatthu X.2 and XX.5 (kv10.2, kv20.5), with its commentary, CS §§573–575, 872–875. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma: VII §17 and §22, VII §§30–33 with the Guides, VIII §11, VII §§38–40 with the Guides, Table 7.3; II §§6, 15, 19 with the Guides; Guide to I §§30–31; IX §§22, 28–29, 34 with the Guides, Table 9.2. Commentaries: Sammohavinodanī on Vibh 4, CS §205 (many moments before, one at the path) and on Vibh 11, CS §493 (the five-factored round); Atthasālinī CS §299 (one abstinence at a time), §301 (right livelihood) and §350 (the path's jhāna level); Papañcasūdanī on MN 8, CS §83 (wrong mindfulness), and on MN 117, CS §142 (five right views); Ledi Sayadaw, Paramatthadīpanī, CS §§163, 165; Visuddhimagga XXI §§797–798.

The tree of purification

The path of insight pictured as a tree: the soil, the roots, a trunk of seven purifications, the knowledges that climb it, and the single moment at its crown.

Manual IX §§22–44 (insight: purifications, knowledges, emancipations, individuals, attainments)

The Visuddhimagga, Buddhaghosa’s path of purification, pictures the path of insight as something that grows. The things to be understood, the aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, truths and dependent origination, are the soil. Purification of virtue and purification of mind are the roots. The five purifications of wisdom are the trunk (Vism XIV §430). The Visuddhimagga stops there; the tree, and liberation at its crown, are this site’s way of drawing the image out.

The image is useful because it is organic. Nothing on the trunk can grow without the roots, and nothing at the crown without the trunk.

Seven purifications

The scheme of seven purifications comes from a sutta in which Sāriputta and Puṇṇa compare the path to a relay of seven chariots: each takes the traveller only as far as the next, and the last arrives (MN 24). The commentaries make it the frame for insight.

Purification of virtue is restraint of body and speech. Purification of mind is concentration, access or absorption, the work of calm. For one who goes by pure insight, without calm first, the Guide reckons momentary concentration, as steady as access, in its place (Guide to IX §29); the sub-commentary on the Visuddhimagga already pairs pure insight with momentary concentration; Ten knowledges, one by one has more. These two are the roots; the five that follow are the trunk.

Purification of view is seeing mind and matter, nāmanāma · mind mind: citta with its factors, which “bend” toward objects; the word also means “name” and rūpa, as they are, with no being or person behind them. Purification by overcoming doubt is seeing their conditions, in the present and in the past and future. Purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path is the critical one: the meditator, seeing rise and fall, meets brilliant experiences, light, rapture, tranquillity, strong faith, and must recognise that attachment to them is not the path.The Visuddhimagga lists ten such “imperfections of insight”. They are not bad in themselves; they are dangerous because they are so attractive that they stop the work.

Purification by knowledge and vision of the way is the run of insight knowledges below, from rise and fall to conformity. Purification by knowledge and vision is the path itself.

The knowledges

The Manual lists ten insight knowledges along the trunk. Comprehension sees dhammas in terms of the three marks, tilakkhaṇatilakkhaṇa · the three marks impermanence, suffering and non-self: the marks that insight sees. Knowledge of rise and fall sees each one arising and ceasing. Knowledge of dissolution sees only the ceasing. Then knowledges of fearfulness, of danger and of disenchantment: what dissolves so constantly cannot be a refuge. Then desire for deliverance, reflection, and equanimity toward formations, a balanced, unshakeable seeing of everything conditioned. Last comes conformity, which adapts the mind to the path. Ten knowledges, one by one takes each in turn, and notes that the Paṭisambhidāmagga counts fear, danger and disenchantment as one knowledge, and the next three as one.

Three doors

Insight that is about to break through dwells on one mark more than the others, and that mark is the door it enters by. Dwelling on impermanence, it enters by the signless. Dwelling on suffering, by the desireless. Dwelling on not-self, by the void, emptiness. The doors differ; what lies beyond them does not.

The crown

At the top of the tree a single process carries the change. After conformity comes change-of-lineage, gotrabhūgotrabhū · change-of-lineage the javana that leaves the sense-sphere lineage for jhāna, or turns to Nibbāna, the first citta in the process to take Nibbāna as its object, the moment that passes from the worldling’s lineage to the noble one’s. Before the three higher paths this moment is called cleansing, vodāna, since the meditator is already noble (Guide to IX §34). Then the path citta, maggamagga · path (citta) a supramundane citta that arises once, cutting defilements, with Nibbāna as object, for one moment only, with the factors of the noble eightfold path all present together; it cuts the fetters it is able to cut. Then two or three moments of fruition, phalaphala · fruition the supramundane resultant citta that follows its path, also taking Nibbāna as object, enjoying the same object: three in one of keen faculties, whose process skips the preparation moment, two in others (Guide to IV §22). Then the life-continuum resumes, and the person is different for good.

Four paths cut ten fetters, saṃyojanasaṃyojana · fetter one of ten defilements that bind to rebirth; the four paths cut them. Stream-entry cuts three: identity view, doubt, and clinging to rules and rites. Once-returning ends the gross forms of sensual desire and ill will, leaving only subtle ones (Paṭisambhidāmagga ps1.1:349; Vism XXII §830); in the Manual’s words, lust, hatred and delusion are attenuated (IX §39). Non-returning cuts sensual desire and ill will. Arahantship cuts the last five: desire for fine-material and immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness and ignorance. Each of the four kinds of person this makes is followed in Four noble persons.

One moment is enough because of what a path does. It does not add anything. It removes the conditions for certain cittas ever arising again, and from then on they simply do not come.

To reflect on. Insight is said to enter liberation by one of three doors, set by whichever mark it dwelt on most: impermanence, suffering or not-self. Which of the three is most alive for you, and what keeps the others at a distance?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, IX §§22–44. Visuddhimagga XIV–XXII: the soil, roots and trunk (XIV §430, CS), the purifications and the knowledges. MN 24, Rathavinīta Sutta: seven purifications as a relay of chariots. Paṭisambhidāmagga I.1, the once-returner's emergence from the gross fetters of sensual lust and aversion (SuttaCentral ps1.1:349.1–349.2), as taken up in Visuddhimagga XXII §§827, 830 (CS). SN 22.59, Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta: the characteristic of not-self.

Ten knowledges, one by one

What insight looks at, the groundwork it needs, and the ten knowledges the Manual lists, from comprehension to conformity, each with what it sees and why it gives way to the next.

Manual IX §§22–37 with the Guides and Table 9.2 (the marks, purification of view and of overcoming doubt, the ten insight knowledges, the imperfections, insight leading to emergence, the three doors)

The tree of purification gave the frame: seven purifications, and within them ten insight knowledges. This reading takes the knowledges one at a time: what each looks at, what it sees, and why it gives way to the next. The Manual lists them in a single line (IX §25) and opens them out in a few paragraphs (IX §§32–34); the Guide and the Visuddhimagga fill in the rest.

What insight looks at

Insight, vipassanāvipassanā · insight seeing mind and matter as impermanent, suffering and non-self, is wisdom that sees. Its field is narrow by design. It looks only at formations, the conditioned dhammas of the three planes: mind and matter, citta, its factors and rūpa. It does not take concepts as its object, and it does not take Nibbāna (IX §32; Guide to III §18). What it sees in formations is their three marks, tilakkhaṇatilakkhaṇa · the three marks impermanence, suffering and non-self: the marks that insight sees: impermanence, suffering and non-self (IX §23). For each mark there is a contemplation (IX §24), and each knowledge below is a stage in how clearly the marks are seen.

The Manual gives each mark a single word. Formations are impermanent because they are destroyed (khaya), suffering because they are a source of fear (bhaya), non-self because they have no core (asāraka) (IX §32). The Guide spells out each word.

Groundwork: view and doubt

Two purifications come before any of the ten. Under them lie purification of virtue and purification of mind, the roots of the tree, which the tree describes.

Purification of view discerns mind and matter by their characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause (IX §30). It takes its name from the view it clears away, the view of a self (Guide to IX §30). The Visuddhimagga sums up what is seen: only mind and matter, no being and no person (Vism XVIII §672). The Visuddhimagga gives two ways in. A meditator who already has jhāna starts from the factors of the jhāna; one who goes by pure insight starts from the four elements (Vism XVIII §§663–664). Either way the result is the same: only mind and matter, no being.Where teachers differ: calm first, or pure insight. The canon knows more than one route: Ānanda lists calm before insight, insight before calm, the two yoked together, and a mind that settles after restlessness about the Dhamma (AN 4.170). The Visuddhimagga defines purification of mind as the attainments with their access (Vism XVIII §662), and names a pure-insight vehicle that begins from the four elements (§664). That the pure-insight meditator’s concentration is momentary concentration, khaṇika-samādhikhaṇika-samādhi · momentary concentration concentration that holds each passing event in turn; the term is in the Visuddhimagga; the Guide reckons it as purification of mind for the pure-insight meditator, is said in Dhammapāla’s sub-commentary (on Vism I §§3–4); the term itself is in the Visuddhimagga (Vism IV §72, VIII §235). The Guide reckons it, being as steady as access, as purification of mind for one who goes by dry insight (Guide to IX §29). The Mahasi school in Burma teaches insight in this way (Mahasi Sayadaw, The Progress of Insight).

Purification by overcoming doubt discerns the conditions of that same mind and matter (IX §31). Here the meditator brings dependent origination to what was just seen. Mind and matter are seen to have causes, neither none nor a lord’s; the body is produced by ignorance, craving, clinging and kamma and sustained by nutriment; and as now, so in the past and the future (Vism XIX §§678–679; Guide to IX §31). Doubts about the self in the three times fall away (Vism XIX §§678–691).The Visuddhimagga calls a meditator who has reached this point a “lesser stream-enterer”, with a fixed destiny, which the sub-commentary reads as a good one so long as this knowledge is not lost (Vism XIX §691). The name is commentarial; it is not a path, and the person is still a worldling.

These two are not counted among the ten. They are the ground the ten stand on.

The ten in order

The Manual names ten knowledges: comprehension, rise and fall, dissolution, fear, danger, disenchantment, desire for deliverance, reflection, equanimity about formations, and conformity (IX §25). The first two belong to the fifth purification, of what is and is not the path; the rest, beginning with rise and fall again, to the sixth, the purification of the way (IX §§32–33; Table 9.2). Rise and fall is counted once but appears twice, first tender and then mature.Where teachers differ: ten, or sixteen. The Manual counts ten knowledges, and the Visuddhimagga has the same knowledges: comprehension and rise and fall in XX, then eight knowledges and conformity as the nine of the way (Vism XXI §737). The “sixteen knowledges” familiar from modern teaching add defining mind and matter and discerning conditions before the ten, and change-of-lineage, path, fruition and reviewing after. Every item is in Vism XVIII–XXII; the count of sixteen is a later arrangement used in modern teaching, for example in Mahasi Sayadaw’s The Progress of Insight, not a number found in the Visuddhimagga. The “sixteen kinds of knowledge-conduct” named for the attainment of cessation are a different list (Vism XXIII §868).

1. Comprehension

The knowledge of comprehension, sammasana-ñāṇasammasana-ñāṇa · comprehension the first insight knowledge, assigning the three marks to formations gathered in groups, still works with groups. The meditator gathers the formations already discerned into the five aggregates, all materiality whether past, future or present, inner or outer, gross or subtle, and so on, and the same for feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. Then each group is assigned the three marks (IX §32 with the Guide).

It works by duration, continuity and moment. By duration, one starts with a whole lifetime and shortens the span step by step, to a decade, a year, a day, an hour, until even the formations of a single step are seen as impermanent, suffering and non-self (Guide to IX §32; Vism XX §§692–722). It works on formations in groups, by spans of time, before the knowledges that watch present formations arise and pass.

2. Rise and fall, tender

The knowledge of rise and fall, udayabbaya-ñāṇaudayabbaya-ñāṇa · rise and fall knowledge seeing dhammas arise and pass; first tender, then mature, turns to formations in the present. It sees them arise and pass in two ways: by condition, as each arises with the arising of its conditions and ceases with their ceasing; and by moment, as they are generated and break up now (IX §32; Vism XX §§723–731).Ledi Sayadaw, in his commentary on the Manual (Paramatthadīpanī, CS §171), holds that a disciple cannot see the rise and fall of single moments of mind and matter; “by moment” must include short runs of them.

It is in this first, tender phase that the imperfections arise.

The ten imperfections

As rise and fall gains momentum, ten experiences arise that the Visuddhimagga calls the imperfections of insight, vipassanupakkilesavipassanupakkilesa · imperfections of insight ten bright experiences, such as light and zest, that arise with early rise and fall and can be clung to (Vism XX §§732–736). In its order they are: light, knowledge, zest, tranquillity, happiness, resolution, exertion, mindfulness, equanimity, and attachment. The Manual’s verse lists the same ten in a different order (IX §32).

What is strange about the list is that most of it is good. Zest, tranquillity, mindfulness and equanimity are wholesome factors; knowledge is wisdom itself. The Visuddhimagga says plainly that the first nine are imperfections not because they are unwholesome but because they are a basis for defilement: each can be taken up by view (“my light has arisen”), by conceit (“what a fine light”) or by craving, relishing it, so that ten become thirty (Vism XX §735). Only the tenth, attachment, nikantinikanti · attachment the subtle liking for insight's bright experiences; the tenth imperfection, is both a defilement and a basis for defilement, and so subtle that it is hard to recognise as one (Vism XX §§734–735).

They come, the Visuddhimagga adds, only to one who is practising rightly; not to one who has given up, nor to one who has already reached a path (Vism XX §732). The danger is a simple misreading: taking the light and the calm for the goal, and stopping there. The Visuddhimagga describes the meditator who decides “I have reached path and fruit”, leaves the meditation subject and sits relishing the light (Vism XX §733). The canon knows the problem under another name: restlessness about the Dhamma, a mind stirred up by its own good states, which the Paṭisambhidāmagga works out as these ten (AN 4.170; Paṭis, Yuganaddhakathā, quoted at Vism XX §732).

Purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path is the answer (IX §32). The meditator sees the ten for what they are, impermanent, suffering and non-self, not mine, not I, not my self, and so knows: this is not the path; insight free of these is. The Visuddhimagga makes both steps explicit, seeing them by the marks and then marking path from not-path (Vism XX §736).

The way: from mature rise and fall to conformity

With the imperfections seen through, the sixth purification begins: nine knowledges, from rise and fall to conformity (IX §33).

2 again. Rise and fall, mature

The same knowledge, practised again, now without the imperfections, and stronger and clearer (Guide to IX §33). The Visuddhimagga says what had been hiding the marks: continuity hid impermanence, the shifting of postures hid suffering, and the appearance of a solid mass hid non-self (Vism XXI §§737–740).

3. Dissolution

As the knowledge grows keen, formations show up quickly, and mindfulness comes to rest on their destruction and cessation alone. This is the knowledge of dissolution, bhaṅga-ñāṇabhaṅga-ñāṇa · dissolution insight knowledge that attends only to the ending of formations (Vism XXI §741; Guide to IX §33). The meditator sees not only the object dissolving but also the knowing of it, and infers that it was so in the past and will be so in the future (Vism XXI §§741–745). Among its benefits the Visuddhimagga lists the giving up of attachment to life and, notably, fearlessness (Vism XXI §749).

4–6. Fear, danger, disenchantment

Then three knowledges that sound like feelings and are not.

The knowledge of fear, or of appearance as fearful, finds every dissolving formation, of whatever realm and time, a thing to be feared (Vism XXI §750; Guide to IX §33). The knowledge of danger finds no shelter or refuge anywhere in becoming: whatever arises is a danger, and safety is in non-arising, which is Nibbāna (Vism XXI §§752–753). The knowledge of disenchantment, nibbidānibbidā · disenchantment turning away from formations, seen as fearful and dangerous; an insight knowledge, follows from that: the mind turns away from formations of every kind and finds no pleasure in them (Vism XXI §754; Guide to IX §33).

The Visuddhimagga is careful here. The knowledge of fear does not itself fear. It only judges, as a man standing by three pits of glowing embers judges that whoever falls in will burn, without being in them or afraid of them (Vism XXI §751). The fear is in what is seen, the fearfulness of formations, not in the seer. These are judgements, knowledges, and the texts treat them that way.Where teachers differ: the “dark night”. Some modern teachers group the knowledges from dissolution to reflection as a hard passage. The name “dark night” for it is best known from Daniel Ingram (Mastering the Core Teachings of the Buddha, 2008; 2nd ed. 2018), who takes it from the Christian mystics. It is not a Pāli term; the Visuddhimagga and its commentaries give these knowledges no name for hardship. The Visuddhimagga’s reading is that they are judgements, and that dissolution brings fearlessness (Vism XXI §§749, 751).

The Paṭisambhidāmagga counts the three as one knowledge with three names, and the Visuddhimagga agrees (Vism XXI §755).

7–9. Desire for deliverance, reflection, equanimity

Seeing formations so, the mind clings to none of them and wants to be free of the whole field: the knowledge of desire for deliverance, muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇamuñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa · desire for deliverance insight knowledge that wants release from the whole field of formations. The Visuddhimagga compares it with a fish in a net, or a frog in a snake’s mouth (Vism XXI §756).

To get free, the meditator looks again at the same formations and lays the three marks on them in many ways. This is the knowledge of reflection, paṭisaṅkhā-ñāṇapaṭisaṅkhā-ñāṇa · reflection insight knowledge that re-examines formations by the three marks, as the means of release: re-examination as the means of release (Guide to IX §33; Vism XXI §§757–759).

Formations are now seen as void of self and of anything belonging to a self (Vism XXI §760), and the mind, dropping both fear and delight, looks on them evenly, neither drawn nor repelled. This is equanimity about formations, saṅkhārupekkhāsaṅkhārupekkhā · equanimity about formations insight knowledge that looks on all formations evenly, with neither fear nor delight (Vism XXI §767; Guide to IX §33). The Visuddhimagga gives it a long treatment, with the many ways in which formations are seen as void (Vism XXI §§760–781). It also says something useful about its shape. If this knowledge sees Nibbāna as peace, it moves on toward the path; if not, it turns back to formations, again and again, like a ship’s crow released to find land that returns to the mast when it sees none (Vism XXI §767).

Again the Paṭisambhidāmagga counts these three as one knowledge, and again the Visuddhimagga follows it (Vism XXI §§778–781). The Paṭisambhidāmagga’s own list is shorter still, with no separate conformity; the ten unfold it.

10. Conformity

The last is conformity, anulomaanuloma · conformity the javana that fits the mind to what follows, just before change-of-lineage, also called adaptation: insight in the last two or three sense-sphere javanas before change-of-lineage, still taking formations by one of the three marks (IX §34). The Visuddhimagga likens it to a king who agrees with his eight judges and with the ancient law: it agrees with the eight knowledges before it and with the thirty-seven aids to awakening to come (Vism XXI §804).

Emergence, and the path

When equanimity about formations and conformity are full grown they are called insight leading to emergence, the peak of insight (IX §34). The Visuddhimagga includes change-of-lineage in that peak as well (Vism XXI §782). The path is “emergence” because it rises out of formations to take Nibbāna as object, and out of the defilements (Guide to IX §34).

The rest is one process. Two or three moments of insight, called preparation, access and conformity, are followed by change-of-lineage, gotrabhūgotrabhū · change-of-lineage the javana that leaves the sense-sphere lineage for jhāna, or turns to Nibbāna, the first citta to take Nibbāna as object; then a single moment of path; then fruition and reviewing (IX §34). Change-of-lineage belongs to neither the sixth purification nor the seventh (Table 9.2; Vism XXII §806). The details are in The tree of purification, and what each of the four paths cuts is in Four noble persons.

Three doors

At its peak, insight settles on one of the three marks, and that mark is its door (IX §35). Contemplating non-self, which lets go of clinging to a self, is the door of the void. Contemplating impermanence, which lets go of the false sign of permanence, is the door of the signless. Contemplating suffering, which lets go of craving’s longing, is the door of the desireless. The commentaries add that faith leans toward impermanence, concentration toward suffering and wisdom toward non-self (Guide to IX §35).

The path is then named by its door: the void, the signless or the desireless emancipation, and the fruit takes the same name (IX §36). In later attainments of fruition, the name follows the insight used that time (IX §37). But by their object and their own quality, every path and fruit is all three at once, since Nibbāna is void, signless and desireless alike (Guide to IX §37).The Visuddhimagga records that the Abhidhamma books themselves name only two kinds of path, the void and the desireless. By the strict method, it explains, insight still has formations as its sign and so is not strictly signless; the threefold naming, from the Paṭisambhidāmagga, holds in a looser sense (Vism XXI §770).

To reflect on. The Visuddhimagga says the knowledge of fear does not itself fear: it judges that whatever dissolves is no refuge, as a man looking at pits of embers judges that whoever falls in will burn. What is the difference between seeing that something is dangerous and being afraid of it?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, IX §§22–37 with the Guide, and Table 9.2; Guide to IX §29 (the two vehicles and momentary concentration). Visuddhimagga XVIII §§662–677 (purification of view; the two vehicles at §§663–664), XIX §§678–691 (overcoming doubt), XX §§692–736 (comprehension, rise and fall, the ten imperfections), XXI §§737–805 (the knowledges of the way; §751 on fear; §§755 and 778–781 on the knowledges counted as one; §767 on equanimity turning back; §782 on insight leading to emergence), XXII §806 (change-of-lineage). Paragraph numbers are those of the Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana edition. Paṭisambhidāmagga, the list of knowledges (SuttaCentral ps1.0) and the treatise on emancipation, which counts fear, danger and disenchantment as one knowledge, and desire for deliverance, reflection and equanimity as one (SuttaCentral ps1.5). MN 24, Rathavinīta Sutta: the seven purifications as a relay of chariots (SuttaCentral). AN 4.170, Yuganaddha Sutta: four ways to arahantship, including insight before calm and restlessness about the Dhamma (SuttaCentral). Paṭisambhidāmagga, the treatise on the pair yoked together: restlessness about the Dhamma worked out as ten (SuttaCentral ps2.1). Dhammapāla's sub-commentary on the Visuddhimagga, on Vism I §§3–4: momentary concentration as the pure-insight meditator's concentration (sub-commentarial). Ledi Sayadaw, Paramatthadīpanī, CS §171: what 'by moment' can mean for a disciple. Modern: Mahasi Sayadaw, The Progress of Insight, tr. Nyanaponika Thera (Buddhist Publication Society); Daniel Ingram, Mastering the Core Teachings of the Buddha (2008; 2nd ed. 2018).

Thirty-seven requisites, fourteen states

The Buddha gathered his teaching on practice into seven sets: thirty-seven items in all. The Abhidhamma counts what they are made of and finds fourteen states, with energy and mindfulness doing most of the work.

Manual VII §§24–33 with the Guide and Table 7.3 (the requisites and their fourteen states)

Near the end of his life, the Buddha reminded the monks of what he had taught them to practise: seven sets of qualities, thirty-seven items in all (DN 16). The suttas occasionally call such qualities bodhipakkhiyā dhammābodhipakkhiyā dhammā · 37 requisites the suttas' 37 aids to awakening, which reduce to 14 states, the states on the side of awakening, or the requisites of enlightenment; later tradition made it the name for exactly these thirty-seven. They are requisites because they lead to the knowledge of the four paths (VII §24).

The noble eightfold path took the last of the seven sets on its own. This reading takes all seven, and then does what the Abhidhamma always does with a list: asks what it is made of.

The seven sets

Four foundations of mindfulness, satipaṭṭhānasatipaṭṭhāna · foundation of mindfulness mindfulness set up on one of four fields: body, feelings, states of mind, mental objects; together, right mindfulness: mindfulness set up on the body, on feelings, on states of mind, and on mental objects, such as the hindrances, the aggregates, the sense bases, the factors of enlightenment and the four truths (§24). It is one practice applied to four fields, and the Guide equates it with right mindfulness.

Four supreme efforts, sammappadhānasammappadhāna · supreme effort energy in four tasks: discard arisen evil, prevent unarisen evil, develop unarisen good, increase arisen good; together, right effort: the effort to abandon evil states that have arisen, to keep out those that have not, to bring about good states not yet arisen, and to increase those that have (§25). One mental factor, energy, doing four jobs; together they are right effort.

Four means to accomplishment, iddhipādaiddhipāda · means to accomplishment desire, energy, consciousness or investigation, when it leads the mind toward the goal of the teaching: desire, energy, consciousness and investigation (§26). They are the four predominants, adhipatiadhipati · predominance the one factor leading a citta: desire, energy, citta or investigation; or, as object predominance, an object held in high regard, the factors that can lead a whole citta, but they count as means to accomplishment only when they lead it toward the goal of the teaching.

Five faculties and five powers, indriyaindriya · faculty a dhamma that governs its own domain; 22 faculties, and condition 16 and balabala · power a state unshaken by its opposite; nine, among them faith, energy and wisdom: faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration and wisdom, twice (§27–28). As faculties they govern their own fields: deciding, exerting, noticing, steadying, discerning. As powers they are the same five, now too strong to be shaken by their opposites. The Guide adds the teaching on balance: faith with wisdom, so that faith is not blind and wisdom not merely clever; energy with concentration, so that the mind is neither restless nor sluggish; and mindfulness always, since it is never in excess.

Seven factors of enlightenment, bojjhaṅgabojjhaṅga · enlightenment factor seven: mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, zest, tranquillity, concentration, equanimity: mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, zest, tranquillity, concentration and equanimity (§29). Investigation, energy and zest lift a sluggish mind; tranquillity, concentration and equanimity calm an excited one; mindfulness watches both. Equanimity here is the mental factor of neutrality, not a neutral feeling.

Eight path factors, maggaṅgamaggaṅga · path factors twelve: eight right factors and four wrong ones; the eight right ones in path consciousness are the truth of the path: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration (§30).

Fourteen states

Now the Abhidhamma’s move. Each of the thirty-seven is a mental state the earlier chapters have already counted, under a different name. Right view is wisdom. Right intention is initial application turned toward renunciation, goodwill and harmlessness. Right speech, action and livelihood are the three abstinences. The four foundations of mindfulness are one factor, mindfulness; the four supreme efforts are one factor, energy (§31). Collected, the thirty-seven are fourteen states: thirteen mental factors and consciousness itself (§32).

The counts are the point (§33). Energy serves nine times: four efforts, a means to accomplishment, a faculty, a power, a factor of enlightenment and right effort. Mindfulness serves eight times, wisdom five, concentration four and faith twice. The other nine serve once each: desire, consciousness, initial application, zest, tranquillity, equanimity and the three abstinences. The path, seen this way, is not thirty-seven separate virtues. It is a handful of qualities, named again at each stage and in each use.

Where they are found

At the moment of a path, all of them are present together, the Manual says, with two exceptions. Right intention is initial application, which the second and higher jhānas have left behind; zest drops away at the fourth jhāna. So a path citta of a higher jhāna lacks one or both (§33), while every bare-insight path, reached without jhāna, is at the first-jhāna level (Guide to I §§30–31), and so, by II §19, eightfold. Before that, in ordinary practice, the requisites appear in different combinations, according to the work in hand, through the six stages of purification that lead up to the path (see The tree of purification).

That is the practical lesson of the grid. No one has to cultivate thirty-seven things. Develop mindfulness and energy, balance faith with wisdom and energy with concentration, and the rest of the list fills itself in. The paths they lead to, and what each one cuts away, are followed in Four noble persons.

To reflect on. Energy turns up nine times among the thirty-seven and faith only twice. In your own practice, which do you find you have to supply most often, and which comes on its own?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, VII §§24–33 with the Guide, and Table 7.3; IX §22 (the stages of purification). DN 16 and MN 77, where the Buddha lists the seven sets; DN 22 and MN 10 on the foundations of mindfulness. SN 48.51 and DN 27, where the suttas use the term bodhipakkhiyā dhammā (SuttaCentral sn48.51, dn27); Guide to VII §24.

Four noble persons

Stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arahant: what each of the four paths cuts away for good, the kinds of person on each step, and the two attainments that only the noble know.

Manual IX §§38–44 with the Guides and Table 9.3 (the four paths, what each abandons, attainments)

The tree of purification ends at a single process: change-of-lineage, then a path citta taking Nibbāna as its object, then two or three moments of fruition. That process happens four times, and each time something is cut that never grows back. The Manual closes its account of insight by naming the four kinds of person this makes, and what each has left behind (IX §38–41).

Entering the stream

The first path is stream-entry, sotāpattisotāpatti · stream-entry the first path, entering the stream of the noble path; it ends identity view, doubt and clinging to rules and rituals. The stream is the noble eightfold path itself, which once entered leads only one way. The stream-enterer has cut the three coarsest fetters: identity view, the belief that there is a self in or behind the aggregates; doubt about the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha and the training; and clinging to rules and rituals as if they could free by themselves. With them goes any defilement strong enough to lead to a woeful rebirth. The Guide describes the result in human terms: unshakable confidence in the three jewels, and the five precepts scrupulously kept (Guide to IX §38).

Of the fourteen unwholesome mental factors, stream-entry ends four: wrong view and doubt, and, the commentaries add, envy and avarice.

What each path cuts

The Guide to these sections and Table 9.3 track the paths against three lists at once: the unwholesome factors of chapter II, the ten fetters of the suttas, and the four taints. The pattern is the same in all three. Stream-entry clears what is wrong in understanding; non-returning clears what binds to the sense world; arahantship clears everything that is left.

The second path ends no factor outright. It thins greed, hatred and delusion instead, as the once-returner’s section below explains.

The stream-enterer

A stream-enterer will be reborn at most seven more times, and only in the human and heavenly worlds (IX §38). The Guide names three kinds by how many births remain: the “seven-times-at-most”, sattakkhattuparamasattakkhattuparama · seven times at most a stream-enterer with at most seven more births, in the human and heavenly worlds; the one who goes “from family to family” two or three times; and the “one-seed”, reborn just once more before the goal.

The once-returner

The path of once-returning does not uproot greed, hatred and delusion, but it thins them: they still arise, but rarely and without their old grip (IX §39). In terms of the fetters, the gross forms of sensual lust and ill will fall away (Paṭisambhidāmagga; Vism XXII §830), which is why the figure hatches those two rows at the second path. The once-returner comes back to “this world” only once more. Which world that is, the commentaries do not agree. On one reading it is the human world, returned to from a heaven; on the other it is the sense-sphere world, returned to from a Brahmā world. Ledi Sayadaw, cited in the Guide, thinks the canon favours the second.

The commentary to the Puggalapaññatti counts five kinds of once-returner, by where the fruition is reached, where the next birth falls, and where final Nibbāna comes. One of them is born twice more, once in a heaven and once as a human, yet keeps the name: the human world is returned to only once (Guide to IX §39).

The non-returner

The third path ends sensual lust and ill will completely (IX §40). With them go the taint of sensual desire, the factors hatred and worry, and every form of greed that takes a sense object. The five fetters cut so far are called the lower fetters, because they bind to the lower, sensuous world. A non-returner who does not reach arahantship in this life is reborn in a fine-material world and reaches Nibbāna there, never returning to the sense sphere.

The Pure Abodes, the five highest fine-material planes of Thirty-one planes, are only for non-returners. But the Guide is careful: not every non-returner is reborn there. The texts name five kinds, by when and how the final path comes: before the midpoint of that heavenly life, after it, without exertion, with exertion, or after passing upward from realm to realm until the highest, Akaniṭṭha.

The arahant

The fourth path ends the five higher fetters: lust for fine-material and for immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance (IX §41). It destroys the last two taints, attachment to existence and ignorance, which is why the arahant is called khīṇāsavakhīṇāsava · one whose taints are destroyed the arahant, in whom the four taints have ended, one whose taints are destroyed. And it ends the last eight unwholesome factors, the eight still standing: delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, restlessness, the rest of greed, conceit, sloth and torpor. Nothing unwholesome can arise again. The arahant’s javanas are functional cittas, which act without making kamma; they have their own place in A map of the eighty-nine.

Fruition and cessation

Two attainments belong only to the noble (IX §42–44).

Fruition, phalasamāpattiphalasamāpatti · attainment of fruition a noble one's absorption in their own fruition, with Nibbāna as object, is open to all four, each to their own fruition. A noble person resolves to attain it and develops insight again from the knowledge of rise and fall; then fruition cittas run, taking Nibbāna as object. It is, the Guide says, for experiencing the bliss of Nibbāna here and now.

Cessation, nirodha-samāpattinirodha-samāpatti · attainment of cessation the temporary stopping of citta and mental factors, open only to non-returners and arahants with all eight jhānas, is open only to non-returners and arahants who have mastered all eight jhānas, and only in the sense or fine-material worlds, since the four fine-material jhānas it requires cannot be entered in the immaterial ones. The meditator enters each jhāna in turn and, emerging, sees its factors as impermanent, suffering and non-self, up to the base of nothingness. Then come four preliminary resolutions: that requisites belonging to others, kept with the meditator, come to no harm; that the meditator emerge if the Saṅgha needs them; that they emerge if the Buddha calls; and that they first check death is not due within seven days. Then the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception runs for two javanas, and the stream of consciousness stops.

On emerging, a single fruition citta arises, of non-returning or of arahantship, and the mind sinks into the life-continuum; then reviewing knowledge looks back on what happened. It is the one place in the Abhidhamma where, for a time, there is matter without mind in a being who has both.Cessation is sometimes compared with the non-percipient beings, who also have matter without mind. The difference is that cessation is entered by choice, for a set time, by one who has insight; the non-percipient birth is a result, and ends in a return to ordinary existence.

To reflect on. Stream-entry is said to end identity view, doubt and clinging to rules and rituals, yet it leaves greed, hatred and conceit in place, except in the grade that could lead to a woeful rebirth. Why might the tradition put the end of a view before the end of a passion?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, IX §38–44 with the Guide, and Table 9.3. Puggalapaññatti and its commentary: the kinds of once-returner; AN 3.86: the kinds of stream-enterer and non-returner. Visuddhimagga XXII (the four paths and what they abandon) and XXIII (fruition and cessation). Paṭisambhidāmagga I.1, the once-returner's emergence from the gross fetters of sensual lust and aversion (SuttaCentral ps1.1:349.1–349.2); Visuddhimagga XXII §§827, 830 (CS).

Looking back

One moment, every lens

The mango moment once more, read through ten of the Abhidhamma's frameworks in turn, to see how the whole system bears on a single sight.

Manual Review: I, II, III §§8–22, IV §6, VI §§9–22, VIII

A man sees a ripe mango and wants it. That moment has run through these readings since The mango and the moment. Here it is read once more, lens by lens, to see the whole system at work on one small event.

Two truths. Conventionally, “I see a mango and want it”. Ultimately: cittas, mental factors, an eye-base and a visible form, with no owner behind them. Both statements are true. The second is what the rest of the lenses examine.

Cittas. Seven kinds of citta run in the active part of the process: five-door adverting, eye-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, the javana, and registration. The javana here is greed with joy, unprompted, without wrong view. Each has its number on the map of the eighty-nine.

Factors. In each javana, the seven universals and the six occasionals are present, with the four unwholesome factors that come with every unwholesome citta, and greed. Conceit may join them; wrong view does not, in this citta. None of the beautiful factors is present.

Matter. The eye’s sensitivity and the colour of the mango are matter, each in its group of eight or more. The colour’s group lasts seventeen mind-moments, exactly the length of the process. If the man reaches for the fruit, mind-born matter moves the hand: a citta willed it. The Vibhāvinī adds that the moving comes from javanas of the mind-door processes that follow, since five-door javanas are too weak to produce intimation.

The process. Three moments of the life-continuum, five that turn to, see and settle the object, seven javanas, two of registration: the seventeen moments of a strong object at the eye door. Only the javanas make kamma.

Conditions. The mango helps the seeing as object. The eye helps it as support and as a prenascent base. Each citta helps the next by proximity. The factors of each citta help one another by conascence and mutuality. Past habits of liking mangoes help the javanas by decisive support. And each javana but the last helps the next by repetition.That is eight of the twenty-four conditions in one glance; a fuller reading, in One moment, twenty-four questions, finds twenty or more for a single javana. The Manual gathers all twenty-four under four: object, decisive support, kamma and presence.

Dependent origination. Contact, feeling, craving: three links of the wheel in a single process. The Vibhaṅga teaches the whole series within one moment of citta, and the mango moment shows why that is not a forced reading. The feeling of the sight is a result; the wanting is new.

Kamma. The volition in the greed-rooted javanas is unwholesome kamma. It is small, and it is reserve kamma, unlikely to ripen at death unless repeated until it becomes habitual. Repeated, it becomes a habit, and that habit is a decisive support for the next sight of a mango.

Planes. The cittas are all of the sense sphere. A Brahmā of the fine-material worlds has eyes and could see the mango, but the commentators say its nose, tongue and body lack sensitivity, so it could not smell, taste or touch it. A being of the immaterial worlds, with no body at all, would not have this process. The man’s plane sets what his mind can meet.

The path. The same seventeen moments are where practice works. Seeing is given. At adverting and determining, where attention turns, wise attention could have led to wholesome javanas: seeing the colour as colour, the wanting as wanting. In an arahant the javanas would be functional, merely seeing, and leave no result.

What the lenses share

Laid side by side, the ten readings agree on a few things. Every one of them describes the moment completely in its own terms. None of them needs a self to finish the account. And most of them point to the same small place, the javanas, as where something new is done.

That is what the Abhidhamma is, seen whole: not ten theories, but ten ways of looking at the same ground, each sharpening the others. The lists exist so that a single moment, like this one, can be seen clearly enough to be let go of.

To reflect on. Take one ordinary moment from today, a sound, a craving, a flash of irritation, and read it through three lenses from this essay. What does each show that the others miss?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma: I, II, III §§8–22, IV §6, VI §§9–22, VIII. Atthasālinī: the mango simile. Vibhaṅga, the Abhidhamma section on dependent origination in a single moment.

Two moments, side by side

The same ripe mango, seen twice: once wanted, once given away. Identical up to determining, the two processes part at the javanas, and everything downstream parts with them.

The previous reading looked at one moment through many lenses. This one looks at two moments through one: the same mango, seen twice. In the first moment the man wants it. In the second, a friend is hungry, and he gives it away.

Contrast is how the categories become clear. Set the two processes side by side, moment by moment, and look for where they differ.

The same, up to determining

For eight moments the two run alike. The same mango strikes the same eye. The life-continuum vibrates and is arrested in the same way. Five-door adverting turns toward it; eye-consciousness sees it; receiving, investigating and determining do their work. Every one of these is a result or merely functional. None of them is a choice. The Atthasālinī places the turn of attention, wise or unwise, at adverting and determining; what it turns into first shows in the javanas.

Seeing is never the problem.

Where they part

At the javanas the two processes part. In the first, the javanas are rooted in greed: lobhalobha · greed grasping at an object; roots eight cittas; as craving, a root of the wheel with joy, the four unwholesome universals with it, delusion hiding what the mango is. In the second, they are rooted in non-greed and non-hatred, perhaps with understanding: generosity with joy, faith, mindfulness, and the nineteen beautiful factors present in every beautiful citta.

The feeling can be the same in both: joy. That is one of the lessons of the contrast. Joy goes with opposite qualities. The roots decide what the moment is.The figure below runs both processes through the lenses of One moment, every lens, row by row, and marks where they differ. Most rows change only from the javanas on.

Everything downstream

From the javanas on, everything differs. The kamma made is unwholesome in one case and wholesome in the other. What it conditions is different: one strengthens a habit of wanting, the other a habit of giving. The link from feeling to craving is made in one process and not in the other. Even the matter produced differs: the hand that reaches to take and the hand that reaches to give are moved by different cittas, in the mind-door processes that follow.

What the contrast teaches

Three things stand out. Seeing is the same in both; the first eight moments are given. Feeling is the same in both; joy does not tell you which kind of moment you are in. And kamma is made only where the two processes differ, in seven moments of javana.

That is much of the Abhidhamma’s practical teaching in miniature. It does not ask you to stop seeing mangoes, or to stop enjoying them. It points to the seven moments where the difference is made, and asks you to watch them.

To reflect on. Take one ordinary moment of liking from today and imagine its wholesome twin. Which parts of the experience would change, and which would stay exactly the same?

Sources. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, I–V. Atthasālinī: the role of attention at adverting and determining. Papañcasūdanī (MA) on covetousness.

Other maps of the same ground

Other Indian schools also took experience apart into elements, and reached different counts. Comparing the maps shows which choices were open, and why the Theravāda made the ones it did.

Manual Introduction (other schools)

The Theravāda was not the only school to build an Abhidhamma. In northern India the Sarvāstivāda developed its own seven books, and later Vasubandhu summarised its system, often critically, in the Abhidharmakośa, a handbook much as Anuruddha’s Abhidhammattha Saṅgaha, the text of the Manual, would later be for the Theravāda. The Yogācāra school took the method further still. All three began from the same early lists and the same aim. They reached different maps.

Counting the same way

To compare the maps fairly, count the same way. If citta is counted as one element, the Theravāda list has eighty-two items in four categories: one citta, fifty-two mental factors, twenty-eight kinds of matter, and Nibbāna.

The Sarvāstivāda counted seventy-five: eleven kinds of matter, one mind, forty-six mental factors, fourteen “formations dissociated from mind”, and three unconditioned dharmas. The Yogācāra counted a hundred: eight consciousnesses, fifty-one mental factors, eleven kinds of matter, twenty-four dissociated formations, and six unconditioned.These counts are the classical summaries. Within each school, earlier texts give variant lists; the plate notes where a figure rests on secondary sources.

The differences are not arbitrary. Each marks a decision about what is real.

A fifth category

The northern lists have a category the Theravāda lacks: formations dissociated from mind. They include possession, the force that makes a dharma belong to a particular stream; the life force; the marks of arising, enduring, decaying and ceasing; and words, phrases and syllables.

The Theravāda treats most of these differently. Words and names are concepts, paññattipaññatti · concept a concept: a name, or what a name refers to, such as “chariot”, not realities. The marks of arising and decay are aspects of matter and mind, not separate things. Life is a faculty, one in matter and one in mind. Possession it does not need, because a stream is held together by conditions alone.

Time

The Sarvāstivāda’s name means “the doctrine that all exists”: its teachers held that dharmas exist in the past, present and future, and that only their activity is present. This explained how a past deed could bring a result, and how memory could know the past.

The Kathāvatthu argues against this at length. For the Theravāda, of conditioned dhammas only present ones exist. Past ones have ceased and future ones have not arisen (Kv I.6). Yet both can be objects of a present citta (Kv IX.6), and a past volition still conditions its result, as asynchronous kamma condition (VIII §14, Guide). A past kamma conditions its result without existing now, as a kamma condition across time; a memory is a present citta taking a past dhamma as its object.

The base of mind

Yogācāra added two consciousnesses below the six of the senses: a storehouse consciousness, ālaya-vijñāna, which carries the seeds of past action from moment to moment and life to life, and a defiled mind, manas, which mistakes the storehouse for a self.

The Theravāda’s bhavaṅgabhavaṅga · life-continuum the resultant citta, of the same kind as rebirth-linking, that runs between processes is often compared to it. Both explain continuity when no active process is running. The difference is instructive. For the Theravāda the bhavaṅga is a series of momentary resultant cittas and stores nothing; continuity is carried by conditions, not by a container.

The unconditioned

The Sarvāstivāda counted three unconditioned dharmas: space, and two kinds of cessation. Yogācāra counted six. The Theravāda counts one: nibbānanibbāna the unconditioned: the ending of craving; object of path and fruition. Space, for it, is in one sense a feature of matter, the gap that delimits groups (VI §4); the space left when a kasiṇa is removed, and “unentangled” space, are mere concepts (Kathāvatthu commentary on Kv VI.6). The Milindapañha pairs space with Nibbāna as the two things not born of kamma, cause or season, but the Kathāvatthu rejects the view that space is unconditioned (Kv VI.6).

That single entry is characteristic. The Theravāda list is the most economical of the three. It admits as real only what it cannot reduce further, and it reduces almost everything. Laid beside the others, its choices become visible as choices, and the reader can ask of each one what it was meant to protect.

To reflect on. The Sarvāstivāda held that dhammas exist in past, present and future; the Theravāda held that only present dhammas exist. Which view fits better with your experience of memory?

Sources. Kathāvatthu I.6: the debate on "everything exists". Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa: the seventy-five dharmas. Vasubandhu, Mahāyānaśatadharmaprakāśamukha: the hundred dharmas of Yogācāra. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma, Introduction.

Eighteen ideas

Two truths conventional, ultimate

Two ways of speaking: of persons and things, and of the ultimate dhammas they resolve into. The starting point of the Abhidhamma.

The Abhidhamma speaks in two registers. Conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) names persons, chariots and selves; it is valid for living and speaking, and it is not a lie. Ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca) speaks of dhammasdhamma an ultimate reality, bearing its own nature; not a mere name or concept: phenomena that bear their own nature (sabhāvasabhāva · own nature the nature a dhamma bears by itself, which makes it an ultimate reality rather than a concept) and cannot be analysed further. Names and the things they designate are concepts (paññattipaññatti · concept a concept: a name, or what a name refers to, such as “chariot”) and belong to the first register; the four ultimate realities belong to the second. Moving between them does not deny the world. It redescribes it so that the view of a lasting self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) finds no ground.

How the Manual presents it

The Manual opens by naming what the Abhidhamma speaks of, taken at the level of ultimate reality: four things only, citta, cetasika, rūpa and Nibbāna (I §2). Counted out, that is 89 (or 121) kinds of citta, 52 mental factors, 28 kinds of matter and the one Nibbāna. The first three are conditioned; Nibbāna alone is not.

The Guide to I §2 sets the frame. Conventional realities (sammutisammuti · convention conventional truth: speech about persons and things; true, but not ultimate) are what ordinary thought and speech refer to: beings, persons, men and women, and the seemingly stable objects of the everyday world. Ultimate realities (paramatthaparamattha · ultimate what remains after analysis: citta, cetasika, matter and Nibbāna, from parama, highest, and attha, thing) are the dhammas that have a nature of their own (sabhāvasabhāva · own nature the nature a dhamma bears by itself, which makes it an ultimate reality rather than a concept) and cannot be broken down any further. They are ultimate in two senses: as what finally exists, and as what right knowledge finally knows. The Guide likens the analysis to pressing oil out of sesame seed.

Two ways of teaching

Bodhi's Introduction to the Manual ties the two truths to two styles of teaching. The suttas use conventional speech (vohāra) and speak freely of "I", "you" and living beings; this is the figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā), adapted to its hearers. The Abhidhamma confines itself to dhammas, their characteristics, functions and relations: the literal teaching (nippariyāya-desanā). The Introduction adds that this is a difference of emphasis, not a wall: each Piṭaka uses both registers.

The suttas already know the distinction. Bhikkhunī Vajirā says that "being" is a word for a heap of formations, as "chariot" is for assembled parts (SN 5.10), and AN 2.25 contrasts a teaching whose meaning must be drawn out with one whose meaning is already drawn out. The technical pair sammutisammuti · convention conventional truth: speech about persons and things; true, but not ultimate and paramatthaparamattha · ultimate what remains after analysis: citta, cetasika, matter and Nibbāna is worked out in the Kathāvatthu and above all in the commentaries.

Concepts in their place

Concepts (paññattipaññatti · concept a concept: a name, or what a name refers to, such as “chariot”) are what is left when the four ultimates have been counted (VIII §29). The Guide to §30 sorts the meanings that concepts make known into six kinds: forms such as land and mountain, collections such as house and chariot, directions, times such as morning and month, spaces such as a well or a cave, and the signs of meditation such as the kasiṇa sign. A concept is not real in the ultimate sense, yet it can be the object of a citta (VIII §30). It also conditions mind as object and as decisive support (VIII §17). The counterpart sign of jhāna and the "beings" of loving-kindness are concepts (IX §17–18). The summary verse (VIII §32) shows a word being understood: an ear-door process hears the sound, and later mind-door processes grasp the meaning. The names themselves are sorted a second way, also into six (VIII §31): from "feeling", a name for something real, to "king's son", where neither part is real. For the long story, see the reading Names and the named.

Common misunderstandings

"Conventional" does not mean false. Saying "I" or "my bowl" is not a lie, and the Buddha used such speech throughout the suttas. What the analysis rejects is the belief that the word names a lasting, independent owner.

"Ultimate" does not mean permanent or hidden behind appearances. Every conditioned dhamma lasts a single moment of arising, standing and dissolving. "Own nature" means only that hardness is hardness and feeling is feeling, each with its own mark. It does not mean that a dhamma exists apart from conditions or in all three times. The Theravāda rejected that view, held by the Sarvāstivāda, in the Kathāvatthu (Kv I.6); see the reading Other maps of the same ground. And Nibbāna is ultimate, not a concept, even though it is mostly described by negations.

Why it matters

The Guide to I §2 notes that an untrained mind does not see the ultimates: it sees the everyday shapes that concepts lay over them. Wise attention (yoniso manasikārayoniso manasikāra · wise attention attending in a way that leads to wholesome javanas; unwise attention leads to unwholesome) is what gets beneath them. This is where insight starts. Purification of view (IX §30) is the discerning of mind and matter, nāma and rūpa, in place of "a being". The meditation subjects of calm may be concepts, but the objects of insight must be ultimate, conditioned dhammas, for only those show rise and fall.

In the texts. SN 5.10; DN 9 (Poṭṭhapāda); AN 2.25 (Neyyattha/Nītattha). The technical pair sammuti/paramattha first appears in the Kathāvatthu; the commentaries (the Aṅguttara commentary, the Visuddhimagga) and the Manual's chapter I systematize it.

To reflect on. If a person is only a convention, who is responsible for a deed?

Citta consciousness

Consciousness: one moment of knowing an object. The Abhidhamma counts 89 kinds.

Consciousness is the bare knowing of an object (ārammaṇa-vijānana); in the Dhammapada’s words, mind is the forerunner (pubbaṅgamapubbaṅgama · forerunner what goes before: the mind as forerunner of states, as in the first verse of the Dhammapada) of states. It never arises without its mental factors, and it never lasts: each citta arises, stands and dissolves in three sub-moments (uppāda, ṭhiti, bhaṅga), and conditions the next as it goes. The 89 kinds are sorted by plane (bhūmibhūmi · plane one of 31 planes of existence, each matched to a kind of mind), by kind (jātijāti · birth the arising of the aggregates in a new existence; the eleventh link, and the characteristic of matter called production: wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional), by roots and by feeling. Mind here is not a substance but a continuity (santatisantati · continuity Continuity: the renewed arising of matter in a series.) of such events, with no owner behind them.

How the Manual presents it

Chapter I sorts consciousness first by plane (I §3): 54 sense-sphere cittas, 15 fine-material, 12 immaterial and 8 supramundane, 89 in all.

The 54 break down into 12 unwholesome (8 rooted in greed, 2 in hatred, 2 in delusion; I §4–7), 18 rootless (7 unwholesome-resultant, 8 wholesome-resultant, 3 functional; I §8–11) and 24 sense-sphere beautiful (8 wholesome, 8 resultant, 8 functional; I §12–16). The fine-material cittas are five jhānas, each wholesome, resultant or functional. The immaterial ones are four, in the same three kinds. The supramundane are four paths and four fruitions. If each path and fruition is counted at each of the five jhānas, the 8 become 40 and the total is 121 (I §30–31).

By kind (jātijāti · birth the arising of the aggregates in a new existence; the eleventh link, and the characteristic of matter called production) the 89 are 21 wholesome, 12 unwholesome, 36 resultant and 20 functional.

What makes one citta differ from another

Each type is fixed by a handful of variables. They are its plane; its kind; its roots, none, one, two or three of the six (III §5–7); and its feeling, which is joy, equanimity, displeasure, bodily pleasure or bodily pain (III §2–4). For the greed- and hate-rooted cittas, prompting (and for greed, wrong view) count too; for the sense-sphere beautiful cittas, knowledge and prompting: whether the citta is prompted (sasaṅkhārikasasaṅkhārika · prompted arising after urging or persuasion, by oneself or by another) or spontaneous (I §§4–5, 13).

Chapter III adds what a citta does and where it stands. There are 14 functions, performed at 10 stations of the process (III §8–11), and further distinctions by door and by base (III §12–21). Some facts follow from these variables. Displeasure occurs only in the two cittas rooted in hatred. Bodily pain occurs only in one unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness. And the ten sense consciousnesses, eye-consciousness among them, carry only the seven universal factors, the barest cittas there are (II §28).

The commentarial picture

The commentators define citta three ways (Guide to I §3). As agent, it is what cognizes an object. As instrument, it is that by which the factors cognize. As activity, it is just the cognizing. The third is the most exact, because it leaves no agent standing behind the act. In the four-part definition the commentaries use for every dhamma, citta's characteristic is knowing an object, its function is to go before (pubbaṅgamapubbaṅgama · forerunner what goes before: the mind as forerunner of states, as in the first verse of the Dhammapada), it shows itself as continuity, and its proximate cause is mentality-materiality.

The Milindapañha gives the image for continuity. A lamp burns all night: the flame of the last watch is neither the flame of the first nor a different one (Milindapañha 3.2.1). The Guide to II §1 gives the image for company. Citta is like a king who never travels without his retinue, the mental factors.

Common misunderstandings

The 89 are kinds, not 89 minds housed in a person. Cittas arise one at a time, each in three sub-moments, and a single unit of matter lasts as long as seventeen of them (IV §6). "Beautiful" is not the same as "wholesome": the 24 sense-sphere beautiful cittas include resultants and the arahant's functionals. "Resultant" does not mean unimportant. Seeing, hearing, rebirth-linking and the life-continuum are all results, the places where past kamma is felt.

For the full map, see the readings A map of the eighty-nine and What each citta does.

In the texts. Dhp 1-2; AN 1.51; SN 12.61. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī lists the cittas without totals; the counts of 89 and 121 come from the commentaries and manuals (Atthasālinī, introduction; Vism XIV §455; Abhidhammāvatāra ch. 1 v. 64 and ch. 3 vv. 90–91; the Manual I §§29–32).

To reflect on. The Abhidhamma counts 89 kinds of citta. What is gained by counting minds instead of describing a mind?

Cetasika mental factors

The mental factors that colour each citta.

Mental factors are the qualities that arise with consciousness and give it its character. Each is a dhamma in its own right, a real quality with its own mark. They are joined to citta by four marks of association (sampayutta-lakkhaṇa): they arise together, cease together, share one object and one base. Fifty-two are counted: seven universals (sabbacitta-sādhāraṇasabbacittasādhāraṇa · universals the seven factors present in every citta, from contact to attention), six occasionals (pakiṇṇakapakiṇṇaka · occasionals six ethically variable factors that join some cittas but not all), fourteen unwholesome and twenty-five beautiful (sobhanasobhana · beautiful the 59 cittas other than unwholesome and rootless ones, and their 25 factors). The ethical quality of a moment is decided by its factors, above all by its roots (hetuhetu · root one of six factors that steady a citta: greed, hatred, delusion, or their opposites): greed, hatred and delusion, or their opposites.

How the Manual presents it

A mental factor is defined by four marks of association: it arises with citta, ceases with it, takes the same object and has the same base (II §1). The Manual sorts the 52 into three classes: 13 ethically variable, 14 unwholesome and 25 beautiful (II §2–9). The first class divides into 7 universals and 6 occasionals, which gives the four groups used across this site: universals, occasionals, unwholesome and beautiful.

The ethically variable factors (aññasamāna) number 13. Seven are universal: contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, life faculty and attention. Six are occasional: initial application, sustained application, decision, energy, zest and desire-to-act.

The unwholesome factors number 14. Four are present in every unwholesome citta: delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing and restlessness. Then come the greed group (greed, wrong view, conceit), the hatred group (hatred, envy, avarice, worry), sloth and torpor, and doubt.

The beautiful factors number 25. Nineteen are present in every beautiful citta: among them faith, mindfulness, shame, fear of wrongdoing, non-greed, non-hatred, neutrality of mind, and six pairs (tranquillity, lightness, malleability, wieldiness, proficiency and rectitude, each of the mental body and of consciousness). Then come the three abstinences, the two illimitables (compassion and appreciative joy) and wisdom.

Two ways of reading the list

The Manual reads the list from both sides. The method of association (II §10–17) takes each factor and asks which cittas it joins. The method of combination (II §18–29) takes each citta and asks which factors it holds. The extremes show the range. Eye-consciousness has only the seven universals, while the first sense-sphere wholesome citta can hold 38 (II §23, Table 2.3).

Eleven factors are "unfixed" (II §17): envy, avarice, worry, the three abstinences, compassion, appreciative joy, conceit, and sloth and torpor. They arise only sometimes in the cittas they belong to. The illimitables and the abstinences, when they arise, come one at a time. In path and fruition, by contrast, the three abstinences are always present together, as right speech, action and livelihood (II §15). Eight of the 52 are the factors of the path; see the concept The noble eightfold path.

The commentarial picture

The commentaries describe each factor by its characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause, the scheme the Guide uses for every entry. Their similes fix one property at a time. Initial application strikes the object like a stick on a bell; sustained application is the ringing that goes on (Vism IV). Volition is like a senior pupil who says his own lesson and sets the others to saying theirs. Feeling is the king who sits down to the meal; the other factors are like the cook, who gets no more than a taste while making it.
