The Guide gives both similes (Guide to II §2), and they go back to the Atthasālinī and Vism XIV. See the reading The commentators' picture-book.

Distinctions that matter

Feeling and perception are each a single factor, and each is an aggregate of its own. The aggregate of formations is the other fifty. Volition is in every citta, results included. It becomes kamma only in wholesome and unwholesome cittas, and these always occur as javanas (III §9).

Opposed factors never meet in one citta: greed and non-greed, or wrong view and wisdom. The thirteen variables take their colour from the company they keep. The ethical quality of a citta is settled by its roots, the six of III §5. For more, see the readings An ensemble of fifty-two and Which factors meet which cittas.

In the texts. Dhs §1; MN 43; MN 111. The term cetasika is Abhidhamma usage; the list of 52 is a later synthesis from the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and the Atthasālinī.

To reflect on. Contact, feeling, perception, volition and attention arise with every citta. What would a moment without volition be like, and why can there be none?

Rūpa matter

Matter: 28 kinds, always arising in groups of eight or more.

Matter (rūparūpa · matter matter: the third reality, 28 kinds; as an aggregate it is called form) is the physical side of experience: the body, its senses and the objects they meet. The word means what is “afflicted” (ruppati), altered by cold, heat, hunger and thirst. Its core is the four great elements (mahābhūtamahābhūta · great elements earth, water, fire and air: the primary matter all other matter depends on): earth as hardness, water as cohesion, fire as heat, air as motion and support; twenty-four kinds are derived from them (upādā-rūpaupādā-rūpa · derived matter the 24 kinds of matter that depend on the four great elements). Matter knows no object (anārammaṇaanārammaṇa · without object without object; said of Nibbāna in Ud 8.1, which the Udāna commentary reads as: unlike a mind, it takes no object (cf. Kv XIX.6)). It arises in inseparable groups (kalāpakalāpa the smallest group of matter: eight or more kinds arising and ceasing together) of eight or more, from four origins (kamma, citta, temperature, nutriment), and a unit of it lasts seventeen mind-moments.

How the Manual presents it

There are four great essentials and twenty-four kinds of derived matter, twenty-eight in all (VI §2–5). Eighteen are "concretely produced" (nipphannanipphanna · concrete matter the 18 kinds with a nature of their own, fit objects for insight), with a nature of their own. They are the four elements; the five sensitivities of eye, ear, nose, tongue and body; four objects (visible form, sound, smell and taste); the female and male faculties; the heart-base; the life faculty; and nutritive essence. The tangible is not a separate kind: it is earth, fire and air as touched.

Ten are not concretely produced (anipphannaanipphanna · non-concrete matter the 10 qualities and modes of concrete matter, such as space and decay). They are modes or marks of the others: space; bodily and vocal intimation; lightness, malleability and wieldiness; and the four characteristics of production, continuity, decay and impermanence.

Origins and groups

Matter has four origins (VI §9–15): kamma, citta, temperature (the fire element) and nutriment. Eighteen kinds can be kamma-born, fifteen mind-born, thirteen temperature-born and twelve nutriment-born. The four characteristics come from none of them.

Matter never occurs alone. It arises in groups (kalāpakalāpa the smallest group of matter: eight or more kinds arising and ceasing together), of which the Manual lists twenty-one: nine kamma-born, six mind-born, four temperature-born and two nutriment-born (VI §16–22). Every group holds the eight inseparables (avinibbhogaavinibbhoga · inseparables the eight kinds in every kalāpa: four elements, colour, smell, taste, nutritive essence): the four elements with colour, smell, taste and nutritive essence. Kamma-born matter arises at every sub-moment from rebirth-linking on, and it stops at the seventeenth citta before death. What remains is a temperature-born body (VI §24–25).

A unit of matter lasts seventeen mind-moments. The exceptions are intimation, which lasts one mind-moment, and the four characteristics (Guide to IV §6 and its note).

Distinctions that matter

The elements are qualities, not stuffs. Earth is hardness or softness, water is cohesion, fire is heat or cold, air is motion or support. Water cannot be touched: cohesion is known only by the mind. Matter as a whole is rootless, without an object, mundane and of the sense sphere (VI §6).

The Manual also sorts matter by pairs (VI §7). Internal matter is the five sensitivities. The bases are those five and the heart. The doors are the five and the two intimations. The faculties are the five, the two sex faculties and life. The gross kinds are twelve and the subtle sixteen.

On the heart-base, the canonical Paṭṭhāna says only "that matter" on which mind depends. It is the commentaries that identify it with the heart (Guide to III §20).

Common misunderstandings

Kalāpas are not atoms in the Greek sense: they are not hard bits of stuff, and they cannot be seen. They are groups of qualities that arise and cease together. Nor is matter treated as the opposite of mind: each conditions the other in set ways, through base, object, the postnascence condition and the four origins (VIII §15–16).

The suttas use the analysis as practice: the body is viewed as "just elements", like a butcher at the crossroads who no longer thinks "cow" (MN 10; worked out in Vism XI). See the readings How matter is made and Mind and matter together.

In the texts. SN 22.79; MN 28; MN 140. The count of 28, the groups (kalāpa) and the four origins of matter are mostly Abhidhamma and commentarial.

To reflect on. Matter knows nothing. Why does a teaching about liberation list 28 kinds of it?

Nibbāna unconditioned

The one unconditioned reality, known in the moments of awakening called path and fruition.

Nibbāna is the one unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātuasaṅkhata-dhātu · unconditioned element Nibbāna, the one element not made by conditions). It does not arise, stand or cease, and nothing produces it; yet it serves as object for path and fruition consciousness, which know it directly, and for change-of-lineage and reviewing. The commentaries give its characteristic as peace (santisanti · peace peace; the characteristic of Nibbāna (Vism XVI §556)). It is described by negation, as the destruction of greed, hatred and delusion (SN 38.1; the commentaries take this as a figure: Nibbāna is that on which their ending depends, Vism XVI §559), and by image, as the deathless (amataamata · the deathless the deathless; a name of Nibbāna in the suttas (SN 43.25)). It is ultimate, not a concept, yet it lies outside the five aggregates and outside past, present and future. It is spoken of with residue (sa-upādisesasa-upādisesa · with residue the Nibbāna element with residue: the defilements ended while an arahant's aggregates remain (It 44; VI §31)), while the aggregates of an arahant remain, and without residue (anupādisesaanupādisesa · without residue the Nibbāna element without residue: named by the absence of aggregates after an arahant's last citta (It 44; VI §31 with the Guide; Vism XVI §561)), when they cease (It 44).

How the Manual presents it

The Manual treats Nibbāna briefly, at the end of the chapter on matter (VI §30–32). It is supramundane, to be realised by the knowledge of the four paths, and it is the object of paths and fruitions. The Manual explains its name as a departure (nikkhanta) from craving, which entangles (vāna). The Guide notes that the commentators prefer this derivation to the etymological one, "blowing out" of the fires.

By its own nature it is one. By the basis of distinction it is two: with residue, while an arahant's aggregates remain, and without residue, after his death. The commentaries call these the extinction of the defilements and the extinction of the aggregates. By aspect it is three: void (suññatasuññata · void void; an aspect of Nibbāna itself (VI §31), and, with signless and desireless, one of the three emancipations named after the insight that leads to the path), signless (animittaanimitta · signless without sign; an aspect of Nibbāna (VI §31), and the emancipation reached through the contemplation of impermanence) and desireless (appaṇihitaappaṇihita · desireless without hankering; an aspect of Nibbāna (VI §31), and the emancipation reached through the contemplation of suffering) (VI §31). These three name Nibbāna itself; the three doors of insight with the same names are contemplations of the conditioned (IX §35). The summary verse calls it deathless, endless, unconditioned and unsurpassed (VI §32).

Where it sits in the system

Nibbāna is one of the four ultimates, but it is no aggregate (VII §40). Among the bases and elements it belongs to the mental-object base and the mental-object element (VII §§36–37, 39). It is free of time (kālavimuttakālavimutta · free of time free of time: said of Nibbāna, which never arises or passes, and of concepts, which have no nature of their own (III §17 with the Guide), III §17 with the Guide): what it is has no arising, change or ceasing, whereas a concept stands outside time because it has no nature of its own to arise. It is called "name" (nāmanāma · mind mind: citta with its factors, which “bend” toward objects; the word also means “name”, from a root meaning "to bend") only in the sense that it makes things bend toward it: as objective predominance it draws the supramundane cittas toward itself (Guide to VIII §29).

It is a condition in three ways, all of them as object: as object, as object predominance and as object decisive support (VIII §17, §19; Table 8.3). It is never conditioned (Guide to VIII §1). Its knowers are the eight supramundane cittas. Just before the first path, change-of-lineage (gotrabhūgotrabhū · change-of-lineage the javana that leaves the sense-sphere lineage for jhāna, or turns to Nibbāna), a sense-sphere citta with knowledge, takes it as object; before the higher paths the same moment is called cleansing (vodānavodāna · cleansing the name of the change-of-lineage javana in the processes of the three higher paths) (IX §34 with the Guide). After each path, reviewing knowledge looks back on it in an ordinary mind-door process, mind-door adverting included (IX §34; Guide to III §18; PaṭṭhānaPaṭṭhāna the seventh Abhidhamma book: relates all dhammas by 24 conditions, Kusalattika, CS §410). A worldling short of the path can know of it only by inference (Vibhāvinī on VI §30).

The commentarial picture

The VisuddhimaggaVisuddhimagga · Path of Purification Buddhaghosa's fifth-century manual of practice and doctrine; source of Plates 12–13 gives its characteristic as peace (santisanti · peace peace; the characteristic of Nibbāna (Vism XVI §556)), its function as not passing away, or comforting, and its manifestation as the signless, or freedom from proliferation (Vism XVI §556). It then argues that Nibbāna is not mere absence: if it were, right practice would be fruitless; and it is not mere destruction, for arahantship too is described as destruction, and a destruction would be temporary and conditioned. The suttas call Nibbāna destruction figuratively, since it is the decisive support for that ending (Vism XVI §§557–559; SN 38.1–38.2). The path reaches it but does not produce it (§560), and it is one goal for all who reach it (§561). Later manuals add that, if Nibbāna were destruction, change-of-lineage and the path would have no object (Abhidhammāvatāra ch. 11), and argue by inference that something other than formations and concepts must be the object that cuts defilements (Vibhāvinī on VI §30).

The Milindapañha compares it to the wind, real though no one can show its shape or colour. The suttas speak of it plainly: there is an unborn, unmade, unconditioned; were there not, no escape from the born would be known (Ud 8.3; It 43).

Common misunderstandings

Nibbāna is not annihilation. Without residue, the aggregates simply arise no more, and no self was there to be destroyed. It is not a place, a heaven or a universal consciousness, for it is not a citta and lies outside all thirty-one planes. Nor is it a concept: concepts are exactly what is left once the four ultimates, Nibbāna among them, have been counted (VIII §29). And the path does not produce it. The path realises it (sacchikātabba); it was not made. Nor is it the attainment of cessation, which the VisuddhimaggaVisuddhimagga · Path of Purification Buddhaghosa's fifth-century manual of practice and doctrine; source of Plates 12–13 calls neither conditioned nor unconditioned (Vism XXIII §884).

For how it is reached, see the readings The tree of purification and Four noble persons; for the whole account, Nibbāna, the unconditioned.

In the texts. Ud 8.1; Ud 8.3; It 43; It 44; SN 38.1; SN 43.1. The Udāna's inspired sayings on Nibbāna (Ud 8.1–4) speak of it directly; Ud 8.3, repeated in It 43, is the passage on the unborn, unmade and unconditioned, and It 44 names the two elements, with and without residue.

To reflect on. Nibbāna is unconditioned and is not a citta. How can a citta take it as its object?

Life-continuum bhavaṅga

The quiet stream of mind that runs whenever nothing is actively being known, as in dreamless sleep.

Bhavaṅgabhavaṅga · life-continuum the resultant citta, of the same kind as rebirth-linking, that runs between processes, literally “factor of becoming” and usually rendered life-continuum, is the resultant citta (one produced by past kamma) that keeps a life continuous whenever no active process is running, as in dreamless sleep. It is the same kind of citta as rebirth-linking (paṭisandhipaṭisandhi · rebirth-linking the first citta of a life: a resultant that links it to the last) and death (cuticuti · death consciousness the last citta of a life, of the same kind as its life-continuum), and it takes the same object, the one presented at the end of the previous life. It is not a soul or a hidden self: it arises and dissolves like any other citta. It shows how continuity is possible without an enduring subject.

How the Manual presents it

The life-continuum is one of the fourteen functions of citta (III §8). Nineteen resultant cittas can perform it: the two investigating cittas with equanimity, for a rootless rebirth; the eight great resultants; and the nine sublime resultants (III §9–10). In any one life a single type does three jobs. It is rebirth-linking at the start, life-continuum in between and death at the end, and it always takes the object of the last process of the previous life.

V §41 describes the continuity directly. From the moment after rebirth-linking, that same citta with that same object runs on unbroken like a river current whenever no process is running, until it becomes death consciousness. Then rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death keep rolling round like a cartwheel. The Guide adds that sixteen moments of life-continuum follow rebirth-linking. Then comes the first process of the new life, at the mind door: seven greed-rooted javanas without wrong view, which take the rebirth-linking citta as object and so cling to the new existence (bhava-nikanti; Guide to V §41).

Its place in the process

When an object strikes a door, three moments of life-continuum are named (IV §6). The first is past life-continuum (atīta-bhavaṅgaatīta-bhavaṅga · past life-continuum the life-continuum moment during which the object arises, before it registers at the door; counted first of the 17), during which the object is present but not yet felt. The second is vibration (bhavaṅga-calanabhavaṅga-calana · vibration of the life-continuum the life-continuum moment that is shaken when an object comes into range; the next is the arrest). The third is arrest (bhavaṅgupacchedabhavaṅgupaccheda · arrest of the life-continuum the last life-continuum moment before a process; after it the stream stops and adverting arises). Then adverting turns the mind toward the object. With a very slight object nothing happens beyond the vibration (IV §9). Every process ends by sinking back into the life-continuum.

One special case shows the rules at work. Joy and displeasure cannot follow each other directly. So when javanas of displeasure end, in someone whose life-continuum is joyful, and no registration follows, the commentarial teachers say that an equanimous investigating citta arises once as a buffer before the return. This is the "adventitious life-continuum" (IV §18).

Sources and the commentarial picture

The term appears in the Paṭṭhāna and the Milindapañha. The full theory belongs to the commentaries and the Manual. In the mango simile, the man asleep under the tree is the life-continuum (Atthasālinī). The Atthasālinī's version ends with the eating; later tradition added his falling asleep again, for the return to the life-continuum (note to IV §6).

The Aṅguttara commentary identifies the "luminous mind" of AN 1.51–52 with the life-continuum. That identification is commentarial, not the sutta's own.

Common misunderstandings

It is not a blank. It is a citta with an object, only not a fresh one, which is why nothing seems to be known. Nor is it a storehouse. The Abhidhamma keeps no memories or drives "in" the life-continuum: latent tendencies and kamma are carried by the continuum of cittas as a whole, as conditions.

It does no kamma: it is resultant, every moment of it. And it is not a self, since it arises and dissolves like every citta. See the readings The mango and the moment and Kamma, death and rebirth.

In the texts. AN 1.51; DN 28 / DN 34; SN 12.61. Mainly post-canonical: the term appears in the Paṭṭhāna; the theory is worked out in the Milindapañha and the Atthasālinī.

To reflect on. In dreamless sleep the life-continuum flows unbroken. Does that make it the self that lasts?

Cognitive process 17 mind-moments

The fixed sequence in which cittas take an object.

When you see a sight or hear a sound, the Abhidhamma holds, the knowing happens as a fixed series of cittas, the order of mind (citta-niyāma). An object strikes a door, the life-continuum vibrates and is arrested, and adverting, sense consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, javana (impulsion, where kamma is made, except in an arahant) and registration follow, each conditioning the next by proximity (anantaraanantara · proximity Each citta, as it ceases, makes way for the next and determines what kind can follow, so the stream of mind has no gaps.). Nobody directs the sequence; it is a lawful succession of impersonal events. Knowing a whole thing takes many such processes, at the five sense doors and at the mind door, in turn.

How the Manual presents it

Chapter IV begins with six sixes (IV §2): six bases, six doors, six objects, six kinds of consciousness, six processes, and a sixfold way objects are presented. The processes are grouped into five-door processes and mind-door processes.

The model case is a "very great" object at a sense door, which runs to seventeen mind-moments (IV §6). There is one moment of past life-continuum, then one of vibration and one of arrest. Then come five-door adverting, the sense consciousness (seeing, say), receiving, investigating and determining. Seven javanas follow, then two moments of registration.

The count matters, because a sense object lives exactly seventeen mind-moments. If it strikes after more moments of life-continuum have passed, the process is cut short. With a great object registration drops out (IV §7). With a slight object there are no javanas, and determining repeats two or three times (IV §8). With a very slight one there is only vibration (IV §9). These four grades give the four courses at the five doors (IV §10). At the mind door the Manual has two grades, clear and obscure (IV §12); Ledi Sayadaw adds two more, making four (Guide to IV §12). The absorption process of jhāna and path has its own form (IV §14).

The rules that govern it

The Guide to IV §6 calls this the fixed order of consciousness (citta-niyāma). Each citta arises in a lawful sequence, linked to the next by proximity and contiguity, and none is skipped or chosen. Further rules are set out in IV §17–22. Registration occurs only after sense-sphere javanas, in sense-sphere beings, with vivid objects. Its feeling must be compatible with the javana's. Javanas normally run seven times, six with a very weak object, and five near death (IV §21).

Only the javanas vary in ethical quality. Everything from adverting to determining, and registration, is resultant or functional.

How a thing gets known

A five-door process knows only a present sense datum: a patch of colour, a sound. Recognition comes later, at the mind door. Following Ledi Sayadaw, the Guide to IV §12 lays out the sequel in seven steps. First a mind-door process repeats the object just past. Then one grasps it as a whole, the way a whirled firebrand looks like a circle. Then one recognises the colour, one grasps the thing, one recognises the thing, one grasps the name and one recognises the name. Together they may run to many thousands of processes, Ledi Sayadaw says. This sequence is the account of a later commentator, not of the Manual's own text. Ledi Sayadaw's Paramatthadīpanī gives both these seven and, more briefly, four kinds of grasping that follow each sense door: of the past object, of the whole, of the thing and of the name.

The commentarial picture and misunderstandings

The mango simile (Atthasālinī; Guide to IV §6) maps the stages. A man asleep is struck by a falling mango and wakes. He looks, picks it up, squeezes it, smells it and eats it. Seeing is the looking, receiving the picking up, investigating the squeezing, determining the smelling, javana the eating. The Atthasālinī stops there. The Vibhāvinī adds the swallowing for registration and his falling asleep again for the return to the life-continuum (note to IV §6).

Nobody sits behind the process watching or steering it, the Guide insists. Each citta does its one job and hands on to the next; whatever wholeness the act of knowing has comes from the way they condition one another (Guide to IV §6). Nor does a person live through one long process. Knowing a single thing takes many processes, alternating between the doors faster than anyone can notice. The seventeen-moment process belongs to the commentaries and the Manual, not to the suttas. See the readings The mango and the moment, Other processes and Who has which cittas.

In the texts. MN 18; SN 35.93; Paṭṭh (anantara, samanantara). The 17-moment vīthi is commentarial (the Visuddhimagga, the Atthasālinī and the Manual), not canonical.

To reflect on. If seeing is over before you know you are seeing, what is the "I see" that follows?

Javana impulsion

The active phase of a cognitive process, where volition becomes kamma (except in an arahant).

Javanajavana · impulsion the active phase of a process, usually seven alike cittas; here kamma is made, impulsion, is the active phase of a process: usually seven cittas of one kind in which the moment’s ethical quality is fixed. Only here is kamma made, by worldlings and trainees; in an arahant the javanas are merely functional (kiriyakiriya · functional a citta that neither makes kamma nor results from it, such as adverting) and leave no result. It is here that wise or unwise attention (yoniso / ayoniso manasikāra) bears fruit, so the javana is where training can make a difference, though the javanas too arise from conditions.

How the Manual presents it

Javana ("running", "impulsion") is the phase in which the mind runs over the object it has determined. Fifty-five cittas can perform it (III §9). They are the 12 unwholesome; the 21 wholesome; the 4 fruitions; and the 18 functionals, which are all the functionals except the two adverting cittas.

How many javanas run depends on the process (IV §21–22). In a sense-sphere process there are normally seven, or six with a very weak object, and five in the feeble process at the moment of dying. The commentators add that five also run in a faint (Guide to IV §21). The Buddha's reviewing at the Twin Miracle ran four or five. A beginner's first absorption runs a single jhāna javana, and direct knowledge always runs one. A path lasts one moment and is followed by two or three fruitions. In attainments such as jhāna and fruition, javanas may follow one another without set limit. Entering cessation, the fourth immaterial javana runs twice before consciousness stops (IV §22).

Javana and kamma

Here, for worldlings and trainees, volition becomes kamma. The arahant's javanas are functional (kiriyakiriya · functional a citta that neither makes kamma nor results from it, such as adverting) and make none. The fruitions are javanas too, but as resultants they make none either. In a sense-sphere process the javanas are all of one type. In an absorption or path process, three or four preliminary sense-sphere javanas give way to a sublime or supramundane one (IV §14). A mundane javana followed by another of the same kind, wholesome, unwholesome or functional, supports it by repetition (āsevanaāsevana · repetition Repetition is the way each javana strengthens the next, as a lesson is learned by reciting it.); the last preliminary javana so supports even the path. A path gives none, since what follows it is fruition, a resultant (Guide to VIII §13).

The commentaries, as the Guide reports, tie the timing of kamma's results to a javana's position (Guide to V §20). The first javana, the weakest of the seven, can ripen only in this life, or else it lapses. The seventh, the next weakest, can ripen only in the next life. The middle five can ripen in any life after the next, whenever they find the chance, and never lapse while the round lasts.

Where the room for choice lies

The cittas up to and including determining are results or functionals; they make no choice. Which kind of javana follows depends on conditions, above all on whether attention is wise or unwise (yoniso / ayoniso manasikāra), and on habit, background and company. These work as natural decisive support (VIII §17). A desirable object, the result of good kamma, can be met with greed, or with generosity and understanding.

The same rules say why bare will cannot simply seize the javana. Attention itself arises from conditions, and it is training and good company that make wise attention more likely.

Common misunderstandings

"Seven like javanas" does not mean seven separate decisions; they are one type, repeated. Javana is not slow deliberation either: a whole process is far quicker than reflection. Not every javana is ethically loaded. In an arahant all are functional, and the smile-producing citta is a rootless functional javana that only arahants have (I §10).

The term as a technical stage of the process is Abhidhamma and commentarial, not sutta usage. See the readings The mango and the moment, Two moments, side by side and Other processes.

In the texts. SN 35.95; MN 18; SN 36.6. Term javana as a technical stage: Abhidhamma and commentarial; absent in suttas.

To reflect on. Seeing is the result of past kamma, but the javanas make new kamma. Where is the room for choice in a moment of seeing?

24 conditions Paṭṭhāna

The ways in which one dhamma supports another.

The Paṭṭhāna analyses every relation between dhammas into twenty-four modes: root, object, predominance, proximity, conascence, mutuality, support, decisive support, kamma, nutriment and the rest. A condition (paccayapaccaya · condition a dhamma that helps another to arise or persist, in a specific way) is a dhamma that helps another, the conditioned (paccayuppannapaccayuppanna · conditioned state the dhamma that a condition helps to arise or persist), to arise or to persist. The scheme puts a web of mutual support where other systems put a creator or a first cause: nothing arises from a single cause, and nothing from no cause. A moment of seeing, for example, depends at once on the eye as its support, the visible form as its object, and the citta just before it by proximity.

How the Manual presents it

Chapter VIII gives two methods of conditionality (VIII §2). Dependent arising shows simply that this arises when that is present. The method of the Paṭṭhāna names the specific force by which one thing conditions another.

The Guide to VIII §1 fixes the terms: the conditioning state (paccaya-dhamma), the conditioned state (paccayuppannapaccayuppanna · conditioned state the dhamma that a condition helps to arise or persist), and the conditioning force (paccaya-satti). A condition is a dhamma that is helpful (upakāraka) to the arising or persistence of another. All conditioned things, and also Nibbāna and concepts, can condition. Only cittas, cetasikas and matter (except the four characteristics of matter) are conditioned.

The 24 conditions are listed in VIII §11: root, object, predominance, proximity, contiguity, conascence, mutuality, support, decisive support, prenascence, postnascence, repetition, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, absence, disappearance, non-disappearance.

Six relations, four master conditions

The Manual sorts them by what conditions what (VIII §12–18). Mind conditions mind in 6 ways: proximity, contiguity, absence, disappearance, repetition and association. Mind conditions mind-and-matter in 5: root, jhāna and path factors, kamma and result. Mind conditions matter in 1, postnascence. Matter conditions mind in 1, prenascence. Concepts and mind-and-matter condition mind in 2, object and decisive support. Mind-and-matter conditions mind-and-matter in 9: predominance, conascence, mutuality, support, nutriment, faculty, dissociation, presence and non-disappearance.

All 24 can be gathered under four master conditions (VIII §27, Table 8.4): object, decisive support, kamma and presence.

Distinctions that matter

Several conditions have sub-kinds. Predominance is by object or conascent (VIII §19). The four conascent predominants (desire, energy, citta and investigation) work one at a time, and only in javanas with two or three roots. Decisive support is threefold (VIII §17): by object; by proximity; and natural decisive support, which takes in lust, faith, pleasure, pain, a person, food, climate and lodging. Kamma is conascent, as volition with its own citta, or asynchronous, as past volition producing results (VIII §14).

A condition need not be present. Proximity works from a citta that has just ceased; asynchronous kamma may work from long ago. Postnascence runs backward: later cittas sustain a body that arose before them, as later rain sustains plants already grown (Guide to VIII §15).

The commentarial picture and why it matters

The Guide gives the familiar similes, drawn from the commentaries. Root is like the roots of a tree, which give it stability (Guide to VIII §14). Mutuality is like a tripod, each leg holding up the others (Guide to VIII §21). Support is like the earth for trees, or canvas for a painting (Guide to VIII §22).

What the scheme rules out matters as much as what it describes. Nothing arises from a single cause, from no cause, or from a first cause. Each named condition marks a place where change can begin: what one attends to, whom one keeps company with, what one repeats. See the reading The web of twenty-four conditions.

In the texts. SN 12.20; Paṭṭh; SN 12.67. The Paṭṭhāna, which sets out the 24 conditions, is canonical, the seventh book of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.

To reflect on. The Paṭṭhāna names twenty-four ways one thing helps another. Why would liberation need so much detail about conditions?

Dependent origination 12 links, 3 lives

The twelve links, read across three lives.

“When this is, that is; from the arising of this, that arises” (SN 12.21). The twelve links show how ignorance and craving keep the round (vaṭṭavaṭṭa · round one of three cycles turning in the wheel: defilements, kamma, results) of existence turning. The commentaries, and the Manual after them, spread the links over three lives: past causes, present results, present causes, future results. Saṃsāra, the round of births, appears as a process with no self that transmigrates, which avoids both eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhisassata-diṭṭhi · eternalism the view of a self that lasts for ever; one of the two extreme views) and annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhiuccheda-diṭṭhi · annihilationism the view that a self is destroyed at death; the other extreme view). SN 12.1 also states the chain in its cessation form: with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease, and so on to the end of the whole mass of suffering.

How the Manual presents it

VIII §3 gives the twelve links. Ignorance conditions formations, then consciousness, mentality-materiality, the six bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and ageing and death with sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair. VIII §4 lists seven ways to analyse the chain: three periods, twelve factors, twenty modes, three connections, four groups, three rounds and two roots (VIII §4–10, Table 8.1).

The periods (VIII §5) put ignorance and formations in the past life, birth and ageing and death in the future, and the eight middle links in the present.

What each link is

The Guide to VIII §3 names the dhammas behind the links. Formations are the volitions in the 29 mundane wholesome and unwholesome cittas. Consciousness is the 32 mundane resultant cittas, from rebirth-linking on. Mentality-materiality is the factors joined to them, with kamma-born matter. Becoming is twofold. Kamma-becoming (kamma-bhavakamma-bhava · kamma-process becoming becoming as the active side: the wholesome and unwholesome volitions that make for a new existence) is the kamma-making process. Rebirth-becoming (upapatti-bhavaupapatti-bhava · rebirth-process becoming becoming as the passive side: the resultant cittas, their factors and kamma-born matter of a new existence) is the 32 resultants with their factors and kamma-born matter.

The Guide adds a detail about feeling: neutral feeling too conditions craving, through its peacefulness.

Groups, connections, rounds, roots

There are four groups of five (VIII §7). The past causes are ignorance, formations, craving, clinging and becoming. The present results run from consciousness to feeling. The present causes are the same five, at work now. The future results are the same five results, shown as birth and ageing and death. That makes the twenty modes.

The three connections fall between formations and consciousness, between feeling and craving, and between becoming and birth. The three rounds (VIII §8) are defilements (ignorance, craving, clinging), kamma (formations and kamma-becoming) and results (the rest). The two roots (VIII §9) are ignorance, running from the past to feeling, and craving, running from the present to ageing and death.

Readings and misunderstandings

The Manual follows the commentaries (Vism XVII) in spreading the links over three lives (VIII §5). The Guide treats the three periods as a frame for showing the causal pattern, not a timetable: no link is confined to its period, and in any one life all twelve are at work and imply one another (Guide to VIII §5; see VIII §7). Vism XVII also works out which of the 24 conditions operate at each link. The suttas show variants. DN 15 runs a two-way bond between consciousness and mentality-materiality. The Vibhaṅga's Abhidhamma section reads the whole chain within a single moment of citta.

The chain is not a first-cause story. Ignorance has its own condition, the taints (MN 9). It is not a row of single causes either, since each link stands in many relations at once. "Birth" means the arising of the aggregates at rebirth-linking, not the day of delivery. SN 12.1 also states the chain in its cessation form: with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease, and so on to the end of the whole mass of suffering (SN 12.1). The two orders are two of the four truths: the arising order is the origin of suffering, the ceasing order its cessation (AN 3.61, 13.6–17.4; see the concept The four noble truths). See the readings The wheel across three lives and One moment, every lens.

In the texts. SN 12.1; SN 12.2; DN 15. Three-lives reading is commentarial; texts show variants.

To reflect on. Dependent origination is usually read across three lives. Where, in a single moment, could you watch one link become the next?

Kamma volition

Volition, and the way it ripens.

Kamma is volition (cetanācetanā · volition the willing that organises the other factors; as kamma, it bears results): “It is intention, monks, that I call kamma” (AN 6.63). The volition ceases at once, but it leaves a potency in the mental continuum that ripens, when conditions allow, as resultant consciousness (vipākavipāka · resultant a citta that is the ripening of past kamma; it makes no new kamma) and kamma-born matter. Kamma is not fate: it is one condition among many, and each present volition is new. The Manual sorts it four ways: by function, by order of ripening, by time of ripening and by place of ripening.

How the Manual presents it

The Manual sorts kamma four ways (V §18–21). By function it is productive, supportive, obstructive or destructive. By order of ripening it is weighty, death-proximate, habitual or reserve. The weighty kinds are, on the unwholesome side, the five heinous crimes and fixed wrong view, and on the wholesome side, jhāna. By time it ripens in this life, in the next, at some later time, or becomes defunct. By place it is unwholesome, sense-sphere wholesome, fine-material wholesome or immaterial wholesome.

Kamma by door and its results

Unwholesome kamma runs along ten courses (V §22). By body: killing, stealing and sexual misconduct. By speech: false speech, slander, harsh speech and idle chatter. By mind: covetousness, ill will and wrong view. V §23 sorts these by root: killing, harsh speech and ill will spring from hatred; sexual misconduct, covetousness and wrong view from greed; the rest from either. Sense-sphere wholesome kamma has ten bases of merit (V §24). They are giving, virtue, meditation, reverence, service, sharing merit, rejoicing in others' merit, hearing the Dhamma, teaching it and straightening one's views.

Results follow grade as well as kind (V §29). Superior three-rooted wholesome kamma, done with a clean mind before and after, gives a three-rooted rebirth. Inferior three-rooted kamma, or superior two-rooted, gives a two-rooted rebirth. Inferior two-rooted kamma gives a rootless rebirth. The jhānas give rebirth in the matching Brahmā planes, graded limited, medium or superior (V §31).

Distinctions that matter

Kamma is the volition, not the deed's outward effect, and not its result (vipākavipāka · resultant a citta that is the ripening of past kamma; it makes no new kamma). Seeing a pleasant sight is a result; how one meets it in the javanas is new kamma. Volition is present in every citta, but it is kamma only in wholesome and unwholesome ones. Strictly, the three mental courses are the factors themselves: covetousness is greed, ill will is hatred, wrong view is the factor of wrong view. The other seven are the volition that drives the act (Guide to V §23). As a condition it is either conascent or asynchronous (VIII §14). The position of a javana sets when its kamma can ripen (Guide to V §20).

Common misunderstandings

Not everything is the result of past kamma. SN 36.21 names bile, phlegm, wind, their combination, climate, careless conduct and assault alongside it. The commentaries count kamma as one of five natural orders (niyāmaniyāma · order, law a fixed order of nature; the commentaries count five, among them the order of mind, which the cognitive process follows), with temperature, seeds, mind and the Dhamma.

Kamma is not fate: present volition is always new, and one kamma can be blocked or cut off by another. Arahants make no new kamma. Kamma they made earlier can still ripen while they live (Guide to V §20), and the commentaries tell Moggallāna's violent death this way. See the readings Kamma, death and rebirth and From kamma to its results.

In the texts. AN 6.63; MN 135; AN 3.76-77. The grouping of kamma into twelve kinds (by function, weight and time of ripening) is the Visuddhimagga's (XIX); the Manual adds a fourth set, by place of ripening, for sixteen (V §§18–21).

To reflect on. Kamma is volition. Why does the same gift bear different results when given with or without understanding?

Death and rebirth rebirth-linking

The last citta of one life and the first of the next, with nothing passing between.

Death (cuticuti · death consciousness the last citta of a life, of the same kind as its life-continuum) is the cutting off of the life faculty in one existence. Rebirth-linking (paṭisandhipaṭisandhi · rebirth-linking the first citta of a life: a resultant that links it to the last), the first citta of the next, follows without interval, conditioned by the kamma that ripens at death and taking the object shown to the last javanas: a kamma, a sign of kamma or a sign of destiny. Nothing passes across. The Visuddhimagga compares it to a seal and its impression, or an echo and its sound, and the Milindapañha calls the new being “neither the same nor another” (na ca so na ca añño).

How the Manual presents it

Death is the cutting off of the life faculty within one existence. It comes in four ways (V §34): the lifespan runs out; the productive kamma runs out; both run out together; or a destructive kamma cuts life short.

As death nears, the kamma that is about to ripen presents an object in one of three forms (V §35). It may be the kamma itself, recalled. It may be a sign of the kamma (kamma-nimittakamma-nimitta · kamma sign at death, an object linked with a past deed, such as offered flowers), something used or seen in doing it. Or it may be a sign of destiny (gati-nimittagati-nimitta · destiny sign at death, an image of the coming birth), an image of the coming world.

The last process runs only five weak javanas (IV §21; V §38). They have no rebirth-producing power of their own; they are the channel for the past kamma now set to produce the next birth (Guide to V §37). Death consciousness may follow the javanas at once, or after two moments of registration, or after some moments of life-continuum (Guide to V §37). Rebirth-linking arises immediately after. It takes the object of that last process, rests on the heart-base or, in the immaterial worlds, on no base, and is produced by a formation rooted in latent ignorance and craving (V §37).

Kinds of rebirth-linking

The Manual names four (V §9–17), by world. Rebirth in the woeful planes uses the unwholesome-resultant investigating citta. In the happy sense-sphere it uses the wholesome-resultant investigating citta, for those born deficient and for some lower deities, or one of the eight great resultants. The fine-material worlds have five rebirth cittas and the immaterial worlds four. That makes nineteen in all. Non-percipient beings are reborn with matter alone, a vital nonad (VI §28).

The objects differ by world (V §38–39). A sense-sphere rebirth takes a sense-sphere object, present or past. A fine-material rebirth takes a concept. An immaterial rebirth takes a concept or a sublime citta. The plane one dies in limits where one can go (V §40). A worldling dying in an immaterial world is reborn in the same or a higher one, or in the sense sphere with three roots. From the fine-material worlds there is no rootless rebirth.

The commentarial picture

Vism XVII (CS §631) gives four images of a connection without transfer: an echo, a lamp, a seal and a reflection in a mirror. Nothing moves from the voice to the echo, yet the echo depends on the voice. The Milindapañha has two lamp images: a flame that burns through the night, neither the same flame nor another, and a lamp lit from another lamp, with nothing passing across.

The Theravāda allows no intermediate existence between death and rebirth-linking. The Kathāvatthu argues against one (Kv VIII.2), and in the Manual the two cittas are simply consecutive.

Common misunderstandings

The last thought does not choose the next life. Which kamma ripens follows an order: weighty kamma first, then kamma close to death, then habitual kamma, then reserve (V §19). The death-moment process only carries it.

Nor does the body simply outlast the mind. Kamma-born matter stops arising seventeen cittas before death, so the last of it ceases with the death citta, and the corpse that remains is temperature-born matter (VI §25). And the new life does not begin with a blank. The first process after rebirth is a clinging to the new existence: greed-rooted javanas that take the rebirth-linking citta as their object (Guide to V §41). See the readings Kamma, death and rebirth and The wheel across three lives.

In the texts. MN 38; DN 15; SN 12.38-40. The sequence of death, rebirth-linking and life-continuum cittas is Abhidhamma and commentarial, not sutta.

To reflect on. Nothing passes from the dying moment to rebirth-linking. What connects the two lives?

31 planes worlds of mind

The worlds, matched to levels of mind.

The cosmos is laid out as thirty-one planes of existence, matched to levels of mind: four woeful planes, seven happy sense-sphere planes, sixteen fine-material and four immaterial Brahmā worlds. Each is reached by the kamma or the jhāna that corresponds to it, so each world mirrors a kind of mind, and rebirth there is that mind’s result. Every plane belongs to saṃsāra and is impermanent; even the longest lifespan ends.

How the Manual presents it

The Manual groups the thirty-one planes into four (V §3–7). The four woeful planes are hell, the animal realm, the ghosts (petapeta · ghost a being of one of the woeful planes, tormented by hunger and thirst) and the titans (asuraasura · titan a being of the woeful plane of the asuras, or, in another sense, of the warring titans). The seven happy sense-sphere planes are the human world and six heavens: the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tusita gods, the gods who delight in creating, and the gods who wield power over others' creations. The sixteen fine-material planes are three for each of the first three jhānas and seven for the fourth: Great Fruit, the non-percipient beings and the five Pure Abodes. Then come the four immaterial planes.

Mind matched to world

Each world is reached by the matching kind of citta. Unwholesome kamma leads to the woeful planes, and sense-sphere wholesome kamma to the human and heavenly worlds. The jhānas lead to the Brahmā worlds, graded limited, medium or superior (V §31). The first jhāna yields Brahmā's Retinue, his Ministers or the Great Brahmās. The Abhidhamma counts five jhānas where the suttas count four, so its second and third jhānas yield the second-jhāna planes; the fourth yields the third-jhāna planes; and the fifth yields Great Fruit. The fifth jhāna developed with dispassion for perception yields the non-percipient plane. Only non-returners are reborn in the Pure Abodes. Each immaterial attainment yields its own immaterial plane.

The same cittas also occur during life, which is why "plane" can name a level of mind as well as a world. But the world limits what can arise in it. The immaterial planes have no matter, and so no eye, no seeing and no five-door process. The non-percipient plane has no mind at all (IV §27–29).

Lifespans

In the woeful planes, and among humans, there is no fixed span: it depends on the kamma (Guide to V §12). The Four Great Kings live 500 celestial years, nine million human years. The highest sense-sphere gods live 16,000 celestial years, about 9,216 million human years (V §12). Brahmā's Retinue lives a third of an aeon (an incalculable aeon, say the commentators), and the Highest Pure Abode 16,000 great aeons (V §14). The immaterial planes run from 20,000 to 84,000 great aeons (V §16). The Guide explains the aeon with the sutta image of a mountain of granite worn away by a silk cloth (SN 15.5).

Common misunderstandings

No plane is permanent; even 84,000 aeons ends. The Great Brahmā is not a creator. The suttas show him mistaken about his own origin (DN 1) and unable to answer where the elements cease (DN 11).

The thirty-one is a count assembled by the later tradition; no single sutta lists them all. Treating the planes only as states of mind loses something the Abhidhamma insists on: rebirth in them is real. The tradition holds that the human plane, with its mix of pain and ease, is the one best suited to practice. See the readings Thirty-one planes and From kamma to its results.

In the texts. MN 12; AN 9.24; DN 33. The count of 31 is a later synthesis; no single sutta lists them all.

To reflect on. The thirty-one planes are worlds, and each also matches kinds of citta. Is a plane a place or a state of mind?

The four noble truths ariya-sacca

The Buddha's four truths, which the Abhidhamma reads as a sorting of every mundane reality, with Nibbāna and the supramundane path set apart.

The four noble truths (ariya-saccaariya-sacca · noble truth suffering, its origin, its cessation, the path: the four noble truths) are suffering, its origin, its cessation and the path to its cessation, set out in the Buddha’s first sermon (SN 56.11). Each has its task: suffering is to be fully understood, its origin abandoned, its cessation realised, the path developed. Every Buddhist school teaches the four truths, though not every school makes them its frame or reads them alike. What the Theravāda Abhidhamma adds is a sorting. On its analysis each truth is a set of ultimate realities: every mundane citta, mental factor and kind of matter falls under the first two truths, Nibbāna is the third, and the fourth is eight mental factors of the path moment. On the Manual’s strict count, only the eight supramundane cittas and their factors, apart from the path’s eight factors, are left outside (Guide to VII §38; VII §40).

How the Manual presents it

The Manual ends its survey of the whole with the four noble truths (VII §§38–40). The Guide gives four reasons for the word "noble". The noble ones penetrate them; they are the truths of the Noble One, the Buddha; discovering them makes a person noble; and they are real, never otherwise than they are (Guide to VII §38).

Then each truth is named in ultimate realities. Suffering is what the suttas list, from birth, ageing and death to the five aggregates of clinging that sum the list up. As realities it is everything of the three mundane planes except craving. Counted out, that is the 81 mundane cittas, all their mental factors but greed, and all 28 kinds of matter; the Guide says only "except craving", and the counts are this site's spelling-out. The origin is craving, which is the factor greed, in three aspects: craving for sense pleasures, for existence and for non-existence. Cessation is Nibbāna. The path is the eight path factors, but only as they arise in the four supramundane path cittas (Guide to VII §38).

The summary verse names what is left over. Strictly speaking, the path citta itself and its other factors, and the four fruitions with all of theirs, belong to no truth (VII §40; Guide to VII §40). That is the Manual's strict count, not the only one (see Two methods below). One overlap needs sorting. The suttas sum up suffering as the five aggregates of clinging, and those include craving. Buddhaghosa answers with a fourfold table: the clinging aggregates other than craving are both suffering and its noble truth, while the states that go with the path, and the fruitions, are suffering only as conditioned formations, not the truth the holy life is lived to understand (Vism XVI §566, commentarial).

Tasks, turnings, one moment

In the first sermon each truth is turned three times: this is suffering; it is to be fully understood; it has been fully understood. Four truths by three turnings make twelve aspects, and the Buddha claimed awakening only when all twelve were complete (SN 56.11). Each truth has its own task: suffering is to be fully understood, its origin abandoned, its cessation realised, the path developed (SN 56.29).

Before the path, knowing the truths is following knowledge (anubodha). It is mundane, and it reaches cessation and the path only by learning and hearsay. Penetration (paṭivedha) is supramundane and takes all four at once (Vism XVI §563). At the path moment one knowledge, with Nibbāna as its object, does the four tasks together (Guide to IX §34). This happens four times, once at each path, and each path abandons only its share of the defilements: the first cuts wrong view and doubt, and craving is gone entirely only at the fourth (IX §§38–41 with the Guides). The commentaries liken it to a lamp, which in one moment burns the wick, dispels the dark, makes light and uses up the oil; and in the same way to the sun, and to a boat that leaves one shore, crosses the stream, carries its cargo and reaches the far shore (Vism XXII §§839–841).

Distinctions that matter

Two senses of saccasacca · truth truth, and what is real: the four noble truths; in another sense also the two truths, conventional and ultimate. The two truths, conventional and ultimate (see the concept Two truths), are two levels of speaking. The four noble truths are something else: four sets of realities. Saccasacca · truth truth, and what is real: the four noble truths; in another sense also the two truths, conventional and ultimate means both "true" and "real", and the Guide's last reason for calling them noble is that they are real and unalterable (Guide to VII §38); on this reading 'noble realities' would fit as well as 'noble truths'.

Three kinds of suffering. Dukkhadukkha · bodily pain painful bodily feeling: only in unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness is wider than pain. The suttas name three kinds: the suffering of pain, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioned existence (SN 38.14; SN 45.165). Buddhaghosa assigns painful feeling to the first, pleasant feeling to the second, and neutral feeling with the other formations of the three planes to the third (Vism XVI §539, commentarial). So the first truth takes in pleasant and wholesome mundane states too. They are conditioned, they pass, and they belong to the round. The word shifts sense, then. As feeling, dukkhadukkha · bodily pain painful bodily feeling: only in unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness is pain; as a characteristic it marks everything conditioned, the path included; as the first truth it is what is conditioned and can be clung to. The noble truths use the third (Vism XVI §566, commentarial).

Two methods. The Manual's count matches the sutta method, with craving alone as the origin. The Vibhaṅga's Abhidhamma section drops the word "noble" and widens the origin step by step: craving, then all defilements, all unwholesome states, the wholesome roots with taints, and all tainted wholesome states. Each time, suffering is the rest (Vibh 4). Once the word "noble" is dropped, then, the good moments of ordinary practice can count under the origin rather than under suffering.

Truths and the wheel. The arising order of dependent origination is the origin of suffering, and its ceasing order is cessation (AN 3.61, 13.6–17.4). In the sutta explanation, ignorance, the first link, is not knowing these four truths (Guide to VIII §3).

Common misunderstandings

Suffering is not to be abandoned; it is to be fully understood. Abandoning is the task for craving. Cessation is not developed or produced; it is realised. Not every good state is the path: in the teaching of the noble truths only the eight factors of a supramundane path moment are the fourth truth, and a mundane kind thought, however useful in practice, counts with what is to be understood (Guide to VII §38; Vism XVI §564). Nor are the truths seen one by one. The Theravāda holds that all four are penetrated in a single moment (SN 56.30; Kv II.9).

Nor is the physician's diagnosis the tradition's own frame for the truths. The commentaries do give disease, its cause, its cure and the medicine, but as one image among several, beside a burden, taking it up, laying it down and the means of laying it down, and famine, drought, plenty and rain (Vism XVI §565). See the readings The four noble truths and The noble eightfold path.

In the texts. SN 56.11; SN 56.30; MN 141; AN 3.61. Twelve aspects and four tasks are canonical (SN 56.11). Sorting realities under the truths, with a remainder outside, is the Abhidhamma's (Vibh 4; CMA VII §§38–40).

To reflect on. In the teaching of the noble truths a kind thought and a moment of mindfulness fall under the truth of suffering. What is gained by calling them that?

The noble eightfold path ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga

Eight factors, right view to right concentration. In the strict sense, eight mental factors arising together in the moment of a supramundane path.

The noble eightfold path (ariya aṭṭhaṅgika maggaariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga · noble eightfold path right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration; in the strict sense, eight mental factors arising together in a supramundane path citta) is the fourth truth: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. The suttas gather them into three trainings: virtue, concentration and wisdom (MN 44). The Theravāda Abhidhamma reads each factor as a mental factor (cetasikacetasika · mental factor a mental factor: arises and ceases with a citta, sharing its object and base): wisdom, initial application, the three abstinences, energy, mindfulness and one-pointedness. The factors can be mundane, developed a few at a time, or supramundane. In the strict sense the path of the four truths is all eight arising together in one supramundane path citta, with Nibbāna as object.

How the Manual presents it

Among the requisites of enlightenment the Manual lists the eight path factors and names the mental factor behind each (VII §30 and Guide; VII §32 and Table 7.3). Right view is wisdom. Right intention is initial application, turned to renunciation, goodwill and harmlessness. Right speech, right action and right livelihood are the three abstinences (II §6). Right effort is energy, working as the four supreme efforts. Right mindfulness is mindfulness, as the four foundations. Right concentration is one-pointedness, defined by the four jhānas.

In its mixed categories the Manual counts twelve path factors: these eight and four wrong ones, wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort and wrong concentration (VII §17 and Guide). They come to nine mental factors, since the last three wrong ones are initial application, energy and one-pointedness in unwholesome company, and only wrong view is a factor of its own. Path factors arise only in rooted cittas (VII §22).

Of their occurrence the Manual says that in the mundane the path factors arise according to circumstances, in the course of the six purifications, and that in the supramundane they arise together, with right intention dropping out above the first jhāna (VII §33; Guide to VII §§32–33). Only those supramundane eight are the fourth noble truth (Guide to VII §38).

Four senses of “path”

The word "path" has four senses here, and the Abhidhamma keeps them apart. First, the twelve path factors of the mixed categories, right and wrong. Wrong view and its companions are a path too, a road to the woeful planes (Guide to VII §17). Second, the path among the requisites of enlightenment: the eight right factors, mundane or supramundane (VII §§30, 33). Third, the fourth noble truth: the eight only as they arise in the four supramundane path cittas (Guide to VII §38). Fourth, the path citta itself (maggamagga · path (citta) a supramundane citta that arises once, cutting defilements, with Nibbāna as object), taken as a whole. On the Manual's strict count, apart from its eight factors it stands outside the four truths, and so do the four fruitions (VII §40; Guide to VII §40).

It follows that mundane right view and mundane right effort belong, in the teaching of the noble truths, to the truth of suffering (Guide to VII §38; Vism XVI §564). They are still the practice. As realities they are among what is to be understood.

Before and at the path

In ordinary wholesome moments the factors come a few at a time. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī already counts a five-factored path in the first wholesome citta of the sense sphere: view, intention, effort, mindfulness and concentration (Dhs §89). The abstinences arise in the mundane only in the eight great wholesome cittas, only when one actually refrains, one at a time, and only for the kind of wrong in view; they do not arise in mundane jhāna or in an arahant's functional cittas (II §6 and §15 with the Guides). The commentaries call this gradual development the preliminary path (pubbabhāga-maggapubbabhāga-magga · preliminary path a commentarial name for the path factors as developed in ordinary moments, before the supramundane path).

At the path moment the factors are together in one citta, on one object, Nibbāna. All three abstinences are present, and each works in full, cutting the disposition to every form of its wrong (Guide to II §15). A path at the level of the first jhāna has all eight. From the second jhāna up, initial application is absent and seven remain (Guide to VII §§32–33; II §19). One who reaches the path by bare insight, without jhāna, has a path at the first-jhāna level (Guide to I §§30–31), and so, the commentaries say, an eightfold one (Vism XXI §798). The same factors recur in fruition, as results (Guide to II §15), but fruition is not the fourth truth (Guide to VII §40).

Common misunderstandings

The eight are not steps done one after another. They are factors, and at the path they arise at once. Right speech is not pleasant talk: as a path factor it is the abstinence from wrong speech. The Abhidhamma counts no factor of wrong mindfulness and no separate factors of wrong speech, action or livelihood, though the suttas use those names (MN 117), so its wrong path factors number four (Guide to VII §17). Good habits are not the fourth truth: they belong to the mundane path, which in the teaching of the noble truths counts with suffering. See the readings The noble eightfold path and The four noble truths.

In the texts. SN 45.8; MN 117; MN 44; SN 56.11. The factors and their definitions are canonical (SN 45.8; MN 117). That at the path they are eight mental factors in one citta is the Abhidhamma's reading (Dhs §277; Vibh 11).

To reflect on. If the noble path in the strict sense lasts one moment, what is someone who 'practises the eightfold path' doing?

Calm samatha

Training the mind to rest on one object, from access concentration to the five jhānas, the meditative absorptions.

Calm (samathasamatha · calm meditation that develops concentration, up to the jhānas) is the training of one-pointedness (ekaggatāekaggatā · one-pointedness unifies the mind on its object; when strong it is concentration (samādhi)) on a meditation subject until the five hindrances (sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, doubt) are suppressed and the mind enters absorption (appanāappanā · absorption the jhāna or path javana itself, after access; the third stage of concentration) as jhāna. Jhāna is a sublime (mahaggata) state in which the jhāna factors (initial and sustained application, zest, happiness, one-pointedness) are refined step by step. Calm suppresses the defilements but does not uproot them; it serves as the basis (pādaka) for insight.

How the Manual presents it

The Manual lists forty subjects (IX §2–12): ten kasiṇas, ten kinds of foulness, ten recollections, four illimitables, one perception (the repulsiveness of food), one analysis (of the four elements) and four immaterial states. It matches them to six temperaments (IX §3, §13). Foulness and the parts of the body suit the lustful. The illimitables and the four colour kasiṇas suit the hating. Breathing suits the deluded and the discursive. The first six recollections suit the faithful. Death, peace, food and the elements suit the intellectual. The rest suit every temperament.

Stages, signs and reach

Development has three stages: preliminary, access and absorption. Its objects have three signs: preliminary, learning and counterpart (IX §14–17). The counterpart sign is a concept born of meditation, free of the original object's flaws. It arises in only twenty-two subjects: the kasiṇas, foulness, the parts of the body and breathing (IX §16, §18). Ten subjects reach only access, never absorption: eight recollections, the perception of food and the analysis of elements (IX §14).

The subjects differ in how far they can take the mind (IX §15). The kasiṇas and breathing reach all five jhānas. Foulness and the body reach only the first, because they need initial application. The first three illimitables reach four, since they are joyful. The fourth illimitable, equanimity, reaches only the fifth. After the first jhāna come the five masteries: adverting, attaining, resolving, emerging and reviewing (IX §18). The immaterial attainments follow from a kasiṇa removed to leave space (IX §19). The direct knowledges come from the fifth jhāna (IX §21).

Jhāna factors and hindrances

The first jhāna has five factors: initial application, sustained application, zest, happiness and one-pointedness. In the Abhidhamma's fivefold scheme they drop away one at a time, and in the fifth jhāna equanimity replaces happiness. The suttas' fourfold scheme drops both kinds of thought at once. The commentaries pair each factor with the hindrance it holds down (Guide to I §§18–20; Vism IV). One-pointedness checks sensual desire, zest checks ill will, initial application checks sloth and torpor, happiness checks restlessness and worry, and sustained application checks doubt.

In the process, the first absorption of a beginner lasts a single javana, after three or four sense-sphere moments of preparation, access, conformity and change-of-lineage (IV §14, §22). With mastery, the jhāna javanas run on in long succession.

Calm and insight

Jhāna suppresses the hindrances; it does not uproot them. It is weighty kamma, and it leads to rebirth in the Brahmā worlds. Access and absorption together make up purification of mind (IX §29), the ground on which insight builds; for one who goes by dry insight, momentary concentration, as steady as access, counts instead (Guide to IX §29). Calm may rest on a concept, but insight must turn to the conditioned dhammas themselves. The commentaries distinguish one who goes by the vehicle of calm from the practitioner of dry insight, who reaches the path with only the concentration that insight itself brings (Guide to IX §29; Vism XVIII). Even so, the path citta is always counted at some level of jhāna, the first for the practitioner of dry insight (Guide to I §§30–31). See the readings Forty meditation subjects and Thirty-one planes.

In the texts. DN 2; MN 118; AN 2.30. The list of forty subjects is set out in the Visuddhimagga; the subjects themselves are scattered through the suttas.

To reflect on. Jhāna suppresses the hindrances but does not uproot them. What is it good for on the way out?

Insight vipassanā

The knowledges that see mind and matter rise and fall.

Insight (vipassanāvipassanā · insight seeing mind and matter as impermanent, suffering and non-self) is wisdom (paññāpaññā · wisdom understanding things as they are; also called non-delusion and the faculty of wisdom) that sees mind and matter as they are: marked by impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkhadukkha · bodily pain painful bodily feeling: only in unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness) and non-self (anattā). It unfolds within the seven purifications, from purification of virtue to purification by knowledge and vision, and within them through the ten insight knowledges, from comprehension to conformity (IX §25). Insight takes conditioned dhammas as its object: it ripens the mind for the path, but it does not itself realise Nibbāna.

How the Manual presents it

Chapter IX sets out the field of insight (IX §22–27). There are seven purifications, from the relay-chariots of MN 24. There are three characteristics: impermanence, suffering and non-self. There are three contemplations, one for each characteristic. There are ten insight knowledges, in the order they arise: comprehension, rise and fall, dissolution, fearfulness, danger, disenchantment, desire for deliverance, reflection, equanimity about formations and conformity. Last come the three emancipations and the three doors to them.

The purifications step by step

Purification of virtue is fourfold: restraint by the Pātimokkha, restraint of the senses, pure livelihood, and right use of the requisites (IX §28). Purification of mind is access and absorption concentration (IX §29; Vism XVIII §662). For one who goes by dry insight, momentary concentration, as steady as access, counts instead (Guide to IX §29); the pairing of pure insight with momentary concentration is in the Visuddhimagga's sub-commentary (on Vism I §§3–4). Purification of view discerns mind and matter by characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause (IX §30; Vism XVIII §§662–677). Overcoming doubt discerns their conditions in past, present and future (IX §31; Vism XIX §§678–691).

Path and not-path is the next purification (IX §32). Formations of past, future and present are gathered into groups, by aggregate and so on, and comprehended by the three marks (Vism XX §§692–722); then an early knowledge of rise and fall arrives (Vism XX §§723–731). With it come ten imperfections of insight. In the VisuddhimaggaVisuddhimagga · Path of Purification Buddhaghosa's fifth-century manual of practice and doctrine; source of Plates 12–13's order they are light, knowledge, zest, tranquillity, happiness, resolution, exertion, mindfulness, equanimity, and a subtle attachment to them all (Vism XX §§732–736); the Manual's verse gives the same ten in another order (IX §32). The meditator must see them as impermanent, suffering and non-self, and so see that they are not the path (Vism XX §736).

Purification of the way covers nine knowledges, from mature rise and fall to conformity (IX §33; Vism XXI §§737–805). Purification by knowledge and vision is the path knowledge itself (IX §34). Change-of-lineage falls between the last two purifications and belongs to neither (Table 9.2; Vism XXII §806).

Distinctions that matter

Insight is wisdom in sense-sphere cittas: the great (sense-sphere) wholesome cittas with knowledge, or functional ones in an arahant. Its objects are conditioned, mundane dhammas, never concepts and never Nibbāna. Nibbāna is known first by change-of-lineage, then by path and fruition, and afterwards by the reviewing cittas that look back on it (Guide to III §18; IX §34).

The mark that leads out gives the path its name (IX §35–36). Seeing non-self opens the void emancipation, impermanence the signless, and suffering the desireless. The commentaries add which faculty favours which door: faith leans toward impermanence, concentration toward suffering, wisdom toward non-self (Guide to IX §35; Vism XXI §§768–769, 772–774). When equanimity about formations and conformity are fully developed, they are called "insight leading to emergence" (IX §34); the VisuddhimaggaVisuddhimagga · Path of Purification Buddhaghosa's fifth-century manual of practice and doctrine; source of Plates 12–13 counts change-of-lineage in it too (Vism XXI §782).

Insight sees formations: the first truth, and craving among them. Its knowledge of the truths is following knowledge (anubodha), which is mundane and reaches cessation and the path only by learning and hearsay. Path knowledge penetrates all four at once (Vism XVI §563; Guide to IX §34). See the concept The four noble truths.

Common misunderstandings

The "sixteen knowledges" of many modern manuals are the Manual's ten with additions. Before them come defining mind and matter and discerning conditions. After them come change-of-lineage, path, fruition and reviewing. The items are all in Vism XVIII–XXII, but the count is a later arrangement used in modern teaching, for example in Mahasi Sayadaw's The Progress of Insight. The canon's own list, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, is shorter: it counts fear, danger and disenchantment as one knowledge, and desire for deliverance, reflection and equanimity as one (Vism XXI §§755, 778–781).

Insight is not only thinking about impermanence. Comprehension works on formations in groups, by spans of time, before the knowledges that watch present formations arise and pass; dissolution then infers past and future from what it sees in the present (Vism XX; Vism XXI §745). Bright lights and bliss are imperfections, not attainments. The knowledges of fear and danger are judgements, not moods: the knowledge of fear does not itself fear (Vism XXI §751). Insight does not realise Nibbāna itself; it ripens the mind until the path does. See the readings Ten knowledges, one by one, The tree of purification and Mind and matter together.

In the texts. SN 22.59; DN 22/MN 10; AN 3.137. The Manual lists ten insight knowledges (IX §25); the sixteen-knowledge scheme is a later arrangement of items found in Vism XVIII–XXII, used in modern teaching, for example in Mahasi Sayadaw's The Progress of Insight.

To reflect on. Insight looks at the same dhammas the Abhidhamma lists. What changes when a list becomes something seen?

Path and fruition four paths

The four moments of awakening that cut defilements for good, each followed by its fruition.

Path and fruition (magga, phala) are the supramundane (lokuttaralokuttara · supramundane beyond the world: the four paths, four fruitions and Nibbāna) cittas that take Nibbāna as object. Each of the four paths arises only once and abandons defilements for good (samuccheda-pahānasamuccheda-pahāna · abandoning by cutting off the path's way of abandoning a defilement: for good, never to arise again): stream-entry, once-return, non-return, arahantship. Fruition follows at once, on the same object. With the fourth path the round of kamma and rebirth is cut at its roots, ignorance and craving.

How the Manual presents it

There are eight supramundane cittas: four paths, which are wholesome, and four fruitions, which are resultant. Counted by the jhāna on which each rests, they become forty (I §26–28, §30–31).

In the path process (IV §14; IX §34), two or three insight moments of preparation, access and conformity come first. Then change-of-lineage, taking Nibbāna as object, crosses from the worldling's lineage to the noble one's. The path follows for a single moment. Two or three moments of fruition come next, three for one of keen faculties, whose preparation moment drops out. Then the mind falls back into the life-continuum, and reviewing follows. Reviewing looks back over path, fruition and Nibbāna, and often, though not always, over what has been abandoned and what is still left (IX §34).

What each path cuts

In one moment the path does four tasks (IX §34). It fully understands suffering, abandons its origin, realises cessation and develops the path. Its path factors arise together in that one moment, the three abstinences among them (II §15). All eight are there only in a path at the level of the first jhāna; at higher levels right intention, which is initial application, drops out, and seven remain (VII §33; II §19). A bare-insight path is at the first-jhāna level (Guide to I §§30–31), and so, the commentaries say, eightfold (Vism XXI §798).

The four persons follow from what is cut (IX §38–41, Table 9.3). The stream-enterer cuts identity view, doubt and clinging to rules and rituals. He is free of the woeful planes and has at most seven more lives, and he is of three kinds: seven-times-at-most, family-to-family and one-seed. Of the fourteen unwholesome factors he has removed wrong view and doubt, and, say the commentaries, envy and avarice. The once-returner weakens lust, hatred and delusion. The non-returner removes sensual lust and ill will entirely, and with them hatred, worry and greed for sense objects; if he dies before arahantship, he is reborn in a fine-material world. The arahant cuts the five higher fetters: lust for fine-material and for immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness and ignorance.

Fruition and cessation

Each noble person can re-enter his own fruition, an absorption with Nibbāna as object (IX §42). The attainment of cessation is open only to non-returners and arahants who have mastered all eight jhānas. It cannot be entered in the immaterial worlds. The meditator ascends through the jhānas, contemplating each with insight up to the base of nothingness, then attends to four preliminary duties (pubbakicca); the last is not a command over death but a check that his life will last the seven days (Guide to IX §43; Vism XXIII §874, §878). Then two javanas of neither-perception-nor-non-perception run, and mind stops. On emergence a single moment of non-return or arahant fruition arises (IX §43–44; IV §22).

Common misunderstandings

A path never repeats. Each arises only once in the whole of saṃsāra, and its work is permanent abandoning (samuccheda-pahānasamuccheda-pahāna · abandoning by cutting off the path's way of abandoning a defilement: for good, never to arise again). Stream-entry leaves greed and hatred in place, except in the grade that could lead to a woeful rebirth (Vism XXII §830): it ends views before passions. The path does not create Nibbāna; it realises it. The names void, signless and desireless come from the insight that led to the path (IX §36); by object and quality every path and fruit has all three (IX §37), since Nibbāna itself is void, signless and desireless (VI §31). The reviewing count of nineteen, five for each of the first three paths and four for the arahant, who has nothing left to review, is commentarial (Guide to IX §34). See the readings Four noble persons, The four noble truths and The noble eightfold path.

In the texts. Dhs §277; SN 55.2; AN 10.13. That a path lasts a single citta is an Abhidhamma teaching.

To reflect on. A path lasts a single moment, yet it changes a person for good. How can one moment do so much?

Dhammas

The 52 mental factors

What colours each moment of knowing: seven present in every citta, six that come and go, fourteen unwholesome and twenty-five beautiful. Manual II §§1–9.

contact phassa
The meeting of mind and object. Contact is what makes an experience happen at all: the coming together of a sense base, an object and consciousness. Feeling follows from it.
feeling vedanā
The tone of an experience: pleasant, painful or neither. Feeling is said to "enjoy" the object, the way a king enjoys a meal that others have only tasted. Five kinds are counted: bodily pleasure and pain, joy, displeasure, and equanimity.
perception saññā
Perception marks an object so that it can be known again, as a carpenter marks timber. It recognises by signs, which is why it can also mislead, as a scarecrow fools deer.
volition cetanā
Volition gathers the other factors and directs them on the object, like a foreman who works and keeps others working. In wholesome and unwholesome cittas it is kamma.
one-pointedness ekaggatā
