One-pointedness holds the citta on its single object without wavering. Present in every moment, developed it becomes concentration, the factor that defines jhāna.
life faculty jīvitindriya
The life faculty sustains the mental factors it arises with for the span of their moment, as water keeps lotuses alive. Matter has a life faculty of its own.
attention manasikāra
Attention turns the mind toward the object, as a rudder steers a ship. Whether it turns wisely (yoniso) or unwisely decides much of what follows.
initial application vitakka
Initial application lifts the mind onto its object, like striking a bell. It is the first factor of the first jhāna and falls away in the higher ones; as wrong or right intention it is also a path factor.
sustained application vicāra
Sustained application keeps the mind moving over its object, like the bell's resonance after the strike. It is subtler than initial application and lasts one jhāna longer in the fivefold scheme.
decision adhimokkha
Decision settles the mind on its object, like a firm pillar. It is absent from moments of doubt, since doubt is exactly the failure to settle.
energy viriya
Energy supports the other factors and keeps them from collapsing, like new timbers propping a sagging house. It serves wholesome and unwholesome states alike; rightly directed it is right effort.
zest pīti
Zest is delight in the object, the gladness that refreshes body and mind. The commentaries describe five grades, from a slight thrill to an uplifting rapture. It occurs only with joyful feeling.
desire to act chanda
Desire to act is wanting to do something with the object. It is not greed: it can be the wish to give, to learn or to practise, and as a predominant it can lead the whole mind.
delusion moha
Delusion blinds the mind to the true nature of its object. It is the root of all unwholesome states and is present in every one of them.
shamelessness ahirika
Shamelessness is the absence of disgust at wrongdoing, the lack of an inner conscience that would recoil from it.
fearlessness of wrongdoing anottappa
Fearlessness of wrongdoing is the absence of dread at the consequences of bad action, the lack of the outer conscience that would hold one back.
restlessness uddhacca
Restlessness is the mind's agitation, like water whipped by wind. It is present in every unwholesome citta and gives its name to one of the two delusion-rooted cittas.
greed lobha
Greed grasps its object and does not let go, like birdlime. It ranges from faint liking to raging lust and appears in more of the Manual's lists of defilements than any other factor.
wrong view diṭṭhi
Wrong view is adherence to a mistaken interpretation, above all the view of a self. It accompanies only greed-rooted cittas, since holding to a view is itself a kind of grasping.
conceit māna
Conceit is measuring oneself against others, as better, equal or worse. It arises only in greed-rooted cittas, never together with wrong view.
hatred dosa
Hatred is the mind's striking out against its object, from mild irritation to fury. It always comes with displeasure, and roots two cittas.
envy issā
Envy is resentment at another's success or good fortune. It arises only in the hate-rooted cittas, and only occasionally.
avarice macchariya
Avarice is the wish to keep one's own good fortune from others. It arises only in hate-rooted cittas, never with envy or worry.
worry kukkucca
Worry is regret over what was done or left undone, the mind going back over the past with distress.
sloth thīna
Sloth is the mind's sluggishness, its loss of drive. It occurs only in the prompted unwholesome cittas, always with torpor.
torpor middha
Torpor is the unwieldiness of the mental factors, their heaviness. With sloth it forms one of the five hindrances.
doubt vicikicchā
Doubt is the mind's indecision about the Buddha, the Dhamma, the path and the nature of things. It is not a root: it occurs in one citta only, the delusion-rooted citta accompanied by doubt, and stream-entry ends it.
faith saddhā
Faith is confidence in what deserves it, which clears the mind as a water-clearing gem settles mud. It is present in every beautiful citta and is the first of the five faculties.
mindfulness sati
Mindfulness keeps the mind from floating away from its object, as a post anchors a boat. It is present in every beautiful citta and is the seventh path factor.
shame hiri
Shame is recoiling from wrongdoing out of self-respect: the inner guardian of the world, the commentaries call it.
fear of wrongdoing ottappa
Fear of wrongdoing is recoiling from it out of regard for its consequences and for others: the outer guardian of the world.
non-greed alobha
Non-greed is not clinging to the object, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. It shows as generosity and renunciation.
non-hatred adosa
Non-hatred is the mind's not opposing its object: friendliness and patience, not only the absence of ill will. Developed toward beings it becomes loving-kindness.
neutrality of mind tatramajjhattatā
Neutrality of mind keeps the citta and its factors in balance, as a charioteer watches well-trained horses. Developed toward beings it becomes the equanimity of the illimitables.
tranquillity of factors kāya-passaddhi
Tranquillity of the mental factors calms their disturbance; it is the opposite of restlessness and worry.
tranquillity of consciousness citta-passaddhi
Tranquillity of consciousness calms the citta itself, as tranquillity of factors calms its companions.
lightness of factors kāya-lahutā
Lightness of the mental factors removes their heaviness; it is the opposite of sloth and torpor.
lightness of consciousness citta-lahutā
Lightness of consciousness removes heaviness from the citta itself, so that it does not drag; it is the opposite of sloth.
malleability of factors kāya-mudutā
Malleability of the mental factors removes their rigidity, the stiffness of views and conceit.
malleability of consciousness citta-mudutā
Malleability of consciousness makes the citta itself supple, free of the stiffness that conceit and wrong view bring.
wieldiness of factors kāya-kammaññatā
Wieldiness of the mental factors makes them fit for work, like gold made workable.
wieldiness of consciousness citta-kammaññatā
Wieldiness of consciousness makes the citta itself fit for any task.
proficiency of factors kāya-pāguññatā
Proficiency of the mental factors is their health and skill, the opposite of faithlessness and sickliness of mind.
proficiency of consciousness citta-pāguññatā
Proficiency of consciousness is the citta's own health and skill, the opposite of faithlessness.
rectitude of factors kāyujjukatā
Rectitude of the mental factors is their straightness, the opposite of deceit and crookedness.
rectitude of consciousness cittujjukatā
Rectitude of consciousness is the straightness of the citta itself, free of hypocrisy and deceit.
right speech sammā-vācā
Right speech is the deliberate abstaining from false, divisive, harsh and idle speech. It is present only when one actually refrains, and always in the moment of the path.
right action sammā-kammanta
Right action is the deliberate abstaining from killing, stealing and sexual misconduct, when an occasion for them arises. In the path it is always present.
right livelihood sammā-ājīva
Right livelihood is the deliberate abstaining from wrong ways of making a living. It arises on occasions of actual restraint, and always in the path.
compassion karuṇā
Compassion is the wish that suffering be removed from others; its near enemy is grief, its far enemy cruelty. It occurs occasionally, and never in the path.
appreciative joy muditā
Appreciative joy is gladness at others' success. The Visuddhimagga names its near enemy as worldly joy and its far enemy as discontent; envy is what it most directly overcomes. Like compassion it occurs occasionally and is a basis for jhāna.
wisdom paññindriya
Wisdom understands things as they are, like a lamp lighting a dark room. It is non-delusion, the third wholesome root, and as right view it leads the path.

The 28 kinds of matter

Four great elements and twenty-four kinds derived from them, with the four origins that produce them. Manual VI §§2–15.

earth pathavī
The earth element: extension, felt as hardness or softness. It is the foundation the other kinds of matter stand on.
water āpo
The water element: cohesion and fluidity. It holds the other elements together and cannot be touched directly.
fire tejo
The fire element: heat and cold. It ripens and matures matter, and as temperature it is one of the four origins of matter.
air vāyo
The air element: motion and support, felt as pressure and distension. It moves and steadies the body.
eye-sensitivity cakkhu
Eye-sensitivity: the sensitive matter in the eye that visible form can strike. It is the base and door of seeing.
ear-sensitivity sota
Ear-sensitivity: the matter in the ear that sound can strike. It is the base and door of hearing.
nose-sensitivity ghāna
Nose-sensitivity: the matter in the nose that smells can strike. It is the base and door of smelling, and takes its object only by contact.
tongue-sensitivity jivhā
Tongue-sensitivity: the matter in the tongue that tastes can strike. It is the base and door of tasting; the relish comes afterwards, in the mind.
body-sensitivity kāya
Body-sensitivity: the matter spread through the body that tangibles can strike. Its object is three of the great elements themselves.
visible form vaṇṇa
Visible form: colour, the object of seeing. Shape, as the commentaries note, is inferred rather than seen.
sound sadda
Sound: the object of hearing. It is the only sense object that is not one of the eight inseparables.
smell gandha
Smell: the object of the nose. As one of the eight inseparables it is in every group of matter, whether or not anyone smells it.
taste rasa
Taste: the object of the tongue. One of the eight inseparables, it is distinct from the nutritive essence that actually feeds.
femininity itthibhāva
Femininity: the kamma-born faculty that shapes the marks and manner of a female body.
masculinity purisabhāva
Masculinity: the kamma-born faculty that shapes the marks and manner of a male body.
heart-base hadaya
The heart-base: the matter named by the commentaries as the physical support of mind-consciousness. The canonical Paṭṭhāna speaks only of "that matter" on which mind depends.
life faculty jīvita
The material life faculty: it sustains the kamma-born matter of its group for that group's span, as water sustains lotuses (Visuddhimagga XIV).
nutritive essence ojā
Nutritive essence: the nourishment in matter. It is one of the eight inseparables, and taken as food it is one of the four origins of matter.
space ākāsa
Space: the gap that separates one group of matter from another. It is not a thing but the boundary between things.
bodily intimation kāya-viññatti
Bodily intimation: the movement by which a body expresses an intention, the gesture that makes a mind known.
vocal intimation vacī-viññatti
Vocal intimation: the movement by which speech expresses an intention.
lightness lahutā
Lightness of matter: its buoyancy, the body's ease of movement in health.
malleability mudutā
Malleability of matter: its pliancy, the opposite of stiffness.
wieldiness kammaññatā
Wieldiness of matter: its fitness for action.
production upacaya
Production: the first arising of a material series, as when the body's first groups arise at conception.
continuity santati
Continuity: the renewed arising of matter in a series.
decay jaratā
Decay: matter's ageing, its maturing toward dissolution.
impermanence aniccatā
Impermanence: matter's breaking up and vanishing.

The 24 conditions

The ways one dhamma helps another, from the Paṭṭhāna, sorted by direction between mind and matter. Manual VIII §§11–28.

1. root hetu
The six roots, greed, hatred, delusion and their opposites, make the states they arise with firm, like the roots of a tree.
2. object ārammaṇa
Anything at all that a citta takes as its object helps it simply by being known: a colour, a thought, a concept, Nibbāna.
3. predominance adhipati
A predominant leads the mind, as a king leads ministers: desire, energy, consciousness or investigation in its conascent kind, or a highly esteemed object in its object kind.
4. proximity anantara
Each citta, as it ceases, makes way for the next and determines what kind can follow, so the stream of mind has no gaps.
5. contiguity samanantara
Contiguity is proximity seen from another angle: the immediate, seamless succession of one citta by the next.
6. conascence sahajāta
States that arise together help one another to arise, as a flame and its light: a citta and its factors, the four great elements.
7. mutuality aññamañña
Mutuality is help in both directions at once, like the legs of a tripod: each state supports and is supported by the others.
8. support nissaya
Support is help by being a foundation, as the earth supports trees: the great elements for derived matter, the eye for seeing.
9. decisive support upanissaya
Decisive support is strong help, often from far away: a good friend, a climate, a past habit, a resolve, even Nibbāna as an object.
10. prenascence purejāta
Prenascence is help from something that arose earlier and still exists: a sense base or an object already present when the citta arises.
11. postnascence pacchājāta
Postnascence is help from something that arises later, to matter already there: later cittas sustain the body, as later rain helps plants that have already grown.
12. repetition āsevana
Repetition is the way each javana strengthens the next, as a lesson is learned by reciting it.
13. kamma kamma
A volition helps its result: at the same moment, by organising the citta, and across time, as past kamma that ripens later.
14. result vipāka
Resultant states help one another by their passivity, effortlessly, as fruit ripens.
15. nutriment āhāra
The four nutriments sustain what they feed: edible food the body; contact, volition and consciousness the states they arise with.
16. faculty indriya
A faculty controls its own domain, as a governor rules a province: the sense faculties, the life faculties, and the mental faculties such as faith and wisdom.
17. jhāna jhāna
The jhāna factors help by making the mind look closely at its object, in ordinary moments as well as in meditation.
18. path magga
The path factors lead the mind toward a destination, a good one or a bad one.
19. association sampayutta
Association is the help mental states give one another by sharing a base, an object, an arising and a ceasing.
20. dissociation vippayutta
Dissociation is help between mind and matter, which cannot be associated but still support each other.
21. presence atthi
Presence is help by being there at the same time, without which the other could not stand.
22. absence natthi
Absence is help by ceasing: a citta that has gone gives the next its opportunity.
23. disappearance vigata
Disappearance is a citta helping the next by vanishing; it is absence seen from the side of the going.
24. non-disappearance avigata
Non-disappearance is help by not yet having vanished, as a base or a meal still sustains what depends on it; it is presence under another name.

Glossary

121 · the cittas counted in detail
the 89, with each path and fruition counted at five jhāna levels
abhidhamma
the “higher teaching”: experience analysed into ultimate realities, dhammas
Abhidhamma Piṭaka
the third basket of the Pāli Canon: seven books of analysis
Abhidhammattha Saṅgaha
Anuruddha's manual of the whole Abhidhamma in nine chapters; Bodhi's CMA translates it
abhiññā · direct knowledge
a mundane power worked from the fifth jhāna, such as the divine eye or recalling past lives; its citta runs for one moment
abyākata · indeterminate
neither wholesome nor unwholesome: resultants, functionals, matter and Nibbāna
accuta · not passing away
not passing away, often rendered deathless; a name of Nibbāna (VI §32)
āciṇṇa · habitual kamma
what one does again and again; next in line after death-proximate kamma
adhimokkha · decision
resolves on the object; absent from doubt and from sense consciousness
adhipati · predominance
the one factor leading a citta: desire, energy, citta or investigation; or, as object predominance, an object held in high regard
āgantuka-bhavaṅga · adventitious life-continuum
an equanimous investigating citta that bridges displeasure in the javanas and a joyful life-continuum
āhāra · nutriment (four)
edible food, contact, volition and consciousness, each sustaining its results
ahetuka · rootless
a citta with none of the six roots; there are 18
ahirika · anottappa
shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing: no self-respect, no dread of evil's results
ahosi · defunct kamma
kamma whose chance to ripen has passed
ākāra · mode
one of twenty factors in the three-life reading: five for each group
akusala · unwholesome
unhealthy, blameworthy, bringing painful results; rooted in greed, hatred or delusion
ālaya-vijñāna · storehouse consciousness
Yogācāra's eighth consciousness, said to hold the seeds of past action
alobha · adosa · amoha
non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion: the three wholesome roots; non-delusion is wisdom
amata · the deathless
the deathless; a name of Nibbāna in the suttas (SN 43.25)
anāgāmī · non-returner
has cut sensual desire and ill will; reborn only in higher planes
ānantariya · heinous deeds
killing mother, father or an arahant, wounding a Buddha, splitting the Saṅgha
anārammaṇa · without object
without object; said of Nibbāna in Ud 8.1, which the Udāna commentary reads as: unlike a mind, it takes no object (cf. Kv XIX.6)
animitta · signless
without sign; an aspect of Nibbāna (VI §31), and the emancipation reached through the contemplation of impermanence
anipphanna · non-concrete matter
the 10 qualities and modes of concrete matter, such as space and decay
aniṭṭha · undesirable
of an object, undesirable; met through unwholesome kamma
anuloma · conformity
the javana that fits the mind to what follows, just before change-of-lineage
anupādisesa · without residue
the Nibbāna element without residue: named by the absence of aggregates after an arahant's last citta (It 44; VI §31 with the Guide; Vism XVI §561)
anusaya · latent tendencies
seven (six factors) that lie latent, unabandoned and gone to strength, ready to arise when conditions meet; only the paths remove them
apāya · woeful planes
hell, animals, ghosts and titans: the four unhappy destinations
āpo · water element
cohesion, which holds matter together; known by mind, not by touch
appamaññā · illimitables (factors)
compassion and appreciative joy as mental factors, taking suffering or happy beings as object
appamaññā · illimitables (meditation)
loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity, toward all beings: the divine abidings
appanā · absorption
the jhāna or path javana itself, after access; the third stage of concentration
appaṇihita · desireless
without hankering; an aspect of Nibbāna (VI §31), and the emancipation reached through the contemplation of suffering
arahant
one who has cut all ten fetters; makes no new kamma and ends rebirth
ārammaṇa · object
whatever a citta knows: a sight, a sound, a thought, a concept, Nibbāna
ārammaṇa-purejāta · object prenascence
a present object of matter, arisen earlier, helping the cittas that take it
ārammaṇādhipati · object predominance
an object held weighty, which dominates the mind that takes it
ariya · noble one
anyone who has reached a path or fruition, from stream-entry up
ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga · noble eightfold path
right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration; in the strict sense, eight mental factors arising together in a supramundane path citta
ariya-sacca · noble truth
suffering, its origin, its cessation, the path: the four noble truths
arūpāvacara · immaterial sphere
the 12 cittas of formless jhāna and the 4 formless planes
asaṅkhārika · unprompted
arising spontaneously, without urging by oneself or another
asaṅkhata-dhātu · unconditioned element
Nibbāna, the one element not made by conditions
asaṅkheyya · incalculable (the Bodhisatta's career)
in the Bodhisatta's story, a countless number of great aeons
asaṅkheyya-kappa · incalculable aeon (Plate 11)
a quarter of a great aeon, one phase of a world-cycle
āsanna · death-proximate kamma
done or recalled just before death; it ripens next if no weighty kamma does
asaññasatta · non-percipient beings
a fine-material plane of matter with no mind, for 500 great aeons
āsava · ogha · yoga
taints, floods, bonds: sense desire, desire for existence, views, ignorance
asura · titan
a being of the woeful plane of the asuras, or, in another sense, of the warring titans
atīta-bhavaṅga · past life-continuum
the life-continuum moment during which the object arises, before it registers at the door; counted first of the 17
attha-paññatti · meaning-concept
a concept as what is made known: the meaning a name conveys, such as the idea of a chariot
aṭṭhaka · navaka · dasaka
kalāpa sizes: octad eight kinds, nonad nine, decad ten, undecad eleven
Atthasālinī · The Expositor
Buddhaghosa's commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī; source of the mango simile
avijjā · ignorance
not knowing the four noble truths; delusion as a root of the wheel
avinibbhoga · inseparables
the eight kinds in every kalāpa: four elements, colour, smell, taste, nutritive essence
āyatana · base (the twelve)
one of twelve bases: six internal (five sense organs and the mind base) and their six objects
ayoniso manasikāra · unwise attention
attention that turns the mind the wrong way, toward greed, hatred or confusion; the opposite of wise attention
bala · power
a state unshaken by its opposite; nine, among them faith, energy and wisdom
bhaṅga-ñāṇa · dissolution
insight knowledge that attends only to the ending of formations
bhava · kamma-becoming
link 10, active side: volition and the deeds that lead to rebirth
bhava · rebirth-becoming
link 10, passive side: the new life's resultant mind and kamma-born matter
bhavaṅga · life-continuum
the resultant citta, of the same kind as rebirth-linking, that runs between processes
bhavaṅga-calana · vibration of the life-continuum
the life-continuum moment that is shaken when an object comes into range; the next is the arrest
bhavaṅgupaccheda · arrest of the life-continuum
the last life-continuum moment before a process; after it the stream stops and adverting arises
bhūmi · plane
one of 31 planes of existence, each matched to a kind of mind
bodhipakkhiyā dhammā · 37 requisites
the suttas' 37 aids to awakening, which reduce to 14 states
Bodhisatta
a being bound for Buddhahood; the Buddha in his past lives and before awakening
bojjhaṅga · enlightenment factor
seven: mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, zest, tranquillity, concentration, equanimity
Brahmā
a being of the fine-material planes, reborn there through jhāna
carita · temperament
a person's dominant tendency, such as lustful or faithful, guiding the choice of subject
cetanā · volition
the willing that organises the other factors; as kamma, it bears results
cetasika · mental factor
a mental factor: arises and ceases with a citta, sharing its object and base
chanda · desire-to-do
the wish to act or attain; not greed, and can be wholesome
citta · consciousness
one moment of knowing an object; 89 kinds, or 121 counted in detail
cittakkhaṇa · mind-moment
the life of one citta, in three sub-moments: arising, presence, dissolution
cittaviprayukta · dissociated formations
a northern category of things neither mind nor matter, such as life force
cuti · death consciousness
the last citta of a life, of the same kind as its life-continuum
deva
a being of the six sense-sphere heavens, above the human world
dhamma
an ultimate reality, bearing its own nature; not a mere name or concept
Dhammasaṅgaṇī
the first Abhidhamma book: lists every kind of citta and its factors
dhātu · element (the eighteen)
one of eighteen elements: the twelve bases, with the mind base split into seven
diṭṭhi · wrong view
a mistaken belief, such as a lasting self; joins four greed-rooted cittas
domanassa · displeasure
painful mental feeling; only in the two hate-rooted cittas
dosa · hatred
aversion, from irritation to rage; root of two cittas, always with displeasure
duhetuka · two-rooted
a being reborn by a great resultant citta without knowledge; jhāna and the path are closed to them in that life
dukkha · bodily pain
painful bodily feeling: only in unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness
dukkha · suffering
the unsatisfactoriness of all that is conditioned; first noble truth and second mark; three kinds: pain, change, conditioned existence
dvāra · door
the channel by which a process meets its object: five senses and mind
dvāravimutta · door-freed
rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death: cittas that arise without any door
ekaggatā · one-pointedness
unifies the mind on its object; when strong it is concentration (samādhi)
gantha · tie, knot
four ties of the mental and physical body: covetousness, ill will, rites and rituals, the dogma 'this alone is true'
garuka · weighty kamma
jhāna kept to death, a heinous deed or fixed wrong view; ripens first
gati-nimitta · destiny sign
at death, an image of the coming birth
gotrabhū · change-of-lineage
the javana that leaves the sense-sphere lineage for jhāna, or turns to Nibbāna
hadaya-vatthu · heart-base
in beings with bodies, the matter supporting every citta except sense consciousness
hasituppāda · smile-producing
an arahant's rootless functional citta that causes smiling at sense-sphere things
hetu · root
one of six factors that steady a citta: greed, hatred, delusion, or their opposites
hiri · ottappa
moral shame and moral dread: recoiling from evil from self-respect, and fear of results
iddhipāda · means to accomplishment
desire, energy, consciousness or investigation, when it leads the mind toward the goal of the teaching
indriya · faculty

Stories

How a story is read here is a study aid, not the tradition's own reading.

Foundations

Where the Abhidhamma was first taught

The Buddha's life · Atthasālinī, introduction · Tāvatiṃsa heaven and Lake Anotatta, in the seventh rains retreat after the awakening

In the seventh year after his awakening, the commentaries say, the Buddha performed the Twin Miracle at Sāvatthī, and then, as every Buddha does, went up to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for the rains. He sat on Sakka's stone seat beneath the coral tree, and devas from ten thousand world-systems gathered to hear him. At their head was his mother. She had died seven days after his birth and was reborn as a deva; the Dhammapada commentary has her come down from the Tusita heaven to listen. The teaching he gave, with his mother as its chief witness, was the Abhidhamma; modern teachers often call it a debt repaid to the one who had carried him.

The teaching went on without a break for three months. At the hour for alms the Buddha created a likeness of himself to carry on the discourse, went to gather food, and ate beside Lake Anotatta in the Himalaya. Sāriputta waited on him there, and the Buddha gave him the method of that day's teaching in outline: "this much has been taught". Sāriputta, with his gift for analysis, could unfold the whole from the outline, and he taught it to the five hundred monks who were his pupils. The commentary adds that in the time of the Buddha Kassapa they had been bats hanging in a cave. They caught only the sound of two monks reciting the Abhidhamma, not its sense, and that was enough to bring them to a deva world. Now, reborn as men and ordained under Sāriputta, they learned all seven books just as the Buddha's teaching in heaven came to its end.

At the end of the rains, on the full-moon day of Pavāraṇā, the Buddha came down at the city of Saṅkassa by a stairway of jewels, with devas on stairways of gold and silver on either side. The place became one of the great pilgrimage sites. The textual order of the Abhidhamma as monks recite it, and the numerical series of the Paṭṭhāna, the commentary says, were laid down by Sāriputta. Does that make him the first master of the Abhidhamma? No, the commentary answers: the Buddha is, for he penetrated it under the Bodhi tree. Sāriputta is the first to pass it on.

This is the tradition's account of where the seven books described in “The library” came from, and why Sāriputta is honoured as the one who first passed it on.

The last line of every Jātaka

Jātaka · Jātaka, closing identification · The end of each of the 547 birth stories

A Jātaka has a fixed shape. It opens with a story of the present: something happens among the monks, and the Buddha says this is not the first time. Then comes the story of the past, usually set when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, with verses spoken at its turning points. Last comes the connection (samodhāna), in which the Buddha names who was who.

The connection always takes the same form, as in this composite: “At that time Devadatta was the king, Ānanda was the minister, the Buddha's following was the company of ascetics, and I myself was the teacher.” The cast changes roles from tale to tale. Devadatta is a cruel king, a jealous monkey, a greedy brahmin; Ānanda is often a loyal companion; Sāriputta a wise adviser. The Bodhisatta is a king, a hare, a monkey, a merchant, a tree spirit.

Only the verses of the Jātakas belong to the canon. The prose that carries them, the frame story and the closing identification are commentary, collected in Sri Lanka and put into Pāli around the fifth century. The tales teach the perfections the Bodhisatta fulfilled; the closing line adds a lesson of its own: across all these bodies and births, the same name is used for one ongoing stream.

Conventional truth at work (“A chariot of parts”). Ultimately there is only a stream of cittas and matter, each moment conditioning the next. “The Bodhisatta” names the stream: in Nāgasena's words to King Milinda, neither the same person, nor a different one.

Vakkali and the body

Disciples · SN 22.87 · A potter's shed in Rājagaha, and Black Rock on the slope of Isigili

The commentary says Vakkali was a brahmin of Sāvatthī who went forth for one reason: so that he could always see the Buddha, whose body he found beautiful beyond anything. He followed him about and neglected his practice. At last the Buddha sent him away. In despair Vakkali climbed Vulture Peak to throw himself off, and the Buddha appeared before him and taught him.

In the sutta, Vakkali lies sick in a potter's shed in Rājagaha and asks for the Buddha to come. When the Buddha arrives, Vakkali tries to rise from his bed, and is told to lie still. He says he has long wanted to come and see the Buddha but had no strength. The Buddha answers: “Enough, Vakkali. Why do you want to see this foul body? One who sees the Dhamma sees me; one who sees me sees the Dhamma.”

Then the Buddha questions him, as he questioned the first five disciples: is form permanent or impermanent? Feeling, perception, formations, consciousness? Whatever is impermanent, is it fit to be regarded as “mine, I, my self”? Vakkali answers rightly each time.

Vakkali asks to be carried to Black Rock on the slope of Isigili, saying a monk like him should not die inside a house. That night two devas tell the Buddha that Vakkali is intent on release, and in the morning the Buddha sends word to him: do not fear; your death will not be a bad one. Vakkali sends back word that he has no doubt the five aggregates are impermanent, and no desire for them. Then he takes the knife. The Saṃyutta commentary explains what follows: he had overrated himself, and seeing no defilement stir, believed he was already an arahant. In the pain of the wound he saw that he was still an ordinary person, took up his meditation subject again at once, and became an arahant as he died. Afterwards the Buddha shows the monks a smoky cloud moving in all directions: Māra, searching for the place where Vakkali's consciousness has been established. It is nowhere, the Buddha says: Vakkali has attained final Nibbāna.

The commentary takes this Dhamma as the ninefold supramundane Dhamma; the sutta goes straight on to teach him the five aggregates, impermanent and not self. Seen that way, even “the Buddha” is a convention for aggregates, the shift “A chariot of parts” asks of you.

Nun Vajirā's chariot

Disciples · SN 5.10 · The Blind Men's Grove outside Sāvatthī

In the morning Vajirā went into Sāvatthī for alms, and after her meal she went to the Blind Men's Grove to sit for the day under a tree. Māra wanted to make her afraid and break her concentration, and came to her with a question in verse: by whom was this being created? Where is the one who makes beings? Where does a being arise, and where does it cease?

Vajirā knew at once who was speaking. Her answer, in three verses, became one of the most quoted passages in the canon. Why do you assume “a being”? Is that your view, Māra? This is a mere heap of formations; no being is found here. Just as the word “chariot” is used when the parts are put together, so “a being” is the convention when the aggregates are there.

Her last verse goes further: it is only suffering that comes to be, suffering that stands and falls away. Nothing but suffering comes to be, nothing but suffering ceases. Māra, knowing he had been seen through, vanished, sad and disappointed.

Centuries later the monk Nāgasena used the same chariot to answer King Milinda: is the axle the chariot? the wheels? the pole? Neither the parts nor something apart from them, and yet “chariot” is a true name; and he quoted Vajirā's verse to seal the point.

Her reply is the hinge of “A chariot of parts”: the five aggregates underneath, the convention “a being” on top of them.

Rohitassa and the end of the world

Disciples · AN 4.45; SN 2.26 · Jetavana at Sāvatthī, late at night

Late one night a young deva named Rohitassa came to the Buddha at Jetavana, lighting up the whole grove, and asked: is it possible, by travelling, to know or see or reach the end of the world, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away and arise again? No, said the Buddha: that end of the world cannot be reached by going.

The deva was delighted, and told him why. In a former life he had been a seer called Rohitassa, with the power to travel through the air. His speed was that of a light arrow shot by a skilled archer across the shadow of a palm tree, and his stride reached from the eastern ocean to the western. With that speed he had set out to reach the end of the world. Stopping only to eat, drink, sleep and relieve himself, he walked for a hundred years, and died on the way.

The Buddha answered: without reaching the end of the world there is no making an end of suffering. But it is in this very fathom-long body, with its perception and its mind, that I make known the world, its arising, its ending, and the way that leads to its ending. Then he spoke verses: the end of the world is never reached by travelling; the wise one, who knows the world, goes to its end with the holy life lived out.

In SN 35.116 the Buddha gives the same teaching in brief, and the monks ask Ānanda to explain it. That in the world by which one perceives the world and conceives the world, Ānanda says, is called the world in the noble discipline: the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body and the mind.

The world that cannot be reached by walking is the world of “The All, counted twice”: six doors, what comes through them, and the knowing of it, inside a fathom-long body.

The honey-ball

Disciples · MN 18 · The Banyan Park at Kapilavatthu, among the Sakyans

One day the Sakyan Daṇḍapāṇi, out walking with his stick, came to the Buddha and asked what he taught. The Buddha said: such a teaching that one does not quarrel with anyone in the world, and perceptions no longer lie latent in the one who lives free of sensual desire, without doubt and without craving for any kind of being. Daṇḍapāṇi shook his head, raised his eyebrows until three lines stood on his forehead, and went off leaning on his stick.

That evening the Buddha told the monks, and added a short saying: whatever the source from which perceptions and notions born of proliferation (papañca) beset a person, if nothing is found there to delight in, welcome or hold to, that is the end of the underlying tendencies, of quarrels and weapons. Then he rose and went into his dwelling. The monks did not understand, and went to Mahākaccāna.

Mahākaccāna explained. Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition there is feeling. What one feels, one perceives; what one perceives, one thinks about; what one thinks about, one proliferates. And from what one has proliferated, perceptions and notions born of proliferation beset a person, about forms seen with the eye, past, future and present. So too for the ear and each of the other doors.

The monks reported this to the Buddha. Mahākaccāna is wise, he said; had you asked me, I would have answered in the same way. Ānanda said it was like a hungry, exhausted man who finds a ball of honey: wherever he tastes it, it is sweet. Then let this teaching be called the Honey-ball Discourse, said the Buddha.

Mahākaccāna's chain runs from realities to concepts: contact, feeling and perception are dhammas, and what they swell into are the names and notions of “Names and the named”. The commentary names what drives the swelling: craving, conceit and views.

Elements

Kisāgotamī and the mustard seed

Disciples · Dhammapada commentary, v. 114 · Sāvatthī and the Jetavana monastery

Gotamī was called Kisā, “lean”, for her thin frame. She came from a poor family and married into a rich one. The Aṅguttara and Therīgāthā commentaries add that she was treated there with contempt until she bore a son, and then honoured. When the boy was old enough to run about, he died.

She could not accept it. Unable to believe he was gone, she carried his body on her hip from door to door in Sāvatthī, asking for medicine for her son. People laughed at her. A wise man, seeing her state, told her there was one who knew the medicine: the Buddha, at Jetavana.

The Buddha told her he did know the medicine. Bring a mustard seed, he said, from a house in which no one has ever died. She went from house to house. Everyone would gladly give a seed; but in every house someone had died: “the living are few, the dead are many.” By evening she understood. This was not her misfortune alone; it was the way of all who live. The commentary says that her heart, soft with love for her son, grew firm; she left his body in the forest and went back.

She told the Buddha she had found no such house. Death, he said, carries off the one who clings to children and herds as a flood carries off a sleeping village; hearing this, she became a stream-enterer, and asked to go forth. As a nun, the commentary says, she was one day watching the flames of a lamp flare up and die down, and saw in them the rising and falling of beings. The Buddha spoke the verse: better one day seeing the deathless than a hundred years without seeing it. She became an arahant, and he named her foremost among the nuns who wore rough robes.

Her grief is displeasure (domanassadomanassa · displeasure painful mental feeling; only in the two hate-rooted cittas), which in “A map of the eighty-nine” occurs only in the two hate-rooted cittas: grief is aversion toward loss. Its soil is attachment (“from the dear comes sorrow”, Dhp 212), and the commentary says her heart, soft with love for her son, had to grow firm before she could let him go. The search turned a private wound into a universal fact, and the verse on death turned that fact into the path.

Why Moggallāna smiled

Disciples · SN 19.1 · The path down from Vulture Peak, outside Rājagaha

Lakkhaṇa and Mahā Moggallāna were living on Vulture Peak. One morning, walking down to Rājagaha for alms, Moggallāna smiled at a certain place. Lakkhaṇa asked why. “This is not the time for that question,” he said. “Ask me in the presence of the Blessed One.”

After the meal, before the Buddha, Lakkhaṇa asked again. Moggallāna said that on the way down he had seen a skeleton travelling through the air, with vultures, crows and hawks following it, pecking between its ribs, and it cried out in pain. It had struck him: how wonderful that there should be such a being.

The Buddha said his disciples live with vision and knowledge. He himself had seen that being before, but had not spoken of it, because those who did not believe it would come to harm through disbelief. It had been a cattle butcher in Rājagaha. After long ages in hell, it was now living out what remained of that deed in such a body. The suttas that follow in the same chapter tell of twenty more such beings, each with its deed.

An arahant smiles with one of five cittas, none of which makes kamma: the smile-producing consciousness found only in arahants (in “A map of the eighty-nine”), or one of the four joyful great functional cittas. What he saw belongs to the woeful planes of “Thirty-one planes”.

Khantivādi, the teacher of patience

Jātaka · Ja 313 · The royal park at Benares, in the reign of King Kalābu

The Buddha told this story about a monk given to anger. Long ago, the Bodhisatta was born to a rich brahmin family, gave away his wealth, and lived as an ascetic in the Himalaya. Coming down to Benares for salt and vinegar, he stayed in the royal park.

King Kalābu came to the park with his dancers, drank, and fell asleep with his head on a favourite's lap. The women, bored, wandered off and found the ascetic, and sat around him listening to him teach. The king woke, found them gone, and came upon them in a rage. “What do you teach, ascetic?” “Patience, great king.” “What is patience?” “Not to be angry when one is abused, struck or insulted.”

“Let us see your patience,” said the king, and called the executioner. The ascetic was flogged with thorny lashes; his hands were cut off, then his feet, then his nose and ears. Each time the king asked what he taught, and each time the answer was the same: patience, which is not in the skin or the limbs but deep in the heart. The king kicked him in the chest and walked away.

The king's commander-in-chief wiped the blood away and begged him to be angry with the king alone, not with the kingdom. “May the king live long,” said the ascetic. “Those like me do not get angry.” As the king left the park the earth split open and he was drawn down into the fires of Avīci. The ascetic died that same day.

“An ensemble of fifty-two” at its sharpest: non-hatred (adosaadosa · non-hatred Non-hatred is the mind's not opposing its object: friendliness and patience, not only the absence of ill will.) and hatred (dosadosa · hatred aversion, from irritation to rage; root of two cittas, always with displeasure) never share a citta. The king's fate returns in “Kamma, death and rebirth” as kamma that ripens in this very life.

The monkey king's bridge

Jātaka · Ja 407 · A great mango tree on the bank of the Ganges, in the Himalaya

The Buddha told this story when the monks praised him for working for his kinsmen's good. The monkey king lived with his troop in a mango tree whose branches spread over the Ganges. Knowing the danger, he had every fruit on the branches over the water eaten while still small. One mango, hidden by an ant's nest, ripened and fell into the river, and floated down to Benares, where it was caught in the king's bathing nets.

The king tasted it, and longed for more. He went upstream with his men, found the tree and the monkeys eating, and surrounded it with archers to shoot them at dawn. The monkeys, trapped, came trembling to their king.

He leapt to the far bank, cut a long cane, tied one end to a tree there and the other round his waist, and leapt back; but he had forgotten the length round his waist, and fell short by the length of his own body. So he caught a branch of the mango tree with both hands, made himself the last stretch of the bridge, and told the troop to cross. Eighty thousand monkeys crossed over his back. Last came one who had always hated him, and leapt down hard on his back, and his heart broke.

The king of Benares had watched it all. He had the monkey king lowered gently, bathed, robed and laid on a couch, and asked him why he had given his life for them. A king, the monkey answered, should be like this: he should seek the welfare of all who depend on him, even at the cost of his own life. Then he died, and the king honoured him as a king.

Compassion (karuṇākaruṇā · compassion Compassion is the wish that suffering be removed from others; its near enemy is grief, its far enemy cruelty.) is one of the variable beautiful factors in “An ensemble of fifty-two”. It joins a wholesome citta only now and then, when the suffering of others is the object. The Jātaka's own lesson is for rulers: one who leads should seek the good of all who depend on him.

Dhammadinnā on feeling

Disciples · MN 44 · The Bamboo Grove at Rājagaha

The commentary tells the background. Visākha, a merchant of Rājagaha, heard the Buddha teach and in time became a non-returner. When he came home he no longer smiled at his wife as before. When she learned why, she asked to go forth, and soon became an arahant. Then Visākha came to put questions to her.

He asked her about identity: what the Buddha calls “personality”, how identity view arises and how it ends; about the noble path and the three trainings; about formations of body, speech and mind, and the attainment of cessation. Then he asked about feeling: pleasant, painful and neutral, and what lies latent in each.

Lust lies latent in pleasant feeling, she said, aversion in painful feeling, ignorance in neutral feeling; but not in every pleasant feeling. The pleasure of the first jhāna abandons lust; the pain of longing for liberation, a grief of the mind, abandons aversion; the neutral feeling of the fourth jhāna abandons ignorance.

He pressed on: what is the counterpart of pleasant feeling? of neutral feeling? of ignorance? of liberation? And what is the counterpart of Nibbāna? “You have gone too far, friend Visākha,” she said. “The holy life is lived with Nibbāna as its culmination.” Visākha reported all this to the Buddha, who said: “The nun Dhammadinnā is wise. If you had asked me, I would have answered in the same way.”

This joins the colours of feeling in “A map of the eighty-nine” to the wheel in “The wheel across three lives”: feeling (link 7) is where craving (link 8) takes hold.

Pukkusāti and the elements

Disciples · MN 140 · The potter Bhaggava's workshop in Rājagaha, one night

The commentary says Pukkusāti was the king of Takkasilā, far to the north-west, and a friend by letter of King Bimbisāra. Bimbisāra once sent him, engraved on a gold plate, an account of the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha. Pukkusāti read it, shaved his head, put on a robe, and walked alone the whole way to Rājagaha.

In the sutta, the Buddha arrives at Rājagaha and asks the potter Bhaggava for a night in his workshop. A monk is already there: Pukkusāti, who has gone forth under the Buddha's name without ever seeing him. Both sit in silence most of the night. Then the Buddha asks whom he follows, and offers to teach.

He teaches that a person is made of six elements: earth, water, fire, air, space and consciousness. Each is examined, inside the body and outside it: whatever is hard in the body, the hair, nails, teeth, bones, is earth, and it is to be seen as “this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.” What remains is a pure, bright equanimity, and even that is seen as conditioned. Pukkusāti understands that this is the Teacher, and asks forgiveness for having called him “friend”.

He asks for full ordination. The Buddha does not ordain one without bowl and robes, so Pukkusāti goes out to find them, and a cow gores him to death. The monks ask what has become of him. He was wise, the Buddha says, and practised in line with the Dhamma: he has broken the five lower fetters and will reach Nibbāna from the Pure Abodes without returning.

The four great elements are the core of the 28 kinds of matter in “How matter is made”. Analysing the body into elements is also one of the subjects in “Forty meditation subjects”.

Nakulapitā, sick in body, not in mind

Disciples · SN 22.1 · The Deer Park in Bhesakaḷā Grove, at Suṃsumāragira in the Bhagga country

Nakulapitā came to the Buddha and said: I am old, venerable sir, worn out, at the last stage of life, sick in body and often ill, and I seldom get to see the Blessed One and the monks. Let the Blessed One teach me something for my lasting good. The Buddha agreed: your body is afflicted, householder, and for anyone carrying such a body to claim even a moment's health would be foolish. So train yourself thus: though I am afflicted in body, my mind will not be afflicted.

Nakulapitā went to Sāriputta, who saw at once that his faculties were serene and his face bright, and asked if he had heard a talk on the Dhamma. He told him what the Buddha had said, and Sāriputta asked whether he had asked how far a body can be afflicted without the mind. Nakulapitā had not; he would come a long way to hear it. Sāriputta explained.

The untaught ordinary person regards form as self, or self as having form, or form in self, or self in form, and lives obsessed with the idea “I am form, form is mine”. When that form changes, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair arise: such a one is afflicted in body and in mind. So too with feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. The noble disciple does not regard them so; when the body changes, the mind does not follow it into grief. He is afflicted in body, but not in mind.

Elsewhere the couple are named together as the foremost among lay followers who were intimate with the Buddha, and in AN 4.55 they tell him that they have never been unfaithful to each other even in thought, and wish to meet again in future lives. The commentary says they had been his parents in many former births, and that on first seeing him Nakulapitā called him “son”.

In “Feeling, roots and objects” bodily feeling alone is painful or pleasant, and mental pain comes only with the two hate-rooted cittas. Nakulapitā's training is the gap between the two.

Two sheaves of reeds

Disciples · SN 12.67 · The Deer Park at Isipatana, near Bārāṇasī

One evening, after the afternoon's meditation, Mahākoṭṭhita came to Sāriputta in the Deer Park and put a series of questions. Is aging and death made by oneself, friend, or by another, or by both, or does it arise by chance, made by neither? None of these, said Sāriputta: with birth as condition, aging and death. And so back through the links, birth, becoming, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six bases, to name-and-form.

Is name-and-form made by oneself, or by another? Neither: with consciousness as condition, name-and-form. And consciousness? With name-and-form as condition, consciousness. Mahākoṭṭhita pressed him: how are we to understand that? Sāriputta gave the simile. Just as two sheaves of reeds might stand leaning against each other, so with name-and-form as condition there is consciousness, and with consciousness as condition there is name-and-form. If one sheaf were drawn away, the other would fall; and so with these two. With their ceasing, the whole mass of suffering ceases.

Mahākoṭṭhita rejoiced. He went on to ask who may be called a speaker on the Dhamma, and Sāriputta answered: one who teaches for disenchantment with aging and death, for its fading and ceasing. Mahākoṭṭhita said it was wonderful how well every question had been answered.

The two sheaves are consciousness on one side and name-and-form on the other (the mental factors and matter); “Mind and matter together” models the same mutual support: two currents that hold each other up, and that arise together at conception.

Buddhaghosa and the tangle

Disciples · Cūḷavaṃsa 37 · Near the tree of awakening in India, then the Mahāvihāra at Anurādhapura, in the reign of King Mahānāma

Near the tree of awakening, the chronicle says, there lived a young brahmin who knew the Vedas and every art, and went about India looking for debates. One night in a monastery he recited his own doctrine, and the elder Revata, hearing him, answered it, then recited a passage of the Abhidhamma that the brahmin could not follow. Whose teaching is that? The Buddha's. He asked to learn it, was told he must first go forth, and did. Because his voice was deep like the Buddha's, he was called Buddhaghosa, voice of the Buddha.

Revata told him that only the texts had been kept in India; the commentaries survived in Sinhala, in Sri Lanka. So Buddhaghosa crossed over to the Mahāvihāra at Anurādhapura, heard the Sinhala commentaries, and asked to translate them. The elders gave him a test: two verses from the Saṃyutta. A deva asks the Buddha about a tangle within and a tangle without, and who can untangle it. The Buddha answers that one who stands firm in virtue, wise, developing mind and understanding, can untangle it. Show your skill on these, they said.

He wrote the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, laying out the whole teaching under virtue, concentration and understanding. The devas, the chronicle says, hid the book to show his skill, and he wrote it a second time, and they hid that too, and he wrote it a third time. When the first two were brought back and the three were read side by side, they agreed in every word. Then the elders gave him the books, and he put the commentaries into Pali.

The heap of coins, the struck bell and the gliding bird of “The commentators' picture-book” are read in the Visuddhimagga; this is the tradition's account of how that book came to be written.

Mālukyaputta's teaching in brief

Disciples · SN 35.95 · Late in the life of an aged monk who wanted to live alone

Mālukyaputta came to the Buddha and asked for a short teaching, so that he could go off alone and practise. What shall I say to the young monks, the Buddha replied, when an old man like you, aged and far along in years, asks for a teaching in brief? Mālukyaputta asked again: even if he was old, perhaps he would understand, and become an heir of the teaching.

So the Buddha asked him. Are there forms known by the eye that you have not seen, have never seen, do not see now and do not expect to see; would you have desire or lust or affection for those? No, venerable sir. And so for sounds, smells, tastes, touches and ideas. Then, he said, let the seen be only the seen, the heard only the heard, the sensed only the sensed, the known only the known. When that is so, you will be neither here nor beyond nor in between, and that is the end of suffering.

Asked whether he had understood, Mālukyaputta answered in verses. Seeing a form with mindfulness lost, attending to its pleasing sign, one feels it with an infatuated mind and holds on; feelings born of the sight multiply, covetousness and harm unsettle the mind, and one is far from Nibbāna. But one who sees a form mindfully is not inflamed by it; he feels it with a mind detached, and as he sees and feels, suffering wears away instead of piling up. The Buddha approved every verse. Mālukyaputta went off alone, and before long he was one of the arahants.

Seeing is one of the fourteen jobs of “What each citta does”, done by a resultant citta that cannot be otherwise. The harm in Mālukyaputta's verses begins after it, in attending to the pleasing sign, at the one station where the javanas run and kamma is made.

The royal cook's sauce

Disciples · Milindapañha, the questions on distinguishing marks · Sāgala, King Milinda's city in the north-west

The king and the elder had been going through the factors of mind one at a time, each by its mark. Contact is known by touching, Nāgasena said, like two rams butting, the eye one ram, the form the other, and their meeting the contact. Feeling is known by being felt, perception by perceiving, volition by willing, initial application by fixing the mind on its object. Earlier, answering whether there is a knower inside, he had said that where eye-consciousness arises, contact arises with it, and feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, the life faculty and attention.

Then the king asked the harder question. Once these states are blended into one, can they be taken apart, so that one could show the difference: this is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness? They cannot, said Nāgasena. Suppose a king's cook made a sauce or a curry, with curds, salt, ginger, cumin, pepper and the rest. Could anyone take from it the taste of the curds alone, or the taste of the salt? No, said the king, but each taste is there by its own mark. Just so with these states.

The cook's sauce is a picture of one column of “Which factors meet which cittas”: a single citta assembled from a fixed menu of factors, each present by its own mark and none separable from the moment.

Process

Bāhiya: in the seen, only the seen

Disciples · Ud 1.10 · Suppāraka on the western coast, then the streets of Sāvatthī

Bāhiya lived at Suppāraka by the sea, dressed in bark, and people honoured him as an arahant. The commentary says he had been shipwrecked and came ashore naked, covered himself in bark, and was taken for a holy man. One day the thought came to him: am I one of those who are arahants? A deva who had once been his kinsman came to him and said: you are not, and you are not even on the way. There is one in Sāvatthī who is.

Bāhiya set out at once, and travelled, the commentary says, the whole way in one night. At Jetavana he was told the Buddha had gone into the city for alms. He hurried after him, fell at his feet in the street and begged to be taught. “It is not the time,” said the Buddha; “I am on alms round.” Bāhiya asked a second time, and a third: “It is hard to know how long the Blessed One will live, or how long I will.”

Then the Buddha taught him, standing there: “Bāhiya, train yourself thus: in the seen there will be only the seen, in the heard only the heard, in the sensed only the sensed, in the cognized only the cognized. When that is so, you will not be ‘with that’; when you are not ‘with that’, you will not be ‘in that’; then you will be neither here nor beyond nor between the two. This is the end of suffering.”

Bāhiya's mind was freed on the spot. Soon after the Buddha left, a cow with a young calf attacked and killed him. Returning from his round, the Buddha had the monks cremate the body and build a mound for it, and declared that Bāhiya had attained final Nibbāna. He later named him foremost among those who understand quickly.

“The mango and the moment” shows where the instruction bites, and the Udāna commentary reads it the same way: let the javanas stay at the measure of eye-consciousness, which neither lusts, hates nor is deluded. Seeing itself, at moment 5, is a result and makes no kamma. Liking, disliking and “I” enter only in the javanas.

Nanda, guardian of the doors

Disciples · Ud 3.2; AN 8.9; AN 1.230 · Kapilavatthu, Jetavana, and a journey to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven

The commentary tells how it began. On the Buddha's first visit home, on the day of Nanda's wedding and consecration, the Buddha handed him his bowl and walked away. Nanda, out of respect, followed him to the monastery holding it, and his bride called after him, hair half combed: “Come back soon, my lord.” At the monastery the Buddha asked if he would go forth, and Nanda could not bring himself to refuse.

In the Udāna, Nanda tells the monks he is not happy in the holy life: he keeps thinking of the Sakyan girl and her parting words, and means to give up the training. The Buddha takes him by the arm and, as quickly as one might bend an arm, takes him to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, where five hundred nymphs with feet like doves are waiting on Sakka. Which is lovelier, he asks, your bride or these? Beside them, says Nanda, she is like a scorched she-monkey with her ears and nose cut off. The Buddha promises him the nymphs if he practises.

Back at Jetavana, the other monks hear of it and call Nanda a hireling, a monk bought for nymphs. Ashamed, he goes off alone and practises with all his strength, and soon becomes an arahant. He comes to release the Buddha from his promise; the Buddha already knows.

In AN 8.9 the Buddha praises him: Nanda is strong, handsome and passionate, and yet he lives the holy life in full, because he guards the doors of his senses, eats with moderation, stays wakeful, and is mindful. If he looks to the east, he looks having considered it fully, so that longing and grief do not flood in.

The Buddha met Nanda's desire where it was and led it past itself: once free, Nanda wanted nothing of the promise. The doors he then learned to guard are the doors of “The mango and the moment”. Guarding them means the seeing is not followed by unwholesome javanas.

Makhādeva's first grey hair

Jātaka · Ja 9 · Mithilā, capital of Videha

The Buddha told this story when the monks were talking about his own going forth. Makhādeva lived in an age when lives were long: the tale gives him eighty-four thousand years as a prince, as many as viceroy, and as many as king.

One day he told his barber: “When you see a grey hair on my head, tell me.” Many years later the barber found one, drew it out with tweezers and laid it in the king's hand. The king looked at it and felt as if the king of death had come and was standing beside him. He called it a messenger of the gods (devadūta).

He gave the barber a village, called his eldest son, and handed him the kingdom, asking him to do the same when his own first grey hair appeared. Then he went forth in a mango grove near the city, cultivated the four divine abidings, and after death was reborn in the Brahmā world.

His line kept the custom for eighty-four thousand kings. The last of them was Nimi, whose story is told in Ja 541: the Bodhisatta born again at the end of his own line, to close the circle.

A small object can carry a large process: the same grey hair can stir vanity or urgency (saṃvega), depending on how it is attended to (“The mango and the moment”). MN 83 adds the Buddha's own point: Makhādeva's good custom led to the Brahmā world; the custom he himself founded, the noble eightfold path, leads to Nibbāna.

Rāhula and the mirror

The Buddha's life · MN 61 · Ambalaṭṭhikā, in the Bamboo Grove at Rājagaha

Seeing the Buddha coming in the evening, Rāhula set out a seat and water for his feet. The Buddha washed his feet and left a little water in the vessel. “Do you see this little water left, Rāhula? Just so little is the recluseship of those who are not ashamed to tell a deliberate lie.” He threw the water away: just so is their recluseship thrown away. He turned the vessel upside down, and then upright, empty: just so overturned, just so empty.

Then an elephant: a royal tusker that goes into battle using its feet, its body, its tusks and its tail, but keeps its trunk back, has not yet given its life to the fight. When it uses its trunk too, there is nothing it will not do. So with one who is not ashamed to lie: there is no evil he will not do. “Train thus, Rāhula: I will not tell a lie even as a joke.”

Then the mirror. “What is a mirror for?” “For reflection, venerable sir.” So, before doing an action with the body, while doing it and after it, one should reflect: does this lead to my own affliction, to others', or to both? Is it unwholesome, with painful results? If so, do not do it; stop it; and if it is done, confess it to the teacher or a wise companion and restrain yourself in future. The same for speech; but a deed of mind already done is not confessed: one should be troubled by it, ashamed of it, and turn from it. If the act was good, abide happy and glad, training day and night.

Reflection is a discipline for the javanas, where volition becomes kamma (“The mango and the moment” and “Kamma, death and rebirth”).

Ānanda lies down

Disciples · Vinaya, Cūḷavagga XI · Rājagaha, on the night before the First Council

After the Buddha's death Mahā Kassapa chose the monks who would recite the teaching at Rājagaha: four hundred and ninety-nine arahants, and Ānanda, who had heard more of the Buddha's words than anyone but was still a trainee. He could not be left out, and he could not be counted with the others as he was.

On the night before the council, the Vinaya says, Ānanda spent much of the night mindful of the body. The commentaries add that he walked up and down his walking path, striving hard, and remembered that the Buddha had told him in his last days that he would soon be free. Seeing no result, he saw that he had pushed too hard, so that energy was tipping into restlessness, and he resolved to balance it.

Towards dawn he went into his dwelling to lie down. As he inclined his body, with his feet off the ground and his head not yet on the pillow, his mind was freed from the taints without clinging. The commentaries treasure the detail: he became an arahant in none of the four postures, neither walking, standing, sitting nor lying.

In the morning he took his seat in the assembly. The commentaries tell that he came by his power, rising up through the earth or through the air, so that the others would know without being told. Asked by Mahā Kassapa where each discourse was spoken and to whom, he recited the suttas, beginning “Thus have I heard”, after Upāli had recited the Discipline.

The path process in “Other processes” runs at the mind door and needs no posture at all: preparation, access, conformity, cleansing (the name change-of-lineage takes for the higher paths), then path and fruition, in the space between standing and lying down.

Pilindavaccha's old word

Disciples · Ud 3.6; Dhammapada commentary, v. 408 · Among the monks at Rājagaha

The monks went to the Buddha: venerable Pilindavaccha addresses the monks as vasala. The Buddha had him called and asked whether it was true, and he said it was. The Buddha turned his mind to Pilindavaccha's former lives, and then told the monks not to be offended. Vaccha does not address you so from hatred within. For five hundred lives in unbroken succession he was born in a brahmin family, and that word has long been his habit.

Then the Buddha spoke a verse: one in whom there is no deceit and no conceit, with greed gone, owning nothing, wanting nothing, anger put out, cooled within; he is a brahmin, he is an ascetic, he is a monk.

The Dhammapada commentary tells the same complaint, and has the Buddha add that one whose taints are destroyed has no harsh, wounding speech: my son, he said, speaks so from habit. Then he spoke the verse: one who speaks words that are gentle, clear and true, and that offend no one, him I call a brahmin.

An arahant has lost every wholesome and unwholesome javana, as “Who has which cittas” explains. Pilindavaccha's rough word is moved by a functional citta: there is no hatred in it and no kamma is made, though the habit of the word remains.

Relations

The night of awakening

The Buddha's life · MN 36; Ud 1.1–1.3 · The foot of the Bodhi tree at Uruvelā, on the bank of the Nerañjarā

Having given up the austerities and eaten again, he sat beneath the tree and entered the four jhānas. With his mind concentrated, pure and pliant, he turned it to knowledge.

In the first watch of the night he recollected his past lives: one birth, two, a hundred thousand, through many aeons of the world's contraction and expansion, with names, families, food, pleasures and pains, and the way each life ended. In the second watch, with the divine eye, he saw beings dying and being reborn, inferior and superior, fortunate and unfortunate, according to their deeds. In the third watch he knew the four noble truths, and the taints of sensual desire, becoming and ignorance were destroyed. “Ignorance was dispelled and knowledge arose, darkness was dispelled and light arose.”

The Udāna adds what followed. For seven days he sat in one posture at the foot of the tree, experiencing the bliss of release. At the end of the week he attended to dependent origination: in the first watch in forward order, how suffering arises; in the second in reverse, how it ceases; in the third in both. At the end of each watch he spoke a verse that opens the same way: when things become clear to the ardent, meditating brahmin. After the first, his doubts vanish because he understands things with their cause; after the second, because he has known the ending of conditions; after the third, he stands scattering Māra's army, like the sun lighting up the sky.

The three watches map onto the readings: past lives across the planes (“Thirty-one planes”), beings reborn by kamma and its fruit (“Kamma, death and rebirth”), and the wheel with its ending (“The wheel across three lives” and “The tree of purification”).

Assaji's four lines

Disciples · Vinaya, Mahāvagga I.23 · The streets of Rājagaha, then the Bamboo Grove

Upatissa and Kolita, two young brahmins of good family, had gone forth together under the wanderer Sañjaya. They had learned all he could teach and found no end of suffering in it. They made a pact: whichever of them first found the deathless would tell the other.

In Rājagaha, Upatissa saw a monk on alms round whose bearing was so calm, going and coming, looking ahead and looking aside, that he thought: if anyone is an arahant, this monk is. He followed him until the meal was over and then asked: whom do you follow, friend? What does your teacher say? Assaji answered that he was new to the teaching and could not explain it at length, but would give its meaning in brief.

Then he spoke the verse: “Of those things that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has told the cause, and also what their cessation is: this is the doctrine of the great recluse.” As he heard it, the dustless eye of Dhamma arose in Upatissa: whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation.

He went to Kolita, who saw from his face what had happened, and on hearing the verse attained the same. They went to the Buddha at the Bamboo Grove with two hundred and fifty of Sañjaya's followers. Seeing them coming, the Buddha said: these two will be my chief pair of disciples. The commentaries add that Moggallāna became an arahant within a week, Sāriputta within a fortnight.

The shortest summary of “The web of twenty-four conditions” and “The wheel across three lives”: whatever is conditioned has conditions, and they can cease. Sāriputta went on, the commentary says, to pass the Abhidhamma on to its first human disciples (“The library”).

“Do not say so, Ānanda”

The Buddha's life · DN 15 · Kammāsadhamma, a market town of the Kurus

Ānanda came to the Buddha and said: it is wonderful, venerable sir, how deep this dependent origination is, and how deep it appears; and yet to me it seems as clear as clear can be.

“Do not say so, Ānanda,” the Buddha answered. “It is deep and it appears deep. It is through not understanding and not penetrating this teaching that this generation has become like a tangled skein, a knotted ball of thread, like matted reeds and rushes, and does not pass beyond the plane of misery, the bad destinations, the lower world, saṃsāra.”

Then he took Ānanda through it again, link by link, asking at each step: is there a specific condition for aging and death? For birth? For becoming? In this telling the chain runs back to consciousness and name-and-form, which condition each other, and stops there: “to this extent one may be born, age and die.” A second chain shows how craving leads to seeking, gain, possessiveness and at last to quarrels and the taking up of weapons. The sutta ends with the ways people describe a self, and the eight liberations.

“The web of twenty-four conditions” and “The wheel across three lives” make the structure visible, but reading a diagram is learning (suta). Seeing a link happen is development (bhāvanā).

Rays from the Jewel House

The Buddha's life · Atthasālinī, introduction · The Ratanaghara, “jewel house”, near the Bodhi tree, in the fourth week after the awakening

The commentaries spend each of the seven weeks after the awakening at a different spot near the Bodhi tree. In the fourth he sat to the north-west of the tree, at the place called the jewel house. Not a house of jewels, the Atthasālinī says, but the spot where he contemplated the seven books, the jewels of the Abhidhamma; the Jātaka introduction has the devas build a jewelled house there. He sat and went over the Abhidhamma in his mind, book by book.

He went through the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, then the Vibhaṅga, the Dhātukathā, the Puggalapaññatti, the Kathāvatthu and the Yamaka, and nothing happened. Then he came to the Paṭṭhāna, with its twenty-four conditions and their numberless combinations. Here, the commentary says, his omniscient knowledge found room at last, like the great fish Timirapiṅgala turning in the ocean, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep.

As his mind moved in that vastness, rays of six colours streamed from his body: blue from his hair and the dark of his eyes, yellow from his skin, red from his flesh and blood, white from his bones, teeth and the whites of his eyes, crimson from various parts of his body, and a shining blend of all five. They spread through the universe. This was neither a power willed nor a power of meditation, the commentary says: as he contemplated, his blood, the heart-base and his skin grew clear, and colour born of mind stood around him.

In 1885 a committee in Colombo designed a flag from these six colours for the Vesak holiday, and the American Henry Steel Olcott helped adapt it for wider use. It is now the Buddhist flag across the world.

The tradition marks the Paṭṭhāna, the book behind “The web of twenty-four conditions”, as the vastest of all. Its colours inspired the modern Buddhist flag.

Ariṭṭha and the ten pictures

Disciples · MN 22 · Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika's park at Sāvatthī

Ariṭṭha announced his view: as he understood the Dhamma, the things the Blessed One called obstructions could not obstruct anyone who engaged in them. Monks went to him and pressed him. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, they said. He has called sensual pleasures a skeleton, a piece of meat, a grass torch, a pit of coals, a dream, borrowed goods, fruit on a tree, a butcher's knife and block, a stake of swords, a snake's head: much suffering, much despair, and the danger in them greater. Ariṭṭha held to his view all the same. (The commentary says he meant sexual relations, for a monk.)

Brought before the Buddha, he was asked from whom he had heard the Dhamma taught that way. He sat silent, shoulders drooping, head down, with nothing to say. The Buddha went through the ten pictures again himself. Elsewhere, in the Potaliya Sutta, he draws them out one by one: the hungry dog gnawing a bone with no meat on it, the bird with a scrap of meat chased by the others, the man carrying a burning torch against the wind, the dream that is gone on waking, the borrowed goods their owner takes back, the man up a fruit tree while another fells it.

Then he spoke of how the teaching itself can be grasped. Some learn it for the sake of finding fault and winning arguments; they hold it like a man who seizes a snake by the tail, and it turns and bites him. Others grasp it well, like a man who pins the snake down with a forked stick and takes it behind the head. And the teaching, he said, is like a raft: for crossing over, not for carrying on one's head once across.

Ten pictures for one thing, sensual pleasures: the objects that greed fastens on, each picture showing a different danger. As “The lists reduced to their factors” shows for the taints, floods, bonds and fetters, many names can point to one factor, greed, each name catching it in a different act.

Lives and worlds

Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī's last thought

Disciples · Dhammapada commentary, v. 2 · Sāvatthī

In Sāvatthī lived a brahmin so mean that he was called Adinnapubbaka, “one who never gave”. To save the goldsmith's fee he hammered out a pair of earrings for his only son himself, and the boy was called Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, “Burnished Earrings”.

At sixteen the boy fell ill with jaundice. The father would not pay a physician; he asked doctors what they gave for such an illness and treated the boy himself with bark, and the boy grew worse. When it was clear he would die, the father carried him out to the veranda, so that people coming to mourn would not see the wealth inside the house.

That morning the Buddha, surveying the world, saw the boy. On his alms round he stopped at the door and sent out a ray of light. The boy turned and saw him. Because of his father, he thought, he had never served the Buddha, given to him or heard him teach, and now his hands would not obey him; all he could do was make his mind bright. He set his heart on him in faith, and died with that thought. He was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden mansion.

The father went to the charnel ground every day to weep. The young deva, seeing it, took his old form and wept beside him. Asked why, he said he wanted a pair of wheels for his golden chariot, and the only ones that would do were the sun and the moon. “You fool,” said the brahmin, “you weep for what cannot be had.” “The sun and moon can at least be seen,” said the boy. “You weep for one who is gone and cannot be seen. Which of us is the fool?” Then he revealed who he was. The brahmin invited the Buddha to a meal, and the Buddha spoke the second verse of the Dhammapada: mind goes before all things; if one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness follows like a shadow that never leaves.

Death-proximate kamma in “Kamma, death and rebirth”: the last javanas were full of faith, and the rebirth-linking that followed took up their object.

Queen Mallikā's seven days

Disciples · Dhammapada commentary, v. 151 · Sāvatthī, the court of King Pasenadi of Kosala

Mallikā was the daughter of a garland-maker. As a girl she gave her own meal to the Buddha, and soon after King Pasenadi, meeting her by chance, made her his queen. She became one of the Buddha's most devoted followers. In one sutta she tells the king that no one is dearer to her than herself, and asks him; he has to say the same of himself; in another, when the king is disappointed that she has borne a daughter, the Buddha tells him a woman may prove better than a man.

The commentary tells of one fault. In the bath-house she let her dog behave improperly with her, and the king saw it through a window. When he spoke of it, she told him the room had a trick to it: whoever went in would look doubled to one outside. She sent him in, and claimed to see him with a she-goat. He believed her.

When she was dying, she did not think of her great gifts, but of this deed and the lie that covered it, and she was reborn in the Avīci hell for seven days. The grieving king went to the Buddha meaning to ask where she was reborn. Each day the Buddha turned the talk so that he forgot to ask: had he heard she was in hell, the commentary says, he would have decided that giving is useless and stopped his daily alms to five hundred monks. On the eighth day she was reborn in the Tusita heaven, and the Buddha told the king.

On the eighth day the Buddha came to the palace on alms round and sat in the chariot hall. Whose chariot is this, he asked, and this? The king's grandfather's, his father's, his own. Then the verse: even the splendid chariots of kings wear out, and so does the body; but the Dhamma of the good does not grow old.
