The other face of death-proximate kamma: one unwholesome last thought outweighed a good life, but only for a while. Her stored good kamma then took its turn (“Kamma, death and rebirth”).

Aṅgulimāla and the stones

Disciples · MN 86 · The kingdom of Kosala, the road to Aṅgulimāla's forest, and Sāvatthī

The commentary tells how a gifted student called Ahiṃsaka, “harmless”, was slandered by jealous fellow students, and his teacher, to be rid of him, demanded a fee of a thousand human fingers. In the sutta he is already a bandit in the realm of King Pasenadi, wearing a garland of fingers, who has laid waste villages and towns.

One morning the Buddha took the road toward his forest. Cowherds and farmers warned him that men in groups of ten, twenty, thirty, even forty had gone that way and fallen to Aṅgulimāla. He walked on in silence. Aṅgulimāla saw him and ran after him with sword and shield, but, running his hardest, could not catch the Buddha walking at his ordinary pace. “Stop, recluse!” he shouted. “I have stopped, Aṅgulimāla,” said the Buddha. “You stop too.” I have stopped, he explained, because I have laid down the rod toward all beings; you have not. Aṅgulimāla threw his weapons into a chasm, bowed, and asked to go forth.

King Pasenadi rode out with five hundred horsemen to take him, and found him sitting at Jetavana with shaven head. The king, amazed, offered him robes and requisites, which he declined, having all a forest monk needs: “what we could not tame with force and weapons, the Blessed One has tamed without them.” On alms round Aṅgulimāla saw a woman in a difficult childbirth, and the Buddha gave him words to say to her: since I was born with the noble birth, I do not recall ever taking a life; by this truth may you and your child be well. She was safe. The verse is still chanted for women in labour.

He became an arahant. One day he came back from alms round with a broken head, his bowl smashed and his robe torn, from a stone, a stick and a potsherd thrown at him. The Buddha said: “Bear it, brahmin. You are experiencing here and now the result of deeds for which you might have been tormented in hell for many years.” His verses close the sutta: one who was heedless and later is heedful lights up the world like the moon freed from a cloud.

Kamma by time (“Kamma, death and rebirth”): what could ripen in this life did. With arahantship there is no next life, so kamma waiting for later lives could never ripen.

Devadatta's weighty kamma

Disciples · Vinaya, Cūḷavagga VII; Dhammapada commentary, v. 17 · Rājagaha, Vulture Peak, Gayāsīsa, and the gate of Jetavana

Devadatta went forth with the Sakyan princes Bhaddiya, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu and Kimbila, and the barber Upāli. He gained psychic powers, and with them won the favour of Prince Ajātasattu, appearing in his lap as a boy wearing a girdle of snakes. With gain and honour, the Vinaya says, came the wish to lead the Saṅgha.

He asked the Buddha, now old, to hand the Saṅgha over to him, and was refused. He urged Ajātasattu to kill his father and take the throne, and he himself would kill the Buddha. He sent archers, who were converted. He hurled a rock from Vulture Peak; it broke, and a splinter cut the Buddha's foot and drew blood. He had the fierce elephant Nāḷāgiri loosed in the Buddha's path; the elephant was calmed by the Buddha's loving-kindness and knelt.

Then he proposed five strict rules: monks should live only in the forest, eat only alms food, wear only rag robes, live at the foot of trees, and never eat fish or meat. The Buddha allowed each as a choice but would not make them binding. Devadatta took this as his cause, and led five hundred newly ordained monks of Vesālī away to Gayāsīsa: a schism. Sāriputta and Moggallāna went there and brought them back, and the Vinaya says hot blood gushed from Devadatta's mouth.

The Dhammapada commentary tells his end. After nine months of illness he wished to see the Buddha and was carried towards Jetavana on a litter. When it was set down by the pond at the gate, he stood, and the earth opened and drew him down. Going down, he spoke a verse taking refuge in the Buddha with his bones and his last breath. He was reborn in Avīci; and the commentary adds that after a hundred thousand aeons he will become a paccekabuddha.

Wounding a Buddha and splitting the Saṅgha are two of the five heinous deeds: weighty kamma, which ripens before any other kind (“Kamma, death and rebirth”). His last act was to take refuge, a wholesome thought at death, and still the weighty kamma came first. The commentary still holds out hope: the Buddha ordained him, it says, knowing that as a monk he could lay a condition for his eventual release, and he will be a paccekabuddha a hundred thousand aeons from now.

Why Moggallāna was beaten

Disciples · Dhammapada commentary, vv. 137–140 · Black Rock on the slope of Isigili, near Rājagaha

Moggallāna used to visit the heavens and the hells and come back to tell people what he had seen: followers of the Buddha enjoying the fruit of their deeds, followers of other teachers suffering. The naked ascetics, the commentary says, saw their support draining away, and paid bandits a thousand coins to kill him.

The bandits surrounded his dwelling at Black Rock. He knew, and slipped out through the keyhole. They came back another time, and he rose through the roof into the sky. The third time he did not escape. He saw that an old deed was waiting for its chance, and let them take him. They beat him until his bones were broken like grains of rice, and left him for dead.

He held himself together by the power of jhāna, went to the Buddha to take his leave, and returned to Black Rock to attain final Nibbāna. When the monks asked why such a death had come to such a disciple, the Buddha told of a past life. Moggallāna had been a devoted son to blind parents; his wife resented caring for them and turned him against them. He took them into the forest by cart, pretended that bandits were attacking, and beat them himself.

Here the versions part. In the Dhammapada commentary the parents, thinking robbers were attacking, cried out to their son to save himself, and he beat them to death all the same; he burned in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, and in a hundred lives since had been beaten to death in the same way. In the Jātaka commentary's telling their cry touched him; he stopped, comforted them and took them home, and the deed waited for its chance like embers under ash. In both, this life was its last. King Ajātasattu had the killers found and executed, and with them the naked ascetics who had hired them. The verses spoken were Dhammapada 137–140: whoever harms the harmless meets one of ten misfortunes.

Kamma that can ripen “in any later life” (“Kamma, death and rebirth”) waits for its chance, even for an arahant; so the Jātaka telling says. In the Dhammapada telling the deed was the killing of his parents, a heinous deed that ripened first in hell; what met him at the end was its remainder. Either way, what arahantship ends is new kamma and any further rebirth.

King Nimi's chariot

Jātaka · Ja 541 · Mithilā, the hells, and the Tāvatiṃsa heaven

The Buddha smiled one evening in Makhādeva's mango grove near Mithilā, and Ānanda asked why. He told the story of the last king of that line. Nimi was so generous and so careful in keeping the precepts that his people followed him, and many were reborn among the devas. He wondered which bears more fruit, giving or the holy life, and Sakka came down to answer him: the holy life.

The devas of Tāvatiṃsa wished to see this king, and Sakka sent his charioteer Mātali with the chariot drawn by a thousand thoroughbreds. Mātali asked which way he would go: by the road of those who did evil, or of those who did good? Nimi asked to see both.

Mātali drove him first over the hells. At each one he named the deed: those who had been cruel to the weak, those who had cheated in trade, those who had harmed recluses, those who had killed, stolen, lied. Then he drove up through the heavens, past mansion after mansion, and at each he named the deed: a woman who gave food to monks, a man who built a rest-house, one who cared for his parents.

Nimi was received in the Sudhamma hall, and Sakka invited him to stay. Nimi declined. He did not want to enjoy, he said, what had been given by another; he would go back and make merit of his own. He returned and told his people what he had seen, and when his first grey hair appeared, he went forth like Makhādeva.

A guided tour of the hells and sense-sphere heavens of “Thirty-one planes”. Each world is paired with a kind of deed, the same pairing as kamma “by place” in “Kamma, death and rebirth”.

The brahmins of Sālā

Disciples · MN 41 · Sālā, a brahmin village in Kosala

The brahmins of Sālā heard that the recluse Gotama had arrived, and went to see him. Some bowed, some greeted him politely, some held out joined hands, some announced their name and clan, and some sat down in silence. They asked: what is the reason why some beings, when the body breaks up after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, even in hell, and others in a good destination, even in a heaven world?

Conduct not in line with the Dhamma, the Buddha said, unrighteous conduct, is the reason for the first; conduct in line with the Dhamma, the reason for the second. They asked him to say it in detail. By body, three kinds: killing living beings, taking what is not given, and misconduct in sensual pleasures. By speech, four: false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech and idle chatter. By mind, three: coveting another's wealth, ill will that wishes beings slain or destroyed, and wrong view, which holds that there is nothing given, no fruit of good and bad deeds, no this world and no other world.

Then the ten in reverse, each an abstaining or its opposite: one who has given up killing lives with the rod laid down, kind and compassionate; one who has given up harsh speech speaks words that are gentle and pleasing to the ear. If such a person wishes, the Buddha said, he may reappear among wealthy nobles or brahmins, among the devas of any heaven up to the Brahmā worlds and the formless realms; or, if he wishes, he may by the ending of the taints realise liberation here and now. The brahmins went for refuge.

The ten courses of “Ten ways to act”, as the Buddha first taught them: the three doors, and a deed matched to every world of “Thirty-one planes”.

Subha and the dog

Disciples · MN 135, with the Majjhima commentary · Tudigāma near Sāvatthī, and Jetavana

Todeyya, the commentary says, was King Pasenadi's chaplain and lord of Tudigāma near Sāvatthī, very rich and very mean. He taught his son that wealth is kept the way ants build an anthill and bees gather honey, little by little, and lost the way a pot of eye-black is used up. He gave nothing, and when he died he was reborn as a dog in his own house, where Subha grew fond of it.

Seeing at dawn that this would bring Subha to the refuges, the Buddha came to the house on his alms round, and the dog ran out barking. The Buddha addressed it by its former name, and it crept away and lay down in the ashes by the hearth. Subha, who believed his father had been reborn in the Brahmā world, went angrily to the monastery to accuse the Buddha of lying. Ask the dog, said the Buddha, to show you the treasure your father hid. Subha did, and the dog went to the spot and scratched at it, and the treasure was found.

In the sutta Subha comes to the Buddha with fourteen questions in seven pairs. Why are some human beings short-lived and some long-lived, some sickly and some healthy, some ugly and some beautiful, some without influence and some influential, some poor and some rich, some low-born and some high-born, some unwise and some wise? Beings are owners of their kamma, the Buddha answers, heirs of their kamma; kamma is what divides them into inferior and superior.

Then he takes each pair. One who kills, if he comes back as a human, is short-lived; one who harms beings is sickly; one who is angry and irritable is ugly; one who is envious has little influence; one who does not give is poor; one who is obstinate and proud is low-born; one who never asks the wise what is good is unwise. The opposite deeds give the opposite lives. Subha went for refuge.

“From kamma to its results” in seven pairs: one kind of deed gives the rebirth, and the same deed, ripening within a later human life, shapes its length, health, looks and wealth.

The frog who heard the Buddha's voice

Disciples · Vimānavatthu 5.1, with its commentary · The bank of the Gaggarā lotus lake at Campā

The commentary tells that the Buddha was teaching one evening beside the Gaggarā lake at Campā. A frog came up out of the water and settled at the edge of the gathering, taking the sound of the Buddha's voice as its object, pleased by it without understanding a word, only knowing that this was the Dhamma.

A cowherd came to listen too, and stood leaning on his staff. Without seeing it, he set the point of the staff on the frog's head, and the frog died at once, its mind still bright with that pleasure. It was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, in a golden mansion, among a company of nymphs.

Waking there as if from sleep, the young deva wondered what he had done to come to such a place, and saw nothing but the sound of a voice by a lake. He came down with his mansion and his company to where the Buddha was still teaching. Asked who he was, he answered in verse: in my former birth I was a frog, living in the water; listening to your Dhamma, a cowherd killed me. The Buddha taught him, and the commentary says he and many in the gathering realised the fruit of stream-entry.

“Who is reborn where” says a being's next life depends on what it dies with. The frog lived in a woeful plane, but died with a wholesome sense-sphere citta, and its rebirth-linking was among the devas.

Practice

The rose-apple tree

The Buddha's life · MN 36 · Kapilavatthu in his childhood, and Uruvelā during the austerities

In MN 36 the Buddha tells the debater Saccaka about his years of striving. He had pressed his tongue to his palate and crushed mind with mind until sweat ran from his armpits. He had stopped his breath until his head felt split by a sword. He had lived on a handful of beans a day, until his spine stood out like a string of beads and the hair rotted from his skin. Whatever pain any recluse had ever felt, this was the utmost; and it had not brought him knowledge.

Then he remembered a day in childhood. His father the Sakyan was at work, and he was sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states, and he entered the first jhāna, with its rapture and happiness. “Could that be the path to awakening?” And the knowledge came: that is the path.

Why be afraid of that pleasure, he asked himself, which has nothing to do with sensual desire? But such a pleasure could not be reached with so starved a body. So he ate rice and porridge again, and the five ascetics who had waited on him left in disgust: he had given up the struggle. With his strength back he sat down, entered the jhānas, and that night awakened.

The commentaries fill in the childhood day. It was the royal ploughing festival. The nurses left the boy alone under the tree to watch the ceremony, and returned to find him sitting cross-legged in meditation; and though the shadows of the other trees had moved with the sun, the shadow of the rose-apple tree had not.

On the tree in “The tree of purification”, concentration is a root. The commentaries say his subject was the breath, one of the eleven in “Forty meditation subjects” that can reach all five jhānas.

Cūḷapanthaka's white cloth

Disciples · Dhammapada commentary, v. 25 · Rājagaha, the gateway of the monastery, and the physician Jīvaka's house

Their mother was the daughter of a rich family of Rājagaha who ran away with a servant. Both her sons were born by the roadside on the way back to her parents, and so they were called Panthaka, “road-child”, the elder and the younger. The elder, Mahāpanthaka, went forth, became an arahant, and brought his brother into the Saṅgha.

Cūḷapanthaka could not learn. For four months he tried to memorise one verse, in praise of the Buddha as a fragrant red lotus, and as he learned each line the last slipped away. Mahāpanthaka, who was arranging the monks for a meal at the house of Jīvaka the physician, left him off the list, and told him he was no use in the teaching and should go home.

At dawn he set out to return to lay life. The Buddha was waiting at the gateway; he stroked his head, led him in, and gave him a clean white cloth. Sit facing east, he said, rub it, and repeat: rajoharaṇaṃ, “removing dirt”. As he rubbed, the cloth grew soiled from his hand. He thought: this was clean, and by this body it has become dirty; so are all conditioned things. As insight grew, the Buddha appeared before him in a radiance: the dirt is not only in the cloth, he said; lust, hate and delusion are the real dust, and these are what to remove. Lust is dust, not dirt, ran the verses he spoke; so too hate, so too delusion. As the verses ended Cūḷapanthaka became an arahant with the analytical knowledges.

At Jīvaka's house the Buddha would not begin the meal: there was a monk still at the monastery. A messenger went and found the mango grove full of monks, a thousand of them, all mind-made by Cūḷapanthaka, and each said his name was Panthaka. Told to take the first who spoke, the messenger brought him back. The Buddha spoke the verse: by effort, heedfulness, restraint and self-control, the wise make an island no flood can overwhelm. He was named foremost among those who create mind-made bodies.

A subject fitted to the person (“Forty meditation subjects”): a simple object you can see and touch, which ripened into insight (“The tree of purification”). The Buddha's verses then turned the outer dirt into the three unwholesome roots of “A map of the eighty-nine”: what is to be removed is lust, hate and delusion.

The goldsmith and the lotus

Disciples · Dhammapada commentary, v. 285; Ja 25 · Jetavana

A goldsmith's son went forth under Sāriputta. Thinking that young men are prone to lust, Sāriputta gave him the foulness of the body as his subject. He worked at it for four months without the least success. Sāriputta took him to the Buddha.

The Buddha saw what a disciple could not: for five hundred lives this monk had been a goldsmith, working with beautiful, pure, red gold. A repulsive subject did not suit him. By his power he made a lotus of gold, water dripping from its leaves and stem, and gave it to the monk: set it on a heap of sand at the edge of the monastery, sit before it, and attend to it: “red, red.”

The monk's mind settled at once, and he passed through the jhānas. Then the Buddha made the lotus wither. Its colour faded and its petals fell, from the edges inwards, until only the seed-pod was left. Watching it, the monk saw that whatever has a beginning has an ending, and that his own body was like it. The Buddha sent out his radiance and spoke the verse: cut off the love of self, as one plucks an autumn lotus with the hand; cultivate the path of peace, Nibbāna, taught by the Well-Gone. The monk became an arahant.

The Jātaka linked to it tells of a royal horse that would not bathe at a ford where common horses had bathed. The king's groom was baffled; the Bodhisatta, a minister, saw that the horse was fastidious and had it bathed at another ford, where it went in at once. What suits one being is not what suits another.

“Forty meditation subjects” in action, with a twist: by the rule, a young man prone to lust is given foulness, but five hundred lives of handling red gold had shaped this mind, and only a beautiful object suited it.

Āḷāra and Uddaka

The Buddha's life · MN 26 · Magadha, during the search; then the road to Bārāṇasī after the awakening

In MN 26, “the noble search”, the Buddha tells how he went forth while young, against his weeping parents' wishes, seeking what is unborn, unaging, deathless. He went first to Āḷāra Kālāma, quickly learned his teaching by word, and asked how far it went. To the base of nothingness, said Āḷāra. The Bodhisatta thought: not only Āḷāra has faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration and wisdom; I have them too. He soon reached it himself. Āḷāra was delighted, and offered to lead his community jointly with him.

But he saw that this teaching did not lead to disenchantment and peace, only to rebirth in the base of nothingness, and he left. Under Uddaka Rāmaputta the same thing happened with the base of neither perception nor non-perception, which Rāma had reached. Uddaka offered to make him the sole teacher. Again he saw it did not lead to Nibbāna, and left, and went to Uruvelā.

After the awakening, when he had resolved to teach, he thought first of Āḷāra: he is wise and has little dust in his eyes; he will understand quickly. A deva told him Āḷāra had died seven days before. Then of Uddaka: he had died the night before. “A great loss,” he said. So he went to the five ascetics at Isipatana. On the road a wanderer, Upaka, asked who his teacher was; told he had none and had awakened by himself, Upaka said, “May it be so, friend,” shook his head, and took a side path.

The highest calm leads to the highest immaterial planes of “Thirty-one planes”, with lifespans of 60,000 and 84,000 aeons, but not out of the round. That is why the tree in “The tree of purification” needs a trunk of insight.

Paṭācārā and the water

Disciples · Therīgāthā 112–116; Dhammapada commentary, v. 113 · The road to Sāvatthī, the river Aciravatī, and the nuns' dwelling

The commentary tells her life before. She was the daughter of a rich merchant of Sāvatthī, and ran away with a servant of the house. Pregnant with her second child, she set out for her parents' home with her husband and her little son. A storm broke; her husband went to cut sticks for a shelter, was bitten by a snake, and died. She gave birth in the night, crouching over both children in the rain.

In the morning she found her husband dead. At the river Aciravatī, swollen with the rain, she could not carry both children across. She took the newborn over, laid it on the far bank, and turned back for the elder. Midstream, a hawk took the baby. She threw up her arms and screamed, and the elder boy, thinking she called him, stepped into the river and was swept away.

Near Sāvatthī she asked a traveller about her family. In the night's storm their house had fallen; her father, mother and brother were burning on one pyre, there, where the smoke rose. She went out of her mind. Her clothes fell from her, and she wandered, and came to Jetavana, where the Buddha said to her: “Sister, recover your mindfulness.” She came to herself. He told her that the tears she had shed in the round of births were more than the waters of the four oceans. She entered the stream, and went forth.

Her own verses tell the rest. (The Dhammapada commentary ends differently: as she watched the water the Buddha appeared to her in a ray of light and spoke verse 113, on seeing rise and fall, and she became an arahant there.) Men plough their fields and sow, and prosper; why do I, keeping the training, not reach Nibbāna? Washing her feet, she watched the water run down the slope, and her mind became still like a well-trained horse. She took her lamp into her cell, sat on the bed, and drew down the wick with a pin. As the lamp went out, her mind was freed. She became the foremost of the nuns in the discipline, and a teacher of many.

The knowledge of rise and fall in “The tree of purification”, seen first in water and then in her own mind. In her verse the lamp going out is the image of the mind's release, Nibbāna, not of death.

Koṇḍañña's eye of Dhamma

The Buddha's life · SN 56.11 · The Deer Park at Isipatana, near Bārāṇasī

In the Vinaya and MN 26, the five ascetics saw him coming and agreed not to rise or greet him: he had given up the struggle. As he came near they could not keep to it. He told them not to call him “friend”: he had found the deathless.

He taught them that there are two extremes not to be followed, the pursuit of sensual pleasure and the pursuit of self-torment, and a middle way between them: the noble eightfold path. Then the four noble truths, each in three turnings: this is suffering; it is to be fully understood; it has been fully understood. Only when his knowledge of all twelve was clear, he said, did he claim to be awakened.

While he was speaking, the dustless eye of Dhamma arose in Koṇḍañña: whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation. The earth devas raised a cry, and it passed from heaven to heaven up to the Brahmā world; the ten-thousandfold world system shook, and a great light appeared. Then the Buddha exclaimed: “Koṇḍañña has understood! Koṇḍañña has understood!” and so he came to be called Aññā Koṇḍañña.

The Jātaka introduction (Nidānakathā) says Koṇḍañña had been the youngest of the eight brahmins who examined the baby prince's marks, and the only one who said without hedging that he would become a Buddha. Over the following days the other four entered the stream; with the next teaching, on non-self, all five became arahants.

“The four noble truths” reads this sermon the Abhidhamma way: each truth a set of realities with its own task, and all four seen in a single moment. The commentaries take Koṇḍañña's insight as stream-entry: path knowledge took Nibbāna as its object and the first three fetters fell away.

Kāla, the paid listener

Disciples · Dhammapada commentary, v. 178 · Sāvatthī, Anāthapiṇḍika's house and Jetavana

Anāthapiṇḍika had given his wealth and his heart to the Buddha, but his son Kāla had no wish even to see him. The father thought: if he goes on like this he will go to a bad destination. So he offered him a hundred coins to spend a fast day at the monastery. Kāla went, slept the day away in a corner, and came home in the morning asking for the money before he would eat.

Then the father offered a thousand if he would learn a single verse from the Buddha and come back with it. Kāla went and sat before the Buddha, meaning to learn the verse and leave. The Buddha, the commentary says, saw to it that the words would not stay with him, so that each time he had to listen again and listen harder. Listening to learn, the commentary says, is listening with respect, and such listening gives the paths. He entered the stream.

The next day he walked behind the Buddha and the monks to his father's house for the meal. Anāthapiṇḍika had the thousand coins brought and set before him in front of everyone. Kāla would not take them. The father told the Buddha how it had been, and the Buddha said that his son had now gained something greater than any treasure, and spoke the verse: better than sole rule over the earth, better than going to heaven, better than lordship over all the worlds, is the fruit of stream-entry.

Stream-entry in “Four noble persons”: the first path cuts identity view, doubt and clinging to rites for good, and a stream-enterer will never again be reborn in a woeful plane.

Soṇa's lute

Disciples · AN 6.55; Vinaya, Mahāvagga V · The Cool Grove (Sītavana) at Rājagaha

The Vinaya tells that Soṇa had grown up so delicately that hair grew on the soles of his feet. When he went forth he set himself to walking meditation in the Cool Grove with all his strength, until the walking path was stained with blood from his feet like a place where cattle are slaughtered.

Alone, he thought: I am one of the most energetic of the Buddha's disciples, and yet my mind is not freed from the taints. My family is wealthy. I could go back, enjoy that wealth and make merit. The Buddha knew his thought, and as quickly as a strong man stretches out his arm, he left Vulture Peak and stood before Soṇa in the Cool Grove.

When you lived at home, Soṇa, were you skilled at the lute? Yes, sir. When its strings were too taut, was it tuneful and fit to play? No, sir. When they were too slack? No, sir. When they were neither too taut nor too slack, but set at an even pitch? Then it was tuneful, sir, and fit to play. Just so, said the Buddha: energy roused too strongly leads to restlessness, energy too lax leads to laziness. Resolve on evenness of energy, find the evenness of the faculties, and take up your object there.

Soṇa did so, and before long he became an arahant. He came to the Buddha and declared it in six things his mind was now set on: renunciation, solitude, non-ill will, the ending of craving, the ending of clinging, and non-confusion. Sights, sounds and thoughts, he said, no longer shake such a mind, as a rock mountain is not shaken by storms from any quarter. In the Vinaya, the Buddha allowed monks to wear sandals because of him.

The five faculties of “Thirty-seven requisites, fourteen states” tuned like strings: no one of them may run ahead, and energy has to be kept in balance with concentration, with mindfulness watching both.

The whole of the holy life

Disciples · SN 45.2 · Nāgaraka, a town of the Sakyans

Ānanda came to the Buddha, sat down, and said: venerable sir, this is half of the holy life: good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship. Not so, Ānanda, the Buddha answered. It is the entire holy life. When a monk has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, it is to be expected that he will develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path.

How? He develops right view, right intention and each of the other factors in a way that rests on seclusion, on fading away and on cessation, and ripens in letting go. And this is how you may know it, Ānanda: by relying on me as a good friend, beings subject to birth are freed from birth, beings subject to aging, sickness and death are freed from them.

In SN 3.18 King Pasenadi of Kosala tells the Buddha he has been thinking that the Dhamma is for one with good friends, not for one with bad friends. The Buddha agrees, and tells the king this same conversation with Ānanda, and advises him that a ruler with good friends should live by heedfulness in good things.

In “The noble eightfold path” the path, in the strict sense, is eight factors in one citta at the moment of the path; this story is about how they come to arise at all. A good friend is a natural decisive support from outside.

Synthesis

Sumedha's vow

Jātaka · Buddhavaṃsa II; Jātaka introduction · The city of Amaravatī, and the road to Rammaka, four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand aeons ago

Sumedha was a brahmin of Amaravatī whose parents died young, leaving him great wealth. Looking over the treasure his family had stored for seven generations, he thought: they all took nothing with them. Birth is suffering, ageing is suffering, death is suffering; as there is heat and also cold, there must be a way out. He gave everything away, went to the Himalaya as an ascetic, and mastered the jhānas and the powers.

One day, flying over the city of Rammaka, he saw people clearing and decorating a road. It was for the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. He asked for a stretch of it to prepare himself, and was given a muddy patch. Before he had finished, the Buddha came, with four hundred thousand arahants.

Sumedha loosened his hair, spread his bark robe and deerskin on the mud, and lay down across it so that the Buddha would not soil his feet. Lying there, he thought: if I wished, I could end my defilements today. But what use is crossing alone? I will become a Buddha, and carry many across. Dīpaṅkara stopped at his head and declared: after four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more, this ascetic will be a Buddha named Gotama.

When the Buddha had gone, Sumedha sat and searched out the qualities that make a Buddha, and found ten perfections: giving, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, resolution, loving-kindness and equanimity. The rest of the Jātaka collection, life after life, is the record of their fulfilling.

One volition (“An ensemble of fifty-two”), renewed and fulfilled across lives (“Kamma, death and rebirth”), in worlds measured in aeons (“Thirty-one planes”): the whole study in a single vow.

Vessantara's gifts

Jātaka · Ja 547 · Jetuttara, capital of the Sivi kingdom, and Mount Vaṅka

The Buddha told this story on his first visit home to Kapilavatthu, when a rain fell that wet only those who wished to be wet: such a rain had fallen once before, he said. Vessantara, son of King Sañjaya of the Sivis, had loved giving since birth. When brahmins came from drought-stricken Kaliṅga to ask for the kingdom's white elephant, whose presence brought rain, he gave it.

The people were furious and demanded his banishment. Before leaving he gave the great gift of seven hundreds: elephants, horses, chariots, women, cows, slaves and wealth. Maddī his wife would not stay behind, and went with their two small children. On the road he gave away the horses and the chariot, and they walked to a hermitage on Mount Vaṅka.

An old brahmin, Jūjaka, came there. His young wife had been mocked by the village women for drawing water herself, and sent him to get her servants. While Maddī was out gathering fruit, held back by devas in the form of wild beasts, Jūjaka asked for the children, and Vessantara gave them. The children hid in a pond and had to be called out. They clung to his feet weeping, and his own tears fell on them. Before he gave them he set a price on each so that they could buy their freedom: a thousand pieces of gold for Jāli, and for Kaṇhājinā a hundred of everything, so that no low-born man could buy her. Then he poured the water of gift, wishing that it be a condition for a Buddha's omniscience, which he said was a hundred thousand times dearer to him than his children. When Maddī came home she searched all night and fell unconscious. Then Sakka came, disguised as a brahmin, and asked for Maddī, and Vessantara gave her too. Sakka revealed himself, gave her back, and granted him boons.

Led by the devas, Jūjaka took the children to the Sivi capital, where their grandfather ransomed them; Jūjaka ate so much at the feast that he died. The king and the people went to Mount Vaṅka, the family was reunited, and Vessantara was brought home as king. The earth shook, and a rain of jewels fell.

Sense-sphere wholesome kamma at its fullest (“Kamma, death and rebirth”). The tradition counts it as the completion of the perfection of giving, made for the sake of a Buddha's awakening; the Jātaka tells the gift of the children as the hardest of all, made in tears and with their ransom already set.

Ajātasattu's lost chance

Disciples · DN 2 · The mango grove of Jīvaka at Rājagaha, on a full-moon night

It was the full-moon night of Komudī, at the end of the rains. The king sat on his palace roof among his ministers and said: how lovely the night is; what recluse or brahmin might we visit, to bring peace to my heart? One minister named Pūraṇa Kassapa, others the other well-known teachers. Jīvaka the physician sat silent, and when asked, said the Buddha was staying in his mango grove.

They set out on elephants by torchlight. Near the grove the king grew afraid: there were twelve hundred and fifty monks there and not a sound, not a cough. Was this a trap? Jīvaka reassured him. Seeing the monks seated in silence like a clear lake, the king said: may my son Udāyibhadda have such calm.

He asked the Buddha what visible fruit there is in the life of a recluse, here and now, as there is in a craft or a trade; he had asked the six other teachers and got no answer. The Buddha answered step by step, from the respect even a slave who goes forth would receive, through virtue, sense restraint and contentment, to the jhānas, the knowledges, and the end of the taints. The king went for refuge and confessed that he had killed his father. The Buddha accepted the confession: to see a fault as a fault and make amends, he said, is growth in the noble discipline.

When he had gone, the Buddha said: “The king is wounded, monks, the king is uprooted. Had he not taken the life of his father, a righteous king, the dustless eye of Dhamma would have arisen in him in this very seat.” The commentary adds that from that night he could sleep again; that he became a great supporter of the Saṅgha after the Buddha's death; and that he will one day be a paccekabuddha.

Weighty kamma (“Kamma, death and rebirth”) can bar the path (“The tree of purification”). A heinous deed closes the door to path attainment in that life (AN 6.87). It does not close the door to refuge, confession and good kamma.

The last night at Kusinārā

The Buddha's life · DN 16 · The sāla grove of the Mallas at Kusinārā

Ill after his last meal at the house of Cunda the smith, the Buddha walked to Kusinārā and lay down on his right side between twin sāla trees, which flowered out of season and scattered their blossoms over him. Ānanda went aside and wept, and the Buddha called him back: have I not told you that we must part from all that is dear? You have served me long and well; make the effort, and you will soon be free.

A wanderer named Subhadda came, wanting to ask a question. Ānanda turned him away three times, not to tire the Buddha. The Buddha overheard and let him in. Subhadda asked whether the other famous teachers had all understood. Leave that aside, said the Buddha: where the noble eightfold path is found, there are true recluses. Subhadda went forth that night, the last disciple the Buddha received himself, and soon became an arahant.

To the monks the Buddha said: after I am gone, the Dhamma and the Discipline I have taught will be your teacher. Three times he asked if anyone had a doubt about the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the path or the practice; all were silent. Then his last words: “All conditioned things are subject to decay. Strive on with diligence.” (vayadhammā saṅkhārā, appamādena sampādetha)

He entered the first jhāna and rose through all the jhānas to the cessation of perception and feeling. Ānanda said: the Blessed One has passed away. Not yet, said Anuruddha: he has entered cessation. The Buddha came down through the jhānas to the first, rose again to the fourth, and emerging from the fourth, attained final Nibbāna. The earth shook, and Brahmā, Sakka, Anuruddha and Ānanda each spoke a verse. Sakka's is still chanted at funerals: impermanent are all formations, their nature is to arise and pass away.

Every level at once: the jhānas of “A map of the eighty-nine” and “Forty meditation subjects”, the planes he would not return to (“Thirty-one planes”), and a death followed by no rebirth-linking (“Kamma, death and rebirth”).

Sāriputta and the elephant's footprint

Disciples · MN 28 · Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika's park at Sāvatthī

He began with the picture. Of all the animals that walk the earth, the elephant leaves the largest print, and every other print fits inside it. In the same way every wholesome state is included in the four noble truths. He took the first truth, and in it the five aggregates affected by clinging, and began with matter: the four elements in the body and outside it. Even the great earth element outside, vast as it is, he said, is seen to be impermanent, liable to destruction and change; what then of this body, held together for a short while by craving? None of it is mine, none of it is I, none of it is my self.

He showed what follows for practice. If others abuse a monk, strike him or wound him, the monk understands: a painful feeling born of ear-contact has arisen in me, and it is dependent, not independent; dependent on contact. He sees that contact is impermanent, and feeling, and perception, and formations, and consciousness, and his mind settles in what it is attending to.

Then he turned to the eye. If the eye within is intact, but no forms come into its range and there is no matching engagement of the mind, no eye-consciousness appears. If forms come into range but there is no engagement, still none appears. Only when all three meet does the matching kind of consciousness come about. And in what has come to be thus, the form belongs to the aggregate of form, the feeling to the aggregate of feeling, and so with perception, formations and consciousness.

Last he laid the same moment on the widest lens. The Blessed One has said, Sāriputta reminded them, that one who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma, and one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination. These five aggregates are dependently arisen. Desire and clinging for them is the origin of suffering; removing desire for them is its cessation. He went through every door the same way, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, and the monks were delighted.

Sāriputta does in a few lines what “One moment, every lens” does with the mango: one moment of seeing, read as matter, as five aggregates, as dependent origination and as the truths. Each reading is complete in its own terms, and none of them needs a self to finish the account.

Moggaliputta Tissa and the points of controversy

Disciples · Samantapāsādikā, introduction; Mahāvaṃsa V · The Asokārāma at Pāṭaliputta, in the reign of King Asoka

When the king's gifts to the Saṅgha grew lavish, the Theravāda chronicles tell, ascetics of other sects who had lost their support shaved their heads and put on robes, and went on teaching their own doctrines as the Dhamma. The true monks would not hold the observance with them, and at the Asokārāma it lapsed. A minister sent to restore it misunderstood his order and began to behead the monks who refused, until the king's own brother, himself a monk, sat down in front of the sword.

The king, afraid the deaths were on his head, sent upriver for Moggaliputta Tissa, who had withdrawn to a mountain retreat. The elder taught him that where there is no intention there is no kamma, and then taught him the Dhamma for seven days. Then, with the elder seated behind a curtain, the king called the monks sect by sect and asked each: what did the Fully Awakened One teach? Those who answered with eternalism and the other views were sent out of the Saṅgha in white clothes. Those who answered that he taught analysis, vibhajjavāda, the elder confirmed, and the observance was held in harmony again.

Then, the commentary says, the elder chose a thousand learned monks, recited the Dhamma with them in a third council, and set out the Kathāvatthu, the Points of Controversy, as the fifth book of the Abhidhamma. Its first debate asks whether a person is found as a real and ultimate thing. Its sixth asks whether everything exists, in past, future and present alike. The commentary names the other side in each: the schools that held to the person, and the Sabbatthivāda, the Sarvāstivāda of the north.

The tradition adds one more step. The Buddha himself, it says, had laid down the outline of the book in the heaven of the Thirty-three, foreseeing the disputes, so that the elder only filled in what was already there, and the book could be counted as the Buddha's word.

The Kathāvatthu is where the Theravāda argued with the other maps of “Other maps of the same ground”: against a person who is more than the elements, and against the Sarvāstivāda's claim that past and future dhammas exist.

The second dart

Disciples · SN 36.6 · A teaching to the monks, in the Saṃyutta's chapter on feeling

The Buddha put the question to the monks. An untaught ordinary person feels pleasant feeling, painful feeling and neither; so does a taught noble disciple. What, then, is the distinction between them? The monks asked him to explain, since their teachings were rooted in him.

When the untaught person is touched by painful feeling, he sorrows, grieves and laments, beats his breast and is distraught. He feels two feelings, one of the body and one of the mind, as if a man were struck by a dart and then, straight after, by a second, and felt the pain of both. Touched by pain, he resists it, and the tendency to aversion lies behind that. Then he looks for delight in sensual pleasure, because he knows no other way out of pain, and the tendency to lust lies behind that.

When the taught noble disciple is touched by painful feeling, he does not sorrow or lament. He feels one feeling, of the body, not of the mind, like a man struck by one dart and not by a second. He does not resist the pain, and he does not run to sensual pleasure for escape, because he knows another way out. Whatever he feels, pleasant, painful or neither, he feels it detached.

The same pain, met twice. As in “Two moments, side by side”, the moments that receive the object are results and are the same in both people; the two processes part at the javanas, and the second dart is made there.
